paragraphs: Dynamic Cell Structures are neural architectures that learn both a representation of data and connections describing its topology. Here, topology concerns the neighborhood relationships along the feature manifold. The approach supports unsupervised learning as well as supervised function approximation, making the learned organization useful beyond simply displaying or grouping inputs.

Two learning mechanisms perform complementary jobs. A modified Kohonen rule adjusts the units’ weight vectors, while competitive Hebbian learning builds lateral connections that reflect the data’s structure. For supervised tasks, each unit supplies a radial basis function, and a linear output layer learns through a delta rule. Representation learning and prediction therefore operate within the same architecture.

The distinctive proposal is to learn and use a topology-preserving map concurrently in an RBF approximation system. Simulations apply the idea to the Growing Cell Structure algorithm on selected CMU benchmarks, where the resulting method can outperform conventional models on similar tasks. These findings support the usefulness of adapting neighborhood structure alongside the numerical parameters used for approximation.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Cell Structures jointly learn data topology and neural representations, using that organization for unsupervised learning and supervised approximation.

title: Dynamic Cell Structures

abstract: Model Predictive Control (MPC), a control algorithm which uses an optimizer to solve for the optimal control moves over a future time horizon based upon a model of the process, has become a stan(cid:173) dard control technique in the process industries over the past two decades. In most industrial applications, a linear dynamic model developed using empirical data is used even though the process it(cid:173) self is often nonlinear. Linear models have been used because of the difficulty in developing a generic nonlinear model from empirical data and the computational expense often involved in using non(cid:173) linear models. In this paper, we present a generic neural network based technique for developing nonlinear dynamic models from em(cid:173) pirical data and show that these models can be efficiently used in a model predictive control framework. This nonlinear MPC based approach has been successfully implemented in a number of indus(cid:173) trial applications in the refining, petrochemical, paper and food industries. Performance of the controller on a nonlinear industrial process, a polyethylene reactor, is presented.

paragraphs: Model predictive control chooses control actions by optimizing predicted process behavior over a future horizon. Its usefulness depends on the model used for those predictions. The paper addresses a common mismatch: industrial processes can be nonlinear, while their controllers often use linear models because nonlinear modeling and optimization can be difficult or computationally expensive.

The authors present a general neural-network technique for learning nonlinear dynamic process models from empirical data. They also show that these models can be used efficiently within model predictive control. The approach therefore addresses both constructing a nonlinear model and incorporating it into the optimization that selects control actions.

The paper reports successful industrial implementations in refining, petrochemicals, paper production, and food processing. It presents controller performance for a polyethylene reactor as a specific nonlinear industrial application. These implementations support the practical feasibility of the approach: learned nonlinear dynamics can participate in predictive control, connecting modeling from observed data with decisions about how an industrial process should be operated.
summary.tldr: Neural networks learn nonlinear process models that can be used efficiently in model predictive control, with successful industrial implementations.

title: Neural Network Based Model Predictive Control

abstract: We investigate a general semi-Markov Decision Process (SMDP) framework for modeling concurrent decision making, where agents learn optimal plans over concurrent temporally extended actions. We introduce three types of parallel termination schemes { all, any and continue { and theoretically and experimentally compare them.
originalAbstract: We investigate a general semi-Markov Decision Process (SMDP) framework for modeling concurrent decision making, where agents learn optimal plans over concurrent temporally extended actions. We introduce three types of parallel termination schemes { all, any and continue { and theoretically and experimentally compare them.

paragraphs: The paper investigates decision making in which an agent can undertake several actions concurrently and those actions extend over time. The planning problem must therefore account for overlapping activity as well as which actions to select. The authors use a general semi-Markov decision process framework to model this setting and support learning optimal plans within it.

A central design choice is how concurrent actions terminate. The paper introduces three parallel termination schemes, named all, any, and continue. Treating termination as an explicit part of the framework makes the handling of concurrent activity part of the decision problem, alongside the selection of the actions themselves.

The authors compare the schemes both theoretically and experimentally. The contribution described is thus a framework for learning with concurrent, temporally extended actions together with an analysis of alternative termination rules. Its significance is to bring action duration and concurrency into the planning formulation, allowing different ways of organizing parallel activity to be examined within a shared mathematical setting.
summary.tldr: A semi-Markov decision framework supports learning plans over concurrent, temporally extended actions and comparing three termination schemes.

title: Learning to Take Concurrent Actions

abstract: Prototypes based algorithms are commonly used to reduce the computa- tional complexity of Nearest-Neighbour (NN) classiﬁers. In this paper we discuss theoretical and algorithmical aspects of such algorithms. On the theory side, we present margin based generalization bounds that sug- gest that these kinds of classiﬁers can be more accurate then the 1-NN rule. Furthermore, we derived a training algorithm that selects a good set of prototypes using large margin principles. We also show that the 20 years old Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ) algorithm emerges natu- rally from our framework.
originalAbstract: Prototypes based algorithms are commonly used to reduce the computa- tional complexity of Nearest-Neighbour (NN) classiﬁers. In this paper we discuss theoretical and algorithmical aspects of such algorithms. On the theory side, we present margin based generalization bounds that sug- gest that these kinds of classiﬁers can be more accurate then the 1-NN rule. Furthermore, we derived a training algorithm that selects a good set of prototypes using large margin principles. We also show that the 20 years old Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ) algorithm emerges natu- rally from our framework.

paragraphs: Prototype-based classifiers reduce the computational burden of nearest-neighbor classification by representing data with a selected set of prototypes. The paper studies these methods from both theoretical and algorithmic perspectives. It asks how the choice of prototypes relates to generalization, beyond their role in making classification cheaper.

The authors derive margin-based generalization bounds. These bounds suggest that prototype classifiers can be more accurate than the one-nearest-neighbor rule. The claim is a possibility supported by the analysis, rather than a guarantee that reducing a dataset to prototypes always improves accuracy. Margins provide the principle used to assess the resulting classifier.

The paper also derives a training algorithm that selects prototypes using large-margin principles. Within the same framework, Learning Vector Quantization emerges naturally. This connects an established prototype-learning algorithm with a theoretical account of generalization. The contribution is therefore a common foundation for understanding existing LVQ behavior and constructing prototype-selection procedures whose training objective is motivated by classification margins.
summary.tldr: A margin-based framework supplies generalization bounds and prototype-learning methods while recovering LVQ as a natural case.

title: Margin Analysis of the LVQ Algorithm

abstract: This work presents an architecture based on perceptrons to recognize phrase structures, and an online learning algorithm to train the percep- trons together and dependently. The recognition strategy applies learning in two layers: a ﬁltering layer, which reduces the search space by identi- fying plausible phrase candidates, and a ranking layer, which recursively builds the optimal phrase structure. We provide a recognition-based feed- back rule which reﬂects to each local function its committed errors from a global point of view, and allows to train them together online as percep- trons. Experimentation on a syntactic parsing problem, the recognition of clause hierarchies, improves state-of-the-art results and evinces the advantages of our global training method over optimizing each function locally and independently.

We provide a recognition-based feed- back rule which reﬂects to each local function its committed errors from a global point of view, and allows to train them together online as percep- trons. Experimentation on a syntactic parsing problem, the recognition of clause hierarchies, improves state-of-the-art results and evinces the advantages of our global training method over optimizing each function locally and independently.

paragraphs: Recognizing phrase structure requires several local decisions to combine into a coherent whole. This paper introduces a perceptron-based architecture whose components are trained together through an online algorithm. Its central concern is how to make each component learn from the quality of the complete recognized structure, rather than only from its own isolated decisions.

Recognition proceeds through two layers. A filtering layer identifies plausible phrase candidates and narrows the search space. A ranking layer then recursively constructs the optimal phrase structure. A recognition-based feedback rule attributes errors to local functions from the perspective of the global result, allowing the perceptrons to be trained dependently.

Experiments address clause-hierarchy recognition, a syntactic parsing problem. The reported results improve on the state of the art and show advantages over training each function separately with a local objective. The finding supports coordinated training in this setting: feedback about the assembled structure can guide local components more effectively than optimizing each one independently.
summary.tldr: Joint online training uses whole-structure feedback to improve a two-layer perceptron architecture for phrase recognition.

title: Online Learning via Global Feedback for Phrase Recognition

abstract: A common way of image denoising is to project a noisy image to the sub- space of admissible images made for instance by PCA. However, a major drawback of this method is that all pixels are updated by the projection, even when only a few pixels are corrupted by noise or occlusion. We pro- pose a new method to identify the noisy pixels by (cid:1) 1-norm penalization and update the identiﬁed pixels only. The identiﬁcation and updating of noisy pixels are formulated as one linear program which can be solved efﬁciently. Especially, one can apply the ν-trick to directly specify the fraction of pixels to be reconstructed. Moreover, we extend the linear program to be able to exploit prior knowledge that occlusions often ap- pear in contiguous blocks (e.g. sunglasses on faces). The basic idea is to penalize boundary points and interior points of the occluded area dif- ferently. We are able to show the ν-property also for this extended LP leading a method which is easy to use. Experimental results impressively demonstrate the power of our approach.

paragraphs: Projecting a damaged image onto a space of admissible images can change every pixel, even when only a small region is corrupted. This paper proposes identifying the damaged pixels and updating only those pixels. The aim is to make reconstruction selective when noise or an occluding object affects only part of an image.

The method uses an L1 penalty and combines identification and reconstruction in one linear program that can be solved efficiently. A parameterization called the ν-trick lets the user directly specify the fraction of pixels to reconstruct. This gives the reconstruction procedure an interpretable control over how much of the image it changes.

An extension incorporates the knowledge that occlusions often occupy connected blocks, such as sunglasses across a face. It penalizes boundary pixels differently from pixels inside an occluded region. The authors establish the ν-property for this extended formulation as well and report strong experimental results. The contribution is a selective reconstruction method with an additional mechanism for representing spatially grouped damage.
summary.tldr: A linear program identifies and repairs corrupted pixels selectively, with an extension for contiguous occlusions.

title: Image Reconstruction by Linear Programming

abstract: We propose a “soft greedy” learning algorithm for building small conjunctions of simple threshold functions, called rays, deﬁned on single real-valued attributes. We also propose a PAC-Bayes risk bound which is minimized for classiﬁers achieving a non-trivial tradeoﬀ between sparsity (the number of rays used) and the mag- nitude of the separating margin of each ray. Finally, we test the soft greedy algorithm on four DNA micro-array data sets.
originalAbstract: We propose a “soft greedy” learning algorithm for building small conjunctions of simple threshold functions, called rays, deﬁned on single real-valued attributes. We also propose a PAC-Bayes risk bound which is minimized for classiﬁers achieving a non-trivial tradeoﬀ between sparsity (the number of rays used) and the mag- nitude of the separating margin of each ray. Finally, we test the soft greedy algorithm on four DNA micro-array data sets.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a soft greedy algorithm for constructing small conjunctions of simple threshold rules. Each rule, called a ray, operates on a single real-valued attribute. A conjunction combines these individual conditions, making the learned classifier a collection of attribute-level tests that must hold together.

The accompanying PAC-Bayes risk bound captures a tradeoff between sparsity and the separating margins of the individual rays. Sparsity is measured by the number of rays used, while each margin describes the separation associated with its threshold. The bound is minimized by a non-trivial balance between these properties, so both the size of the rule set and the strength of its separations matter.

The authors test the soft greedy procedure on four DNA microarray datasets. This connects the proposed rule-building method and its theoretical criterion to gene-expression classification. The contribution is a learning approach for compact conjunctions together with a risk bound that explains why choosing a small number of thresholds must be balanced against their individual margins.
summary.tldr: A soft greedy method learns compact threshold conjunctions, guided by a PAC-Bayes tradeoff between sparsity and margins.

title: PAC-Bayes Learning of Conjunctions and Classification of Gene-Expression Data

abstract: Learning in a multiagent system is a challenging problem due to two key factors. First, if other agents are simultaneously learning then the envi- ronment is no longer stationary, thus undermining convergence guaran- tees. Second, learning is often susceptible to deception, where the other agents may be able to exploit a learner's particular dynamics. In the worst case, this could result in poorer performance than if the agent was not learning at all. These challenges are identifiable in the two most com- mon evaluation criteria for multiagent learning algorithms: convergence and regret. Algorithms focusing on convergence or regret in isolation are numerous. In this paper, we seek to address both criteria in a single algorithm by introducing GIGA-WoLF, a learning algorithm for normal- form games. We prove the algorithm guarantees at most zero average regret, while demonstrating the algorithm converges in many situations of self-play. We prove convergence in a limited setting and give empir- ical results in a wider variety of situations. These results also suggest a third new learning criterion combining convergence and regret, which we call negative non-convergence regret (NNR).

paragraphs: Learning becomes difficult when several agents adapt at once. Each agent faces an environment that changes as the others learn, weakening ordinary convergence guarantees. Other agents may also exploit a learner's behavior. The paper addresses both concerns through convergence, which asks whether learning settles down, and regret, which evaluates the cost of the learner's choices.

The authors introduce GIGA-WoLF for normal-form games with the aim of handling these two criteria together. They prove an average-regret guarantee of at most zero. They also investigate self-play, where the learning algorithm interacts with copies of itself, and demonstrate convergence in many such situations.

The convergence evidence has two different strengths: a proof applies in a limited setting, while empirical results cover a wider range of situations. The paper therefore does not establish convergence in all games or all interactions. Its results also motivate negative non-convergence regret, a proposed evaluation criterion combining convergence and regret. The broader contribution is to study stability of learning and protection against unfavorable adaptation within one algorithm.
summary.tldr: GIGA-WoLF guarantees at most zero average regret and shows self-play convergence through a limited proof and broader empirical results.

title: Convergence and No-Regret in Multiagent Learning

abstract: Assume a uniform, multidimensional grid of bivariate data, where each cell of the grid has a count ci and a baseline bi . Our goal is to find spatial regions (d-dimensional rectangles) where the ci are significantly higher than expected given bi . We focus on two applications: detection of clusters of disease cases from epidemiological data (emergency department visits, over-the-counter drug sales), and discovery of regions of increased brain activity corresponding to given cognitive tasks (from fMRI data). Each of these problems can be solved using a spatial scan statistic (Kulldorff, 1997), where we compute the maximum of a likelihood ratio statistic over all spatial regions, and find the significance of this region by randomization. However, computing the scan statistic for all spatial regions is generally computationally infeasible, so we introduce a novel fast spatial scan algorithm, generalizing the 2D scan algorithm of (Neill and Moore, 2004) to arbitrary dimensions. Our new multidimensional multiresolution algorithm allows us to find spatial clusters up to 1400x faster than the naive spatial scan, without any loss of accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper searches for regions where observed counts are unusually high relative to a baseline. Data occupy a uniform multidimensional grid, with each cell containing a count and its expected reference level. Candidate regions are rectangles in the relevant number of dimensions. Applications include detecting disease clusters and locating increased brain activity associated with cognitive tasks.

A spatial scan statistic scores candidate regions using a likelihood ratio, selects the highest-scoring region, and assesses its significance through randomization. The computational obstacle is the number of possible regions: evaluating all of them directly is generally infeasible. The paper develops a fast multidimensional, multiresolution scan algorithm that extends an earlier two-dimensional approach.

The reported speedup reaches 1,400 times that of a naive spatial scan, with no loss of accuracy. This is an upper reported speedup, rather than a promise that every dataset receives that acceleration. The result matters because it makes the specified spatial search substantially faster while preserving its accuracy, allowing the statistical search procedure to be applied more efficiently.
summary.tldr: A multidimensional spatial scan algorithm finds unusually elevated rectangular regions up to 1,400 times faster than naive scanning without losing accuracy.

title: Detecting Significant Multidimensional Spatial Clusters

abstract: Detecting underlying clusters from large-scale data plays a central role in machine learning research. In this paper, we attempt to tackle clustering problems for complex data of multiple distributions and large multi-scales. To this end, we develop an algorithm named Zeta $l$-links, or Zell which consists of two parts: Zeta merging with a similarity graph and an initial set of small clusters derived from local $l$-links of the graph. More specifically, we propose to structurize a cluster using cycles in the associated subgraph. A mathematical tool, Zeta function of a graph, is introduced for the integration of all cycles, leading to a structural descriptor of the cluster in determinantal form. The popularity character of the cluster is conceptualized as the global fusion of variations of the structural descriptor by means of the leave-one-out strategy in the cluster. Zeta merging proceeds, in the agglomerative fashion, according to the maximum incremental popularity among all pairwise clusters. Experiments on toy data, real imagery data, and real sensory data show the promising performance of Zell. The $98.1\%$ accuracy, in the sense of the normalized mutual information, is obtained on the FRGC face data of 16028 samples and 466 facial clusters. The MATLAB codes of Zell will be made publicly available for peer evaluation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Zell, a clustering algorithm intended for complex data containing multiple distributions and scales. It represents the data with a similarity graph and begins with small clusters formed from local links. The distinctive idea is to describe a cluster through the cycles contained in its associated portion of the graph.

A graph zeta function combines information from those cycles into a structural descriptor expressed through a determinant. The authors then define cluster popularity by combining changes in this descriptor when individual members are left out. Clustering proceeds by repeatedly merging the pair of clusters with the largest increase in popularity, linking local graph structure to the overall merging process.

Experiments on artificial data, imagery, and sensory data are reported as promising. On the FRGC face dataset, containing 16,028 samples and 466 facial clusters, the reported normalized mutual information is 98.1%. This is a clustering-agreement measure, so the figure should be understood in that sense. The findings support the potential of cycle-based structure as a guide for assembling larger clusters.
summary.tldr: Zell clusters data by merging graph-based groups according to a popularity measure derived from their cycle structure.

title: Cyclizing Clusters via Zeta Function of a Graph

abstract: We present an approach to low-level vision that combines two main ideas: the use of convolutional networks as an image processing architecture and an unsupervised learning procedure that synthesizes training samples from specific noise models. We demonstrate this approach on the challenging problem of natural image denoising. Using a test set with a hundred natural images, we find that convolutional networks provide comparable and in some cases superior performance to state of the art wavelet and Markov random field (MRF) methods. Moreover, we find that a convolutional network offers similar performance in the blind denoising setting as compared to other techniques in the non-blind setting. We also show how convolutional networks are mathematically related to MRF approaches by presenting a mean field theory for an MRF specially designed for image denoising. Although these approaches are related, convolutional networks avoid computational difficulties in MRF approaches that arise from probabilistic learning and inference. This makes it possible to learn image processing architectures that have a high degree of representational power (we train models with over 15,000 parameters), but whose computational expense is significantly less than that associated with inference in MRF approaches with even hundreds of parameters.

paragraphs: This paper combines convolutional networks with an unsupervised procedure that generates training samples from specified noise models. The resulting image-processing system learns to remove noise from natural images. Synthesizing the training samples connects the learning procedure directly to the kinds of corruption represented by those noise models.

On a test set of one hundred natural images, the networks perform comparably to, and sometimes better than, state-of-the-art wavelet and Markov random field methods. The authors also report that a convolutional network in a blind denoising setting achieves performance similar to other techniques in a non-blind setting. These are empirical comparisons for the evaluated denoising conditions.

The paper additionally relates convolutional networks to Markov random fields through a mean-field theory for a specially designed denoising model. Despite that mathematical connection, the network approach avoids computational difficulties associated with probabilistic learning and inference in the MRF methods. The authors train networks with more than 15,000 parameters while reporting substantially lower computational expense than inference in MRF approaches containing even hundreds of parameters.
summary.tldr: Convolutional networks trained with synthesized noise achieve competitive image denoising while reducing computation relative to the studied MRF approaches.

title: Natural Image Denoising with Convolutional Networks

abstract: Likelihood ratio policy gradient methods have been some of the most successful reinforcement learning algorithms, especially for learning on physical systems. We describe how the likelihood ratio policy gradient can be derived from an importance sampling perspective. This derivation highlights how likelihood ratio methods under-use past experience by (a) using the past experience to estimate {\em only} the gradient of the expected return $U(\theta)$ at the current policy parameterization $\theta$, rather than to obtain a more complete estimate of $U(\theta)$, and (b) using past experience under the current policy {\em only} rather than using all past experience to improve the estimates. We present a new policy search method, which leverages both of these observations as well as generalized baselines---a new technique which generalizes commonly used baseline techniques for policy gradient methods. Our algorithm outperforms standard likelihood ratio policy gradient algorithms on several testbeds.

This derivation highlights how likelihood ratio methods under-use past experience by (a) using the past experience to estimate {\em only} the gradient of the expected return $U(\theta)$ at the current policy parameterization $\theta$, rather than to obtain a more complete estimate of $U(\theta)$, and (b) using past experience under the current policy {\em only} rather than using all past experience to improve the estimates. We present a new policy search method, which leverages both of these observations as well as generalized baselines---a new technique which generalizes commonly used baseline techniques for policy gradient methods. paragraphs: This paper derives likelihood-ratio policy gradients from an importance-sampling perspective. The derivation reveals two ways that these reinforcement-learning methods underuse experience. They use observations to estimate only the gradient of expected return at the current policy parameters, and they restrict that estimation to experience collected under the current policy.

The proposed policy-search method uses both observations to broaden the role of past data. It seeks a more complete estimate of expected return and draws on experience from past policies as well as the current one. It also introduces generalized baselines, extending the baseline techniques commonly used in policy-gradient methods.

The algorithm outperforms standard likelihood-ratio policy-gradient algorithms on several testbeds. These results support the practical value of the proposed experience reuse in the evaluated problems. The conceptual contribution is the connection between importance sampling and policy gradients: it exposes where an established update rule leaves information unused and motivates a search procedure designed to use more of it.
summary.tldr: An importance-sampling view motivates a policy-search method that uses past experience more fully and outperforms standard likelihood-ratio gradients on several testbeds.

title: On a Connection between Importance Sampling and the Likelihood Ratio Policy Gradient

abstract: To understand the relationship between genomic variations among population and complex diseases, it is essential to detect eQTLs which are associated with phenotypic effects. However, detecting eQTLs remains a challenge due to complex underlying mechanisms and the very large number of genetic loci involved compared to the number of samples. Thus, to address the problem, it is desirable to take advantage of the structure of the data and prior information about genomic locations such as conservation scores and transcription factor binding sites. In this paper, we propose a novel regularized regression approach for detecting eQTLs which takes into account related traits simultaneously while incorporating many regulatory features. We first present a Bayesian network for a multi-task learning problem that includes priors on SNPs, making it possible to estimate the significance of each covariate adaptively. Then we find the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation of regression coefficients and estimate weights of covariates jointly. This optimization procedure is efficient since it can be achieved by using convex optimization and a coordinate descent procedure iteratively. Experimental results on simulated and real yeast datasets confirm that our model outperforms previous methods for finding eQTLs.

paragraphs: Detecting genetic locations associated with traits is difficult when the number of candidate locations greatly exceeds the number of samples. This paper addresses that problem by analyzing related traits together and incorporating information about genomic locations. Such information includes conservation scores and transcription factor binding sites, which can help guide the search for relevant genetic variation.

The authors develop a regularized regression approach within a Bayesian network for multi-task learning. Priors on genetic variants allow the importance of individual predictors to be estimated adaptively. The procedure jointly estimates regression coefficients and predictor weights, so the treatment of a location can reflect both the observed data and its regulatory features. Computation alternates between convex optimization and coordinate descent.

Experiments on simulated data and real yeast data report better eQTL detection than previous methods. These findings support the proposed combination of shared learning across traits and adaptive use of genomic information in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a way to bring those sources of evidence into one estimation procedure.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Multi-Task Lasso combines related traits and genomic prior information to improve eQTL detection in simulated and yeast datasets.

title: Adaptive Multi-Task Lasso: with Application to eQTL Detection

abstract: Many time-series such as human movement data consist of a sequence of basic actions, e.g., forehands and backhands in tennis. Automatically extracting and characterizing such actions is an important problem for a variety of different applications. In this paper, we present a probabilistic segmentation approach in which an observed time-series is modeled as a concatenation of segments corresponding to different basic actions. Each segment is generated through a noisy transformation of one of a few hidden trajectories representing different types of movement, with possible time re-scaling. We analyze three different approximation methods for dealing with model intractability, and demonstrate how the proposed approach can successfully segment table tennis movements recorded using a robot arm as haptic input device.

paragraphs: A continuous movement recording may contain a succession of basic actions, such as different kinds of strokes. Recovering those actions requires deciding where one segment ends and another begins, while recognizing repeated movement types. This paper develops a probabilistic method that models a time series as a concatenation of action segments.

Each segment is generated from one of a small number of hidden trajectories representing different movement types. The observed segment can be a noisy transformation of that trajectory and can have a different time scale. This lets the model represent repeated actions whose recorded paths or durations vary, rather than requiring every occurrence to be identical.

Because working with the model directly is intractable, the authors analyze three approximation methods. They demonstrate successful segmentation of table-tennis movements recorded through a robot arm used as a haptic input device. The result shows how recurring trajectory structure and changes between movement segments can jointly support action extraction from the demonstrated continuous recordings.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic trajectory model segments repeated actions while allowing noise and timing variation, demonstrated on recorded table-tennis movements.

title: Movement extraction by detecting dynamics switches and repetitions

abstract: Latent variable mixture models are a powerful tool for exploring the structure in large datasets. A common challenge for interpreting such models is a desire to impose sparsity, the natural assumption that each data point only contains few latent features. Since mixture distributions are constrained in their L1 norm, typical sparsity techniques based on L1 regularization become toothless, and concave regularization becomes necessary. Unfortunately concave regularization typically results in EM algorithms that must perform problematic non-concave M-step maximizations. In this work, we introduce a technique for circumventing this difficulty, using the so-called Mountain Pass Theorem to provide easily verifiable conditions under which the M-step is well-behaved despite the lacking concavity. We also develop a correspondence between logarithmic regularization and what we term the pseudo-Dirichlet distribution, a generalization of the ordinary Dirichlet distribution well-suited for inducing sparsity. We demonstrate our approach on a text corpus, inferring a sparse topic mixture model for 2,406 weblogs.

paragraphs: Mixture models describe observations through combinations of hidden components. For interpretation, it can be useful for each observation to involve only a few components. The paper studies how to encourage that sparsity when mixture weights already have a fixed L1 norm. Under this constraint, an ordinary L1 penalty cannot distinguish sparse mixtures from more spread-out ones.

Concave regularization can encourage sparse weights, but it complicates fitting with expectation maximization. In particular, the maximization step can lose the concavity that would make it easier to handle. The authors use the Mountain Pass Theorem to establish easily checked conditions under which this step remains well behaved despite that loss. The result is conditional, rather than a guarantee for every concave penalty.

The paper also connects logarithmic regularization to a proposed pseudo-Dirichlet distribution, extending the ordinary Dirichlet distribution to better support sparsity. An application learns sparse topic mixtures from 2,406 weblogs. Together, these contributions connect an interpretable modeling preference with conditions that make its associated optimization manageable.
summary.tldr: The paper gives checkable conditions that make concave sparsity penalties manageable when fitting mixture models.

title: A concave regularization technique for sparse mixture models

abstract: Many fundamental questions in theoretical neuroscience involve optimal decoding and the computation of Shannon information rates in populations of spiking neurons. In this paper, we apply methods from the asymptotic theory of statistical inference to obtain a clearer analytical understanding of these quantities. We find that for large neural populations carrying a finite total amount of information, the full spiking population response is asymptotically as informative as a single observation from a Gaussian process whose mean and covariance can be characterized explicitly in terms of network and single neuron properties. The Gaussian form of this asymptotic sufficient statistic allows us in certain cases to perform optimal Bayesian decoding by simple linear transformations, and to obtain closed-form expressions of the Shannon information carried by the network. One technical advantage of the theory is that it may be applied easily even to non-Poisson point process network models; for example, we find that under some conditions, neural populations with strong history-dependent (non-Poisson) effects carry exactly the same information as do simpler equivalent populations of non-interacting Poisson neurons with matched firing rates. We argue that our findings help to clarify some results from the recent literature on neural decoding and neuroprosthetic design.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much information populations of spiking neurons carry and how that information can be decoded optimally. It applies asymptotic statistical-inference theory to large populations carrying a finite total amount of information. Under this setup, the authors establish a simpler description of the information contained in the full population response.

Asymptotically, that response is as informative as one observation from a Gaussian process. Its mean and covariance are explicitly related to network and individual-neuron properties. In certain cases, this Gaussian representation enables optimal Bayesian decoding through simple linear transformations and yields closed-form expressions for the network's Shannon information.

The theory also accommodates non-Poisson network models, including neurons whose activity depends strongly on their histories. Under some conditions, such populations carry exactly the same information as equivalent populations of independent Poisson neurons with matched firing rates. The qualifications matter: this equivalence is conditional, and the Gaussian result is asymptotic. Within those settings, the findings help explain neural decoding results and questions relevant to neuroprosthetic design.
summary.tldr: For large neural populations with finite total information, an asymptotically equivalent Gaussian representation can simplify information calculations and optimal decoding.

title: Information Rates and Optimal Decoding in Large Neural Populations

abstract: An agglomerative clustering algorithm merges the most similar pair of clusters at every iteration. The function that evaluates similarity is traditionally hand- designed, but there has been recent interest in supervised or semisupervised settings in which ground-truth clustered data is available for training. Here we show how to train a similarity function by regarding it as the action-value function of a reinforcement learning problem. We apply this general method to segment images by clustering superpixels, an application that we call Learning to Agglomerate Superpixel Hierarchies (LASH). When applied to a challenging dataset of brain images from serial electron microscopy, LASH dramatically improved segmentation accuracy when clustering supervoxels generated by state of the boundary detection algorithms. The naive strategy of directly training only supervoxel similarities and applying single linkage clustering produced less improvement.

paragraphs: Agglomerative clustering builds groups through a sequence of merges, choosing the most similar pair at each step. Its behavior therefore depends heavily on the similarity function. This paper develops a way to learn that function from ground-truth clustered data rather than designing the merge criterion entirely by hand.

The authors treat similarity as the action-value function of a reinforcement learning problem. This frames the evaluation of a possible merge within the clustering process itself. They apply the general method to image segmentation by merging superpixels, calling the resulting approach Learning to Agglomerate Superpixel Hierarchies, or LASH.

On a challenging dataset of brain images from serial electron microscopy, LASH dramatically improves segmentation accuracy when clustering supervoxels produced by state-of-the-art boundary detectors. Directly training supervoxel similarities and then applying single-linkage clustering produces a smaller improvement. The comparison supports learning the criterion as part of the sequential merging problem: the contribution concerns how existing image regions are assembled into larger segments, building on the initial boundary detection.
summary.tldr: LASH learns a clustering similarity function as a reinforcement-learning action value and substantially improves segmentation of electron-microscopy brain images.

title: Learning to Agglomerate Superpixel Hierarchies

abstract: How should we design experiments to maximize performance of a complex system, taking into account uncontrollable environmental conditions? How should we select relevant documents (ads) to display, given information about the user? These tasks can be formalized as contextual bandit problems, where at each round, we receive context (about the experimental conditions, the query), and have to choose an action (parameters, documents). The key challenge is to trade off exploration by gathering data for estimating the mean payoff function over the context-action space, and to exploit by choosing an action deemed optimal based on the gathered data. We model the payoff function as a sample from a Gaussian process defined over the joint context-action space, and develop CGP-UCB, an intuitive upper-confidence style algorithm. We show that by mixing and matching kernels for contexts and actions, CGP-UCB can handle a variety of practical applications. We further provide generic tools for deriving regret bounds when using such composite kernel functions. Lastly, we evaluate our algorithm on two case studies, in the context of automated vaccine design and sensor management. We show that context-sensitive optimization outperforms no or naive use of context.

paragraphs: An action's value can depend on conditions the decision maker does not control. This paper studies sequential decisions in which context arrives before an action is selected, such as environmental conditions for an experiment or user information for document selection. The learner must gather useful information while also choosing actions expected to perform well in the current context.

The authors model payoff with a Gaussian process over contexts and actions together. Their CGP-UCB algorithm uses upper-confidence reasoning to guide decisions. Kernels for contexts and actions can be combined, allowing the model to express different relationships within the joint decision space. The paper also provides general tools for obtaining regret bounds for these composite kernels.

Evaluations examine automated vaccine design and sensor management. In these case studies, context-sensitive optimization outperforms approaches that ignore context or use it naively. The result supports learning how actions and conditions interact, while the theoretical contribution gives a framework for analyzing performance when different kernel combinations encode those relationships.
summary.tldr: CGP-UCB combines context and action information in a Gaussian process to guide exploration and improve decisions in two case studies.

title: Contextual Gaussian Process Bandit Optimization

abstract: Given a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with $n$ states and $m$ actions per state, we study the number of iterations needed by Policy Iteration (PI) algorithms to converge to the optimal $\gamma$-discounted optimal policy. We consider two variations of PI: Howard's PI that changes the actions in all states with a positive advantage, and Simplex-PI that only changes the action in the state with maximal advantage. We show that Howard's PI terminates after at most $ O \left( \frac{ n m}{1-\gamma} \log \left( \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \right)\right) $ iterations, improving by a factor $O(\log n)$ a result by Hansen et al. (2013), while Simplex-PI terminates after at most $ O \left( \frac{n^2 m}{1-\gamma} \log \left( \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \right)\right) $ iterations, improving by a factor $O(\log n)$ a result by Ye (2011). Under some structural assumptions of the MDP, we then consider bounds that are independent of the discount factor~$\gamma$: given a measure of the maximal transient time $\tau_t$ and the maximal time $\tau_r$ to revisit states in recurrent classes under all policies, we show that Simplex-PI terminates after at most $ \tilde O \left( n^3 m^2 \tau_t \tau_r \right) $ iterations. This generalizes a recent result for deterministic MDPs by Post & Ye (2012), in which $\tau_t \le n$ and $\tau_r \le n$. We explain why similar results seem hard to derive for Howard's PI. Finally, under the additional (restrictive) assumption that the state space is partitioned in two sets, respectively states that are transient and recurrent for all policies, we show that Simplex-PI and Howard's PI terminate after at most $ \tilde O(nm (\tau_t+\tau_r))$ iterations.

paragraphs: Policy iteration improves a decision policy until it reaches an optimal discounted policy in a Markov decision process. The paper studies two versions: Howard's method updates every state with positive advantage, whereas Simplex-PI updates only the state with the largest advantage. Its focus is the number of iterations required.

For n states, m actions per state, and discount factor gamma, the authors sharpen existing bounds for both methods by a logarithmic factor in n. Their bounds scale respectively as nm and n²m, multiplied by a shared term involving 1/(1−gamma) and its logarithm. These are upper bounds on iteration counts, not reported runtime measurements.

The paper also obtains discount-independent bounds under structural assumptions involving transient duration and return times to recurrent states across policies. One result applies to Simplex-PI and generalizes a deterministic-MDP result. A stronger, explicitly restrictive assumption fixes which states are transient or recurrent under every policy and enables bounds for both variants. Thus, additional structural information can replace discount dependence, but the applicable assumptions differ across the results.
summary.tldr: Sharper iteration bounds improve guarantees for two policy-iteration variants, with discount-independent results under additional structural assumptions.

title: Improved and Generalized Upper Bounds on the Complexity of Policy Iteration

abstract: A common problem in knowledge representation and related fields is reasoning over a large joint knowledge graph, represented as triples of a relation between two entities. The goal of this paper is to develop a more powerful neural network model suitable for inference over these relationships. Previous models suffer from weak interaction between entities or simple linear projection of the vector space. We address these problems by introducing a neural tensor network (NTN) model which allow the entities and relations to interact multiplicatively. Additionally, we observe that such knowledge base models can be further improved by representing each entity as the average of vectors for the words in the entity name, giving an additional dimension of similarity by which entities can share statistical strength. We assess the model by considering the problem of predicting additional true relations between entities given a partial knowledge base. Our model outperforms previous models and can classify unseen relationships in WordNet and FreeBase with an accuracy of 86.2% and 90.0%, respectively.

paragraphs: A knowledge graph records facts as relationships between pairs of entities. Given an incomplete graph, the task is to predict additional true relationships. This paper introduces a neural tensor network to model these facts more expressively, addressing weak entity interactions and simple linear projections in earlier approaches.

The model lets entity representations and relations interact multiplicatively. This provides a richer way to represent how a pair of entities fits a particular relationship. The authors also represent an entity by averaging vectors for the words in its name. Shared words then provide an additional source of similarity through which entities can share statistical strength.

Evaluation asks the model to classify unseen relationships using a partial knowledge base. It outperforms previous models in the reported experiments, reaching 86.2% accuracy on WordNet and 90.0% on FreeBase. These findings support combining richer relational interactions with information from entity names. The demonstrated reasoning task is knowledge-base completion: using observed relationships and learned representations to assess additional candidate relationships.
summary.tldr: Neural tensor networks combine multiplicative relational interactions with entity-name representations to improve knowledge-base completion.

title: Reasoning With Neural Tensor Networks for Knowledge Base Completion

abstract: The problem of estimating the kernel mean in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) is central to kernel methods in that it is used by classical approaches (e.g., when centering a kernel PCA matrix), and it also forms the core inference step of modern kernel methods (e.g., kernel-based non-parametric tests) that rely on embedding probability distributions in RKHSs. Previous work [1] has shown that shrinkage can help in constructing “better” estimators of the kernel mean than the empirical estimator. The present paper studies the consistency and admissibility of the estimators in [1], and proposes a wider class of shrinkage estimators that improve upon the empirical estimator by considering appropriate basis functions. Using the kernel PCA basis, we show that some of these estimators can be constructed using spectral filtering algorithms which are shown to be consistent under some technical assumptions. Our theoretical analysis also reveals a fundamental connection to the kernel-based supervised learning framework. The proposed estimators are simple to implement and perform well in practice.

paragraphs: A kernel mean represents a probability distribution through its average in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Estimating it supports tasks ranging from centering kernel PCA matrices to kernel-based nonparametric tests. This paper investigates how shrinkage can improve that estimate relative to the ordinary empirical mean.

The authors study the consistency and admissibility of previously proposed shrinkage estimators, then introduce a broader class that uses appropriate basis functions. The choice of basis matters because it determines the directions in which the estimate is represented and adjusted. With a kernel PCA basis, some of the proposed estimators can be implemented through spectral filtering algorithms.

The paper proves consistency for those spectral procedures under technical assumptions and identifies a fundamental connection to kernel-based supervised learning. This connects distribution representation with an established framework for learning from labeled data. The proposed estimators are also described as simple to implement and effective in practice. Together, the theoretical and practical findings support treating kernel mean estimation as an estimation problem that can benefit from carefully structured shrinkage.
summary.tldr: Basis-aware shrinkage and spectral filtering improve kernel mean estimation, with consistency guarantees under technical assumptions.

title: Kernel Mean Estimation via Spectral Filtering

abstract: Accurate and efficient analysis of multivariate spatio-temporal data is critical in climatology, geology, and sociology applications. Existing models usually assume simple inter-dependence among variables, space, and time, and are computationally expensive. We propose a unified low rank tensor learning framework for multivariate spatio-temporal analysis, which can conveniently incorporate different properties in spatio-temporal data, such as spatial clustering and shared structure among variables. We demonstrate how the general framework can be applied to cokriging and forecasting tasks, and develop an efficient greedy algorithm to solve the resulting optimization problem with convergence guarantee. We conduct experiments on both synthetic datasets and real application datasets to demonstrate that our method is not only significantly faster than existing methods but also achieves lower estimation error.

paragraphs: Data measured across locations and times can contain several variables whose patterns are related. This paper addresses the challenge of modeling these dependencies accurately without making computation prohibitively expensive. It proposes a unified low-rank tensor learning framework, using a multidimensional representation to connect the variable, spatial, and temporal aspects of the data.

The framework can incorporate properties such as spatial clustering and structure shared among variables. These capabilities matter because relationships in the data need not be captured adequately by simple assumptions about how space, time, and variables interact. The authors show how the framework supports both cokriging, which concerns spatial estimation using related variables, and forecasting.

To fit the resulting models, the paper develops an efficient greedy algorithm with a convergence guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real application datasets show significantly faster computation and lower estimation error than existing methods in the comparisons reported. The findings support the combination of a flexible shared representation and an efficient optimization procedure for the examined spatiotemporal analysis tasks.
summary.tldr: A low-rank tensor framework captures shared spatiotemporal structure and achieves faster computation with lower estimation error in the reported experiments.

title: Fast Multivariate Spatio-temporal Analysis via Low Rank Tensor Learning

abstract: To cope with the high level of ambiguity faced in domains such as Computer Vision or Natural Language processing, robust prediction methods often search for a diverse set of high-quality candidate solutions or proposals. In structured prediction problems, this becomes a daunting task, as the solution space (image labelings, sentence parses, etc.) is exponentially large. We study greedy algorithms for finding a diverse subset of solutions in structured-output spaces by drawing new connections between submodular functions over combinatorial item sets and High-Order Potentials (HOPs) studied for graphical models. Specifically, we show via examples that when marginal gains of submodular diversity functions allow structured representations, this enables efficient (sub-linear time) approximate maximization by reducing the greedy augmentation step to inference in a factor graph with appropriately constructed HOPs. We discuss benefits, tradeoffs, and show that our constructions lead to significantly better proposals.

paragraphs: Ambiguous prediction tasks can benefit from several strong, diverse candidate answers. In structured problems, however, each answer may be an entire image labeling or sentence parse, making the possible candidate set exponentially large. Searching directly through that space to assemble a useful collection is therefore a substantial computational challenge.

This paper studies greedy selection by connecting submodular diversity functions with high-order potentials in graphical models. The key condition is that the marginal gain from adding a candidate admits a structured representation. When that condition holds, the next greedy addition can be sought through inference in a factor graph equipped with appropriately constructed high-order potentials.

The authors show through examples that these representations enable approximate maximization in time sublinear in the size of the candidate space. They discuss benefits and trade-offs and report substantially better proposals from their constructions. The result is conditional on exploitable structure in the marginal gains: it supplies a way to use graphical-model inference for diverse candidate selection without claiming efficient optimization for every possible diversity function.
summary.tldr: Structured marginal gains let greedy diversity selection use factor-graph inference to search enormous candidate spaces approximately and efficiently.

title: Submodular meets Structured: Finding Diverse Subsets in Exponentially-Large Structured Item Sets

abstract: To keep up with the Big Data challenge, parallelized algorithms based on dual decomposition have been proposed to perform inference in Markov random fields. Despite this parallelization, current algorithms struggle when the energy has high order terms and the graph is densely connected. In this paper we propose a partitioning strategy followed by a message passing algorithm which is able to exploit pre-computations. It only updates the high-order factors when passing messages across machines. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of joint layout and semantic segmentation estimation from single images, and show that our approach is orders of magnitude faster than current methods.
originalAbstract: To keep up with the Big Data challenge, parallelized algorithms based on dual decomposition have been proposed to perform inference in Markov random fields. Despite this parallelization, current algorithms struggle when the energy has high order terms and the graph is densely connected. In this paper we propose a partitioning strategy followed by a message passing algorithm which is able to exploit pre-computations. It only updates the high-order factors when passing messages across machines. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of joint layout and semantic segmentation estimation from single images, and show that our approach is orders of magnitude faster than current methods.

paragraphs: This paper tackles inference in large Markov random fields with dense connections and high-order terms. These terms connect groups of variables, creating computational demands that existing parallel approaches based on dual decomposition still struggle to handle. Distributing the work across machines alone does not remove the expensive operations associated with this structure.

The authors propose a partitioning strategy followed by a message-passing algorithm that can reuse precomputed quantities. A central feature is its update schedule: high-order factors are updated only when messages pass between machines. This ties those updates to communication across the partitioned model and allows precomputation to contribute to the inference procedure.

The method is demonstrated on jointly estimating scene layout and semantic segmentation from single images. In that application, the authors report inference that is orders of magnitude faster than current methods. The result shows how the organization of a distributed inference problem, together with selective factor updates, can substantially affect computational performance on the evaluated large graphical models.
summary.tldr: Partitioning, reusable precomputations, and selective high-order updates produce orders-of-magnitude inference speedups in the demonstrated image-understanding task.

title: Message Passing Inference for Large Scale Graphical Models with High Order Potentials

abstract: We study contextual bandits with budget and time constraints under discrete contexts, referred to as constrained contextual bandits. The time and budget constraints significantly complicate the exploration and exploitation tradeoff because they introduce complex coupling among contexts over time. To gain insight, we first study unit-cost systems with known context distribution. When the expected rewards are known, we develop an approximation of the oracle, referred to Adaptive-Linear-Programming(ALP), which achieves near-optimality and only requires the ordering of expected rewards. With these highly desirable features, we then combine ALP with the upper-confidence-bound (UCB) method in the general case where the expected rewards are unknown a priori. We show that the proposed UCB-ALP algorithm achieves logarithmic regret except in certain boundary cases.Further, we design algorithms and obtain similar regret analysis results for more general systems with unknown context distribution or heterogeneous costs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that shows how to achieve logarithmic regret in constrained contextual bandits. Moreover, this work also sheds light on the study of computationally efficient algorithms for general constrained contextual bandits.

Those constraints link decisions across time: resources used in one context are unavailable for later opportunities, making the exploration-versus-exploitation tradeoff more complicated.

When expected rewards are known, their Adaptive Linear Programming method approximates an oracle and achieves near-optimal performance while requiring only the ordering of expected rewards. summary.tldr: Adaptive resource allocation combined with upper confidence bounds achieves logarithmic regret for constrained contextual bandits outside certain boundary cases.

title: Algorithms with Logarithmic or Sublinear Regret for Constrained Contextual Bandits

abstract: Practitioners of Bayesian statistics have long depended on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to obtain samples from intractable posterior distributions. Unfortunately, MCMC algorithms are typically serial, and do not scale to the large datasets typical of modern machine learning. The recently proposed consensus Monte Carlo algorithm removes this limitation by partitioning the data and drawing samples conditional on each partition in parallel (Scott et al, 2013). A fixed aggregation function then combines these samples, yielding approximate posterior samples. We introduce variational consensus Monte Carlo (VCMC), a variational Bayes algorithm that optimizes over aggregation functions to obtain samples from a distribution that better approximates the target. The resulting objective contains an intractable entropy term; we therefore derive a relaxation of the objective and show that the relaxed problem is blockwise concave under mild conditions. We illustrate the advantages of our algorithm on three inference tasks from the literature, demonstrating both the superior quality of the posterior approximation and the moderate overhead of the optimization step. Our algorithm achieves a relative error reduction (measured against serial MCMC) of up to 39% compared to consensus Monte Carlo on the task of estimating 300-dimensional probit regression parameter expectations; similarly, it achieves an error reduction of 92% on the task of estimating cluster comembership probabilities in a Gaussian mixture model with 8 components in 8 dimensions. Furthermore, these gains come at moderate cost compared to the runtime of serial MCMC, achieving near-ideal speedup in some instances.

summary.tldr: Variational consensus Monte Carlo learns how to combine parallel posterior samples, improving reported approximation quality with moderate optimization overhead.

title: Variational Consensus Monte Carlo

abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are successfully used in a number of applications. However, their storage and computational requirements have largely prevented their widespread use on mobile devices. Here we present an effective CNN compression approach in the frequency domain, which focuses not only on smaller weights but on all the weights and their underlying connections. By treating convolutional filters as images, we decompose their representations in the frequency domain as common parts (i.e., cluster centers) shared by other similar filters and their individual private parts (i.e., individual residuals). A large number of low-energy frequency coefficients in both parts can be discarded to produce high compression without significantly compromising accuracy. We relax the computational burden of convolution operations in CNNs by linearly combining the convolution responses of discrete cosine transform (DCT) bases. The compression and speed-up ratios of the proposed algorithm are thoroughly analyzed and evaluated on benchmark image datasets to demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Convolutional neural networks can require substantial storage and computation, making deployment on mobile devices difficult. CNNpack addresses both costs by representing convolutional filters in the frequency domain. Its compression strategy considers relationships among filters as well as the weights within each filter.

The method treats filters as images and separates their frequency representations into shared and individual components. Similar filters share a common cluster-center representation, while residuals capture their differences. Many low-energy frequency coefficients can then be removed from both components. The abstract reports that this produces strong compression without significantly compromising accuracy.

CNNpack also reduces convolutional computation by linearly combining responses of discrete cosine transform bases. This connects the compressed representation to a way of performing the network's operations with less computational burden. The paper analyzes compression and speed-up ratios and evaluates them on benchmark image datasets, reporting advantages over state-of-the-art methods. Its central idea is to use frequency structure for both compact storage and more efficient computation.
summary.tldr: CNNpack compresses shared and individual filter structure in the frequency domain and uses DCT basis responses to reduce convolution costs.

title: CNNpack: Packing Convolutional Neural Networks in the Frequency Domain

abstract: Low-rank matrix factorizations arise in a wide variety of applications -- including recommendation systems, topic models, and source separation, to name just a few. In these and many other applications, it has been widely noted that by incorporating temporal information and allowing for the possibility of time-varying models, significant improvements are possible in practice. However, despite the reported superior empirical performance of these dynamic models over their static counterparts, there is limited theoretical justification for introducing these more complex models. In this paper we aim to address this gap by studying the problem of recovering a dynamically evolving low-rank matrix from incomplete observations. First, we propose the locally weighted matrix smoothing (LOWEMS) framework as one possible approach to dynamic matrix recovery. We then establish error bounds for LOWEMS in both the {\em matrix sensing} and {\em matrix completion} observation models. Our results quantify the potential benefits of exploiting dynamic constraints both in terms of recovery accuracy and sample complexity. To illustrate these benefits we provide both synthetic and real-world experimental results.

paragraphs: Many applications represent data with low-rank matrices, including recommendation, topic modeling, and source separation. When the underlying relationships change over time, a static matrix can miss useful temporal structure. This paper investigates how to recover an evolving low-rank matrix from incomplete observations and supplies theory for the potential benefits of using its dynamics.

The authors propose locally weighted matrix smoothing, or LOWEMS, as a framework for dynamic recovery under an exact low-rank constraint. They establish recovery error bounds for two observation settings: matrix sensing and matrix completion. Studying both settings broadens the analysis beyond a single way of observing only part of a matrix.

The bounds quantify how exploiting dynamic constraints can improve recovery accuracy and reduce sample requirements. This provides theoretical support for temporal modeling, whose practical advantages had received more attention than its guarantees. Synthetic and real-world experiments illustrate the potential benefits. The contribution is thus both a recovery framework and an analysis of when temporal information can be valuable.
summary.tldr: LOWEMS recovers evolving low-rank matrices from incomplete observations, with error bounds quantifying potential gains from temporal structure.

title: Dynamic matrix recovery from incomplete observations under an exact low-rank constraint

abstract: Generative state estimators based on probabilistic filters and smoothers are one of the most popular classes of state estimators for robots and autonomous vehicles. However, generative models have limited capacity to handle rich sensory observations, such as camera images, since they must model the entire distribution over sensor readings. Discriminative models do not suffer from this limitation, but are typically more complex to train as latent variable models for state estimation. We present an alternative approach where the parameters of the latent state distribution are directly optimized as a deterministic computation graph, resulting in a simple and effective gradient descent algorithm for training discriminative state estimators. We show that this procedure can be used to train state estimators that use complex input, such as raw camera images, which must be processed using expressive nonlinear function approximators such as convolutional neural networks. Our model can be viewed as a type of recurrent neural network, and the connection to probabilistic filtering allows us to design a network architecture that is particularly well suited for state estimation. We evaluate our approach on synthetic tracking task with raw image inputs and on the visual odometry task in the KITTI dataset. The results show significant improvement over both standard generative approaches and regular recurrent neural networks.

Probabilistic filters and smoothers are widely used for this task, but generative approaches must describe the distribution of sensor readings. Rich inputs such as camera images make that modeling requirement demanding. Discriminative approaches avoid that requirement, although training them with hidden states can be complicated.

The paper treats the parameters of the estimated state distribution as outputs of a deterministic computation graph. This makes it possible to train the estimator directly with gradient descent. The graph can include expressive nonlinear components, such as convolutional neural networks, to process raw images before contributing to state estimation.

The resulting model can be understood as a recurrent neural network whose architecture draws on probabilistic filtering. Evaluations use a synthetic tracking task with raw images and visual odometry on KITTI. The reported improvements over standard generative approaches and ordinary recurrent networks suggest that filtering structure can be useful when learning state estimators from complex observations.
summary.tldr: Backprop KF trains image-based state estimators through a deterministic computation graph that combines neural processing with probabilistic filtering structure.

title: Backprop KF: Learning Discriminative Deterministic State Estimators

abstract: Many applications of machine learning involve structured output with large domain, where learning of structured predictor is prohibitive due to repetitive calls to expensive inference oracle. In this work, we show that, by decomposing training of Structural Support Vector Machine (SVM) into a series of multiclass SVM problems connected through messages, one can replace expensive structured oracle with Factorwise Maximization Oracle (FMO) that allows efficient implementation of complexity sublinear to the factor domain. A Greedy Direction Method of Multiplier (GDMM) algorithm is proposed to exploit sparsity of messages which guarantees $\epsilon$ sub-optimality after $O(log(1/\epsilon))$ passes of FMO calls. We conduct experiments on chain-structured problems and fully-connected problems of large output domains. The proposed approach is orders-of-magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art training algorithms for Structural SVM.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs with interacting parts, and the number of possible outputs can be very large. Training a structural SVM can become prohibitively expensive because it repeatedly calls an inference procedure over that output space. This paper focuses on reducing the cost of those repeated training computations.

The authors decompose structural SVM training into multiclass SVM problems linked by messages. This permits replacement of the expensive structured inference oracle with a factorwise maximization oracle. The replacement supports an implementation whose complexity is sublinear in the factor domain, addressing the cost of searching large local output possibilities.

Their Greedy Direction Method of Multiplier exploits sparse messages and guarantees an objective gap of epsilon after a number of oracle passes proportional to log(1/epsilon). Experiments cover chain-structured and fully connected problems with large output domains. In those evaluations, training is orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art structural SVM training algorithms compared. The contribution connects decomposition, sparse communication between subproblems, and a convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: Decomposing structural SVM training into message-linked subproblems enables cheaper factorwise inference and substantial reported training speedups.

title: Dual Decomposed Learning with Factorwise Oracle for Structural SVM of Large Output Domain

abstract: In this paper, we study the mixed linear regression (MLR) problem, where the goal is to recover multiple underlying linear models from their unlabeled linear measurements. We propose a non-convex objective function which we show is {\em locally strongly convex} in the neighborhood of the ground truth. We use a tensor method for initialization so that the initial models are in the local strong convexity region. We then employ general convex optimization algorithms to minimize the objective function. To the best of our knowledge, our approach provides first exact recovery guarantees for the MLR problem with $K \geq 2$ components. Moreover, our method has near-optimal computational complexity $\tilde O (Nd)$ as well as near-optimal sample complexity $\tilde O (d)$ for {\em constant} $K$. Furthermore, we show that our non-convex formulation can be extended to solving the {\em subspace clustering} problem as well. In particular, when initialized within a small constant distance to the true subspaces, our method converges to the global optima (and recovers true subspaces) in time {\em linear} in the number of points. Furthermore, our empirical results indicate that even with random initialization, our approach converges to the global optima in linear time, providing speed-up of up to two orders of magnitude.
