paragraphs: Mixed linear regression aims to recover several linear models from measurements without labels identifying which model generated each one. The authors propose a nonconvex objective that becomes strongly convex near the true models. A tensor-based initialization places the estimated models inside that favorable neighborhood, after which standard convex optimization algorithms minimize the objective.

The approach provides what the authors describe as the first exact-recovery guarantees for mixed linear regression with two or more components. For a constant number of components, its computational cost is near-optimal in the number of measurements and dimension, and its sample requirement is near-optimal in dimension. The constant-component qualification is part of these complexity claims.

The formulation also extends to subspace clustering. Starting within a sufficiently small constant distance of the true subspaces, it provably recovers them in time linear in the number of points. Experiments additionally report global convergence with random initialization and speedups of up to two orders of magnitude; that random-initialization finding is empirical, distinct from the nearby-initialization guarantee.
summary.tldr: Tensor initialization and a locally strongly convex objective yield exact-recovery guarantees for mixed linear regression, with an extension to subspace clustering.

title: Mixed Linear Regression with Multiple Components

abstract: Machine learning is now being used to make crucial decisions about people's lives. For nearly all of these decisions there is a risk that individuals of a certain race, gender, sexual orientation, or any other subpopulation are unfairly discriminated against. Our recent method has demonstrated how to use techniques from counterfactual inference to make predictions fair across different subpopulations. This method requires that one provides the causal model that generated the data at hand. In general, validating all causal implications of the model is not possible without further assumptions. Hence, it is desirable to integrate competing causal models to provide counterfactually fair decisions, regardless of which causal "world" is the correct one. In this paper, we show how it is possible to make predictions that are approximately fair with respect to multiple possible causal models at once, thus mitigating the problem of exact causal specification. We frame the goal of learning a fair classifier as an optimization problem with fairness constraints entailed by competing causal explanations. We show how this optimization problem can be efficiently solved using gradient-based methods. We demonstrate the flexibility of our model on two real-world fair classification problems. We show that our model can seamlessly balance fairness in multiple worlds with prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: Counterfactual approaches to fair prediction depend on a causal explanation of how the data were generated. Yet the available observations generally cannot validate every causal implication without further assumptions. This paper addresses the resulting uncertainty by considering several competing causal models when learning a fair classifier.

The authors formulate prediction as an optimization problem with fairness constraints supplied by the competing causal explanations. They show that predictions can be approximately fair with respect to multiple models at once, and that the optimization can be solved efficiently with gradient-based methods. This reduces dependence on committing to one exact causal specification.

Experiments on two real-world fair classification problems demonstrate the framework’s flexibility and its ability to balance prediction accuracy with fairness across the considered worlds. The qualification is central: the result concerns approximate fairness relative to multiple supplied causal models. Its value is to bring disagreement about causal assumptions into the learning objective itself, allowing that uncertainty to influence the fairness–accuracy balance.
summary.tldr: Fairness constraints from competing causal models enable predictions that balance accuracy with approximate counterfactual fairness across multiple possible worlds.

title: When Worlds Collide: Integrating Different Counterfactual Assumptions in Fairness

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have recently been applied to the optical flow estimation problem. As training the CNNs requires sufficiently large ground truth training data, existing approaches resort to synthetic, unrealistic datasets. On the other hand, unsupervised methods are capable of leveraging real-world videos for training where the ground truth flow fields are not available. These methods, however, rely on the fundamental assumptions of brightness constancy and spatial smoothness priors which do not hold near motion boundaries. In this paper, we propose to exploit unlabeled videos for semi-supervised learning of optical flow with a Generative Adversarial Network. Our key insight is that the adversarial loss can capture the structural patterns of flow warp errors without making explicit assumptions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed semi-supervised algorithm performs favorably against purely supervised and semi-supervised learning schemes.

paragraphs: Optical flow estimates motion between video frames. Training convolutional networks for this task requires many examples with known motion, so supervised approaches often use synthetic data. Real videos provide plentiful unlabeled observations, but unsupervised methods commonly depend on brightness constancy and spatial smoothness assumptions that break down near motion boundaries.

The paper proposes semi-supervised optical flow learning with a generative adversarial network, allowing unlabeled videos to contribute to training. Its key idea is to use an adversarial loss to capture structural patterns in flow warp errors. This gives the learning procedure a way to evaluate those patterns without explicitly imposing the assumptions identified as problematic.

Extensive benchmark experiments show favorable performance against purely supervised and other semi-supervised schemes. The findings support learning from the structure of warp errors as a useful complement to available supervision. The approach matters because it connects unlabeled real-world video to optical flow training while addressing a specific weakness of objectives built around fixed brightness and smoothness assumptions.
summary.tldr: An adversarial loss learns structural patterns in flow warp errors, enabling semi-supervised optical flow training with unlabeled videos.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning for Optical Flow with Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Modern neural networks are often augmented with an attention mechanism, which tells the network where to focus within the input. We propose in this paper a new framework for sparse and structured attention, building upon a smoothed max operator. We show that the gradient of this operator defines a mapping from real values to probabilities, suitable as an attention mechanism. Our framework includes softmax and a slight generalization of the recently-proposed sparsemax as special cases. However, we also show how our framework can incorporate modern structured penalties, resulting in more interpretable attention mechanisms, that focus on entire segments or groups of an input. We derive efficient algorithms to compute the forward and backward passes of our attention mechanisms, enabling their use in a neural network trained with backpropagation. To showcase their potential as a drop-in replacement for existing ones, we evaluate our attention mechanisms on three large-scale tasks: textual entailment, machine translation, and sentence summarization. Our attention mechanisms improve interpretability without sacrificing performance; notably, on textual entailment and summarization, we outperform the standard attention mechanisms based on softmax and sparsemax.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms assign weights to input elements so a neural network can concentrate on relevant information. This paper develops a framework that also controls how that attention is organized. Instead of only distributing weight across individual elements, attention can become sparse or concentrate on whole segments and groups, making its focus easier to interpret.

The construction starts with a smoothed maximum operator whose gradient converts real-valued scores into probabilities. Softmax and a slight generalization of sparsemax fit within this formulation. Adding structured penalties changes the resulting attention pattern, providing a common mathematical route to several kinds of focus. The authors also derive efficient forward and backward computations so these mechanisms can be trained through backpropagation.

The framework is evaluated on textual entailment, machine translation, and sentence summarization as a replacement for existing attention mechanisms. The reported results improve interpretability without sacrificing performance. On entailment and summarization specifically, the proposed mechanisms outperform standard softmax and sparsemax attention. The contribution therefore combines a unifying formulation with practical evidence that more structured attention can remain effective.
summary.tldr: A regularized attention framework produces sparse or grouped focus, improving interpretability while preserving performance in the reported tasks.

title: A Regularized Framework for Sparse and Structured Neural Attention

abstract: Computing optimal transport distances such as the earth mover's distance is a fundamental problem in machine learning, statistics, and computer vision. Despite the recent introduction of several algorithms with good empirical performance, it is unknown whether general optimal transport distances can be approximated in near-linear time. This paper demonstrates that this ambitious goal is in fact achieved by Cuturi's Sinkhorn Distances. This result relies on a new analysis of Sinkhorn iterations, which also directly suggests a new greedy coordinate descent algorithm Greenkhorn with the same theoretical guarantees. Numerical simulations illustrate that Greenkhorn significantly outperforms the classical Sinkhorn algorithm in practice.
originalAbstract: Computing optimal transport distances such as the earth mover's distance is a fundamental problem in machine learning, statistics, and computer vision. Despite the recent introduction of several algorithms with good empirical performance, it is unknown whether general optimal transport distances can be approximated in near-linear time. This paper demonstrates that this ambitious goal is in fact achieved by Cuturi's Sinkhorn Distances. This result relies on a new analysis of Sinkhorn iterations, which also directly suggests a new greedy coordinate descent algorithm Greenkhorn with the same theoretical guarantees. Numerical simulations illustrate that Greenkhorn significantly outperforms the classical Sinkhorn algorithm in practice.

paragraphs: Optimal transport distances, including earth mover's distance, provide ways to compare distributions by the cost of moving mass between them. They are important in machine learning, statistics, and computer vision. The paper addresses a computational question left open by practical successes: whether general optimal transport distances can be approximated in near-linear time.

The authors establish that Sinkhorn distances achieve this goal through a new analysis of Sinkhorn iterations. The result gives a theoretical efficiency guarantee to an approach already associated with good empirical behavior. It concerns approximation of optimal transport distances, so the speed claim should be understood in that approximation setting.

The analysis also suggests Greenkhorn, a new greedy coordinate-descent algorithm with the same theoretical guarantees. Numerical simulations show that Greenkhorn substantially outperforms classical Sinkhorn in practice. The two contributions reinforce one another: the analysis establishes near-linear approximation, while the new algorithm turns that analysis into a method with an additional empirical advantage in the reported simulations.
summary.tldr: A new Sinkhorn analysis proves near-linear optimal-transport approximation and yields Greenkhorn, which is substantially faster in reported simulations.

title: Near-linear time approximation algorithms for optimal transport via Sinkhorn iteration

abstract: Hierarchical clustering is a data analysis method that has been used for decades. Despite its widespread use, the method has an underdeveloped analytical foundation. Having a well understood foundation would both support the currently used methods and help guide future improvements. The goal of this paper is to give an analytic framework to better understand observations seen in practice. This paper considers the dual of a problem framework for hierarchical clustering introduced by Dasgupta. The main result is that one of the most popular algorithms used in practice, average linkage agglomerative clustering, has a small constant approximation ratio for this objective. Furthermore, this paper establishes that using bisecting k-means divisive clustering has a very poor lower bound on its approximation ratio for the same objective. However, we show that there are divisive algorithms that perform well with respect to this objective by giving two constant approximation algorithms. This paper is some of the first work to establish guarantees on widely used hierarchical algorithms for a natural objective function. This objective and analysis give insight into what these popular algorithms are optimizing and when they will perform well.

This paper develops theoretical guarantees using an objective that is dual to a framework introduced by Dasgupta. The objective supplies a common mathematical standard for examining several familiar clustering strategies.

For average linkage, which builds a hierarchy by merging groups, the authors prove a small constant approximation ratio. This bounds its performance relative to the best hierarchy under the chosen objective. For bisecting k-means, which repeatedly splits groups, they establish a poor lower bound on the approximation ratio, revealing potentially unfavorable behavior under that same standard.

The distinction does not imply that splitting-based approaches are inherently unsuccessful. The paper also provides two divisive algorithms with constant approximation guarantees. Together, these results show why the objective matters when judging a hierarchy: they give specific support for average linkage, identify a weakness of bisecting k-means, and demonstrate that other splitting strategies can retain strong guarantees.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical clustering objective yields constant approximation guarantees for average linkage and two divisive algorithms, while exposing weak worst-case behavior for bisecting k-means.

title: Approximation Bounds for Hierarchical Clustering: Average Linkage, Bisecting K-means, and Local Search

abstract: Synchronous mini-batch SGD is state-of-the-art for large-scale distributed machine learning. However, in practice, its convergence is bottlenecked by slow communication rounds between worker nodes. A natural solution to reduce communication is to use the \emph{``local-SGD''} model in which the workers train their model independently and synchronize every once in a while. This algorithm improves the computation-communication trade-off but its convergence is not understood very well. We propose a non-asymptotic error analysis, which enables comparison to \emph{one-shot averaging} i.e., a single communication round among independent workers, and \emph{mini-batch averaging} i.e., communicating at every step. We also provide adaptive lower bounds on the communication frequency for large step-sizes ($ t^{-\alpha} $, $ \alpha\in (1/2 , 1 ) $) and show that \emph{Local-SGD} reduces communication by a factor of $O\Big(\frac{\sqrt{T}}{P^{3/2}}\Big)$, with $T$ the total number of gradients and $P$ machines.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial time synchronizing workers instead of computing updates. Local stochastic gradient descent reduces that communication by letting workers train independently between synchronization rounds. This paper studies the resulting trade-off: how much communication can be reduced while retaining useful convergence behavior.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic error analysis, describing behavior at finite amounts of computation. It supports comparisons with two endpoints: one-shot averaging, where independent workers communicate once, and mini-batch averaging, where they communicate at every step. The analysis therefore places periodic synchronization within a common framework for assessing these alternatives.

For step sizes decreasing as t to the power of negative alpha, with alpha between one-half and one, the paper gives adaptive lower bounds on communication frequency. It also establishes a communication reduction factor of O(sqrt(T)/P^(3/2)), where T is the total number of gradients and P is the number of machines. This expression makes the stated saving depend explicitly on both computation and worker count.
summary.tldr: A finite-computation analysis quantifies how Local-SGD can reduce synchronization under the studied large-step-size schedules.

title: Communication trade-offs for Local-SGD with large step size

abstract: A recent line of research has shown that gradient-based algorithms with random initialization can converge to the global minima of the training loss for over-parameterized (i.e., sufficiently wide) deep neural networks. However, the condition on the width of the neural network to ensure the global convergence is very stringent, which is often a high-degree polynomial in the training sample size $n$ (e.g., $O(n^{24})$). In this paper, we provide an improved analysis of the global convergence of (stochastic) gradient descent for training deep neural networks, which only requires a milder over-parameterization condition than previous work in terms of the training sample size and other problem-dependent parameters. The main technical contributions of our analysis include (a) a tighter gradient lower bound that leads to a faster convergence of the algorithm, and (b) a sharper characterization of the trajectory length of the algorithm. By specializing our result to two-layer (i.e., one-hidden-layer) neural networks, it also provides a milder over-parameterization condition than the best-known result in prior work.

paragraphs: Theory has shown that gradient-based training can reach a global minimum of the training loss when a randomly initialized deep network is sufficiently wide. The difficulty is how wide the theory requires it to be. Earlier guarantees could demand widths growing as extremely high powers of the number of training examples, making the sufficient conditions very stringent.

This paper improves the analysis of gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent. It establishes global convergence under a milder requirement on network width, accounting for both training-set size and other problem-dependent quantities. The contribution is a stronger theoretical guarantee for these training methods rather than a new optimization algorithm.

Two refinements drive the result: a tighter lower bound on gradients, which supports faster convergence, and a more precise account of the distance traveled during optimization. The analysis also improves the sufficient width requirement for networks with one hidden layer. These results reduce the over-parameterization needed by the guarantees while retaining the focus on minimizing training loss.
summary.tldr: A sharper convergence analysis reduces the sufficient network width needed to guarantee successful gradient-based training.

title: An Improved Analysis of Training Over-parameterized Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Video interpolation is an important problem in computer vision, which helps overcome the temporal limitation of camera sensors. Existing video interpolation methods usually assume uniform motion between consecutive frames and use linear models for interpolation, which cannot well approximate the complex motion in the real world. To address these issues, we propose a quadratic video interpolation method which exploits the acceleration information in videos. This method allows prediction with curvilinear trajectory and variable velocity, and generates more accurate interpolation results. For high-quality frame synthesis, we develop a flow reversal layer to estimate flow fields starting from the unknown target frame to the source frame. In addition, we present techniques for flow refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach performs favorably against the existing linear models on a wide variety of video datasets.

paragraphs: Video interpolation synthesizes frames between recorded frames, helping overcome limits on how frequently a camera captures images. Many existing methods model motion as uniform between consecutive frames. This paper argues that such linear models poorly approximate the more complex movements that occur in real videos.

The proposed method uses a quadratic motion model that incorporates acceleration information. It can represent curved trajectories and changing velocity, giving the interpolation process a richer account of how scene content moves. This changes the motion assumption used to predict the missing frame, allowing more accurate results for the motions addressed by the method.

To synthesize high-quality images, the authors also introduce a flow reversal layer. It estimates motion fields directed from the unknown target frame back toward the source frames, and additional techniques refine those fields. Extensive experiments across a wide variety of video datasets show favorable performance against existing linear models. The contribution combines a more expressive motion model with components for turning that motion estimate into an interpolated frame.
summary.tldr: Quadratic video interpolation models acceleration and curved motion, producing favorable results against linear methods across varied video datasets.

title: Quadratic Video Interpolation

abstract: Predicting the future trajectories of multiple interacting pedestrians in a scene has become an increasingly important problem for many different applications ranging from control of autonomous vehicles and social robots to security and surveillance. This problem is compounded by the presence of social interactions between humans and their physical interactions with the scene. While the existing literature has explored some of these cues, they mainly ignored the multimodal nature of each human's future trajectory which is noticeably influenced by the intricate social interactions. In this paper, we present Social-BiGAT, a graph-based generative adversarial network that generates realistic, multimodal trajectory predictions for multiple pedestrians in a scene. Our method is based on a graph attention network (GAT) that learns feature representations that encode the social interactions between humans in the scene, and a recurrent encoder-decoder architecture that is trained adversarially to predict, based on the features, the humans' paths. We explicitly account for the multimodal nature of the prediction problem by forming a reversible transformation between each scene and its latent noise vector, as in Bicycle-GAN. We show that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance comparing it to several baselines on existing trajectory forecasting benchmarks.

paragraphs: Predicting pedestrian movement requires accounting for interactions among people and with their surroundings. A scene can also admit several plausible future paths for each person. Social-BiGAT addresses this combination by generating multiple realistic trajectory possibilities for interacting pedestrians, rather than treating the future as a single outcome.

A graph attention network learns features that encode social interactions among people in the scene. A recurrent encoder-decoder then uses those features to predict paths and is trained adversarially. These components connect the representation of interpersonal interactions with the generation of future movement.

To explicitly represent multiple possible futures, the framework forms a reversible transformation between each scene and its latent noise vector, following the Bicycle-GAN approach. This gives the latent representation a defined relationship with the scene in the trajectory generation process. Evaluations against several baselines on established trajectory forecasting benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance. The results support combining social interaction features with a generative model that explicitly accounts for multiple plausible trajectories.
summary.tldr: Social-BiGAT combines graph attention and adversarial trajectory generation to model social interactions and multiple plausible pedestrian futures.

title: Social-BiGAT: Multimodal Trajectory Forecasting using Bicycle-GAN and Graph Attention Networks

abstract: Data-driven models are subject to model errors due to limited and noisy training data. Key to the application of such models in safety-critical domains is the quantification of their model error. Gaussian processes provide such a measure and uniform error bounds have been derived, which allow safe control based on these models. However, existing error bounds require restrictive assumptions. In this paper, we employ the Gaussian process distribution and continuity arguments to derive a novel uniform error bound under weaker assumptions. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this distribution can be used to derive probabilistic Lipschitz constants and analyze the asymptotic behavior of our bound. Finally, we derive safety conditions for the control of unknown dynamical systems based on Gaussian process models and evaluate them in simulations of a robotic manipulator.

paragraphs: Models learned from limited, noisy data can make errors, so safety-critical control requires a way to quantify those errors. Gaussian process regression supports uncertainty estimates, and uniform error bounds can support safe control across a domain. This paper develops such a bound under weaker assumptions than those required by existing bounds.

The derivation combines the Gaussian process distribution with continuity arguments. The authors also use that distribution to obtain probabilistic Lipschitz constants, which describe how quickly a function can vary with its input under a probabilistic guarantee. They analyze the asymptotic behavior of the error bound, extending the work beyond its derivation to its behavior in the limit.

The paper then derives safety conditions for controlling unknown dynamical systems using Gaussian process models. Simulations of a robotic manipulator evaluate those conditions. The contribution links uncertainty quantification to concrete control requirements: a learned model supplies predictions, while the bound helps characterize when those predictions can support the stated safety conditions under the framework’s assumptions.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process error bound derived under weaker assumptions supports probabilistic regularity estimates and safety conditions for learned control.

title: Uniform Error Bounds for Gaussian Process Regression with Application to Safe Control

abstract: Structured representations of images that model visual relationships are beneficial for many vision and vision-language applications. However, current human-annotated visual relationship datasets suffer from the long-tailed predicate distribution problem which limits the potential of visual relationship models. In this work, we introduce a self-supervised method that implicitly learns the visual relationships without relying on any ground-truth visual relationship annotations. Our method relies on 1) intra- and inter-modality encodings to respectively model relationships within each modality separately and jointly, and 2) relationship probing, which seeks to discover the graph structure within each modality. By leveraging masked language modeling, contrastive learning, and dependency tree distances for self-supervision, our method learns better object features as well as implicit visual relationships. We verify the effectiveness of our proposed method on various vision-language tasks that benefit from improved visual relationship understanding.

paragraphs: Understanding an image involves relationships among objects as well as the objects themselves. Human-labeled relationship datasets contain highly uneven predicate frequencies, limiting what relationship models can learn from them. This paper proposes learning visual relationships implicitly through self-supervision, without requiring ground-truth annotations of those relationships.

The method combines encodings within each modality with encodings that connect modalities. It also uses relationship probing to discover graph structure within each modality, making relationships part of the learned representation. Its self-supervised signals come from masked language modeling, contrastive learning, and distances in dependency trees. These sources provide complementary guidance for learning object features and relational structure.

The authors evaluate the method on several vision-language tasks that benefit from understanding visual relationships and report evidence of its effectiveness. The stated contribution is improved object representations together with implicitly learned relationships. This matters because it offers a way to develop useful relational information without depending on explicit visual-relationship labels whose uneven distribution constrains existing approaches.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised relationship probing learns useful object features and implicit visual relationships without ground-truth visual-relationship annotations.

title: Self-Supervised Relationship Probing

abstract: Normalization methods such as batch, weight, instance, and layer normalization are commonly used in modern machine learning. Here, we study the weight normalization (WN) method \cite{salimans2016weight} and a variant called reparametrized projected gradient descent (rPGD) for overparametrized least squares regression and some more general loss functions. WN and rPGD reparametrize the weights with a scale $g$ and a unit vector such that the objective function becomes \emph{non-convex}. We show that this non-convex formulation has beneficial regularization effects compared to gradient descent on the original objective. These methods adaptively regularize the weights and \emph{converge linearly} close to the minimum $\ell_2$ norm solution even for initializations far from zero. For certain two-phase variants, they can converge to the min norm solution. This is different from the behavior of gradient descent, which only converges to the min norm solution when started at zero, and thus more sensitive to initialization.

paragraphs: This paper studies how weight normalization changes which solution an optimization method approaches. Its main setting is overparameterized least-squares regression, with additional consideration of more general losses. The authors analyze weight normalization and a related method, reparametrized projected gradient descent, to understand both their convergence and their implicit preference among possible solutions.

Both methods express a weight vector through a scale and a unit-length direction. Although this makes the objective nonconvex, the authors show that the new formulation provides beneficial regularization relative to gradient descent on the original objective. The methods adaptively constrain the weights and converge at a linear rate to a point close to the minimum Euclidean-norm solution, even from initializations far from zero.

Certain two-phase variants can reach the minimum-norm solution itself. In the comparison described by the abstract, ordinary gradient descent reaches that solution only when initialized at zero, making its result more sensitive to initialization. The distinction between approaching the minimum-norm solution and reaching it exactly is central: the stronger conclusion applies to the specified two-phase variants.
summary.tldr: Weight normalization can implicitly favor near-minimum-norm solutions with linear convergence, while certain two-phase variants reach the minimum-norm solution.

title: Implicit Regularization and Convergence for Weight Normalization

abstract: Missing data poses significant challenges while learning representations of video sequences. We present Disentangled Imputed Video autoEncoder (DIVE), a deep generative model that imputes and predicts future video frames in the presence of missing data. Specifically, DIVE introduces a missingness latent variable, disentangles the hidden video representations into static and dynamic appearance, pose, and missingness factors for each object, while it imputes each object trajectory where data is missing. On a moving MNIST dataset with various missing scenarios, DIVE outperforms the state of the art baselines by a substantial margin. We also present comparisons on a real-world MOTSChallenge pedestrian dataset, which demonstrates the practical value of our method in a more realistic setting. Our code can be found in https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/DIVE.

paragraphs: DIVE is a deep generative model for learning from video sequences with missing data. It tackles both filling in missing observations and predicting future frames. The central idea is to represent missingness explicitly alongside the factors describing the objects in a video, so incomplete observations become part of the representation-learning problem.

For each object, the model separates static appearance, dynamic appearance, pose, and missingness into distinct hidden factors. It also imputes the object's trajectory where observations are absent. This connects the representation of what an object looks like and how it changes with the task of reconstructing its unobserved behavior over time.

The authors evaluate DIVE on moving MNIST under several missing-data scenarios and report a substantial improvement over state-of-the-art baselines. They also present comparisons on the MOTSChallenge pedestrian dataset to demonstrate practical value in a more realistic setting. Together, these evaluations support explicitly modeling missingness and object-level factors when completing and forecasting incomplete videos.
summary.tldr: DIVE separates object appearance, pose, and missingness to reconstruct incomplete video trajectories and predict future frames.

title: Learning Disentangled Representations of Videos with Missing Data

abstract: Feature importance ranking has become a powerful tool for explainable AI. However, its nature of combinatorial optimization poses a great challenge for deep learning. In this paper, we propose a novel dual-net architecture consisting of operator and selector for discovery of an optimal feature subset of a fixed size and ranking the importance of those features in the optimal subset simultaneously. During learning, the operator is trained for a supervised learning task via optimal feature subset candidates generated by the selector that learns predicting the learning performance of the operator working on different optimal subset candidates. We develop an alternate learning algorithm that trains two nets jointly and incorporates a stochastic local search procedure into learning to address the combinatorial optimization challenge. In deployment, the selector generates an optimal feature subset and ranks feature importance, while the operator makes predictions based on the optimal subset for test data. A thorough evaluation on synthetic, benchmark and real data sets suggests that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art feature importance ranking and supervised feature selection methods. (Our source code is available: https://github.com/maksym33/FeatureImportanceDL)

paragraphs: Choosing a useful fixed-size feature subset requires searching among many possible combinations. Ranking the selected features adds another interpretability objective. This paper addresses both tasks with two neural networks trained together, connecting feature selection directly to how well a supervised predictor performs when given different subsets of its inputs.

The operator network learns the prediction task using candidate subsets supplied by the selector. The selector learns to predict the operator's learning performance on these candidates, providing guidance about which combinations are promising. An alternating training procedure couples the networks and incorporates stochastic local search to address the combinatorial difficulty of exploring feature subsets.

At deployment, the selector supplies a feature subset and an importance ranking, while the operator predicts from the selected inputs. Evaluations on synthetic, benchmark, and real datasets suggest improvements over several leading ranking and supervised feature-selection methods. The contribution is a joint learning procedure for selection, ranking, and prediction, with its reported advantage supported by those empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: An operator-selector pair jointly learns feature subsets, importance rankings, and predictions through alternating training and stochastic local search.

title: Feature Importance Ranking for Deep Learning

abstract: 3D shape representations that accommodate learning-based 3D reconstruction are an open problem in machine learning and computer graphics. Previous work on neural 3D reconstruction demonstrated benefits, but also limitations, of point cloud, voxel, surface mesh, and implicit function representations. We introduce \emph{Deformable Tetrahedral Meshes} (DefTet) as a particular parameterization that utilizes volumetric tetrahedral meshes for the reconstruction problem. Unlike existing volumetric approaches, DefTet optimizes for both vertex placement and occupancy, and is differentiable with respect to standard 3D reconstruction loss functions. It is thus simultaneously high-precision, volumetric, and amenable to learning-based neural architectures. We show that it can represent arbitrary, complex topology, is both memory and computationally efficient, and can produce high-fidelity reconstructions with a significantly smaller grid size than alternative volumetric approaches. The predicted surfaces are also inherently defined as tetrahedral meshes, thus do not require post-processing. We demonstrate that DefTetmatches or exceeds both the quality of the previous best approaches and the performance of the fastest ones. Our approach obtains high-quality tetrahedral meshes computed directly from noisy point clouds, and is the first to showcase high-quality 3D results using only a single image as input.

DefTet represents volume using tetrahedral meshes and learns both where mesh vertices belong and which regions are occupied. Adjusting geometry and occupancy together provides a way to describe detailed surfaces and complex topology within a volumetric representation.

Demonstrations include high-quality tetrahedral meshes reconstructed directly from noisy point clouds and high-quality 3D results from a single image. These findings support jointly adapting mesh geometry and occupancy as a useful reconstruction strategy.
summary.tldr: DefTet learns vertex positions and occupancy in tetrahedral meshes to produce detailed, efficient 3D reconstructions.

title: Learning Deformable Tetrahedral Meshes for 3D Reconstruction

abstract: We present a generative model for stroke-based drawing tasks which is able to model complex free-form structures. While previous approaches rely on sequence-based models for drawings of basic objects or handwritten text, we propose a model that treats drawings as a collection of strokes that can be composed into complex structures such as diagrams (e.g., flow-charts). At the core of the approach lies a novel auto-encoder that projects variable-length strokes into a latent space of fixed dimension. This representation space allows a relational model, operating in latent space, to better capture the relationship between strokes and to predict subsequent strokes. We demonstrate qualitatively and quantitatively that our proposed approach is able to model the appearance of individual strokes, as well as the compositional structure of larger diagram drawings. Our approach is suitable for interactive use cases such as auto-completing diagrams. We make code and models publicly available at https://eth-ait.github.io/cose.

CoSE approaches drawing generation by treating a drawing as a collection of composable strokes. This shifts attention toward how strokes fit together in structures such as flowcharts, extending beyond the basic objects and handwriting emphasized by earlier sequence-based approaches.

Its central component is an autoencoder that converts strokes of different lengths into representations with a fixed number of dimensions. A relational model then works with these representations to capture dependencies among strokes and predict subsequent ones. This gives the model a common representation for individual strokes while allowing it to reason about their role in the surrounding drawing.

The authors present qualitative and quantitative evidence that CoSE captures both the appearance of individual strokes and the composition of larger diagrams. They also identify interactive diagram completion as a suitable application. The important result is the combination of local stroke modeling with broader structural modeling: generating a plausible mark is only part of the task when that mark must contribute to a coherent diagram.
summary.tldr: CoSE encodes variable-length strokes into fixed-size representations so a relational model can generate strokes within complex diagram structures.

title: CoSE: Compositional Stroke Embeddings

abstract: Neural network architecture design mostly focuses on the new convolutional operator or special topological structure of network block, little attention is drawn to the configuration of stacking each block, called Block Stacking Style (BSS). Recent studies show that BSS may also have an unneglectable impact on networks, thus we design an efficient algorithm to search it automatically. The proposed method, AutoBSS, is a novel AutoML algorithm based on Bayesian optimization by iteratively refining and clustering Block Stacking Style Code (BSSC), which can find optimal BSS in a few trials without biased evaluation. On ImageNet classification task, ResNet50/MobileNetV2/EfficientNet-B0 with our searched BSS achieve 79.29%/74.5%/77.79%, which outperform the original baselines by a large margin. More importantly, experimental results on model compression, object detection and instance segmentation show the strong generalizability of the proposed AutoBSS, and further verify the unneglectable impact of BSS on neural networks.

paragraphs: Neural architecture design often concentrates on the operations inside a network block or the connections within it. AutoBSS examines another design choice: how those blocks are stacked to form a network. The paper argues that this configuration can materially affect performance and deserves systematic search alongside the design of individual blocks.

The method uses Bayesian optimization to search for a block stacking style. It represents candidate configurations through a code, then repeatedly refines and clusters these codes during search. The authors describe this process as finding an optimal stacking configuration in a small number of trials without biased evaluation. Its purpose is to make this architectural choice practical to optimize automatically.

On ImageNet, the searched configurations achieve 79.29% for ResNet50, 74.5% for MobileNetV2, and 77.79% for EfficientNet-B0, improving on the original baselines. Experiments also cover model compression, object detection, and instance segmentation. Together, these findings support the value of block stacking choices across the tested applications and the usefulness of AutoBSS beyond the initial classification setting.
summary.tldr: AutoBSS uses Bayesian optimization to search block stacking configurations, improving several networks and showing benefits across multiple tasks.

title: AutoBSS: An Efficient Algorithm for Block Stacking Style Search

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a powerful class of generative models in the deep learning community. Current practice on large-scale GAN training utilizes large models and distributed large-batch training strategies, and is implemented on deep learning frameworks (e.g., TensorFlow, PyTorch, etc.) designed in a centralized manner. In the centralized network topology, every worker needs to either directly communicate with the central node or indirectly communicate with all other workers in every iteration. However, when the network bandwidth is low or network latency is high, the performance would be significantly degraded. Despite recent progress on decentralized algorithms for training deep neural networks, it remains unclear whether it is possible to train GANs in a decentralized manner. The main difficulty lies at handling the nonconvex-nonconcave min-max optimization and the decentralized communication simultaneously. In this paper, we address this difficulty by designing the \textbf{first gradient-based decentralized parallel algorithm} which allows workers to have multiple rounds of communications in one iteration and to update the discriminator and generator simultaneously, and this design makes it amenable for the convergence analysis of the proposed decentralized algorithm. Theoretically, our proposed decentralized algorithm is able to solve a class of non-convex non-concave min-max problems with provable non-asymptotic convergence to first-order stationary point. Experimental results on GANs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Training a generative adversarial network involves two models learning against one another: a generator and a discriminator. Distributing this work across machines introduces communication costs alongside the optimization challenge. The paper targets settings where limited bandwidth or high latency makes centralized communication particularly costly.

The authors design a gradient-based decentralized algorithm that lets workers communicate multiple times within an iteration while updating the generator and discriminator simultaneously. These choices are central to making the combined optimization and communication process mathematically tractable. The difficulty is that GAN training involves a minimax objective that is neither convex in one side nor concave in the other.

For a specified class of these minimax problems, the paper establishes a finite-iteration convergence guarantee to a first-order stationary point. This describes a particular optimization endpoint, rather than guaranteeing a globally optimal GAN. Experiments on GANs support the algorithm's effectiveness. Together, the theory and experiments provide a foundation for training adversarial models through decentralized coordination.
summary.tldr: A decentralized GAN training algorithm combines local coordination with provable convergence for a class of nonconvex, nonconcave minimax problems.

title: A Decentralized Parallel Algorithm for Training Generative Adversarial Nets

abstract: Learning a stable Linear Dynamical System (LDS) from data involves creating models that both minimize reconstruction error and enforce stability of the learned representation. We propose a novel algorithm for learning stable LDSs. Using a recent characterization of stable matrices, we present an optimization method that ensures stability at every step and iteratively improves the reconstruction error using gradient directions derived in this paper. When applied to LDSs with inputs, our approach---in contrast to current methods for learning stable LDSs---updates both the state and control matrices, expanding the solution space and allowing for models with lower reconstruction error. We apply our algorithm in simulations and experiments to a variety of problems, including learning dynamic textures from image sequences and controlling a robotic manipulator. Compared to existing approaches, our proposed method achieves an \textit{orders-of-magnitude} improvement in reconstruction error and superior results in terms of control performance. In addition, it is \textit{provably} more memory efficient, with an $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ space complexity compared to $\mathcal{O}(n^4)$ of competing alternatives, thus scaling to higher-dimensional systems when the other methods fail. The code of the proposed algorithm and animations of the results can be found at https://github.com/giorgosmamakoukas/MemoryEfficientStableLDS.

paragraphs: Learning a linear dynamical system requires fitting observed behavior, but the resulting dynamics may also need to be stable. This paper develops an optimization method that combines these requirements. Using a characterization of stable matrices, the algorithm maintains stability at every step while iteratively improving reconstruction error through derived gradient directions.

For systems with external inputs, the method updates both the state matrix and the control matrix. Allowing both to change expands the set of candidate solutions compared with approaches that do not jointly update them. This creates opportunities to fit observations more accurately while preserving the stability requirement throughout optimization.

The paper evaluates the algorithm in simulations and experiments, including dynamic textures learned from image sequences and control of a robotic manipulator. It reports orders-of-magnitude improvements in reconstruction error and better control performance than existing approaches. The method also has a proven O(n²) memory requirement, compared with O(n⁴) for competing alternatives, enabling higher-dimensional systems in cases where those alternatives fail.
summary.tldr: A stability-preserving algorithm learns linear dynamical systems with improved reported fit and control performance using O(n²) memory.

title: Memory-Efficient Learning of Stable Linear Dynamical Systems for Prediction and Control

abstract: Score matching (SM) provides a compelling approach to learn energy-based models (EBMs) by avoiding the calculation of partition function. However, it remains largely open to learn energy-based latent variable models (EBLVMs), except some special cases. This paper presents a bi-level score matching (BiSM) method to learn EBLVMs with general structures by reformulating SM as a bi-level optimization problem. The higher level introduces a variational posterior of the latent variables and optimizes a modified SM objective, and the lower level optimizes the variational posterior to fit the true posterior. To solve BiSM efficiently, we develop a stochastic optimization algorithm with gradient unrolling. Theoretically, we analyze the consistency of BiSM and the convergence of the stochastic algorithm. Empirically, we show the promise of BiSM in Gaussian restricted Boltzmann machines and highly nonstructural EBLVMs parameterized by deep convolutional neural networks. BiSM is comparable to the widely adopted contrastive divergence and SM methods when they are applicable; and can learn complex EBLVMs with intractable posteriors to generate natural images.

paragraphs: Score matching offers a way to train energy-based models without calculating the partition function, a normalization quantity that can be difficult to compute. Extending this advantage to models with hidden variables has largely remained unresolved beyond special cases. This paper proposes Bi-level Score Matching, or BiSM, to make score matching applicable to latent-variable models with more general structures.

BiSM rewrites training as two connected optimization problems. The higher level introduces an approximate posterior distribution over hidden variables and optimizes a modified score-matching objective. The lower level improves that approximation by fitting it to the true posterior. A stochastic algorithm uses gradient unrolling to account for this nested optimization, and the authors analyze both the method’s consistency and the algorithm’s convergence.

Experiments cover Gaussian restricted Boltzmann machines and complex models built with deep convolutional networks. BiSM performs comparably to contrastive divergence and ordinary score matching where those methods apply. It also trains models with intractable posteriors to generate natural images, demonstrating the promise of extending score matching to a broader model class.
summary.tldr: BiSM uses nested optimization to extend score matching to general energy-based latent-variable models, including models with intractable posteriors.

title: Bi-level Score Matching for Learning Energy-based Latent Variable Models

abstract: In reinforcement learning, continuous time is often discretized by a time scale $\delta$, to which the resulting performance is known to be highly sensitive. In this work, we seek to find a $\delta$-invariant algorithm for policy gradient (PG) methods, which performs well regardless of the value of $\delta$. We first identify the underlying reasons that cause PG methods to fail as $\delta \to 0$, proving that the variance of the PG estimator can diverge to infinity in stochastic environments under a certain assumption of stochasticity. While durative actions or action repetition can be employed to have $\delta$-invariance, previous action repetition methods cannot immediately react to unexpected situations in stochastic environments. We thus propose a novel $\delta$-invariant method named Safe Action Repetition (SAR) applicable to any existing PG algorithm. SAR can handle the stochasticity of environments by adaptively reacting to changes in states during action repetition. We empirically show that our method is not only $\delta$-invariant but also robust to stochasticity, outperforming previous $\delta$-invariant approaches on eight MuJoCo environments with both deterministic and stochastic settings. Our code is available at https://vision.snu.ac.kr/projects/sar.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often represents continuous time using discrete steps, and performance can depend strongly on the chosen step size. This paper investigates why policy-gradient methods can fail as those steps become extremely small. Under a particular stochasticity assumption, it proves that the variance of the policy-gradient estimator can grow without bound.

Repeating actions over time can reduce sensitivity to the discretization, but previous repetition methods cannot immediately respond to unexpected events in stochastic environments. Safe Action Repetition addresses this issue by adapting to changes in state while an action is being repeated. The method is designed to be applicable to any existing policy-gradient algorithm.

Experiments in eight MuJoCo environments, using deterministic and stochastic settings, show invariance to time discretization and robustness to stochasticity. The method outperforms previous discretization-invariant approaches in those evaluations. Its contribution combines an explanation of a small-time-step failure mode with action repetition that retains the ability to react, addressing both the timing choice and changes encountered during execution.
summary.tldr: Safe Action Repetition reduces policy-gradient sensitivity to time-step size while adapting repeated actions to state changes in stochastic environments.

title: Time Discretization-Invariant Safe Action Repetition for Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: Truncated linear regression is a classical challenge in Statistics, wherein a label, $y = w^T x + \varepsilon$, and its corresponding feature vector, $x \in \mathbb{R}^k$, are only observed if the label falls in some subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$; otherwise the existence of the pair $(x, y)$ is hidden from observation. Linear regression with truncated observations has remained a challenge, in its general form, since the early works of [Tobin'58, Amemiya '73]. When the distribution of the error is normal with known variance, recent work of [Daskalakis et al. '19] provides computationally and statistically efficient estimators of the linear model, $w$. In this paper, we provide the first computationally and statistically efficient estimators for truncated linear regression when the noise variance is unknown, estimating both the linear model and the variance of the noise. Our estimator is based on an efficient implementation of Projected Stochastic Gradient Descent on the negative log-likelihood of the truncated sample. Importantly, we show that the error of our estimates is asymptotically normal, and we use this to provide explicit confidence regions for our estimates.

paragraphs: In truncated linear regression, an observation becomes visible only when its outcome falls within a specified set. Otherwise, both the outcome and its accompanying features are hidden, including the fact that the pair exists. The observed data therefore represent a selected portion of the underlying regression problem, making parameter estimation more difficult.

Earlier efficient estimators described in the abstract handled normally distributed errors with known variance. This paper extends the estimation problem to unknown noise variance, estimating both the regression coefficients and the amount of noise. The authors present their method as the first estimator for this setting that is efficient in both computation and statistical use of data.

The method uses projected stochastic gradient descent to optimize the negative log-likelihood of the truncated observations. Accounting for truncation in that objective is central to learning from the selected sample. The authors also establish asymptotic normality of estimation errors and use it to construct explicit confidence regions. The contribution thus includes uncertainty quantification alongside efficient estimation of the model and noise variance.
summary.tldr: The paper efficiently estimates regression coefficients and unknown noise variance from truncated observations, with asymptotic results supporting explicit confidence regions.

title: Efficient Truncated Linear Regression with Unknown Noise Variance

abstract: The accuracy of simulation-based forecasting in chaotic systems is heavily dependent on high-quality estimates of the system state at the beginning of the forecast. Data assimilation methods are used to infer these initial conditions by systematically combining noisy, incomplete observations and numerical models of system dynamics to produce highly effective estimation schemes. We introduce a self-supervised framework, which we call \textit{amortized assimilation}, for learning to assimilate in dynamical systems. Amortized assimilation combines deep learning-based denoising with differentiable simulation, using independent neural networks to assimilate specific observation types while connecting the gradient flow between these sub-tasks with differentiable simulation and shared recurrent memory. This hybrid architecture admits a self-supervised training objective which is minimized by an unbiased estimator of the true system state even in the presence of only noisy training data. Numerical experiments across several chaotic benchmark systems highlight the improved effectiveness of our approach compared to widely-used data assimilation methods.

paragraphs: Forecasting a chaotic system depends heavily on estimating its state accurately at the forecast's start. Data assimilation combines noisy, incomplete observations with a numerical dynamics model to obtain that estimate. This paper introduces amortized assimilation, a self-supervised framework that learns how to perform this combination.

The architecture joins neural denoising with differentiable simulation. Separate neural networks assimilate particular types of observation, while the simulator and shared recurrent memory connect the subtasks and their gradient flow. This lets the different observation-processing components participate in a shared learning process grounded in the system's dynamics.

The resulting training objective has an unbiased estimator of the true state as a minimizer even when the training observations are noisy. This is a property of the objective, rather than a claim that every trained network necessarily attains that estimator. Numerical experiments across several chaotic benchmark systems show improved effectiveness over widely used assimilation methods. The findings support learning state estimation through the interaction of observations, memory, and simulation.
summary.tldr: Amortized assimilation combines neural denoising, differentiable simulation, and recurrent memory to learn state estimation from noisy observations.

title: Learning to Assimilate in Chaotic Dynamical Systems

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel visual representation learning which relies on a handful of adaptively learned tokens, and which is applicable to both image and video understanding tasks. Instead of relying on hand-designed splitting strategies to obtain visual tokens and processing a large number of densely sampled patches for attention, our approach learns to mine important tokens in visual data. This results in efficiently and effectively finding a few important visual tokens and enables modeling of pairwise attention between such tokens, over a longer temporal horizon for videos, or the spatial content in image frames. Our experiments demonstrate strong performance on several challenging benchmarks for video recognition tasks. Importantly, due to our tokens being adaptive, we accomplish competitive results at significantly reduced computational cost. We establish new state-of-the-arts on multiple video datasets, including Kinetics-400, Kinetics-600, Charades, and AViD.

This results in efficiently and effectively finding a few important visual tokens and enables modeling of pairwise attention between such tokens, over a longer temporal horizon for videos, or the spatial content in image frames. Our experiments demonstrate strong performance on several challenging benchmarks for video recognition tasks. Importantly, due to our tokens being adaptive, we accomplish competitive results at significantly reduced computational cost. We establish new state-of-the-arts on multiple video datasets, including Kinetics-400, Kinetics-600, Charades, and AViD.

paragraphs: Visual attention models often divide images into predefined patches and process many resulting tokens. TokenLearner instead learns to extract a small number of important tokens from the visual input. The representation is adaptive, allowing token selection to respond to the content rather than being fixed by a hand-designed partition.

Using fewer meaningful tokens makes it possible to model pairwise attention efficiently. For video, this supports reasoning across a longer temporal span; for images, it supports attention over spatial content. The method therefore changes how visual information is packaged before attention, making the selection of that information part of representation learning itself.

Experiments demonstrate strong performance on challenging video-recognition benchmarks and competitive results at significantly lower computational cost. The authors report new state-of-the-art results on Kinetics-400, Kinetics-600, Charades, and AViD. These findings support the value of adaptive tokenization for video understanding, while the proposed representation also applies to images. The key result is that a handful of learned tokens can support effective visual reasoning in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: TokenLearner adaptively extracts a few visual tokens, supporting strong video recognition with significantly reduced computation.

title: TokenLearner: Adaptive Space-Time Tokenization for Videos

abstract: We tackle sequential learning under label noise in applications where a human supervisor can be queried to relabel suspicious examples. Existing approaches are flawed, in that they only relabel incoming examples that look "suspicious" to the model. As a consequence, those mislabeled examples that elude (or don't undergo) this cleaning step end up tainting the training data and the model with no further chance of being cleaned. We propose CINCER, a novel approach that cleans both new and past data by identifying \emph{pairs of mutually incompatible examples}. Whenever it detects a suspicious example, CINCER identifies a counter-example in the training set that - according to the model - is maximally incompatible with the suspicious example, and asks the annotator to relabel either or both examples, resolving this possible inconsistency. The counter-examples are chosen to be maximally incompatible, so to serve as \emph{explanations} of the model's suspicion, and highly influential, so to convey as much information as possible if relabeled. CINCER achieves this by leveraging an efficient and robust approximation of influence functions based on the Fisher information matrix (FIM). Our extensive empirical evaluation shows that clarifying the reasons behind the model's suspicions by cleaning the counter-examples helps in acquiring substantially better data and models, especially when paired with our FIM approximation.

paragraphs: In sequential learning, incorrectly labeled examples can remain in the training set long after they arrive. Methods that only inspect suspicious new examples leave earlier mistakes with no further opportunity for correction. CINCER addresses this by asking a human supervisor to resolve conflicts involving both incoming examples and previously collected data.

When a new example appears suspicious, CINCER finds a training example that the model considers strongly incompatible with it. The annotator can then relabel either example or both. The counter-example serves as an explanation of why the model is concerned, making the query a concrete comparison rather than an unexplained request to reconsider a label.

Counter-examples are selected for both incompatibility and influence, so correcting them can provide useful information to the model. CINCER uses an efficient, robust approximation to influence functions based on the Fisher information matrix. The empirical evaluation reports substantially better data and models when counter-examples are also cleaned, especially with this approximation. The approach turns an explanation into an opportunity to repair the model's existing training history.
summary.tldr: CINCER improves label cleaning by showing humans conflicting example pairs and allowing corrections to both new and past data.

title: Interactive Label Cleaning with Example-based Explanations

abstract: Partial Domain Adaptation (PDA) addresses the unsupervised domain adaptation problem where the target label space is a subset of the source label space. Most state-of-art PDA methods tackle the inconsistent label space by assigning weights to classes or individual samples, in an attempt to discard the source data that belongs to the irrelevant classes. However, we believe samples from those extra categories would still contain valuable information to promote positive transfer. In this paper, we propose the Implicit Semantic Response Alignment to explore the intrinsic relationships among different categories by applying a weighted schema on the feature level. Specifically, we design a class2vec module to extract the implicit semantic topics from the visual features. With an attention layer, we calculate the semantic response according to each implicit semantic topic. Then semantic responses of source and target data are aligned to retain the relevant information contained in multiple categories by weighting the features, instead of samples. Experiments on several cross-domain benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method over the state-of-the-art PDA methods. Moreover, we elaborate in-depth analyses to further explore implicit semantic alignment.

Most state-of-art PDA methods tackle the inconsistent label space by assigning weights to classes or individual samples, in an attempt to discard the source data that belongs to the irrelevant classes. However, we believe samples from those extra categories would still contain valuable information to promote positive transfer. In this paper, we propose the Implicit Semantic Response Alignment to explore the intrinsic relationships among different categories by applying a weighted schema on the feature level. Specifically, we design a class2vec module to extract the implicit semantic topics from the visual features. With an attention layer, we calculate the semantic response according to each implicit semantic topic. Then semantic responses of source and target data are aligned to retain the relevant information contained in multiple categories by weighting the features, instead of samples. Experiments on several cross-domain benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method over the state-of-the-art PDA methods. Moreover, we elaborate in-depth analyses to further explore implicit semantic alignment.

paragraphs: Partial domain adaptation transfers learning from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain whose classes form a subset of the source classes. Many methods reduce the influence of source examples from classes absent in the target. This paper asks whether those extra classes can still contribute useful visual information.

The proposed method weights information at the feature level. A class2vec module extracts implicit semantic topics from visual features, and an attention layer measures the response to each topic. The method then aligns these semantic responses between source and target data. This creates a way to retain relevant information distributed across multiple categories, including categories that would otherwise be downweighted as whole groups of examples.

Experiments on several cross-domain benchmarks show the method's effectiveness relative to the compared state-of-the-art partial adaptation approaches. Additional analyses examine the semantic alignment mechanism. The contribution is a finer-grained approach to selective transfer: learning which features are relevant when source and target label spaces differ.
summary.tldr: Aligning semantic responses at the feature level helps partial domain adaptation retain useful information from otherwise irrelevant source classes.

title: Implicit Semantic Response Alignment for Partial Domain Adaptation

abstract: Shift neural networks reduce computation complexity by removing expensive multiplication operations and quantizing continuous weights into low-bit discrete values, which are fast and energy-efficient compared to conventional neural networks. However, existing shift networks are sensitive to the weight initialization and yield a degraded performance caused by vanishing gradient and weight sign freezing problem. To address these issues, we propose S$^3$ re-parameterization, a novel technique for training low-bit shift networks. Our method decomposes a discrete parameter in a sign-sparse-shift 3-fold manner. This way, it efficiently learns a low-bit network with weight dynamics similar to full-precision networks and insensitive to weight initialization. Our proposed training method pushes the boundaries of shift neural networks and shows 3-bit shift networks compete with their full-precision counterparts in terms of top-1 accuracy on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Shift neural networks reduce computational demands by replacing expensive multiplications and representing weights with a small number of discrete values. Their appeal is faster, more energy-efficient computation. However, the paper identifies training difficulties in existing shift networks, including sensitivity to initialization, vanishing gradients, and weights whose signs become frozen.

The proposed S³ method changes how each discrete weight is represented during training. It decomposes the parameter into sign, sparsity, and shift components. This three-part representation is intended to let the low-bit weights evolve more like weights in a full-precision network. The authors report that it also makes training insensitive to weight initialization.

The stated experimental result is that three-bit shift networks can compete with full-precision counterparts on ImageNet top-1 accuracy. This matters because the motivation for shift networks depends on preserving useful predictive performance while simplifying computation. The contribution focuses on making the restricted weight representation train effectively, showing that the reported accuracy gap can be substantially addressed through the parameterization used for learning.
summary.tldr: S³ separates sign, sparsity, and shift to train three-bit shift networks that compete with full-precision models on ImageNet accuracy.

title: S$^3$: Sign-Sparse-Shift Reparametrization for Effective Training of Low-bit Shift Networks

abstract: Transfer Learning has shown great potential to enhance single-agent Reinforcement Learning (RL) efficiency. Similarly, Multiagent RL (MARL) can also be accelerated if agents can share knowledge with each other. However, it remains a problem of how an agent should learn from other agents. In this paper, we propose a novel Multiagent Policy Transfer Framework (MAPTF) to improve MARL efficiency. MAPTF learns which agent's policy is the best to reuse for each agent and when to terminate it by modeling multiagent policy transfer as the option learning problem. Furthermore, in practice, the option module can only collect all agent's local experiences for update due to the partial observability of the environment. While in this setting, each agent's experience may be inconsistent with each other, which may cause the inaccuracy and oscillation of the option-value's estimation. Therefore, we propose a novel option learning algorithm, the successor representation option learning to solve it by decoupling the environment dynamics from rewards and learning the option-value under each agent's preference. MAPTF can be easily combined with existing deep RL and MARL approaches, and experimental results show it significantly boosts the performance of existing methods in both discrete and continuous state spaces.

paragraphs: Agents learning together may improve more quickly by reusing one another’s policies, but useful transfer requires deciding whose behavior to borrow and when to stop borrowing it. The Multiagent Policy Transfer Framework, or MAPTF, treats these decisions as an option learning problem. A transferred policy becomes a behavior that an agent can select and later terminate.

Partial observability complicates this process because the option module must learn from agents’ local experiences. Those experiences may disagree, making estimates of a transferred policy’s value inaccurate or unstable. The authors address this with successor representation option learning, which separates environmental dynamics from rewards and evaluates options according to each agent’s preferences.

The framework can be combined with existing deep reinforcement learning and multiagent reinforcement learning methods. Experiments show significant performance improvements for existing methods in both discrete and continuous state spaces. The contribution is therefore more than sharing policies: it supplies a learned selection and termination mechanism, together with a way to evaluate transferred behavior when agents experience the environment differently.
summary.tldr: MAPTF learns which agent’s policy to reuse and when to stop, while accounting for differences in agents’ experiences and preferences.

title: An Efficient Transfer Learning Framework for Multiagent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Adder neural networks (ANNs) are designed for low energy cost which replace expensive multiplications in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with cheaper additions to yield energy-efficient neural networks and hardware accelerations. Although ANNs achieve satisfactory efficiency, there exist gaps between ANNs and CNNs where the accuracy of ANNs can hardly be compared to CNNs without the assistance of other training tricks, such as knowledge distillation. The inherent discrepancy lies in the similarity measurement between filters and features, however how to alleviate this difference remains unexplored. To locate the potential problem of ANNs, we focus on the property difference due to similarity measurement. We demonstrate that unordered heavy tails in ANNs could be the key component which prevents ANNs from achieving superior classification performance since fatter tails tend to overlap in feature space. Through pre-defining Multivariate Skew Laplace distributions and embedding feature distributions into the loss function, ANN features can be fully controlled and designed for various properties. We further present a novel method for tackling existing heavy tails in ANNs with only a modification of classifier where ANN features are clustered with their tails well-formulated through proposed angle-based constraint on the distribution parameters to encourage high diversity of tails. Experiments conducted on several benchmarks and comparison with other distributions demonstrate the effectiveness of proposed approach for boosting the performance of ANNs.
