paragraphs: Adder neural networks replace costly multiplications with cheaper additions to reduce energy use. Their accuracy, however, can lag behind convolutional networks without additional training techniques. This paper investigates how the different similarity measurement between filters and features affects the geometry of learned features, focusing on distributions with heavy tails.

The authors identify unordered heavy tails as a possible key obstacle to classification performance: broader tails tend to overlap in feature space. They introduce predefined multivariate skew Laplace distributions into the loss function so that feature distributions can be shaped explicitly. This makes the arrangement of the tails a target of learning.

Their method handles existing heavy tails through a modification of the classifier. An angle-based constraint on distribution parameters encourages diverse tail directions as the features form clusters. The intended effect is to organize the tails that would otherwise overlap. Experiments across several benchmarks, including comparisons with alternative distributions, show improved AdderNet performance. The findings support distribution design as a useful approach to the observed accuracy gap without establishing heavy tails as its sole cause.
summary.tldr: Shaping heavy-tailed feature distributions through a modified classifier improves AdderNet performance in the reported experiments.

title: Handling Long-tailed Feature Distribution in AdderNets

abstract: Fitting network models to neural activity is an important tool in neuroscience. A popular approach is to model a brain area with a probabilistic recurrent spiking network whose parameters maximize the likelihood of the recorded activity. Although this is widely used, we show that the resulting model does not produce realistic neural activity. To correct for this, we suggest to augment the log-likelihood with terms that measure the dissimilarity between simulated and recorded activity. This dissimilarity is defined via summary statistics commonly used in neuroscience and the optimization is efficient because it relies on back-propagation through the stochastically simulated spike trains. We analyze this method theoretically and show empirically that it generates more realistic activity statistics. We find that it improves upon other fitting algorithms for spiking network models like GLMs (Generalized Linear Models) which do not usually rely on back-propagation. This new fitting algorithm also enables the consideration of hidden neurons which is otherwise notoriously hard, and we show that it can be crucial when trying to infer the network connectivity from spike recordings.

A common approach chooses parameters that maximize the likelihood of the recordings. The authors show that this fitting objective can yield a model whose own generated activity is unrealistic, exposing a gap between explaining recordings and reproducing their statistical characteristics.

Their solution augments log-likelihood with penalties measuring differences between simulated and recorded activity. These comparisons use summary statistics common in neuroscience. Optimization remains efficient by backpropagating through stochastically simulated spike trains, allowing the generated activity itself to inform parameter updates.

The paper provides theoretical analysis and empirical evidence of more realistic activity statistics, along with improvements over other spiking-network fitting algorithms such as those used for generalized linear models. The method also permits hidden neurons to be included in fitting. The authors show that accounting for these unobserved neurons can be crucial when inferring connectivity from spike recordings, linking simulation realism to the network structure being estimated.
summary.tldr: Matching simulated neural activity statistics alongside likelihood produces more realistic spiking models and supports connectivity inference with hidden neurons.

title: Fitting summary statistics of neural data with a differentiable spiking network simulator

abstract: We study multi-task reinforcement learning (RL) in tabular episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs). We formulate a heterogeneous multi-player RL problem, in which a group of players concurrently face similar but not necessarily identical MDPs, with a goal of improving their collective performance through inter-player information sharing. We design and analyze a model-based algorithm, and provide gap-dependent and gap-independent regret upper and lower bounds that characterize the intrinsic complexity of the problem.
originalAbstract: We study multi-task reinforcement learning (RL) in tabular episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs). We formulate a heterogeneous multi-player RL problem, in which a group of players concurrently face similar but not necessarily identical MDPs, with a goal of improving their collective performance through inter-player information sharing. We design and analyze a model-based algorithm, and provide gap-dependent and gap-independent regret upper and lower bounds that characterize the intrinsic complexity of the problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies how several reinforcement-learning agents can learn together when their environments resemble one another without being identical. Each player interacts with its own episodic Markov decision process, and the collective goal is to improve performance through information sharing. The setting is tabular, meaning states and actions are represented explicitly.

The authors formulate this as a heterogeneous multi-player learning problem and design a model-based algorithm. The important distinction is that related tasks need not have exactly the same dynamics. The formulation therefore places task differences inside the learning problem while still allowing agents to benefit from information gathered by other players.

The theoretical analysis supplies both regret upper bounds for the algorithm and lower bounds describing inherent difficulty. It includes gap-dependent results, which account for differences in the values of competing choices, and gap-independent results, which do not rely on those separations. Together, these bounds characterize the intrinsic complexity of the stated transfer problem and give a mathematical basis for assessing collective learning across related environments.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a model-based algorithm and regret bounds for agents sharing information across similar but nonidentical tabular episodic environments.

title: Provably efficient multi-task reinforcement learning with model transfer

abstract: Machine learning models trained on uncurated datasets can often end up adversely affecting inputs belonging to underrepresented groups. To address this issue, we consider the problem of adaptively constructing training sets which allow us to learn classifiers that are fair in a {\em minimax} sense. We first propose an adaptive sampling algorithm based on the principle of \emph{optimism}, and derive theoretical bounds on its performance. We also propose heuristic extensions of this algorithm suitable for application to large scale, practical problems. Next, by deriving algorithm independent lower-bounds for a specific class of problems, we show that the performance achieved by our adaptive scheme cannot be improved in general. We then validate the benefits of adaptively constructing training sets via experiments on synthetic tasks with logistic regression classifiers, as well as on several real-world tasks using convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

paragraphs: A classifier trained on an uncurated dataset can perform poorly for groups that appear less often in its training examples. This paper addresses that problem through the construction of the training set itself. Its objective is minimax fairness: learning with attention to the group facing the worst classification performance.

The authors propose an adaptive sampling algorithm based on optimism and establish theoretical bounds on its performance. Sampling is therefore part of the learning strategy, rather than a fixed preliminary choice. They also develop heuristic extensions intended to make the approach usable for larger practical problems.

To assess what improvement is possible, the paper derives lower bounds that apply regardless of the algorithm for a particular class of problems. These show that the adaptive method's performance cannot generally be improved. Experiments with logistic regression on synthetic tasks and convolutional networks on real-world tasks support the benefits of adaptive dataset construction. Together, the results connect a fairness objective to both a sampling procedure and limits on achievable performance.
summary.tldr: Adaptive training-data sampling improves minimax fairness, with theoretical guarantees and supporting experiments.

title: Adaptive Sampling for Minimax Fair Classification

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control typically employs distributions whose support covers the entire action space. In this work, we investigate the colloquially known phenomenon that trained agents often prefer actions at the boundaries of that space. We draw theoretical connections to the emergence of bang-bang behavior in optimal control, and provide extensive empirical evaluation across a variety of recent RL algorithms. We replace the normal Gaussian by a Bernoulli distribution that solely considers the extremes along each action dimension - a bang-bang controller. Surprisingly, this achieves state-of-the-art performance on several continuous control benchmarks - in contrast to robotic hardware, where energy and maintenance cost affect controller choices. Since exploration, learning, and the final solution are entangled in RL, we provide additional imitation learning experiments to reduce the impact of exploration on our analysis. Finally, we show that our observations generalize to environments that aim to model real-world challenges and evaluate factors to mitigate the emergence of bang-bang solutions. Our findings emphasise challenges for benchmarking continuous control algorithms, particularly in light of potential real-world applications.

paragraphs: Continuous-control reinforcement learning usually represents actions with distributions that cover the full action range. Yet trained agents often favor the extremes. This paper investigates that behavior by replacing Gaussian action distributions with Bernoulli distributions that choose only the two boundaries along each action dimension, producing a bang-bang controller.

The authors connect this behavior to optimal control theory and test it across several reinforcement-learning algorithms. Despite the restricted choices, the resulting controllers achieve state-of-the-art performance on several continuous-control benchmarks. Additional imitation-learning experiments reduce the influence of exploration, helping separate that factor from learning and the properties of the final controller.

The observations also extend to environments intended to capture real-world challenges, and the paper evaluates factors that can reduce bang-bang behavior. The practical distinction is that robotic hardware introduces energy and maintenance considerations that influence controller choice. The findings therefore raise questions about what benchmark success measures: strong scores can coexist with extreme-action behavior whose suitability depends on the costs represented by the task.
summary.tldr: Policies restricted to extreme actions perform surprisingly well on continuous-control benchmarks, highlighting questions about their relevance to physical control.

title: Is Bang-Bang Control All You Need? Solving Continuous Control with Bernoulli Policies

abstract: Learning efficiently from small amounts of data has long been the focus of model-based reinforcement learning, both for the online case when interacting with the environment, and the offline case when learning from a fixed dataset. However, to date no single unified algorithm could demonstrate state-of-the-art results for both settings.In this work, we describe the Reanalyse algorithm, which uses model-based policy and value improvement operators to compute improved training targets for existing data points, allowing for efficient learning at data budgets varying by several orders of magnitude. We further show that Reanalyse can also be used to learn completely without environment interactions, as in the case of Offline Reinforcement Learning (Offline RL). Combining Reanalyse with the MuZero algorithm, we introduce MuZero Unplugged, a single unified algorithm for any data budget, including Offline RL. In contrast to previous work, our algorithm requires no special adaptations for the off-policy or Offline RL settings. MuZero Unplugged sets new state-of-the-art results for Atari in the standard 200 million frame online setting as well as in the RL Unplugged Offline RL benchmark.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can collect new experience through interaction or learn entirely from a fixed dataset. This paper develops a unified approach for both cases, centered on extracting more useful training information from experience already available. Its Reanalyse algorithm revisits existing data points and uses model-based policy and value improvement operations to produce improved training targets.

The authors combine Reanalyse with MuZero to create MuZero Unplugged. Recomputing targets allows the algorithm to use planning with a learned model across data budgets differing by several orders of magnitude. It can also operate without new environment interactions, and the proposed algorithm requires no special adaptations for offline or off-policy learning.

The reported results set new state-of-the-art performance on Atari in the standard 200-million-frame online setting and on the RL Unplugged offline benchmark. These findings support the usefulness of revisiting stored experience with improved model-based targets. The same overall algorithm succeeds in both evaluated regimes, connecting online learning and fixed-dataset learning through a shared planning-based training procedure.
summary.tldr: MuZero Unplugged uses Reanalyse to improve targets for stored experience, achieving strong online and offline reinforcement learning with one algorithm.

title: Online and Offline Reinforcement Learning by Planning with a Learned Model

abstract: Given a set of $n$ points in $d$ dimensions, the Euclidean $k$-means problem (resp. Euclidean $k$-median) consists of finding $k$ centers such that the sum of squared distances (resp. sum of distances) from every point to its closest center is minimized. The arguably most popular way of dealing with this problem in the big data setting is to first compress the data by computing a weighted subset known as a coreset and then run any algorithm on this subset. The guarantee of the coreset is that for any candidate solution, the ratio between coreset cost and the cost of the original instance is less than a $(1\pm \varepsilon)$ factor. The current state of the art coreset size is $\tilde O(\min(k^{2} \cdot \varepsilon^{-2},k\cdot \varepsilon^{-4}))$ for Euclidean $k$-means and $\tilde O(\min(k^{2} \cdot \varepsilon^{-2},k\cdot \varepsilon^{-3}))$ for Euclidean $k$-median. The best known lower bound for both problems is $\Omega(k\varepsilon^{-2})$. In this paper, we improve these bounds to $\tilde O(\min(k^{3/2} \cdot \varepsilon^{-2},k\cdot \varepsilon^{-4}))$ for Euclidean $k$-means and $\tilde O(\min(k^{4/3} \cdot \varepsilon^{-2},k\cdot \varepsilon^{-3}))$ for Euclidean $k$-median. In particular, ours is the first provable bound that breaks through the $k^2$ barrier while retaining an optimal dependency on $\varepsilon$.

paragraphs: Euclidean k-means chooses k centers to minimize total squared distance to the nearest center; k-median uses unsquared distances. For large datasets, a coreset replaces the full input with a smaller weighted subset. Its guarantee preserves the cost of every candidate set of centers within a multiplicative factor of 1 plus or minus epsilon.

The paper improves the number of points needed for such coresets. Ignoring logarithmic factors, its k-means bound is the smaller of k^(3/2)/epsilon^2 and k/epsilon^4. For k-median, it is the smaller of k^(4/3)/epsilon^2 and k/epsilon^3. The improvement replaces the previously quadratic dependence on k in the branches with epsilon^-2 dependence.

This matters because the compressed dataset can be used by a subsequent clustering algorithm while preserving candidate costs. The authors establish the first bounds that move below quadratic dependence on k while retaining optimal dependence on epsilon. The stated lower bound remains proportional to k/epsilon^2, so the results improve the gap without claiming to close it completely.
summary.tldr: The paper proves smaller coresets for Euclidean k-means and k-median while preserving optimal accuracy dependence in the improved bounds.

title: Improved Coresets for Euclidean $k$-Means

abstract: Conditional inference on arbitrary subsets of variables is a core problem in probabilistic inference with important applications such as masked language modeling and image inpainting. In recent years, the family of Any-Order Autoregressive Models (AO-ARMs) -- closely related to popular models such as BERT and XLNet -- has shown breakthrough performance in arbitrary conditional tasks across a sweeping range of domains. But, in spite of their success, in this paper we identify significant improvements to be made to previous formulations of AO-ARMs. First, we show that AO-ARMs suffer from redundancy in their probabilistic model, i.e., they define the same distribution in multiple different ways. We alleviate this redundancy by training on a smaller set of univariate conditionals that still maintains support for efficient arbitrary conditional inference. Second, we upweight the training loss for univariate conditionals that are evaluated more frequently during inference. Our method leads to improved performance with no compromises on tractability, giving state-of-the-art likelihoods in arbitrary conditional modeling on text (Text8), image (CIFAR10, ImageNet32), and continuous tabular data domains.

In recent years, the family of Any-Order Autoregressive Models (AO-ARMs) -- closely related to popular models such as BERT and XLNet -- has shown breakthrough performance in arbitrary conditional tasks across a sweeping range of domains. But, in spite of their success, in this paper we identify significant improvements to be made to previous formulations of AO-ARMs. First, we show that AO-ARMs suffer from redundancy in their probabilistic model, i.e., they define the same distribution in multiple different ways. We alleviate this redundancy by training on a smaller set of univariate conditionals that still maintains support for efficient arbitrary conditional inference. Second, we upweight the training loss for univariate conditionals that are evaluated more frequently during inference. Our method leads to improved performance with no compromises on tractability, giving state-of-the-art likelihoods in arbitrary conditional modeling on text (Text8), image (CIFAR10, ImageNet32), and continuous tabular data domains.

paragraphs: Arbitrary conditional inference means predicting some variables while observing whichever others are available. Masked language modeling and image inpainting are examples. Any-order autoregressive models support this flexibility, but the paper identifies redundancy in their probabilistic formulation: the same distribution can be represented in multiple different ways.

The authors reduce this redundancy by training on a smaller collection of univariate conditionals, each predicting one variable given others. The reduced collection still supports efficient arbitrary conditional inference. They also adjust training priorities by increasing the loss weights for conditionals that are evaluated more often during inference, tying training emphasis to actual model use.

Together, these changes improve performance without sacrificing tractability. The reported evaluations achieve state-of-the-art likelihoods for arbitrary conditional modeling on Text8, CIFAR10, ImageNet32, and continuous tabular data. The contribution is a refinement of both the training formulation and its weighting: it preserves flexible conditioning while reducing redundant modeling and giving frequently used predictions more attention during learning.
summary.tldr: Reducing redundant conditionals and weighting training by inference frequency improves any-order autoregressive modeling while preserving efficient arbitrary conditioning.

title: Training and Inference on Any-Order Autoregressive Models the Right Way

abstract: Each year, expert-level performance is attained in increasingly-complex multiagent domains, where notable examples include Go, Poker, and StarCraft II. This rapid progression is accompanied by a commensurate need to better understand how such agents attain this performance, to enable their safe deployment, identify limitations, and reveal potential means of improving them. In this paper we take a step back from performance-focused multiagent learning, and instead turn our attention towards agent behavior analysis. We introduce a model-agnostic method for discovery of behavior clusters in multiagent domains, using variational inference to learn a hierarchy of behaviors at the joint and local agent levels. Our framework makes no assumption about agents' underlying learning algorithms, does not require access to their latent states or policies, and is trained using only offline observational data. We illustrate the effectiveness of our method for enabling the coupled understanding of behaviors at the joint and local agent level, detection of behavior changepoints throughout training, discovery of core behavioral concepts, demonstrate the approach's scalability to a high-dimensional multiagent MuJoCo control domain, and also illustrate that the approach can disentangle previously-trained policies in OpenAI's hide-and-seek domain.
originalAbstract: Each year, expert-level performance is attained in increasingly-complex multiagent domains, where notable examples include Go, Poker, and StarCraft II. This rapid progression is accompanied by a commensurate need to better understand how such agents attain this performance, to enable their safe deployment, identify limitations, and reveal potential means of improving them. In this paper we take a step back from performance-focused multiagent learning, and instead turn our attention towards agent behavior analysis. We introduce a model-agnostic method for discovery of behavior clusters in multiagent domains, using variational inference to learn a hierarchy of behaviors at the joint and local agent levels. Our framework makes no assumption about agents' underlying learning algorithms, does not require access to their latent states or policies, and is trained using only offline observational data. We illustrate the effectiveness of our method for enabling the coupled understanding of behaviors at the joint and local agent level, detection of behavior changepoints throughout training, discovery of core behavioral concepts, demonstrate the approach's scalability to a high-dimensional multiagent MuJoCo control domain, and also illustrate that the approach can disentangle previously-trained policies in OpenAI's hide-and-seek domain.

paragraphs: Strong performance in a multiagent task does not by itself explain how the agents behave together. This paper develops a way to analyze recorded behavior, shifting attention from the reward an agent achieves to the patterns of interaction behind that performance. The aim is to connect an understanding of individual agents with an understanding of the group.

The method uses variational inference to discover a hierarchy of behavior clusters at both the joint and local agent levels. It learns entirely from offline observational data. It requires neither access to agents' policies or internal latent states nor assumptions about their learning algorithms, allowing the same analysis framework to be applied to differently constructed agents.

The demonstrations show how this hierarchy can reveal relationships between group and individual behavior, identify changes during training, and uncover recurring behavioral concepts. The authors also demonstrate scalability in a high-dimensional multiagent MuJoCo control setting and separation of previously trained policies in hide-and-seek. Together, these results support behavior analysis as a complementary view of multiagent performance.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy learned from recorded multiagent interactions reveals individual and collective behavior without access to agents' internal policies.

title: Beyond Rewards: a Hierarchical Perspective on Offline Multiagent Behavioral Analysis

abstract: Image classification accuracy on the ImageNet dataset has been a barometer for progress in computer vision over the last decade. Several recent papers have questioned the degree to which the benchmark remains useful to the community, yet innovations continue to contribute gains to performance, with today's largest models achieving 90%+ top-1 accuracy. To help contextualize progress on ImageNet and provide a more meaningful evaluation for today's state-of-the-art models, we manually review and categorize every remaining mistake that a few top models make in order to provide insight into the long-tail of errors on one of the most benchmarked datasets in computer vision. We focus on the multi-label subset evaluation of ImageNet, where today's best models achieve upwards of 97% top-1 accuracy. Our analysis reveals that nearly half of the supposed mistakes are not mistakes at all, and we uncover new valid multi-labels, demonstrating that, without careful review, we are significantly underestimating the performance of these models. On the other hand, we also find that today's best models still make a significant number of mistakes (40%) that are obviously wrong to human reviewers. To calibrate future progress on ImageNet, we provide an updated multi-label evaluation set, and we curate ImageNet-Major: a 68-example "major error" slice of the obvious mistakes made by today's top models -- a slice where models should achieve near perfection, but today are far from doing so.

This paper manually examines and categorizes every remaining mistake made by several leading models on ImageNet's multi-label subset evaluation. In that setting, the best models considered exceed 97% top-1 accuracy.

The review finds that nearly half of the supposed mistakes are actually valid predictions missing from the accepted labels. Adding those valid labels shows that the existing evaluation understates model performance. At the same time, about 40% of the reviewed mistakes are plainly incorrect to human reviewers, revealing substantial recognizable failures among the remaining errors.

The authors provide an updated multi-label evaluation set and ImageNet-Major, a collection of 68 obvious-error examples. The latter targets cases where they argue models should perform almost perfectly but remain far from that standard. These resources separate incomplete annotation from clear recognition failure, making future benchmark gains easier to interpret and directing attention toward errors that remain meaningful despite very high overall accuracy.
summary.tldr: Manual review reveals many apparent ImageNet errors are valid predictions, while a curated 68-example set exposes obvious remaining failures.

title: When does dough become a bagel? Analyzing the remaining mistakes on ImageNet

abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are latent variable models that can generate complex objects and provide meaningful latent representations. Moreover, they could be further used in downstream tasks such as classification. As previous work has shown, one can easily fool VAEs to produce unexpected latent representations and reconstructions for a visually slightly modified input. Here, we examine several objective functions for adversarial attacks construction proposed previously and present a solution to alleviate the effect of these attacks. Our method utilizes the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique in the inference step that we motivate with a theoretical analysis. Thus, we do not incorporate any extra costs during training and the performance on non-attacked inputs is not decreased. We validate our approach on a variety of datasets (MNIST, Fashion MNIST, Color MNIST, CelebA) and VAE configurations ($\beta$-VAE, NVAE, $\beta$-TCVAE), and show that our approach consistently improves the model robustness to adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders learn internal representations and reconstruct inputs, but small visual changes can cause unexpectedly large changes in those outputs. This paper examines adversarial attacks designed to exploit that vulnerability. It considers several previously proposed attack objectives and develops a method to reduce their effect on the model's inference process.

The proposed defense uses Markov chain Monte Carlo during inference, with theoretical analysis motivating this choice. Placing the intervention at this stage means the method adds no training cost. The authors also report that performance on inputs without attacks does not decrease, so the stated benefit combines improved robustness with preserved ordinary-input performance.

The evaluation spans MNIST, Fashion MNIST, Color MNIST, and CelebA, together with beta-VAE, NVAE, and beta-TCVAE configurations. Across these tests, the method consistently improves robustness to adversarial attacks. The contribution is therefore an inference-stage approach supported across several datasets and VAE designs, with the stated aim of alleviating attacks rather than establishing complete immunity.
summary.tldr: An MCMC-based inference method improves VAE robustness to adversarial inputs without adding training costs or reducing reported clean-input performance.

title: Alleviating Adversarial Attacks on Variational Autoencoders with MCMC

abstract: We show that the effectiveness of the well celebrated Mixup can be further improved if instead of using it as the sole learning objective, it is utilized as an additional regularizer to the standard cross-entropy loss. This simple change not only improves accuracy but also significantly improves the quality of the predictive uncertainty estimation of Mixup in most cases under various forms of covariate shifts and out-of-distribution detection experiments. In fact, we observe that Mixup otherwise yields much degraded performance on detecting out-of-distribution samples possibly, as we show empirically, due to its tendency to learn models exhibiting high-entropy throughout; making it difficult to differentiate in-distribution samples from out-of-distribution ones. To show the efficacy of our approach (RegMixup), we provide thorough analyses and experiments on vision datasets (ImageNet & CIFAR-10/100) and compare it with a suite of recent approaches for reliable uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: The paper revisits how Mixup enters a classifier’s training objective. Its proposed change, RegMixup, retains standard cross-entropy training and adds Mixup as a regularizer. This changes the balance of training signals while preserving Mixup’s role in influencing the learned model.

The motivation includes a problem with uncertainty estimation. The authors observe that ordinary Mixup can perform poorly at detecting examples from outside the training distribution. Their empirical analysis suggests a possible explanation: models may produce high-entropy predictions broadly, making familiar and unfamiliar examples difficult to distinguish through predictive uncertainty.

Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10/100 compare RegMixup with recent uncertainty-estimation approaches. The authors report improved accuracy and, in most evaluated cases, significantly better uncertainty estimates under covariate shifts and out-of-distribution detection. The findings show that the way Mixup is combined with the ordinary classification objective can affect both prediction quality and the usefulness of uncertainty, while the high-entropy explanation remains an empirically supported possibility.
summary.tldr: RegMixup adds Mixup to standard cross-entropy as a regularizer, improving accuracy and uncertainty estimation in most evaluated settings.

title: Using Mixup as a Regularizer Can Surprisingly Improve Accuracy & Out-of-Distribution Robustness

abstract: Tremendous progress has been made in reinforcement learning (RL) over the past decade. Most of these advancements came through the continual development of new algorithms, which were designed using a combination of mathematical derivations, intuitions, and experimentation. Such an approach of creating algorithms manually is limited by human understanding and ingenuity. In contrast, meta-learning provides a toolkit for automatic machine learning method optimisation, potentially addressing this flaw. However, black-box approaches which attempt to discover RL algorithms with minimal prior structure have thus far not outperformed existing hand-crafted algorithms. Mirror Learning, which includes RL algorithms, such as PPO, offers a potential middle-ground starting point: while every method in this framework comes with theoretical guarantees, components that differentiate them are subject to design. In this paper we explore the Mirror Learning space by meta-learning a “drift” function. We refer to the immediate result as Learnt Policy Optimisation (LPO). By analysing LPO we gain original insights into policy optimisation which we use to formulate a novel, closed-form RL algorithm, Discovered Policy Optimisation (DPO). Our experiments in Brax environments confirm state-of-the-art performance of LPO and DPO, as well as their transfer to unseen settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning algorithms are often designed through mathematical analysis, intuition, and experimentation. Automatically learning such algorithms could expand the search beyond manually chosen designs, but minimally structured black-box approaches have struggled to outperform established methods. This paper explores automatic discovery within a framework that already supplies theoretical guarantees.

That framework is Mirror Learning, which includes algorithms such as PPO while leaving some components open to design. The authors use meta-learning to discover a drift function within this space, producing Learnt Policy Optimisation, or LPO. They then analyze the learned method and use the resulting insights to formulate a new algorithm with a closed-form expression, called Discovered Policy Optimisation, or DPO.

Experiments in Brax environments report state-of-the-art performance for both LPO and DPO, together with transfer to unseen settings. The approach connects automated search with algorithm interpretation: a learned component supplies useful behavior, and analyzing it yields an explicit policy optimization method. The reported transfer supports the usefulness of the discovered designs beyond their original learning settings.
summary.tldr: Meta-learning within Mirror Learning yields LPO and inspires the closed-form DPO algorithm, both showing strong Brax performance and transfer.

title: Discovered Policy Optimisation

abstract: The need for interpretable models has fostered the development of self-explainable classifiers. Prior approaches are either based on multi-stage optimization schemes, impacting the predictive performance of the model, or produce explanations that are not transparent, trustworthy or do not capture the diversity of the data. To address these shortcomings, we propose ProtoVAE, a variational autoencoder-based framework that learns class-specific prototypes in an end-to-end manner and enforces trustworthiness and diversity by regularizing the representation space and introducing an orthonormality constraint. Finally, the model is designed to be transparent by directly incorporating the prototypes into the decision process. Extensive comparisons with previous self-explainable approaches demonstrate the superiority of ProtoVAE, highlighting its ability to generate trustworthy and diverse explanations, while not degrading predictive performance.

paragraphs: Self-explainable classifiers build explanations into their prediction process. The paper identifies two difficulties in previous approaches: multi-stage training can affect predictive performance, and the resulting explanations may lack transparency, trustworthiness, or coverage of diverse data. ProtoVAE addresses these concerns through a framework based on a variational autoencoder.

The model learns class-specific prototypes through end-to-end training. These prototypes serve as representative patterns and participate directly in the classification decision, making their connection to a prediction explicit. The framework also regularizes its representation space and introduces an orthonormality constraint to promote the trustworthiness and diversity of the learned prototypes.

Comparisons with earlier self-explainable methods report superior performance and explanations that are both trustworthy and diverse, without degrading predictive performance. The approach matters because explanation quality and classification are handled within the same model and training process. Rather than attaching a separate account after a prediction, ProtoVAE makes prototypes part of the mechanism producing it, while its constraints aim to keep those explanatory patterns informative and varied.
summary.tldr: ProtoVAE learns diverse class-specific prototypes that directly support predictions, with reported explanation benefits that do not degrade predictive performance.

title: ProtoVAE: A Trustworthy Self-Explainable Prototypical Variational Model

abstract: The kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy~(MMD) is a popular multivariate distance metric between distributions. The usual kernel-MMD test statistic (for two-sample testing) is a degenerate U-statistic under the null, and thus it has an intractable limiting null distribution. Hence, the standard approach for designing a level-$(1-\alpha)$ two-sample test using this statistic involves selecting the rejection threshold as the $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of the permutation distribution. The resulting nonparametric test has finite-sample validity but suffers from large computational cost, since the test statistic must be recomputed for every permutation. We propose the cross-MMD, a new quadratic time MMD test statistic based on sample-splitting and studentization. We prove that under mild assumptions, it has a standard normal limiting distribution under the null. Importantly, we also show that the resulting test is consistent against any fixed alternative, and when using the Gaussian kernel, it has minimax rate-optimal power against local alternatives. For large sample-sizes, our new cross-MMD provides a significant speedup over the MMD, for only a slight loss in power.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. Kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or MMD, measures differences between distributions, but calibrating its usual test statistic is computationally awkward. Standard testing repeatedly permutes the data to determine a rejection threshold, providing finite-sample validity at the cost of recomputing the statistic many times.

The paper introduces cross-MMD, which splits the samples and rescales the resulting statistic through studentization. Under mild assumptions, its distribution approaches a standard normal distribution when the two underlying distributions are equal. This supplies an asymptotic route to setting the threshold without permutations. Computing the statistic itself still takes quadratic time.

The authors prove consistency against any fixed alternative: with enough data, the test can detect a fixed distributional difference. With a Gaussian kernel, they also establish minimax rate-optimal power against local alternatives. For large samples, the reported benefit is a substantial speedup with only a slight reduction in power, trading repeated permutation computation for asymptotic calibration.
summary.tldr: Cross-MMD uses sample splitting and studentization to avoid permutation calibration, substantially accelerating large-sample testing with a slight loss in power.

title: A permutation-free kernel two-sample test

abstract: Top two algorithms arose as an adaptation of Thompson sampling to best arm identification in multi-armed bandit models for parametric families of arms. They select the next arm to sample from by randomizing among two candidate arms, a leader and a challenger. Despite their good empirical performance, theoretical guarantees for fixed-confidence best arm identification have only been obtained when the arms are Gaussian with known variances. In this paper, we provide a general analysis of top-two methods, which identifies desirable properties of the leader, the challenger, and the (possibly non-parametric) distributions of the arms. As a result, we obtain theoretically supported top-two algorithms for best arm identification with bounded distributions. Our proof method demonstrates in particular that the sampling step used to select the leader inherited from Thompson sampling can be replaced by other choices, like selecting the empirical best arm.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks which option has the highest expected reward, with a specified level of confidence. Top-two algorithms collect evidence by randomizing between two candidates: a leader and a challenger. Although these methods perform well empirically, earlier fixed-confidence guarantees were restricted to Gaussian rewards with known variances.

The paper develops a general analysis that separates the properties needed from the leader, the challenger, and the reward distributions. This makes it possible to reason about top-two methods beyond that Gaussian setting, including distributions that need not belong to a specified parametric family.

The analysis yields theoretically supported algorithms for bounded reward distributions. It also shows that the leader-selection step inherited from Thompson sampling can be replaced by other choices, including selecting the option with the highest observed average reward. This matters because it identifies flexibility within the top-two design: the theoretical support can apply to a broader family of candidate-selection procedures, rather than depending on that particular sampling step.
summary.tldr: A general analysis extends theoretical support for top-two best-arm identification to bounded distributions and alternative leader-selection rules.

title: Top Two Algorithms Revisited

abstract: The increasing reliance on ML models in high-stakes tasks has raised a major concern about fairness violations. Although there has been a surge of work that improves algorithmic fairness, most are under the assumption of an identical training and test distribution. In many real-world applications, however, such an assumption is often violated as previously trained fair models are often deployed in a different environment, and the fairness of such models has been observed to collapse. In this paper, we study how to transfer model fairness under distribution shifts, a widespread issue in practice. We conduct a fine-grained analysis of how the fair model is affected under different types of distribution shifts and find that domain shifts are more challenging than subpopulation shifts. Inspired by the success of self-training in transferring accuracy under domain shifts, we derive a sufficient condition for transferring group fairness. Guided by it, we propose a practical algorithm with fair consistency regularization as the key component. A synthetic dataset benchmark, which covers diverse types of distribution shifts, is deployed for experimental verification of the theoretical findings. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets, including image and tabular data, demonstrate that our approach effectively transfers fairness and accuracy under various types of distribution shifts.

paragraphs: A model that meets fairness goals in its training environment may lose those properties when deployed elsewhere. This paper studies that transfer problem across different kinds of distribution shift. Its analysis finds domain shifts more challenging than subpopulation shifts, showing that the nature of the environmental change matters when assessing whether fairness will persist.

Drawing inspiration from self-training methods that transfer accuracy across domains, the authors derive a sufficient condition for transferring group fairness. They use that condition to design an algorithm centered on fair consistency regularization. The theoretical result supplies a route under which fairness transfer is supported; it does not state that the condition is necessary for every successful transfer.

The authors build a synthetic benchmark covering diverse shifts to examine the theoretical findings. They also evaluate the method on real image and tabular datasets. The experiments show effective transfer of both fairness and accuracy across various shifts. Together, the analysis and results support treating fairness preservation as an explicit adaptation objective when a model moves between environments.
summary.tldr: A sufficient condition for fairness transfer motivates a consistency-regularized algorithm that preserves fairness and accuracy across tested distribution shifts.

title: Transferring Fairness under Distribution Shifts via Fair Consistency Regularization

abstract: Learning medical visual representations directly from paired radiology reports has become an emerging topic in representation learning. However, existing medical image-text joint learning methods are limited by instance or local supervision analysis, ignoring disease-level semantic correspondences. In this paper, we present a novel Multi-Granularity Cross-modal Alignment (MGCA) framework for generalized medical visual representation learning by harnessing the naturally exhibited semantic correspondences between medical image and radiology reports at three different levels, i.e., pathological region-level, instance-level, and disease-level. Specifically, we first incorporate the instance-wise alignment module by maximizing the agreement between image-report pairs. Further, for token-wise alignment, we introduce a bidirectional cross-attention strategy to explicitly learn the matching between fine-grained visual tokens and text tokens, followed by contrastive learning to align them. More important, to leverage the high-level inter-subject relationship semantic (e.g., disease) correspondences, we design a novel cross-modal disease-level alignment paradigm to enforce the cross-modal cluster assignment consistency. Extensive experimental results on seven downstream medical image datasets covering image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks demonstrate the stable and superior performance of our framework.

paragraphs: Medical images and their radiology reports describe related information at several scales. This paper argues that learning only from whole image-report pairs or local correspondences overlooks disease-level relationships across subjects. MGCA addresses this by aligning visual and textual information at the region, individual example, and disease levels.

At the instance level, the framework increases agreement between paired images and reports. For finer details, bidirectional cross-attention learns matches between visual tokens and text tokens, followed by contrastive learning to align them. These components connect the overall correspondence of a report and image with the more specific correspondences within them.

The disease-level component enforces consistency between cluster assignments across the two modalities. This incorporates higher-level semantic relationships across subjects into the representation-learning process. Experiments on seven downstream medical image datasets cover classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, with consistently strong reported performance. The findings support combining several levels of image-text correspondence to learn visual representations useful across different medical imaging tasks.
summary.tldr: MGCA aligns medical images and reports at region, instance, and disease levels to improve representations across several downstream imaging tasks.

title: Multi-Granularity Cross-modal Alignment for Generalized Medical Visual Representation Learning

abstract: We developed a new method PROTES for black-box optimization, which is based on the probabilistic sampling from a probability density function given in the low-parametric tensor train format. We tested it on complex multidimensional arrays and discretized multivariable functions taken, among others, from real-world applications, including unconstrained binary optimization and optimal control problems, for which the possible number of elements is up to $2^{1000}$. In numerical experiments, both on analytic model functions and on complex problems, PROTES outperforms popular discrete optimization methods (Particle Swarm Optimization, Covariance Matrix Adaptation, Differential Evolution, and others).

We tested it on complex multidimensional arrays and discretized multivariable functions taken, among others, from real-world applications, including unconstrained binary optimization and optimal control problems, for which the possible number of elements is up to $2^{1000}$. paragraphs: PROTES tackles black-box optimization over large discrete spaces, including multidimensional arrays and discretized functions of many variables. The central challenge is the enormous number of possible candidates. The paper considers problems whose candidate spaces contain as many as 2¹⁰⁰⁰ elements, making the representation used to guide search a consequential design choice.

The method samples candidates probabilistically from a distribution represented in tensor-train format. This format uses relatively few parameters to describe the sampling distribution. The contribution therefore centers on combining probabilistic search with a compact tensor representation, providing a way to organize exploration of very large multidimensional spaces.

The authors test PROTES on analytic functions and complex problems, including unconstrained binary optimization and optimal control applications. In these numerical experiments, it outperforms popular discrete optimization approaches, including Particle Swarm Optimization, Covariance Matrix Adaptation, and Differential Evolution. The stated findings establish empirical advantages on the evaluated problems; the enormous candidate count describes the search spaces involved, rather than the number of candidates individually evaluated.
summary.tldr: PROTES uses compact tensor-train sampling distributions to outperform popular optimizers on evaluated large discrete search problems.

title: PROTES: Probabilistic Optimization with Tensor Sampling

abstract: Current self-supervised learning (SSL) methods (e.g., SimCLR, DINO, VICReg, MOCOv3) target primarily on representations at instance level and do not generalize well to dense prediction tasks, such as object detection and segmentation. Towards aligning SSL with dense predictions, this paper demonstrates for the first time the underlying mean-shift clustering process of Vision Transformers (ViT), which aligns well with natural image semantics (e.g., a world of objects and stuffs). By employing transformer for joint embedding and clustering, we propose a bi-level feature clustering SSL method, coined Feature-Level Self-supervised Learning (FLSL). We present the formal definition of the FLSL problem and construct the objectives from the mean-shift and k-means perspectives. We show that FLSL promotes remarkable semantic cluster representations and learns an embedding scheme amenable to intra-view and inter-view feature clustering. Experiments show that FLSL yields significant improvements in dense prediction tasks, achieving 44.9 (+2.8)% AP and 46.5% AP in object detection, as well as 40.8 (+2.3)% AP and 42.1% AP in instance segmentation on MS-COCO, using Mask R-CNN with ViT-S/16 and ViT-S/8 as backbone, respectively. FLSL consistently outperforms existing SSL methods across additional benchmarks, including UAV object detection on UAVDT, and video instance segmentation on DAVIS 2017. We conclude by presenting visualization and various ablation studies to better understand the success of FLSL. The source code is available at https://github.com/ISL-CV/FLSL.

paragraphs: Many self-supervised learning methods emphasize a representation of an entire image. Object detection and segmentation also need meaningful representations of the image’s local content. FLSL addresses this mismatch by making feature-level grouping central to self-supervised training, with the aim of learning representations better suited to identifying individual objects and regions.

The paper identifies an underlying mean-shift clustering process in vision transformers that aligns with image semantics. Building on this observation, FLSL uses a transformer to learn embeddings and clusters jointly. Its two-level clustering objectives draw on mean-shift and k-means perspectives, encouraging features to form semantic groups both within a view and across different views.

Together, these results support the value of aligning the structure of self-supervised learning with the local distinctions required by dense prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: FLSL trains vision transformers to cluster local features, improving self-supervised representations for detection and segmentation.

title: FLSL: Feature-level Self-supervised Learning

abstract: This paper presents an end-to-end neural architecture based on Diffusion Models for spatial puzzle solving, particularly jigsaw puzzle and room arrangement tasks.In the latter task, for instance, the proposed system ``PuzzleFusion'' takes a set of room layouts as polygonal curves in the top-down view and aligns the room layout pieces by estimating their 2D translations and rotations, akin to solving the jigsaw puzzle of room layouts. A surprising discovery of the paper is that the simple use of a Diffusion Model effectively solves these challenging spatial puzzle tasks as a conditional generation process. To enable learning of an end-to-end neural system, the paper introduces new datasets with ground-truth arrangements: 1) 2D Voronoi Jigsaw Dataset, a synthetic one where pieces are generated by voronoi diagram of 2D pointset; and 2) MagicPlan Dataset, a real one from a production pipeline by MagicPlan, where pieces are room layouts constructed by augmented reality App by real-estate consumers.The qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms the competing methods by significant margins in all three spatial puzzle tasks. We have provided code and data in https://sepidsh.github.io/puzzlefusion.

paragraphs: PuzzleFusion treats assembling spatial pieces as a conditional generation problem. Its diffusion-based neural architecture tackles tasks including jigsaw puzzles and room arrangement. For room layouts, the input consists of polygonal curves viewed from above, and the system estimates how each piece should translate and rotate in two dimensions.

The approach learns to generate an arrangement conditioned on the supplied pieces. To support end-to-end learning, the authors introduce two datasets with known correct arrangements. The synthetic 2D Voronoi Jigsaw Dataset derives pieces from Voronoi diagrams. The real MagicPlan Dataset contains room layouts produced through an augmented-reality application used by real-estate consumers.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations show significant improvements over competing methods across all three spatial puzzle tasks examined. The authors emphasize that a straightforward use of diffusion models proves effective for these challenging arrangement problems. The result broadens the demonstrated use of diffusion: here, generation determines the positions and orientations of given pieces, providing a learned route to solving spatial assembly tasks.
summary.tldr: PuzzleFusion uses conditional diffusion to arrange spatial pieces, significantly outperforming competing methods across the three evaluated puzzle tasks.

title: Puzzlefusion: Unleashing the Power of Diffusion Models for Spatial Puzzle Solving

abstract: Neurons in early sensory areas rapidly adapt to changing sensory statistics, both by normalizing the variance of their individual responses and by reducing correlations between their responses. Together, these transformations may be viewed as an adaptive form of statistical whitening. Existing mechanistic models of adaptive whitening exclusively use either synaptic plasticity or gain modulation as the biological substrate for adaptation; however, on their own, each of these models has significant limitations. In this work, we unify these approaches in a normative multi-timescale mechanistic model that adaptively whitens its responses with complementary computational roles for synaptic plasticity and gain modulation. Gains are modified on a fast timescale to adapt to the current statistical context, whereas synapses are modified on a slow timescale to match structural properties of the input statistics that are invariant across contexts. Our model is derived from a novel multi-timescale whitening objective that factorizes the inverse whitening matrix into basis vectors, which correspond to synaptic weights, and a diagonal matrix, which corresponds to neuronal gains. We test our model on synthetic and natural datasets and find that the synapses learn optimal configurations over long timescales that enable adaptive whitening on short timescales using gain modulation.

paragraphs: Early sensory neurons adapt when the statistics of their inputs change. They adjust the variability of individual responses and reduce correlations between neurons. Together, these operations resemble statistical whitening. The paper asks how a mechanistic model can accomplish this adaptation using both changing synaptic connections and changing neuronal gains.

The proposed model assigns these mechanisms complementary timescales. Synapses change slowly, learning structural properties shared across statistical contexts. Gains change quickly, adapting responses to the current context. The authors derive this division from a whitening objective that separates an inverse whitening matrix into basis vectors associated with synaptic weights and a diagonal component associated with neuronal gains.

Tests on synthetic and natural datasets show that the synapses learn optimal configurations over longer timescales, enabling rapid whitening through gain changes. The result offers a unified computational account of how slow learning can prepare a sensory system for fast adaptation. It establishes this behavior in the proposed model rather than directly demonstrating that biological neurons implement the same objective.
summary.tldr: A sensory adaptation model combines slow synaptic learning with fast gain changes to whiten responses across changing statistical contexts.

title: Adaptive whitening with fast gain modulation and slow synaptic plasticity

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a privacy-constrained decentralized machine learning paradigm in which clients enable collaborative training without compromising private data. However, how to learn a robust global model in the data-heterogeneous and model-heterogeneous FL scenarios is challenging. To address it, we resort to data-free knowledge distillation to propose a new FL method (namely DFRD).DFRD equips a conditional generator on the server to approximate the training space of the local models uploaded by clients, and systematically investigates its training in terms of fidelity, transferability and diversity. To overcome the catastrophic forgetting of the global model caused by the distribution shifts of the generator across communication rounds, we maintain an exponential moving average copy of the generator on the server. Additionally, we propose dynamic weighting and label sampling to accurately extract knowledge from local models. Finally, our extensive experiments on various image classification tasks illustrate that DFRD achieves significant performance gains compared to SOTA baselines.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines knowledge from clients while keeping their training data private. Building a strong global model becomes harder when clients differ in both their data distributions and model designs. DFRD addresses these two forms of heterogeneity through data-free knowledge distillation, transferring information from uploaded local models without requiring their original training examples.

A conditional generator on the server approximates the training space of those local models. The paper studies its training in terms of fidelity, transferability, and diversity. It also introduces dynamic weighting and label sampling to improve knowledge extraction, making the way local models contribute an explicit part of the distillation process.

The generator's distribution can shift between communication rounds, causing the global model to forget previously learned information. DFRD maintains an exponentially averaged copy of the generator to address that instability. Experiments across image-classification tasks report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the combined approach of synthetic data generation, more stable distillation, and adaptive extraction of client knowledge.
summary.tldr: DFRD combines server-generated data, generator averaging, and adaptive distillation to improve federated learning with heterogeneous clients.

title: DFRD: Data-Free Robustness Distillation for Heterogeneous Federated Learning

abstract: The study of robustness has received much attention due to its inevitability in data-driven settings where many systems face uncertainty. One such example of concern is Bayesian Optimization (BO), where uncertainty is multi-faceted, yet there only exists a limited number of works dedicated to this direction. In particular, there is the work of Kirschner et al., which bridges the existing literature of Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) by casting the BO problem from the lens of DRO. While this work is pioneering, it admittedly suffers from various practical shortcomings such as finite contexts assumptions, leaving behind the main question \textit{Can one devise a computationally tractable algorithm for solving this DRO-BO problem}? In this work, we tackle this question to a large degree of generality by considering robustness against data-shift in $\varphi$-divergences, which subsumes many popular choices, such as the $\chi^2$-divergence, Total Variation, and the extant Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. We show that the DRO-BO problem in this setting is equivalent to a finite-dimensional optimization problem which, even in the continuous context setting, can be easily implemented with provable sublinear regret bounds. We then show experimentally that our method surpasses existing methods, attesting to the theoretical results.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization must make decisions under uncertainty, including uncertainty about whether the data distribution will change. Distributionally robust optimization addresses this by accounting for alternative distributions. Earlier work connected these ideas, but practical obstacles remained, including assumptions that contextual variables take only finitely many values. This paper seeks a computationally tractable formulation that also accommodates continuous contexts.

The authors describe distribution shifts using phi-divergences, a family that includes chi-squared divergence, total variation, and Kullback-Leibler divergence. This provides a common treatment of several ways to specify distributional uncertainty. The key result shows that the resulting robust Bayesian optimization problem is equivalent to a finite-dimensional optimization problem, even when the context itself is continuous.

That equivalence makes the method implementable without requiring a finite context set. The authors also prove sublinear regret bounds, providing a formal guarantee on how accumulated decision loss grows. Experiments report improvements over existing methods. The contribution therefore pairs a broader mathematical treatment of distribution shift with a tractable algorithm and both theoretical and empirical support.
summary.tldr: A finite-dimensional reformulation makes distributionally robust Bayesian optimization tractable across phi-divergences, including with continuous contexts.

title: Distributionally Robust Bayesian Optimization with $\varphi$-divergences

abstract: Gradual Domain Adaptation (GDA), in which the learner is provided with additional intermediate domains, has been theoretically and empirically studied in many contexts. Despite its vital role in security-critical scenarios, the adversarial robustness of the GDA model remains unexplored. In this paper, we adopt the effective gradual self-training method and replace vanilla self-training with adversarial self-training (AST). AST first predicts labels on the unlabeled data and then adversarially trains the model on the pseudo-labeled distribution. Intriguingly, we find that gradual AST improves not only adversarial accuracy but also clean accuracy on the target domain. We reveal that this is because adversarial training (AT) performs better than standard training when the pseudo-labels contain a portion of incorrect labels. Accordingly, we first present the generalization error bounds for gradual AST in a multiclass classification setting. We then use the optimal value of the Subset Sum Problem to bridge the standard error on a real distribution and the adversarial error on a pseudo-labeled distribution. The result indicates that AT may obtain a tighter bound than standard training on data with incorrect pseudo-labels. We further present an example of a conditional Gaussian distribution to provide more insights into why gradual AST can improve the clean accuracy for GDA.

paragraphs: Gradual domain adaptation uses intermediate datasets to help a model move from its original data distribution to a different target distribution. This paper examines adversarial robustness in that setting. It modifies gradual self-training, where a model supplies labels for unlabeled examples and then learns from those predictions.

The proposed method follows pseudo-labeling with adversarial training on the resulting distribution. The authors find improvements in both adversarial accuracy and accuracy on unmodified target examples. Their explanation centers on mistakes in the predicted labels: adversarial training can handle these imperfect training signals better than standard training in the setting studied.

The theoretical analysis provides generalization bounds for multiclass gradual adaptation. It uses the optimal value of a Subset Sum Problem to relate ordinary error on the true distribution to adversarial error on the pseudo-labeled distribution. The resulting comparison indicates that adversarial training may yield a tighter bound when pseudo-labels are incorrect. A conditional Gaussian example further explains how improved clean accuracy can arise.
summary.tldr: Adversarial self-training improves robustness and clean target accuracy in gradual adaptation, with theory linking the gains to imperfect pseudo-labels.

title: Adversarial Self-Training Improves Robustness and Generalization for Gradual Domain Adaptation

abstract: We present a method for text-driven perpetual view generation -- synthesizing long-term videos of various scenes solely, given an input text prompt describing the scene and camera poses. We introduce a novel framework that generates such videos in an online fashion by combining the generative power of a pre-trained text-to-image model with the geometric priors learned by a pre-trained monocular depth prediction model. To tackle the pivotal challenge of achieving 3D consistency, i.e., synthesizing videos that depict geometrically-plausible scenes, we deploy an online test-time training to encourage the predicted depth map of the current frame to be geometrically consistent with the synthesized scene. The depth maps are used to construct a \emph{unified} mesh representation of the scene, which is progressively constructed along the video generation process. In contrast to previous works, which are applicable only to limited domains, our method generates diverse scenes, such as walkthroughs in spaceships, caves, or ice castles.

paragraphs: SceneScape generates extended videos from a text description of a scene and specified camera poses. The challenge is to make successive views depict a geometrically plausible shared environment. The method combines a pretrained text-to-image generator with geometric information supplied by a pretrained monocular depth predictor.

Generation proceeds online, with the scene developing as the video is produced. At test time, the system trains the depth prediction component to encourage the current frame's depth map to agree with the synthesized scene. The resulting depth maps contribute to a unified mesh that grows progressively throughout generation.

That mesh provides a shared geometric representation for the evolving scene, making consistency across views a central part of the generation process. The authors demonstrate diverse environments, including spaceship interiors, caves, and ice castles, extending beyond the limited domains supported by previous work. The contribution is a combination of image generation, depth adaptation, and accumulating geometry for text-directed scene walkthroughs.
summary.tldr: SceneScape combines text-to-image generation, adaptive depth prediction, and a growing mesh to synthesize geometrically consistent scene videos.

title: SceneScape: Text-Driven Consistent Scene Generation

abstract: Over the last decade, deep neural networks have transformed our society, and they are already widely applied in various machine learning applications. State-of-the-art deep neural networks are becoming larger in size every year to deliver increasing model accuracy, and as a result, model training consumes substantial computing resources and will only consume more in the future.Using current training methods, in each iteration, to process a data point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ in a layer, we need to spend $\Theta(md)$ time to evaluate all the $m$ neurons in the layer. This means processing the entire layer takes $\Theta(nmd)$ time for $n$ data points. Recent work [Song, Yang and Zhang, NeurIPS 2021] reduces this time per iteration to $o(nmd)$, but requires exponential time to preprocess either the data or the neural network weights, making it unlikely to have practical usage. In this work, we present a new preprocessing method that simply stores the weight-data correlation in a tree data structure in order to quickly and dynamically detect which neurons fire at each iteration. Our method requires only $O(nmd)$ time in preprocessing and still achieves $o(nmd)$ time per iteration. We complement our new algorithm with a lower bound, proving that assuming a popular conjecture from complexity theory, one could not substantially speed up our algorithm for dynamic detection of firing neurons.

paragraphs: This paper studies the computational cost of determining which neurons activate during neural-network training. For n data points, m neurons, and d input features, evaluating an entire layer conventionally takes time proportional to nmd per iteration. Earlier work reduced the iteration cost below that order, but required exponential preprocessing of the data or weights.

The proposed method stores correlations between weights and data in a tree structure. This structure supports quickly detecting active neurons as training changes the weights. Its preprocessing takes O(nmd) time, while each subsequent iteration still takes o(nmd) time. The contribution therefore removes the exponential setup cost while retaining the stated asymptotic improvement in repeated training work.

The authors also establish a conditional lower bound for dynamically identifying firing neurons. Assuming a conjecture from complexity theory, their algorithm cannot be substantially accelerated for that task. This result places the speedup in a theoretical context: the method improves preprocessing costs, and its dynamic detection component is close to a computational barrier under the conjecture.
summary.tldr: A tree of weight–data correlations reduces neuron-detection costs during training without the exponential preprocessing required by earlier work.

title: Bypass Exponential Time Preprocessing: Fast Neural Network Training via Weight-Data Correlation Preprocessing

abstract: Modern generative models exhibit unprecedented capabilities to generate extremely realistic data. However, given the inherent compositionality of the real world, reliable use of these models in practical applications requires that they exhibit the capability to compose a novel set of concepts to generate outputs not seen in the training data set. Prior work demonstrates that recent diffusion models do exhibit intriguing compositional generalization abilities, but also fail unpredictably. Motivated by this, we perform a controlled study for understanding compositional generalization in conditional diffusion models in a synthetic setting, varying different attributes of the training data and measuring the model's ability to generate samples out-of-distribution. Our results show: (i) the order in which the ability to generate samples from a concept and compose them emerges is governed by the structure of the underlying data-generating process; (ii) performance on compositional tasks exhibits a sudden "emergence" due to multiplicative reliance on the performance of constituent tasks, partially explaining emergent phenomena seen in generative models; and (iii) composing concepts with lower frequency in the training data to generate out-of-distribution samples requires considerably more optimization steps compared to generating in-distribution samples. Overall, our study lays a foundation for understanding emergent capabilities and compositionality in generative models from a data-centric perspective.

paragraphs: Generating realistic examples does not by itself establish that a model can combine familiar concepts in unfamiliar ways. This paper investigates that compositional ability in conditional diffusion models through a controlled synthetic task. The researchers vary properties of the training data and measure generation of combinations outside the training distribution.

Their findings connect the order in which individual concepts and their combinations become learnable to the structure of the data-generating process. They also find that success on a combined task depends multiplicatively on success at its constituent tasks. This dependence can produce an apparently sudden improvement in composition, offering a partial explanation for emergent capabilities in generative models.

The study further finds that composing concepts appearing less frequently in training requires substantially more optimization steps than generating examples within the training distribution. Together, these results show how data structure, concept frequency, and training progress shape composition in the studied setting. The synthetic design supports a controlled explanation of these effects, rather than establishing that the same patterns govern every diffusion model.
summary.tldr: A synthetic study links sudden compositional improvements in diffusion models to multiplicative dependence on constituent abilities.

title: Compositional Abilities Emerge Multiplicatively: Exploring Diffusion Models on a Synthetic Task

abstract: Visual question answering (VQA) has traditionally been treated as a single-step task where each question receives the same amount of effort, unlike natural human question-answering strategies. We explore a question decomposition strategy for VQA to overcome this limitation. We probe the ability of recently developed large vision-language models to use human-written decompositions and produce their own decompositions of visual questions, finding they are capable of learning both tasks from demonstrations alone.However, we show that naive application of model-written decompositions can hurt performance.We introduce a model-driven selective decomposition approach for second-guessing predictions and correcting errors, and validate its effectiveness on eight VQA tasks across three domains, showing consistent improvements in accuracy, including improvements of >20% on medical VQA datasets and boosting the zero-shot performance of BLIP-2 above chance on a VQA reformulation of the challenging Winoground task. Project Site: https://zaidkhan.me/decomposition-0shot-vqa/
