paragraphs: Visual question answering often gives every question a single answering step, regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores whether breaking a question into smaller questions can help vision-language models reason about an image. The motivation is to vary the effort devoted to answering rather than treat every question as equally straightforward.

The authors find that large vision-language models can learn from demonstrations both to use human-written decompositions and to generate decompositions themselves. However, applying model-generated decompositions naively can reduce accuracy. They therefore introduce a selective approach in which the model uses decomposition to reconsider predictions and correct errors, making the decision to decompose part of the method.

Evaluation spans eight visual question-answering tasks across three domains and shows consistent accuracy improvements. Reported gains include improvements greater than 20% on medical datasets and raising BLIP-2 above chance on a question-answering version of Winoground. The findings support selective decomposition as a useful correction strategy, while the negative result for naive decomposition shows why generating subquestions alone is insufficient.
summary.tldr: Selectively decomposing visual questions helps models reconsider errors and improves accuracy, while indiscriminate decomposition can hurt performance.

title: Exploring Question Decomposition for Zero-Shot VQA

abstract: In this paper, we provide the first efficient batched algorithm for contextual linear bandits with large action spaces. Unlike existing batched algorithms that rely on action elimination, which are not implementable for large action sets, our algorithm only uses a linear optimization oracle over the action set to design the policy. The proposed algorithm achieves a regret upper bound $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ with high probability, and uses $O(\log\log T)$ batches, matching the lower bound on the number of batches (Gao et al., 2019). When specialized to linear bandits, our algorithm can achieve a high probability gap-dependent regret bound of $\tilde{O}(1/\Delta_{\min})$ with the optimal $\log T$ number of batches, where $\Delta_{\min}$ is the minimum reward gap between a suboptimal arm and the optimal. Our result is achieved via a novel soft elimination approach, that entails $\text{``}$shaping$\text{"}$ the action sets at each batch so that we can efficiently identify (near) optimal actions.

These are theoretical efficiency guarantees with explicitly probabilistic regret claims.
summary.tldr: Soft elimination enables efficient batched linear-bandit learning over large action sets using only a linear optimization oracle.

title: Efficient Batched Algorithm for Contextual Linear Bandits with Large Action Space via Soft Elimination

abstract: We provide theoretical bounds on the forgetting quantity in the continual learning setting for linear tasks, where each round of learning corresponds to projecting onto a linear subspace. For a cyclic task ordering on $T$ tasks repeated $m$ times each, we prove the best known upper bound of $O(T^2/m)$ on the forgetting. Notably, our bound holds uniformly over all choices of tasks and is independent of the ambient dimension. Our main technical contribution is a characterization of the union of all numerical ranges of products of $T$ (real or complex) projections as a sinusoidal spiral, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper studies forgetting in a mathematical model of continual learning with linear tasks. Each learning step is represented as a projection onto a linear subspace. The tasks occur in a fixed cycle, so the analysis asks how much forgetting remains as the learner repeatedly revisits the same sequence.

For T tasks, each repeated m times, the authors prove an upper bound of O(T²/m) on the forgetting quantity. They describe this as the best known upper bound. It holds uniformly across all choices of tasks in the stated setting and does not depend on the dimension of the surrounding space. The bound decreases with more repetitions and grows quadratically with the number of tasks.

The main mathematical ingredient characterizes the combined numerical ranges of products of T projections as a sinusoidal spiral, covering real and complex projections. That geometric result enables the forgetting analysis and may also have independent mathematical value. The learning guarantee specifically concerns cyclic projection-based linear tasks, providing a precise setting in which repeated revisiting can be analyzed.
summary.tldr: For cyclic learning of linear tasks, the paper proves a dimension-independent forgetting bound of O(T²/m).

title: Nearly Optimal Bounds for Cyclic Forgetting

abstract: There are a number of diverging hypotheses about the neural text degeneration problem, i.e., generating repetitive and dull loops, which makes this problem both interesting and confusing. In this work, we aim to advance our understanding by presenting a straightforward and fundamental explanation from the data perspective. Our preliminary investigation reveals a strong correlation between the degeneration issue and the presence of repetitions in training data. Subsequent experiments also demonstrate that by selectively dropping out the attention to repetitive words in training data, degeneration can be significantly minimized. Furthermore, our empirical analysis illustrates that prior works addressing the degeneration issue from various standpoints, such as the high-inflow words, the likelihood objective, and the self-reinforcement phenomenon, can be interpreted by one simple explanation. That is, penalizing the repetitions in training data is a common and fundamental factor for their effectiveness. Moreover, our experiments reveal that penalizing the repetitions in training data remains critical even when considering larger model sizes and instruction tuning.

paragraphs: Language models sometimes fall into repetitive, uninformative loops. This paper examines that behavior from the perspective of training data, offering a common explanation for several previously proposed accounts. Its preliminary investigation finds a strong correlation between repeated material in the training data and repetition during generation.

The researchers then intervene during training by selectively dropping attention to repetitive words. Their experiments show that this can substantially reduce degeneration. This gives the data-centered explanation support beyond the initial correlation: changing how the model learns from repeated words changes the unwanted generation behavior.

The paper also empirically reexamines earlier approaches involving high-inflow words, the likelihood objective, and self-reinforcement. It argues that penalizing training-data repetition is a shared factor behind their effectiveness. Additional experiments find that such penalties remain important with larger models and instruction tuning. The findings position repetition in training as a useful target for intervention and a unifying interpretation of existing remedies, without establishing it as the only possible cause of degeneration.
summary.tldr: Experiments link repetitive generation to training-data repetition and show that reducing attention to repeated words can substantially mitigate it.

title: Repetition In Repetition Out: Towards Understanding Neural Text Degeneration from the Data Perspective

abstract: Despite its practical importance across a wide range of modalities, recent advances in self-supervised learning (SSL) have been primarily focused on a few well-curated domains, e.g., vision and language, often relying on their domain-specific knowledge. For example, Masked Auto-Encoder (MAE) has become one of the popular architectures in these domains, but less has explored its potential in other modalities. In this paper, we develop MAE as a unified, modality-agnostic SSL framework. In turn, we argue meta-learning as a key to interpreting MAE as a modality-agnostic learner, and propose enhancements to MAE from the motivation to jointly improve its SSL across diverse modalities, coined MetaMAE as a result. Our key idea is to view the mask reconstruction of MAE as a meta-learning task: masked tokens are predicted by adapting the Transformer meta-learner through the amortization of unmasked tokens. Based on this novel interpretation, we propose to integrate two advanced meta-learning techniques. First, we adapt the amortized latent of the Transformer encoder using gradient-based meta-learning to enhance the reconstruction. Then, we maximize the alignment between amortized and adapted latents through task contrastive learning which guides the Transformer encoder to better encode the task-specific knowledge. Our experiment demonstrates the superiority of MetaMAE in the modality-agnostic SSL benchmark (called DABS), significantly outperforming prior baselines.

paragraphs: Masked auto-encoders learn by reconstructing hidden parts of an input from the parts that remain visible. This paper develops that idea into a self-supervised framework intended to work across diverse modalities. Its motivation is that much self-supervised learning progress has concentrated on a few domains and often depends on domain-specific knowledge.

MetaMAE interprets each reconstruction problem as a meta-learning task. The visible tokens provide information that adapts a Transformer-based learner to predict the missing tokens. Building on this interpretation, the method uses gradient-based meta-learning to adapt the encoder’s amortized latent representation and improve reconstruction. Task contrastive learning then aligns the original and adapted latent representations.

That alignment is intended to teach the encoder to represent task-specific information more effectively, connecting its initial representation to one refined through adaptation. The authors evaluate MetaMAE on DABS, a modality-agnostic self-supervised learning benchmark, and report significant improvements over prior baselines. The contribution is both a reinterpretation of masked reconstruction and a concrete method derived from it, with the benchmark results supporting its use across the evaluated modalities.
summary.tldr: MetaMAE treats masked reconstruction as meta-learning and aligns adapted representations to improve self-supervised learning across modalities.

title: Modality-Agnostic Self-Supervised Learning with Meta-Learned Masked Auto-Encoder

abstract: Algorithmic decision-making in high-stakes domains often involves assigning decisions to agents with incentives to strategically modify their input to the algorithm. In addition to dealing with incentives, in many domains of interest (e.g. lending and hiring) the decision-maker only observes feedback regarding their policy for rounds in which they assign a positive decision to the agent; this type of feedback is often referred to as apple tasting (or one-sided) feedback. We formalize this setting as an online learning problem with apple-tasting feedback where a principal makes decisions about a sequence of $T$ agents, each of which is represented by a context that may be strategically modified. Our goal is to achieve sublinear strategic regret, which compares the performance of the principal to that of the best fixed policy in hindsight, if the agents were truthful when revealing their contexts. Our main result is a learning algorithm which incurs $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ strategic regret when the sequence of agents is chosen stochastically. We also give an algorithm capable of handling adversarially-chosen agents, albeit at the cost of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$ strategic regret (where $d$ is the dimension of the context). Our algorithms can be easily adapted to the setting where the principal receives bandit feedback---this setting generalizes both the linear contextual bandit problem (by considering agents with incentives) and the strategic classification problem (by allowing for partial feedback).

paragraphs: In decisions such as lending or hiring, applicants may modify the information presented to an algorithm to obtain a favorable outcome. Meanwhile, the decision-maker may observe feedback only after a positive decision. This paper combines those two difficulties in an online learning model: strategic inputs and one-sided feedback, also called apple-tasting feedback.

The performance target is strategic regret, measured against the best fixed policy in hindsight if agents had reported their contexts truthfully. When agents arrive stochastically, the authors give an algorithm with regret scaling as the square root of the number of rounds, up to logarithmic factors. This provides sublinear growth despite both strategic behavior and incomplete feedback.

For adversarially chosen agents, another algorithm achieves regret scaling as T^((d+1)/(d+2)), again up to logarithmic factors, where d is context dimension. This weaker rate makes the role of dimension explicit. The algorithms also adapt to bandit feedback, linking incentive-aware decision-making with learning settings where only limited feedback about chosen actions is available.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sublinear strategic regret guarantees for online decisions with manipulable inputs and feedback available only after positive decisions.

title: Strategic Apple Tasting

abstract: This paper presents a new gradient flow dissipation geometry over non-negative and probability measures.This is motivated by a principled construction that combines the unbalanced optimal transport and interaction forces modeled by reproducing kernels. Using a precise connection between the Hellinger geometry and the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), we propose the interaction-force transport (IFT) gradient flows and its spherical variant via an infimal convolution of the Wasserstein and spherical MMD tensors. We then develop a particle-based optimization algorithm based on the JKO-splitting scheme of the mass-preserving spherical IFT gradient flows. Finally, we provide both theoretical global exponential convergence guarantees and improved empirical simulation results for applying the IFT gradient flows to the sampling task of MMD-minimization. Furthermore, we prove that the spherical IFT gradient flow enjoys the best of both worlds by providing the global exponential convergence guarantee for both the MMD and KL energy.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization in which the evolving object is a distribution or a non-negative measure. Its contribution is a new geometry describing how such objects move toward lower objective values. The construction combines unbalanced optimal transport with interaction forces represented by reproducing kernels.

The authors use a precise relationship between Hellinger geometry and maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, to define interaction-force transport gradient flows. They also introduce a spherical variant that preserves mass. The construction combines Wasserstein and spherical MMD tensors through infimal convolution, bringing transport and kernel interactions into a shared mathematical framework.

For computation, the paper develops a particle-based algorithm using JKO splitting of the spherical flow. Applied to sampling through MMD minimization, the framework comes with global exponential convergence guarantees and improved empirical simulations. The authors further prove global exponential convergence for the spherical flow with both MMD and KL energies. This extends the theoretical appeal of the geometry across two distinct objectives for comparing distributions.
summary.tldr: Interaction-force transport combines transport geometry and kernel interactions, yielding particle algorithms and global exponential convergence guarantees for distribution optimization.

title: Interaction-Force Transport Gradient Flows

abstract: While the field of 3D scene reconstruction is dominated by NeRFs due to their photorealistic quality, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently emerged, offering similar quality with real-time rendering speeds. However, both methods primarily excel with well-controlled 3D scenes, while in-the-wild data - characterized by occlusions, dynamic objects, and varying illumination - remains challenging. NeRFs can adapt to such conditions easily through per-image embedding vectors, but 3DGS struggles due to its explicit representation and lack of shared parameters. To address this, we introduce WildGaussians, a novel approach to handle occlusions and appearance changes with 3DGS. By leveraging robust DINO features and integrating an appearance modeling module within 3DGS, our method achieves state-of-the-art results. We demonstrate that WildGaussians matches the real-time rendering speed of 3DGS while surpassing both 3DGS and NeRF baselines in handling in-the-wild data, all within a simple architectural framework.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a 3D scene from uncontrolled images is difficult when objects obscure the scene, things move, or illumination changes. Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting offers photorealistic quality and real-time rendering, but its explicit representation struggles with these variations. The paper contrasts this with NeRFs, which can accommodate such conditions using per-image embedding vectors.

WildGaussians adapts Gaussian splatting to handle occlusions and changes in appearance. It combines robust DINO features with an appearance-modeling module integrated into the Gaussian-splatting framework. These components address the mismatch between a shared scene representation and images that show different visibility or lighting conditions. The authors describe the resulting architecture as simple.

The reported evaluations show state-of-the-art results on in-the-wild data, surpassing both Gaussian-splatting and NeRF baselines in handling those conditions. WildGaussians also matches the real-time rendering speed of Gaussian splatting. The central result is therefore a combination of improved reconstruction under uncontrolled capture conditions and retention of the fast rendering that makes this representation attractive in the first place.
summary.tldr: WildGaussians improves reconstruction from uncontrolled images while retaining the real-time rendering speed of 3D Gaussian splatting.

title: WildGaussians: 3D Gaussian Splatting In the Wild

abstract: Extracting scientific understanding from particle-physics experiments requires solving diverse learning problems with high precision and good data efficiency. We propose the Lorentz Geometric Algebra Transformer (L-GATr), a new multi-purpose architecture for high-energy physics. L-GATr represents high-energy data in a geometric algebra over four-dimensional space-time and is equivariant under Lorentz transformations, the symmetry group of relativistic kinematics. At the same time, the architecture is a Transformer, which makes it versatile and scalable to large systems. L-GATr is first demonstrated on regression and classification tasks from particle physics. We then construct the first Lorentz-equivariant generative model: a continuous normalizing flow based on an L-GATr network, trained with Riemannian flow matching. Across our experiments, L-GATr is on par with or outperforms strong domain-specific baselines.

paragraphs: Particle-physics learning problems demand precision and efficient use of data across several different tasks. L-GATr is designed as a shared architectural approach for this setting. It combines a Transformer with a representation of high-energy data in geometric algebra over four-dimensional space-time.

The architecture is Lorentz-equivariant, meaning its behavior respects the transformations associated with relativistic kinematics. This embeds a relevant physical symmetry into the model. At the same time, retaining the Transformer structure supports versatility and scalability to large systems, allowing the architecture to serve more than one narrowly defined physics task.

The authors first demonstrate L-GATr on regression and classification. They then use it to construct what they describe as the first Lorentz-equivariant generative model: a continuous normalizing flow trained with Riemannian flow matching. Across the reported experiments, the method matches or exceeds strong domain-specific baselines. These findings support combining physical symmetry with a broadly usable architecture, extending the same foundation from prediction tasks to generation without claiming an advantage on every individual comparison.
summary.tldr: L-GATr combines Lorentz symmetry with Transformers for particle-physics prediction and generation, matching or outperforming strong specialized baselines in the reported experiments.

title: Lorentz-Equivariant Geometric Algebra Transformers for High-Energy Physics

abstract: Neural network sparsification is a promising avenue to save computational time and memory costs, especially in an age where many successful AI models are becoming too large to naively deploy on consumer hardware. While much work has focused on different weight pruning criteria, the overall sparsifiability of the network, i.e., its capacity to be pruned without quality loss, has often been overlooked. We present Sparsifiability via the Marginal likelihood (SpaM), a sparsification framework that highlights the effectiveness of using the Bayesian marginal likelihood in conjunction with sparsity-inducing priors for making neural networks more sparsifiable. Our approach implements an automatic Occam's razor that selects the most sparsifiable model that still explains the data well, both for structured and unstructured sparsification. In addition, we demonstrate that the pre-computed posterior precision from the Laplace approximation can be re-used to define a cheap pruning criterion, which outperforms many existing (more expensive) approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, especially at high sparsity levels, across a range of different neural network architectures and datasets.

paragraphs: SpaM focuses on how much a neural network can be pruned without losing quality. Many pruning methods concentrate on deciding which weights to remove, while the paper emphasizes making the network itself more amenable to removal. This matters because sparsification offers a route to lower memory use and computational cost.

The framework combines Bayesian marginal likelihood with priors that encourage sparsity. Its model-selection principle balances explaining the data well with favoring a model that can be made sparse. The authors describe this as an automatic Occam's razor and apply it to both structured and unstructured sparsification.

SpaM also reuses posterior precision already computed through a Laplace approximation to construct an inexpensive pruning criterion. The authors report that this criterion outperforms many more expensive alternatives, and demonstrate the framework across multiple architectures and datasets, particularly at high sparsity. The results connect two decisions often treated separately: selecting a model that tolerates pruning and identifying what can be removed from that model.
summary.tldr: SpaM uses Bayesian model selection to encourage prunable networks and reuses posterior information for inexpensive pruning.

title: Shaving Weights with Occam's Razor: Bayesian Sparsification for Neural Networks using the Marginal Likelihood

abstract: Autoregressive language models have achieved remarkable advancements, yet their potential is often limited by the slow inference speeds associated with sequential token generation. Blockwise parallel decoding (BPD) was proposed by Stern et al. [42] as a method to improve inference speed of language models by simultaneously predicting multiple future tokens, termed block drafts, which are subsequently verified by the autoregressive model. This paper advances the understanding and improvement of block drafts in two ways. First, we analyze token distributions generated across multiple prediction heads. Second, leveraging these insights, we propose algorithms to improve BPD inference speed by refining the block drafts using task-independent \ngram and neural language models as lightweight rescorers. Experiments demonstrate that by refining block drafts of open-sourced Vicuna and Medusa LLMs, the mean accepted token length are increased by 5-25% relative. This results in over a 3x speedup in wall clock time compared to standard autoregressive decoding in open-source 7B and 13B LLMs.

paragraphs: Language models usually generate text one token at a time, making each new prediction wait for the previous one. Blockwise parallel decoding tries to reduce this delay by proposing several future tokens together. The autoregressive model then checks these proposed blocks, so the usefulness of parallel prediction depends on how much of each draft survives verification.

This paper studies the token distributions produced by the different prediction heads responsible for those drafts. Using that analysis, the authors develop ways to refine proposed blocks before verification. Their refiners use lightweight n-gram and neural language models to rescore drafts, without requiring a separate scoring approach tailored to each task.

In experiments with Vicuna and Medusa, refinement increases the average number of accepted tokens by 5–25% relative to the unrefined drafts. The resulting decoding achieves more than a threefold wall-clock speedup over standard autoregressive generation in the evaluated 7B and 13B models. The practical contribution is improving the productivity of each verification step by making parallel drafts more acceptable.
summary.tldr: Lightweight draft refinement improves blockwise parallel decoding, enabling over threefold generation speedups in the evaluated language models.

title: Accelerating Blockwise Parallel Language Models with Draft Refinement

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have revolutionized artificial intelligence, achieving impressive results on diverse data types, including images, videos, and texts. However, DNNs still lag behind Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT) on tabular data, a format extensively utilized across various domains. This paper introduces DOFEN, which stands for Deep Oblivious Forest ENsemble. DOFEN is a novel DNN architecture inspired by oblivious decision trees and achieves on-off sparse selection of columns. DOFEN surpasses other DNNs on tabular data, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the well-recognized benchmark: Tabular Benchmark, which includes 73 total datasets spanning a wide array of domains. The code of DOFEN is available at: https://github.com/Sinopac-Digital-Technology-Division/DOFEN

paragraphs: Deep neural networks perform strongly on images, video, and text, yet tabular data remains a setting where gradient boosting decision trees often have an advantage. This paper addresses that gap through architecture design. It introduces DOFEN, a neural network inspired by oblivious decision trees and organized as a deep forest ensemble.

The central property highlighted by the authors is on-off sparse selection of columns. For tabular inputs, columns represent the information available to the model, so selecting them is a direct way to control which inputs participate in its computation. DOFEN brings this tree-inspired selection behavior into a neural architecture, connecting a strength of tabular modeling with deep learning.

The authors evaluate DOFEN on Tabular Benchmark, which contains 73 datasets across many domains. They report that it surpasses other neural networks and achieves state-of-the-art performance on that benchmark. The clearly stated comparison establishes a strong neural approach to tabular prediction; the motivation involving gradient boosting should be kept distinct from the explicit finding about outperforming other neural networks.
summary.tldr: DOFEN uses tree-inspired sparse column selection to achieve leading neural-network performance on a benchmark of 73 tabular datasets.

title: DOFEN: Deep Oblivious Forest ENsemble

abstract: Segment Anything Model (SAM) has recently gained much attention for its outstanding generalization to unseen data and tasks. Despite its promising prospect, the vulnerabilities of SAM, especially to universal adversarial perturbation (UAP) have not been thoroughly investigated yet. In this paper, we propose DarkSAM, the first prompt-free universal attack framework against SAM, including a semantic decoupling-based spatial attack and a texture distortion-based frequency attack. We first divide the output of SAM into foreground and background. Then, we design a shadow target strategy to obtain the semantic blueprint of the image as the attack target. DarkSAM is dedicated to fooling SAM by extracting and destroying crucial object features from images in both spatial and frequency domains. In the spatial domain, we disrupt the semantics of both the foreground and background in the image to confuse SAM. In the frequency domain, we further enhance the attack effectiveness by distorting the high-frequency components (i.e., texture information) of the image. Consequently, with a single UAP, DarkSAM renders SAM incapable of segmenting objects across diverse images with varying prompts. Experimental results on four datasets for SAM and its two variant models demonstrate the powerful attack capability and transferability of DarkSAM. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/CGCL-codes/DarkSAM.

title: DarkSAM: Fooling Segment Anything Model to Segment Nothing

abstract: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) is a large-scale foundation model that has revolutionized segmentation methodology. Despite its impressive generalization ability, the segmentation accuracy of SAM on images with intricate structures is often unsatisfactory. Recent works have proposed lightweight fine-tuning using high-quality annotated data to improve accuracy on such images. However, here we provide extensive empirical evidence that this strategy leads to forgetting how to "segment anything": these models lose the original generalization abilities of SAM, in the sense that they perform worse for segmentation tasks not represented in the annotated fine-tuning set. To improve performance without forgetting, we introduce a novel framework that combines high-quality annotated data with a large unlabeled dataset. The framework relies on two methodological innovations. First, we quantify the uncertainty in the SAM pseudo labels associated with the unlabeled data and leverage it to perform uncertainty-aware fine-tuning. Second, we encode the type of segmentation task associated with each training example using a $\textit{task prompt}$ to reduce ambiguity. We evaluated the proposed Segmentation with Uncertainty Model (SUM) on a diverse test set consisting of 14 public benchmarks, where it achieves state-of-the-art results. Notably, our method consistently surpasses SAM by 3-6 points in mean IoU and 4-7 in mean boundary IoU across point-prompt interactive segmentation rounds. Code is available at https://github.com/Kangningthu/SUM

summary.tldr: SUM combines uncertainty-aware learning from unlabeled images with task prompts to improve SAM segmentation while addressing fine-tuning-induced forgetting.

title: Uncertainty-aware Fine-tuning of Segmentation Foundation Models

abstract: This study presents an Exploratory Retrieval-Augmented Planning (ExRAP) framework, designed to tackle continual instruction following tasks of embodied agents in dynamic, non-stationary environments. The framework enhances Large Language Models' (LLMs) embodied reasoning capabilities by efficiently exploring the physical environment and establishing the environmental context memory, thereby effectively grounding the task planning process in time-varying environment contexts. In ExRAP, given multiple continual instruction following tasks, each instruction is decomposed into queries on the environmental context memory and task executions conditioned on the query results. To efficiently handle these multiple tasks that are performed continuously and simultaneously, we implement an exploration-integrated task planning scheme by incorporating the information-based exploration into the LLM-based planning process. Combined with memory-augmented query evaluation, this integrated scheme not only allows for a better balance between the validity of the environmental context memory and the load of environment exploration, but also improves overall task performance. Furthermore, we devise a temporal consistency refinement scheme for query evaluation to address the inherent decay of knowledge in the memory. Through experiments with VirtualHome, ALFRED, and CARLA, our approach demonstrates robustness against a variety of embodied instruction following scenarios involving different instruction scales and types, and non-stationarity degrees, and it consistently outperforms other state-of-the-art LLM-based task planning approaches in terms of both goal success rate and execution efficiency.

paragraphs: ExRAP helps embodied agents follow ongoing instructions in environments that change over time. A planner needs information about its surroundings, but previously observed facts can become outdated. Exploring constantly also consumes effort. The framework combines environmental memory, retrieval, and exploration so that language-model planning can respond to the current context.

Each instruction becomes a set of queries to environmental memory and actions conditioned on the answers. Exploration is integrated into planning through an information-based scheme, helping the agent balance obtaining fresh information against the burden of investigating its environment. Memory-assisted query evaluation supports multiple tasks performed continually and simultaneously. A temporal consistency refinement further addresses the decay of stored knowledge.

Experiments in VirtualHome, ALFRED, and CARLA cover different instruction types, task scales, and degrees of environmental change. ExRAP consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art language-model planners in goal success and execution efficiency. These findings support the value of managing the freshness of environmental knowledge as part of planning, especially when several instructions must be carried out in changing surroundings.
summary.tldr: ExRAP combines memory retrieval and planned exploration to help embodied agents complete ongoing tasks in changing environments.

title: Exploratory Retrieval-Augmented Planning For Continual Embodied Instruction Following

abstract: We study offline multitask representation learning in reinforcement learning (RL), where a learner is provided with an offline dataset from different tasks that share a common representation and is asked to learn the shared representation. We theoretically investigate offline multitask low-rank RL, and propose a new algorithm called MORL for offline multitask representation learning. Furthermore, we examine downstream RL in reward-free, offline and online scenarios, where a new task is introduced to the agent that shares the same representation as the upstream offline tasks. Our theoretical results demonstrate the benefits of using the learned representation from the upstream offline task instead of directly learning the representation of the low-rank model.

paragraphs: The paper studies how an agent can learn a reusable representation from offline data collected across several reinforcement learning tasks. Its central assumption is that these tasks share a common representation. The learner's goal is to recover that shared structure from existing datasets so it can support learning on a subsequent task.

The authors analyze this question in the setting of low-rank reinforcement learning and introduce MORL, an algorithm for offline multitask representation learning. The upstream stage focuses on learning the representation across tasks. The downstream stage introduces a new task that shares the same representation, making this common structure the basis for transfer.

The theoretical investigation covers downstream reward-free, offline, and online scenarios. Its results demonstrate benefits from reusing the upstream representation compared with directly learning the low-rank model's representation for the new task. This establishes a theoretical reason to combine offline experience across related tasks. The shared-representation assumption is essential to the setting in which the transfer benefits are studied.
summary.tldr: MORL learns a shared representation from offline tasks, with theoretical benefits for new tasks that share that representation.

title: Offline Multitask Representation Learning for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: How (dis)similar are the learning trajectories of vision–language models and children? Recent modeling work has attempted to understand the gap between models’ and humans’ data efficiency by constructing models trained on less data, especially multimodal naturalistic data. However, such models are often evaluated on adult-level benchmarks, with limited breadth in language abilities tested, and without direct comparison to behavioral data. We introduce DevBench, a multimodal benchmark comprising seven language evaluation tasks spanning the domains of lexical, syntactic, and semantic ability, with behavioral data from both children and adults. We evaluate a set of vision–language models on these tasks, comparing models and humans on their response patterns, not their absolute performance. Across tasks, models exhibit variation in their closeness to human response patterns, and models that perform better on a task also more closely resemble human behavioral responses. We also examine the developmental trajectory of OpenCLIP over training, finding that greater training results in closer approximations to adult response patterns. DevBench thus provides a benchmark for comparing models to human language development. These comparisons highlight ways in which model and human language learning processes diverge, providing insight into entry points for improving language models.

Those evaluations can cover a narrow set of abilities and lack direct comparisons with how children and adults actually respond.

Its comparisons focus on response patterns rather than absolute performance. summary.tldr: DevBench compares vision–language models with children and adults across seven language tasks using their patterns of responses.

title: DevBench: A multimodal developmental benchmark for language learning

abstract: We study the problem of training diffusion models to sample from a distribution with a given unnormalized density or energy function. We benchmark several diffusion-structured inference methods, including simulation-based variational approaches and off-policy methods (continuous generative flow networks). Our results shed light on the relative advantages of existing algorithms while bringing into question some claims from past work. We also propose a novel exploration strategy for off-policy methods, based on local search in the target space with the use of a replay buffer, and show that it improves the quality of samples on a variety of target distributions. Our code for the sampling methods and benchmarks studied is made public at [this link](https://github.com/GFNOrg/gfn-diffusion) as a base for future work on diffusion models for amortized inference.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to train diffusion models to sample from a target distribution specified by an unnormalized density or an energy function. The target is therefore described through a function assigning relative weights to possible outcomes. The goal is to learn a sampler that produces useful draws from that distribution.

The authors benchmark several inference methods built around diffusion processes. These include simulation-based variational approaches and off-policy approaches based on continuous generative flow networks. The comparisons clarify relative strengths of existing algorithms and challenge some earlier claims, making the benchmark itself part of the contribution.

The paper also introduces an exploration strategy for off-policy training that combines local search in the target space with a replay buffer. This pairs searching for useful target-space samples with retaining experience for subsequent training. Across a variety of target distributions, the strategy improves sample quality. The released methods and benchmarks provide a basis for further work on learned diffusion samplers for amortized inference.
summary.tldr: A benchmark of diffusion samplers identifies algorithmic tradeoffs, while local search with replay improves off-policy sample quality.

title: Improved off-policy training of diffusion samplers

abstract: Benchmark datasets in computer vision often contain off-topic images, near duplicates, and label errors, leading to inaccurate estimates of model performance.In this paper, we revisit the task of data cleaning and formalize it as either a ranking problem, which significantly reduces human inspection effort, or a scoring problem, which allows for automated decisions based on score distributions.We find that a specific combination of context-aware self-supervised representation learning and distance-based indicators is effective in finding issues without annotation biases.This methodology, which we call SelfClean, surpasses state-of-the-art performance in detecting off-topic images, near duplicates, and label errors within widely-used image datasets, such as ImageNet-1k, Food-101N, and STL-10, both for synthetic issues and real contamination.We apply the detailed method to multiple image benchmarks, identify up to 16% of issues, and confirm an improvement in evaluation reliability upon cleaning.The official implementation can be found at: https://github.com/Digital-Dermatology/SelfClean.

paragraphs: SelfClean addresses errors inside image benchmarks that can distort estimates of model performance. The paper considers three kinds of problems: images unrelated to the dataset's subject, near-duplicate examples, and incorrect labels. It frames cleaning as a systematic auditing task, with outputs suited to either human review or automated decisions.

In the ranking formulation, suspicious examples are ordered so that people can concentrate their inspection effort. In the scoring formulation, decisions can be made from the distribution of issue scores. Both rely on a combination of context-aware, self-supervised representations and distance-based indicators, which the authors find effective for identifying problems without annotation biases.

The method exceeds prior detection performance on benchmarks including ImageNet-1k, Food-101N, and STL-10, covering both deliberately introduced issues and existing contamination. Across the audited benchmarks, the authors identify issue levels reaching 16% and confirm more reliable evaluation after cleaning. The contribution therefore connects finding problematic examples with improving the trustworthiness of the benchmark measurements themselves.
summary.tldr: SelfClean uses self-supervised representations and distance-based indicators to find image dataset issues and improve evaluation reliability.

title: Intrinsic Self-Supervision for Data Quality Audits

abstract: LiDAR data exhibits significant domain gaps due to variations in sensors, vehicles, and driving environments, creating “language barriers” that limit the effective use of data across domains and the scalability of LiDAR perception models. To address these challenges, we introduce the LiDAR Translator (LiT), a framework that directly translates LiDAR data across domains, enabling both cross-domain adaptation and multi-domain joint learning. LiT integrates three key components: a scene modeling module for precise foreground and background reconstruction, a LiDAR modeling module that models LiDAR rays statistically and simulates ray-drop, and a fast, hardware-accelerated ray casting engine. LiT enables state-of-the-art zero-shot and unified domain detection across diverse LiDAR datasets, marking a step toward data-driven domain unification for autonomous driving systems. Source code and demos are available at: https://yxlao.github.io/lit.

paragraphs: LiDAR measurements differ across sensors, vehicles, and driving environments. Those differences make it difficult to reuse data or perception models across datasets. LiDAR Translator, or LiT, tackles this by translating the data between domains, supporting both adaptation to another domain and joint learning from several domains.

The framework combines scene reconstruction with sensor modeling. One module reconstructs foreground objects and background structure. Another statistically models LiDAR rays and simulates ray-drop, accounting for measurements that are absent from the observed scan. A hardware-accelerated ray-casting engine makes the translation process fast. Together, these components address both the scene being measured and the way a sensor samples it.

The authors report state-of-the-art zero-shot and unified-domain detection across diverse LiDAR datasets. These results support direct data translation as a route toward sharing information across otherwise mismatched domains. The contribution is a framework that connects scene geometry, sensor behavior, and efficient simulation to improve the use of heterogeneous LiDAR data for autonomous-driving perception.
summary.tldr: LiT translates LiDAR data across domains using scene reconstruction and sensor simulation, improving cross-domain and unified detection.

title: LiT: Unifying LiDAR "Languages" with LiDAR Translator

abstract: Machine learning craves high-quality data which is a major bottleneck during realistic deployment, as it takes abundant resources and massive human labor to collect and label data. Unfortunately, label noise where image data mismatches with incorrect label exists ubiquitously in all kinds of datasets, significantly degrading the learning performance of deep networks. Learning with Label Noise (LNL) has been a common strategy for mitigating the influence of noisy labels. However, existing LNL methods either require pertaining using the memorization effect to separate clean data from noisy ones or rely on dataset assumptions that cannot extend to various scenarios. Thanks to the development of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) which possess massive knowledge and hold In-Context Learning (ICL) ability, this paper proposes NoiseGPT to effectively leverage MLLMs as a knowledge expert for conducting label noise detection and rectification. Specifically, we observe a \textit{probability curvature} effect of MLLMs where clean and noisy examples reside on curvatures with different smoothness, further enabling the detection of label noise. By designing a token-wise Mix-of-Feature (MoF) technique to produce the curvature, we propose an In-Context Discrepancy (ICD) measure to determine the authenticity of an image-label pair. Subsequently, we repeat such a process to find the best matching pairs to complete our label rectification. Through extensive experiments, we carefully demonstrate the effectiveness of NoiseGPT on detecting and cleansing dataset noise, especially on ILSVRC12, the AUROC of NoiseGPT reached over 0.92. And by integrating with existing methods, the classification performance can be significantly improved on noisy datasets, typically by 22.8\% on 80\% symmetric CIFAR-10 with M-correction. Source code: \url{https://github.com/drunkerWang/NoiseGPT}

paragraphs: NoiseGPT uses a multimodal language model to detect and correct mismatches between images and their labels. The motivation is that incorrect annotations degrade learning, while collecting reliable labels requires substantial resources. The method draws on the model's existing knowledge and in-context learning ability to assess whether an image-label pair is credible.

summary.tldr: NoiseGPT uses multimodal-model probability curvature to detect incorrect image labels and find better matches, improving learning from noisy datasets.

title: NoiseGPT: Label Noise Detection and Rectification through Probability Curvature

abstract: In many machine learning tasks, data is inherently sequential. Most existing algorithms learn from sequential data in an auto-regressive manner, which predicts the next unseen data point based on the observed sequence, implicitly assuming the presence of an \emph{evolving pattern} embedded in the data that can be leveraged. However, identifying and assessing evolving patterns in learning tasks often relies on subjective judgments rooted in the prior knowledge of human experts, lacking a standardized quantitative measure. Furthermore, such measures enable us to determine the suitability of employing sequential models effectively and make informed decisions on the temporal order of time series data, and feature/data selection processes. To address this issue, we introduce the Evolving Rate (EvoRate), which quantitatively approximates the intensity of evolving patterns in the data with Mutual Information. Furthermore, in some temporal data with neural mutual information estimations, we only have snapshots at different timestamps, lacking correspondence, which hinders EvoRate estimation. To tackle this challenge, we propose EvoRate$_\mathcal{W}$, aiming to establish correspondence with optimal transport for estimating the first-order EvoRate. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets including images and tabular data validate the efficacy of our EvoRate.

paragraphs: Sequential prediction assumes that earlier observations contain useful information about how later observations develop. Yet deciding whether a dataset has a meaningful evolving pattern often depends on expert judgment. This paper introduces a quantitative approach intended to help assess that structure and inform the use of sequential models.

Evolving Rate, or EvoRate, uses mutual information to approximate the intensity of evolving patterns. Such a measure can inform choices about temporal ordering and feature or data selection, in addition to model suitability. A practical complication arises when data consists of snapshots at different times without correspondence between observations, making direct estimation difficult.

To address missing correspondence, the authors introduce EvoRate_W, which uses optimal transport to establish correspondence for estimating first-order EvoRate. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, including images and tabular data, support the measure's effectiveness. The contribution combines a proposed numerical description of temporal structure with an estimation approach for snapshots that do not already provide the links needed to follow observations over time.
summary.tldr: EvoRate uses mutual information to quantify evolving patterns, with an optimal-transport variant for temporal snapshots lacking correspondence.

title: Towards Understanding Evolving Patterns in Sequential Data

abstract: Recent works have studied fair resource allocation in social settings, where fairness is judged by the impact of allocation decisions rather than more traditional minimum or maximum thresholds on the allocations themselves. Our work significantly adds to this literature by developing continuous resource allocation strategies that adhere to *equality of impact*, a generalization of equality of opportunity. We derive methods to maximize total welfare across groups subject to minimal violation of equality of impact, in settings where the outcomes of allocations are unknown but have a diminishing marginal effect. While focused on a two-group setting, our study addresses a broader class of welfare dynamics than explored in prior work. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce *Equality of Impact (EoI)*, a fairness criterion defined via group-level impact functions. Second, we design an online algorithm for non-noisy settings that leverages the problem’s geometric structure and achieves constant cumulative fairness regret. Third, we extend this approach to noisy environments with a meta-algorithm and empirically demonstrate that our methods find fair allocations and perform competitively relative to representative baselines.
originalAbstract: Recent works have studied fair resource allocation in social settings, where fairness is judged by the impact of allocation decisions rather than more traditional minimum or maximum thresholds on the allocations themselves. Our work significantly adds to this literature by developing continuous resource allocation strategies that adhere to *equality of impact*, a generalization of equality of opportunity. We derive methods to maximize total welfare across groups subject to minimal violation of equality of impact, in settings where the outcomes of allocations are unknown but have a diminishing marginal effect. While focused on a two-group setting, our study addresses a broader class of welfare dynamics than explored in prior work. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce *Equality of Impact (EoI)*, a fairness criterion defined via group-level impact functions. Second, we design an online algorithm for non-noisy settings that leverages the problem’s geometric structure and achieves constant cumulative fairness regret. Third, we extend this approach to noisy environments with a meta-algorithm and empirically demonstrate that our methods find fair allocations and perform competitively relative to representative baselines.

paragraphs: Fair resource allocation can depend on what resources accomplish for different groups, not simply on how much each group receives. This paper formalizes that perspective through Equality of Impact, a fairness criterion built from group-level impact functions. It generalizes equality of opportunity and guides the allocation of resources that can be divided continuously.

The study focuses on two groups whose allocation outcomes are initially unknown and exhibit diminishing marginal effects: additional resources have progressively smaller effects. Within this setting, the authors develop methods that seek high total welfare while minimizing violations of Equality of Impact. Their formulation accommodates a broader class of welfare dynamics than the prior work they discuss.

For environments without noise, an online algorithm exploits the problem's geometry and achieves constant cumulative fairness regret. This controls accumulated fairness regret over time, rather than asserting that every individual allocation has zero violation. A meta-algorithm extends the approach to noisy environments. Empirical evaluations show that the methods find fair allocations and perform competitively against representative baselines, connecting the fairness criterion to an implementable learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Equality of Impact guides online resource allocation toward fair outcomes and high welfare when group responses are unknown and have diminishing marginal effects.

title: Fair Continuous Resource Allocation with Equality of Impact

abstract: Adapting large-scale foundational flow and diffusion generative models to optimize task-specific objectives while preserving prior information is crucial for real-world applications such as molecular design, protein docking, and creative image generation. Existing principled fine-tuning methods aim to maximize the expected reward of generated samples, while retaining knowledge from the pre-trained model via KL-divergence regularization. In this work, we tackle the significantly more general problem of optimizing general utilities beyond average rewards, including risk-averse and novelty-seeking reward maximization, diversity measures for exploration, and experiment design objectives among others. Likewise, we consider more general ways to preserve prior information beyond KL-divergence, such as optimal transport distances and Rényi divergences. To this end, we introduce Flow Density Control (FDC), a simple algorithm that reduces this complex problem to a specific sequence of simpler fine-tuning tasks, each solvable via scalable established methods. We derive convergence guarantees for the proposed scheme under realistic assumptions by leveraging recent understanding of mirror flows. Finally, we validate our method on illustrative settings, text-to-image, and molecular design tasks, showing that it can steer pre-trained generative models to optimize objectives and solve practically relevant tasks beyond the reach of current fine-tuning schemes.

This paper studies a broader problem: objectives that depend on properties such as risk, novelty, diversity, or usefulness for designing experiments. Those goals need more flexibility than average reward alone provides.

The reported results show that pretrained models can be steered toward objectives beyond the reach of the fine-tuning schemes considered. The contribution is a framework for choosing both richer generation goals and more varied ways of retaining prior knowledge.
summary.tldr: Flow Density Control reduces broad generative optimization objectives to simpler fine-tuning tasks while supporting multiple ways to preserve pretrained knowledge.

title: Flow Density Control: Generative Optimization Beyond Entropy-Regularized Fine-Tuning

abstract: Prior work using Masked Autoencoders (MAEs) typically relies on random patch masking based on the assumption that images have significant redundancies across different channels, allowing for the reconstruction of masked content using cross-channel correlations. However, this assumption does not hold in Multi-Channel Imaging (MCI), where channels may provide complementary information with minimal feature overlap. Thus, these MAEs primarily learn local structures within individual channels from patch reconstruction, failing to fully leverage cross-channel interactions and limiting their MCI effectiveness. In this paper, we present ChA-MAEViT, an MAE-based method that enhances feature learning across MCI channels via four key strategies: (1) dynamic channel-patch masking, which compels the model to reconstruct missing channels in addition to masked patches, thereby enhancing cross-channel dependencies and improving robustness to varying channel configurations; (2) memory tokens, which serve as long-term memory aids to promote information sharing across channels, addressing the challenges of reconstructing structurally diverse channels; (3) hybrid token fusion module, which merges fine-grained patch tokens with a global class token to capture richer representations; and (4) Channel-Aware Decoder, a lightweight decoder utilizes channel tokens to effectively reconstruct image patches. Experiments on satellite and microscopy datasets, CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, and So2Sat, show that ChA-MAEViT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art MCI-ViTs by 3.0-21.5%, highlighting the importance of cross-channel interactions in MCI. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/chaudatascience/cha_mae_vit.

title: ChA-MAEViT: Unifying Channel-Aware Masked Autoencoders and Multi-Channel Vision Transformers for Improved Cross-Channel Learning

abstract: Chip placement is a critical step in the Electronic Design Automation (EDA) workflow, which aims to arrange chip modules on the canvas to optimize the performance, power, and area (PPA) metrics of final designs.Recent advances show great potential of AI-based algorithms in chip placement.However, due to the lengthy EDA workflow, evaluations of these algorithms often focus on intermediate surrogate metrics, which are computationally efficient but often misalign with the final end-to-end performance (i.e., the final design PPA).To address this challenge, we propose to build ChiPBench, a comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the effectiveness of AI-based algorithms in final design PPA metrics.Specifically, we generate a diverse evaluation dataset from $20$ circuits across various domains, such as CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs.We then evaluate six state-of-the-art AI-based chip placement algorithms on the dataset and conduct a thorough analysis of their placement behavior.Extensive experiments show that AI-based chip placement algorithms produce unsatisfactory final PPA results, highlighting the significant influence of often-overlooked factors like regularity and dataflow.We believe ChiPBench will effectively bridge the gap between academia and industry.

paragraphs: Chip placement determines where modules sit on a chip, with consequences for the completed design's performance, power use, and area. Because the full design workflow takes considerable time, placement algorithms are often evaluated using faster intermediate measurements. The problem is that improvements in these surrogate measurements may not correspond to improvements in the finished chip.

ChiPBench evaluates AI-based placement methods using final design outcomes. Its evaluation dataset covers 20 circuits from domains including CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. The authors apply six state-of-the-art AI placement algorithms and analyze their placement behavior alongside the resulting performance, power, and area measurements.

The experiments find unsatisfactory final results from the evaluated algorithms and highlight the influence of factors such as regularity and dataflow. This makes the benchmark useful for examining whether a placement method's apparent progress survives the rest of the design workflow. The contribution is an evaluation framework that connects algorithm assessment more directly to engineering outcomes, with bridging academic research and industrial needs stated as an intended benefit.
summary.tldr: ChiPBench evaluates AI chip placement through final design outcomes and finds that the tested methods deliver unsatisfactory performance, power, and area results.

title: Benchmarking End-To-End Performance of AI-Based Chip Placement Algorithms

abstract: Diffusion models have recently emerged as powerful neural solvers for combinatorial optimization (CO). However, existing approaches fail to reveal how variables are progressively determined during inference, making the final solution opaque until the last step. To address this limitation, we propose a structured denoising diffusion model, StruDiCO, which incrementally constructs solutions through step-wise variable selection. This is achieved via a variable-absorption noising model, wherein the forward process simulates gradual variable deactivation, converging to an empty solution, while the reverse process incrementally selects variables to reconstruct the final solution. This design induces structural continuity across intermediate states, enabling interpretable and trajectory-consistent partial solutions throughout inference. To further improve the reliability of reverse inference, we introduce a constrained consistency sampling strategy, which suppresses low-confidence variable selection at each step to stabilize the reverse process. Leveraging the structure-preserving reverse process, we further propose a lightweight, gradient-free, objective-aware refinement framework, which iteratively improves solution quality by applying structure-aware perturbations to the current solution, performing reverse inference through the constraint consistency model, and decoding with an objective-guided scoring scheme. Extensive experiments on two canonical CO tasks, the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and Maximal Independent Set (MIS), show that StruDiCO outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion-based solvers, achieving up to $3.5\times$ faster inference, 70\% lower GPU memory usage, and significantly improved solution quality, with up to 37.7\% drop reduction on TSP and an average 38.1\% improvement on MIS. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/yuuuuwang/StruDiCO.

title: StruDiCO: Structured Denoising Diffusion with Gradient-free Inference-stage Boosting for Memory and Time Efficient Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback usually models preferences using a reward function that does not distinguish between people. We argue that this is unlikely to be a good design choice in contexts with high potential for disagreement, like in the training of large language models. We formalise and analyse the problem of learning a reward model that can be specialised to a user. Using the principle of empirical risk minimisation, we derive a probably approximately correct (PAC) bound showing the dependency of the approximation error on the number of training examples, as usual, and also on the number of human raters who provided feedback on them. Based on our theoretical findings, we discuss how to best collect pairwise preference data and argue that adaptive reward models should be beneficial when there is considerable disagreement among users. We also propose a concrete architecture for an adaptive reward model. Our approach leverages the observation that individual preferences can be captured as a linear combination of a set of general reward features. We show how to learn such features and subsequently use them to quickly adapt the reward model to a specific individual, even if their preferences are not reflected in the training data. We present experiments with large language models illustrating our theoretical results and comparing the proposed architecture with a non-adaptive baseline. Consistent with our analysis, the benefits provided by our model increase with the number of raters and the heterogeneity of their preferences. We also show that our model compares favourably to adaptive counterparts, including those performing in-context personalisation.

paragraphs: Human-feedback training often uses one reward function for everyone, even when people disagree about what makes an answer good. This paper studies reward models that can adapt to an individual. It formalizes the learning problem and derives a probably approximately correct bound that connects approximation error to both the number of examples and the number of human raters.

The reported benefits grow as the number of raters and the diversity of their preferences increase. The model also compares favorably with approaches using in-context personalization, supporting adaptation particularly where disagreement among users is substantial.
summary.tldr: Shared reward features let a reward model adapt to individual preferences, with reported benefits increasing as raters become more numerous and diverse.

title: Capturing Individual Human Preferences with Reward Features

abstract: Estimating the geometric median of a dataset is a robust counterpart to mean estimation, and is a fundamental problem in computational geometry. Recently, [HSU24] gave an $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differentially private algorithm obtaining an $\alpha$-multiplicative approximation to the geometric median objective, $\frac 1 n \sum_{i \in [n]} \|\cdot - \mathbf{x}_i\|$, given a dataset $D$ of $x_i$ for $i \in [n]$. Their algorithm requires $n \gtrsim \sqrt d \cdot \frac 1 {\alpha\epsilon}$ samples, which they prove is information-theoretically optimal. This result is surprising because its error scales with the effective radius of $D$ (i.e., of a ball capturing most points), rather than the worst-case radius. We give an improved algorithm that obtains the same approximation quality, also using $n \gtrsim \sqrt d \cdot \frac 1 {\alpha\epsilon}$ samples, but in time $\widetilde{O}(nd + \frac d {\alpha^2})$. Our runtime is nearly-linear, plus the cost of the cheapest non-private first-order method due to [CLMPS16]. To achieve our results, we use subsampling and geometric aggregation tools inspired by FriendlyCore [TCKMS22] to speed up the "warm start" component of the [HSU24] algorithm, combined with a careful custom analysis of DP-SGD's sensitivity for the geometric median objective.

paragraphs: The geometric median finds a point minimizing the average distance to the data, providing a robust alternative to estimating a mean. Prior work achieved a differentially private approximation whose error depends on a radius containing most data points, rather than the worst-case radius. It also established an information-theoretically optimal sample requirement.

This paper retains that approximation quality and sample requirement while improving computation. For n points in d dimensions, the runtime is approximately nd plus d divided by the square of the approximation parameter, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The sample requirement scales as the square root of dimension divided by the product of the approximation and privacy parameters, matching the prior result.

The speedup combines subsampling and geometric aggregation to accelerate initialization with a custom sensitivity analysis of private stochastic gradient descent for the geometric median objective. The resulting runtime is nearly linear in the input size plus the cost of the cheapest non-private first-order method cited by the authors. The advance therefore concerns computational efficiency while preserving the established statistical and privacy guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper speeds up differentially private geometric median estimation while preserving prior approximation quality and optimal sample requirements.

title: Private Geometric Median in Nearly-Linear Time

abstract: The performance of a deep learning model on a specific task and dataset depends heavily on its neural architecture, motivating considerable efforts to rapidly and accurately identify architectures suited to the target task and dataset. To achieve this, researchers use machine learning models—typically neural architecture encoders—to predict the performance of a neural architecture. Many state-of-the-art encoders aim to capture information flow within a neural architecture, which reflects how information moves through the forward pass and backpropagation, via a specialized model structure. However, due to their complicated structures, these flow-based encoders are significantly slower to process neural architectures compared to simpler encoders, presenting a notable practical challenge. To address this, we propose FGP, a novel pre-training method for neural architecture encoding that trains an encoder to capture the information flow without requiring specialized model structures. FGP trains an encoder to reconstruct a flow surrogate, our proposed representation of the neural architecture's information flow. Our experiments show that FGP boosts encoder performance by up to 106\% in Precision@1\%, compared to the same encoder trained solely with supervised learning.

paragraphs: Choosing a neural architecture requires estimating how well it will perform on a particular task and dataset. Architecture encoders help by learning representations from which performance can be predicted. Some strong encoders explicitly model information flow during forward computation and backpropagation, but their specialized structures make architectures slower to process.

FGP moves the learning of information flow into a pre-training task. The authors introduce a flow surrogate, a representation of an architecture's information flow, and train the encoder to reconstruct it. This gives the encoder a reason to learn flow-related information without requiring a specialized architecture designed around that information.

Experiments show improvements of up to 106% in Precision@1% compared with training the same encoder using supervised learning alone. The comparison isolates the benefit of the proposed pre-training relative to that encoder's supervised version. The broader significance is that useful structural knowledge can be learned through a reconstruction objective, offering a way to strengthen architecture representations while avoiding the requirement for the complicated structures used by existing flow-based encoders.
summary.tldr: FGP pre-trains architecture encoders to reconstruct information-flow surrogates, improving prediction quality without requiring specialized flow-based model structures.

title: Learning to Flow from Generative Pretext Tasks for Neural Architecture Encoding

abstract: We study the problem of learning in the presence of an adversary that can corrupt an $\eta$ fraction of the training examples with the goal of causing failure on a specific test point. In the realizable setting, prior work established that the optimal error under such instance-targeted poisoning attacks scales as $\Theta(d\eta)$, where $d$ is the VC dimension of the hypothesis class [Hanneke, Karbasi, Mahmoody, Mehalel, and Moran (NeurIPS 2022)]. In this work, we resolve the corresponding question in the agnostic setting. We show that the optimal excess error is $\widetilde\Theta(\sqrt{d\eta})$, answering one of the main open problems left by Hanneke et al. To achieve this rate, it is necessary to use randomized learners: Hanneke et al.\ showed that deterministic learners can be forced to suffer error close to $1$ even under small amounts of poisoning. Perhaps surprisingly, our upper bound remains valid even when the learner’s random bits are fully visible to the adversary. In the other direction, our lower bound is stronger than standard PAC-style bounds: instead of tailoring a hard distribution separately for each sample size, we exhibit a single fixed distribution under which the adversary can enforce an excess error of $\Omega(\sqrt{d\eta})$ infinitely often.

It addresses the agnostic setting, where learning does not assume that the available hypothesis class perfectly explains the data. The central question is how much additional error such targeted poisoning can force.
