summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal agnostic learning rates under targeted poisoning and shows that randomized learners remain effective even when their randomness is visible.

title: Agnostic Learning under Targeted Poisoning: Optimal Rates and the Role of Randomness

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have recently shown impressive capabilities in complex reasoning and tool use via multi-step interactions with their environments. While these agents have the potential to tackle complicated tasks, their problem-solving process—agents' interaction trajectory leading to task completion—remains underexploited. These trajectories contain rich feedback that can navigate agents toward the right directions for solving problems correctly. Although prevailing approaches, such as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), can effectively balance exploration and exploitation, they ignore the interdependence among various trajectories and lack the diversity of search spaces, which leads to redundant reasoning and suboptimal outcomes. To address these challenges, we propose SE-Agent, a Self-Evolution framework that enables Agents to optimize their reasoning processes iteratively. Our approach revisits and enhances former pilot trajectories through three key operations: revision, recombination, and refinement. This evolutionary mechanism enables two critical advantages: (1) it expands the search space beyond local optima by intelligently exploring diverse solution paths guided by previous trajectories, and (2) it leverages cross-trajectory inspiration to efficiently enhance performance while mitigating the impact of suboptimal reasoning paths. Through these mechanisms, SE-Agent achieves continuous self-evolution that incrementally improves reasoning quality. We evaluate SE-Agent on SWE-bench Verified to resolve real-world GitHub issues. Experimental results across five strong LLMs show that integrating SE-Agent delivers up to 55% relative improvement, achieving state-of-the-art performance among all open-source agents on SWE-bench Verified.
originalAbstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have recently shown impressive capabilities in complex reasoning and tool use via multi-step interactions with their environments. While these agents have the potential to tackle complicated tasks, their problem-solving process—agents' interaction trajectory leading to task completion—remains underexploited. These trajectories contain rich feedback that can navigate agents toward the right directions for solving problems correctly. Although prevailing approaches, such as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), can effectively balance exploration and exploitation, they ignore the interdependence among various trajectories and lack the diversity of search spaces, which leads to redundant reasoning and suboptimal outcomes. To address these challenges, we propose SE-Agent, a Self-Evolution framework that enables Agents to optimize their reasoning processes iteratively. Our approach revisits and enhances former pilot trajectories through three key operations: revision, recombination, and refinement. This evolutionary mechanism enables two critical advantages: (1) it expands the search space beyond local optima by intelligently exploring diverse solution paths guided by previous trajectories, and (2) it leverages cross-trajectory inspiration to efficiently enhance performance while mitigating the impact of suboptimal reasoning paths. Through these mechanisms, SE-Agent achieves continuous self-evolution that incrementally improves reasoning quality. We evaluate SE-Agent on SWE-bench Verified to resolve real-world GitHub issues. Experimental results across five strong LLMs show that integrating SE-Agent delivers up to 55% relative improvement, achieving state-of-the-art performance among all open-source agents on SWE-bench Verified.

paragraphs: An agent's sequence of reasoning and tool interactions contains feedback about how it approached a task. SE-Agent treats these complete trajectories as material for further improvement. The paper argues that existing search approaches can underuse relationships between trajectories, leading to repeated reasoning and insufficient diversity in the solution paths being explored.

The framework revisits earlier pilot trajectories through revision, recombination, and refinement. These operations use previous attempts to guide new ones and allow ideas from separate trajectories to inform each other. The intended benefit is a wider search beyond local optima, together with reduced influence from unproductive reasoning paths. Improvement happens through iterative optimization of the agent's problem-solving process.

The authors evaluate SE-Agent on SWE-bench Verified, where agents resolve real GitHub issues, using five strong language models. They report gains of up to 55% relative improvement and state-of-the-art performance among open-source agents on that benchmark. The result supports reusing and combining information across attempts as an effective way to improve multi-step software problem solving.
summary.tldr: SE-Agent revises, combines, and refines previous interaction trajectories to improve multi-step reasoning and software issue resolution.

title: SE-Agent: Self-Evolution Trajectory Optimization in Multi-Step Reasoning with LLM-Based Agents

abstract: We propose a novel energy function for Dense Associative Memory (DenseAM) networks, the log-sum-ReLU (LSR), inspired by optimal kernel density estimation. Unlike the common log-sum-exponential (LSE) function, LSR is based on the Epanechnikov kernel and enables exact memory retrieval with exponential capacity without requiring exponential separation functions. Uniquely, it introduces abundant additional emergent local minima while preserving perfect pattern recovery --- a characteristic previously unseen in DenseAM literature. Empirical results show that LSR energy has significantly more local minima (memories) that have comparable log-likelihood to LSE-based models. Analysis of LSR's emergent memories on image datasets reveals a degree of creativity and novelty, hinting at this method's potential for both large-scale memory storage and generative tasks.

paragraphs: Dense associative memory networks retrieve stored patterns through an energy function whose low points correspond to memories. This paper proposes a different energy function, log-sum-ReLU, inspired by optimal kernel density estimation. It uses the Epanechnikov kernel in place of the log-sum-exponential construction commonly used in these networks.

These observations suggest possible generative uses as well as large-scale storage applications; the generative potential is presented as a promising implication of the observed memories.
summary.tldr: A new associative-memory energy function preserves exact pattern retrieval while producing many additional, potentially useful emergent memories.

title: Dense Associative Memory with Epanechnikov Energy

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning representations without labeled data. Most SSL approaches rely on strong, well-established, handcrafted data augmentations to generate diverse views for representation learning. However, designing such augmentations requires domain-specific knowledge and implicitly imposes representational invariances on the model, which can limit generalization. In this work, we propose an unsupervised representation learning method that replaces augmentations by generating views using orthonormal bases and overcomplete frames. We show that embeddings learned from orthonormal and overcomplete spaces reside on distinct manifolds, shaped by the geometric biases introduced by representing samples in different spaces. By jointly leveraging the complementary geometry of these distinct manifolds, our approach achieves superior performance without artificially increasing data diversity through strong augmentations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on nine datasets across five temporal sequence tasks, where signal-specific characteristics make data augmentations particularly challenging. Without relying on augmentation-induced diversity, our method achieves performance gains of up to 15--20\% over existing self-supervised approaches. Source code: \url{https://github.com/eth-siplab/Learning-with-FrameProjections}

paragraphs: This paper learns time-series representations without relying on strong handcrafted data augmentations. Such augmentations usually provide different views of a sample, but choosing them requires knowledge of which signal changes should preserve meaning. Those choices also impose invariances on the learned representation, potentially restricting how well it generalizes.

The proposed method creates views by expressing samples through orthonormal bases and overcomplete frames. These alternative representation spaces introduce different geometric biases. The authors show that the resulting embeddings occupy distinct manifolds, and their method jointly uses the complementary geometry of those manifolds. View diversity therefore comes from how samples are represented, rather than from strong artificial changes to the data.

The paper reports gains of up to 15–20% over existing self-supervised approaches. Those are the largest reported gains, not a uniform improvement across every task. The findings support representation geometry as a useful source of complementary learning signals without augmentation-induced diversity.
summary.tldr: The method learns time-series representations from complementary frame projections, reporting gains without strong handcrafted augmentations.

title: Learning Without Augmenting: Unsupervised Time Series Representation Learning via Frame Projections

abstract: Discrete diffusion has emerged as a powerful framework for generative modeling in discrete domains, yet efficiently sampling from these models remains challenging. Existing sampling strategies often struggle to balance computation and sample quality when the number of sampling steps is reduced, even when the model has learned the data distribution well. To address these limitations, we propose a predictor-corrector sampling scheme where the corrector is informed by the diffusion model to more reliably counter the accumulating approximation errors. To further enhance the effectiveness of our informed corrector, we introduce complementary architectural modifications based on hollow transformers and a simple tailored training objective that leverages more training signal. We use a synthetic example to illustrate the failure modes of existing samplers and show how informed correctors alleviate these problems. On the Text8 dataset, the informed corrector improves sample quality by generating text with significantly fewer errors than the baselines. On tokenized ImageNet 256x256, this approach consistently produces superior samples with fewer steps, achieving improved FID scores for discrete diffusion models. These results underscore the potential of informed correctors for fast and high-fidelity generation using discrete diffusion.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models can learn a data distribution well yet still generate poor samples when sampling is accelerated. Reducing the number of steps can allow approximation errors to accumulate, creating a gap between model quality and the quality of its outputs. This paper addresses that gap through the sampling procedure.

The proposed predictor-corrector scheme uses information from the diffusion model to guide its corrective updates. These updates are intended to counter accumulating errors more reliably. The authors also introduce complementary changes based on hollow transformers and a tailored training objective that makes use of more training signal. Together, these results show that better-informed corrections can improve the trade-off between sampling cost and output quality in discrete diffusion.
summary.tldr: Model-informed corrective updates reduce sampling errors in discrete diffusion, improving text and image generation with fewer steps.

title: Informed Correctors for Discrete Diffusion Models

abstract: The recent development of zero-shot reinforcement learning (RL) has opened a new avenue for learning pre-trained generalist policies that can adapt to arbitrary new tasks in a zero-shot manner. While the popular Forward-Backward representations (FB) and related methods have shown promise in zero-shot RL, we empirically found that their modeling lacks expressivity and that extrapolation errors caused by out-of-distribution (OOD) actions during offline learning sometimes lead to biased representations, ultimately resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these issues, we propose Behavior-REgularizEd Zero-shot RL with Expressivity enhancement (BREEZE), an upgraded FB-based framework that simultaneously enhances learning stability, policy extraction capability, and representation learning quality. BREEZE introduces behavioral regularization in zero-shot RL policy learning, transforming policy optimization into a stable in-sample learning paradigm. Additionally, BREEZE extracts the policy using a task-conditioned diffusion model, enabling the generation of high-quality and multimodal action distributions in zero-shot RL settings. Moreover, BREEZE employs expressive attention-based architectures for representation modeling to capture the complex relationships between environmental dynamics. Extensive experiments on ExORL and D4RL Kitchen demonstrate that BREEZE achieves the best or near-the-best performance while exhibiting superior robustness compared to prior offline zero-shot RL methods. The official implementation is available at: https://github.com/Whiterrrrr/BREEZE.

summary.tldr: BREEZE improves offline zero-shot reinforcement learning through behavioral regularization, diffusion-based policies, and more expressive representations.

title: Towards Robust Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Motion in the real world takes place in 3D space. Existing Frame Interpolation methods often estimate global receptive fields in 2D frame space. Due to the limitations of 2D space, these global receptive fields are limited, which makes it difficult to match object correspondences between frames, resulting in sub-optimal performance when handling large-motion scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel pipeline for exploring object correspondences based on differential surface theory. The differential surface coordinate system provides a better representation of the real world, enabling effective exploration of object correspondences. Specifically, the pipeline first transforms an input pair of video frames from the image coordinate system to the differential surface coordinate system. Subsequently, within this coordinate system, object correspondences are explored based on surface geometric properties and the surface uniqueness theorem. Experimental findings showcase that our method attains state-of-the-art performance across large motion benchmarks. Our method demonstrates the state-of-the-art performance on these VFI subsets with large motion.

paragraphs: Frame interpolation generates an intermediate view of motion from input video frames. A central difficulty is matching the same objects between frames when they move substantially. This paper argues that estimating correspondences in two-dimensional image space limits existing approaches, because real-world motion occurs in three dimensions.

The proposed pipeline first transforms a pair of frames from image coordinates into a differential surface coordinate system. It then searches for object correspondences using surface geometry and the surface uniqueness theorem. The change of representation is intended to make the geometric structure of the scene more useful for matching objects across the two observations.

The significance lies in where correspondence reasoning takes place: the method introduces surface structure into a problem that is often handled within image coordinates. The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on large-motion frame interpolation benchmarks and subsets. Those findings support the proposed geometric representation for the particular difficulty emphasized by the paper, namely maintaining useful object correspondences when motion between frames is large.
summary.tldr: A surface-coordinate representation improves object matching for frame interpolation and achieves state-of-the-art results on large-motion evaluations.

title: Surface-Aware Feed-Forward Quadratic Gaussian for Frame Interpolation with Large Motion

abstract: Uncertain knowledge graphs (UKGs) associate each triple with a confidence score to provide more precise knowledge representations. Recently, since real-world UKGs suffer from the incompleteness, uncertain knowledge graph (UKG) completion attracts more attention, aiming to complete missing triples and confidences. Current studies attempt to learn UKG embeddings to solve this problem, but they neglect the extremely imbalanced distributions of triple confidences. This causes that the learnt embeddings are insufficient to high-quality UKG completion. Thus, in this paper, to address the above issue, we propose a new semi-supervised Confidence Distribution Learning (ssCDL) method for UKG completion, where each triple confidence is transformed into a confidence distribution to introduce more supervision information of different confidences to reinforce the embedding learning process. ssCDL iteratively learns UKG embedding by relational learning on labeled data (i.e., existing triples with confidences) and unlabeled data with pseudo labels (i.e., unseen triples with the generated confidences), which are predicted by meta-learning to augment the training data and rebalance the distribution of triple confidences. Experiments on two UKG datasets demonstrate that ssCDL consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines in different evaluation metrics.

paragraphs: An uncertain knowledge graph attaches a confidence score to each relationship, so completing it means predicting both missing relationships and their confidence. The paper identifies an obstacle in existing embedding methods: confidence values can be extremely unevenly distributed. Ignoring that imbalance can leave the learned representations poorly suited to completing the graph.

The proposed ssCDL method transforms each confidence score into a distribution, providing a richer supervisory signal across different confidence levels. It then alternates learning from existing relationships with known scores and unseen relationships assigned generated scores. Meta-learning predicts these pseudo-labels, allowing the added examples to expand the training data and rebalance confidence coverage.

This makes confidence distribution learning and semi-supervised augmentation parts of the same iterative process. Existing labeled facts anchor learning, while pseudo-labeled relationships extend the information available to the model. Experiments on two uncertain knowledge graph datasets show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across different evaluation metrics, supporting the value of explicitly addressing confidence imbalance.
summary.tldr: ssCDL improves uncertain knowledge graph completion by learning confidence distributions and using pseudo-labels to rebalance training data.

title: Uncertain Knowledge Graph Completion via Semi-Supervised Confidence Distribution Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of average reward optimization in domains with partial observability, within the modeling framework of linear predictive state representations (PSRs). The key to average-reward computation is to have a well-defined stationary behavior of a system, so the required averages can be computed. If, additionally, the stationary behavior varies smoothly with changes in policy parameters, average-reward control through policy search also becomes a possibility. In this paper, we show that PSRs have a well-behaved stationary distribution, which is a rational function of policy parameters. Based on this result, we define a related reward process particularly suitable for average reward optimization, and analyze its properties. We show that in such a predictive state reward process, the average reward is a rational function of the policy parameters, whose complexity depends on the dimension of the underlying linear PSR. This result suggests that average reward-based policy search methods can be effective when the dimension of the system is small, even when the system representation in the POMDP framework requires many hidden states. We provide illustrative examples of this type.

paragraphs: Optimizing long-run average reward requires a system to have well-defined stationary behavior. Under partial observability, the learner cannot directly see the complete state, making the representation of that behavior important. This paper studies the problem using linear predictive state representations, which describe a system through predictions.

The authors show that the stationary distribution is well behaved and depends on policy parameters through a rational function, meaning a ratio of polynomials. They then define a related predictive-state reward process and establish that its average reward is also a rational function of those parameters. The complexity of this expression depends on the dimension of the underlying linear representation.

This connects representation size to the difficulty of searching for a rewarding policy. The results suggest that average-reward policy search can be effective when the predictive representation is small, even if a partially observable Markov decision process description needs many hidden states. Illustrative examples support that possibility; the abstract presents it as a promising consequence rather than a universal efficiency guarantee.
summary.tldr: Small predictive state representations yield structured average-reward objectives that may make policy search effective despite many hidden states.

title: Average Reward Optimization Objective In Partially Observable Domains

abstract: Most learning methods with rank or sparsity constraints use convex relaxations, which lead to optimization with the nuclear norm or the \ell_1-norm. However, several important learning applications cannot benefit from this approach as they feature these convex norms as constraints in addition to the non-convex rank and sparsity constraints. In this setting, we derive efficient sparse projections onto the simplex and its extension, and illustrate how to use them to solve high-dimensional learning problems in quantum tomography, sparse density estimation and portfolio selection with non-convex constraints.
originalAbstract: Most learning methods with rank or sparsity constraints use convex relaxations, which lead to optimization with the nuclear norm or the \ell_1-norm. However, several important learning applications cannot benefit from this approach as they feature these convex norms as constraints in addition to the non-convex rank and sparsity constraints. In this setting, we derive efficient sparse projections onto the simplex and its extension, and illustrate how to use them to solve high-dimensional learning problems in quantum tomography, sparse density estimation and portfolio selection with non-convex constraints.

paragraphs: Many learning problems constrain a solution to be sparse or to have low rank. A common strategy replaces these difficult constraints with convex alternatives involving the ℓ₁ norm or nuclear norm. This paper considers situations where those norms are already separate constraints, alongside the original sparsity or rank requirement.

In that setting, the usual convex relaxation does not provide the needed way to handle both requirements. The authors derive efficient sparse projections onto the simplex and an extension of it. These projections supply an optimization operation that respects sparsity within the relevant constrained set, addressing the combined constraints directly.

The paper illustrates how to use these operations in high-dimensional quantum tomography, sparse density estimation, and portfolio selection. These applications demonstrate why retaining nonconvex constraints can be important when a convex norm constraint is already part of the problem. The contribution is an efficient computational tool for this particular constraint structure, together with examples of how it can support learning problems across several domains.
summary.tldr: Efficient sparse simplex projections support learning problems that require nonconvex sparsity or rank constraints alongside convex norm constraints.

title: Sparse projections onto the simplex

abstract: Previous analysis of binary SVMs has demonstrated a deep connection between robustness to perturbations over uncertainty sets and regularization of the weights. In this paper, we explore the problem of learning robust models for structured prediction problems. We first formulate the problem of learning robust structural SVMs when there are perturbations in the feature space. We consider two different classes of uncertainty sets for the perturbations: ellipsoidal uncertainty sets and polyhedral uncertainty sets. In both cases, we show that the robust optimization problem is equivalent to the non-robust formulation with an additional regularizer. For the ellipsoidal uncertainty set, the additional regularizer is based on the dual norm of the norm that constrains the ellipsoidal uncertainty. For the polyhedral uncertainty set, we show that the robust optimization problem is equivalent to adding a linear regularizer in a transformed weight space related to the linear constraints of the polyhedron. We also show that these constraint sets can be combined and demonstrate a number of interesting special cases. This represents the first theoretical analysis of robust optimization of structural support vector machines. Our experimental results show that our method outperforms the nonrobust structural SVMs on real world data when the test data distributions is drifted from the training data distribution.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to train structural support vector machines that tolerate perturbations in their feature space. Earlier binary SVM analysis had connected robustness with regularization. The authors extend this line of reasoning to structured prediction, formulating robust learning problems for two classes of allowable perturbations.

For ellipsoidal uncertainty sets, the robust problem is equivalent to adding a regularizer based on the dual norm associated with the uncertainty constraint. For polyhedral sets, the equivalent addition is a linear regularizer in a transformed weight space related to the polyhedron's constraints. These results make the shape of the assumed perturbations directly relevant to the regularizer used in training.

The authors also show how the constraint sets can be combined and examine special cases. Experiments on real-world data report improvements over nonrobust structural SVMs when the test distribution has drifted from the training distribution. The theoretical contribution is the equivalence between specified robustness formulations and regularization; the empirical contribution supports their usefulness under the evaluated distribution shifts.
summary.tldr: Specified feature-perturbation models for structural SVMs are equivalent to additional regularizers, with empirical benefits under distribution shift.

title: On Robustness and Regularization of Structural Support Vector Machines

abstract: Gaussian graphical models (GGM) have been widely used in many high-dimensional applications ranging from biological and financial data to recommender systems. Sparsity in GGM plays a central role both statistically and computationally. Unfortunately, real-world data often does not fit well to sparse graphical models. In this paper, we focus on a family of latent variable Gaussian graphical models (LVGGM), where the model is conditionally sparse given latent variables, but marginally non-sparse. In LVGGM, the inverse covariance matrix has a low-rank plus sparse structure, and can be learned in a regularized maximum likelihood framework. We derive novel parameter estimation error bounds for LVGGM under mild conditions in the high-dimensional setting. These results complement the existing theory on the structural learning, and open up new possibilities of using LVGGM for statistical inference.

paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models often rely on sparsity to make high-dimensional estimation statistically and computationally manageable. Yet observed data may exhibit many dependencies, making a sparse model an inadequate description. This paper studies models in which unobserved variables help explain why the observed relationships appear dense.

The key assumption is conditional sparsity: relationships become sparse when the latent variables are taken into account, although the observed marginal model remains non-sparse. In this setting, the inverse covariance matrix has a low-rank plus sparse structure. This decomposition supports learning through regularized maximum likelihood, with the two components representing the model’s structured departure from ordinary sparsity.

The main contribution is a set of new parameter estimation error bounds for high-dimensional latent variable Gaussian graphical models under conditions described as mild. These results complement existing theory about learning model structure by addressing the accuracy of estimated parameters. The authors present them as opening possibilities for statistical inference with these models, extending the theoretical basis for using latent structure to explain dense observed dependencies.
summary.tldr: The paper derives parameter estimation error bounds for high-dimensional Gaussian graphical models whose latent variables induce low-rank plus sparse structure.

title: Learning Latent Variable Gaussian Graphical Models

abstract: Random projections have played an important role in scaling up machine learning and data mining algorithms. Recently they have also been applied to probabilistic inference to estimate properties of high-dimensional distributions; however, they all rely on the same class of projections based on universal hashing. We provide a general framework to analyze random projections which relates their statistical properties to their Fourier spectrum, which is a well-studied area of theoretical computer science. Using this framework we introduce two new classes of hash functions for probabilistic inference and model counting that show promising performance on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

Recently they have also been applied to probabilistic inference to estimate properties of high-dimensional distributions; however, they all rely on the same class of projections based on universal hashing. We provide a general framework to analyze random projections which relates their statistical properties to their Fourier spectrum, which is a well-studied area of theoretical computer science. Using this framework we introduce two new classes of hash functions for probabilistic inference and model counting that show promising performance on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies random projections used to estimate properties of high-dimensional probability distributions. Such projections already help make machine learning and data mining computations more manageable. The authors identify a restriction in the inference methods they discuss: these methods rely on the same family of projections, built from universal hashing.

Their contribution is a general framework connecting the statistical behavior of random projections to their Fourier spectrum. This turns a question about whether a projection is useful for inference into a question that can draw on established mathematical tools. The framework provides a basis for analyzing projection choices beyond the previously used hashing family.

Using that analysis, the authors introduce two new classes of hash functions for probabilistic inference and model counting. Tests on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show promising performance. The stated result is therefore both analytical and algorithmic: a broader way to study projections leads to concrete alternatives that work encouragingly in the reported evaluations, without establishing that either family is universally preferable.
summary.tldr: A Fourier-based framework for analyzing random projections yields two new hash-function families with promising inference and model-counting results.

title: Beyond Parity Constraints: Fourier Analysis of Hash Functions for Inference

abstract: Expert input can improve clustering performance. In today’s collaborative environment, the availability of crowdsourced multiple expert input is becoming common. Given multiple experts’ inputs, most existing approaches can only discover one clustering structure. However, data is multi-faced by nature and can be clustered in different ways (also known as views). In an exploratory analysis problem where ground truth is not known, different experts may have diverse views on how to cluster data. In this paper, we address the problem on how to automatically discover multiple ways to cluster data given potentially diverse inputs from multiple uncertain experts. We propose a novel Bayesian probabilistic model that automatically learns the multiple expert views and the clustering structure associated with each view. The benefits of learning the experts’ views include 1) enabling the discovery of multiple diverse clustering structures, and 2) improving the quality of clustering solution in each view by assigning higher weights to experts with higher confidence. In our approach, the expert views, multiple clustering structures and expert confidences are jointly learned via variational inference. Experimental results on synthetic datasets, benchmark datasets and a real-world disease subtyping problem show that our proposed approach outperforms competing baselines, including meta clustering, semi-supervised clustering, semi-crowdsourced clustering and consensus clustering.

paragraphs: Different experts can organize the same dataset in legitimately different ways. Methods that merge all expert input into one clustering may therefore erase useful alternative views, especially when no ground truth is available. This paper treats disagreement as a possible sign of multiple clustering structures while also accounting for uncertainty in individual experts.

The authors introduce a Bayesian model that jointly learns expert views, the clustering associated with each view, and expert confidence. Variational inference estimates these coupled quantities. Experts with higher inferred confidence receive more influence within a view, allowing the model to distinguish unreliable input from meaningful differences in how the data should be grouped.

Experiments cover synthetic data, benchmark datasets, and a disease-subtyping application. The approach outperforms the compared meta-clustering, semi-supervised, semi-crowdsourced, and consensus-clustering baselines. The reported contribution is thus both representational and practical: it discovers multiple organizations of the data while improving clustering quality within those views, rather than requiring all experts to agree on one answer.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model separates expert disagreement into multiple clustering views while learning how much to trust each expert.

title: Multiple Clustering Views from Multiple Uncertain Experts

abstract: We study the problem of causal structure learning when the experimenter is limited to perform at most $k$ non-adaptive experiments of size $1$. We formulate the problem of finding the best intervention target set as an optimization problem, which aims to maximize the average number of edges whose directions are resolved. We prove that the corresponding objective function is submodular and a greedy algorithm suffices to achieve $(1-\frac{1}{e})$-approximation of the optimal value. We further present an accelerated variant of the greedy algorithm, which can lead to orders of magnitude performance speedup. We validate our proposed approach on synthetic and real graphs. The results show that compared to the purely observational setting, our algorithm orients the majority of the edges through a considerably small number of interventions.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph involves determining which way its connections point. Observations can leave some directions unresolved, while experiments can provide additional information. This paper studies how to choose experiments when only a limited number are available. Its setting permits at most k experiments, each targeting one variable, with all targets chosen before experimental results arrive.

The authors formulate target selection as an optimization problem: maximize the average number of edge directions that the experiments resolve. They prove that this objective is submodular, meaning that additional targets have diminishing returns. This structure supports a greedy selection algorithm with a guarantee of at least a 1 − 1/e fraction of the optimal objective value.

They also introduce an accelerated version that can produce orders-of-magnitude speedups. On synthetic and real graphs, their approach resolves most edge directions with relatively few interventions compared with using observations alone. The contribution connects a restricted experimental budget to both a principled selection rule and a quantified approximation guarantee.
summary.tldr: A greedy experiment-selection method has a provable approximation guarantee and resolves most causal edge directions with few interventions in the reported evaluations.

title: Budgeted Experiment Design for Causal Structure Learning

abstract: Sign random projections (SRP) is a technique which allows the user to quickly estimate the angular similarity and inner products between data. We propose using additional information to improve these estimates which is easy to implement and cost efficient. We prove that the variance of our estimator is lower than the variance of SRP. Our proposed method can also be used together with other modifications of SRP, such as Super-Bit LSH (SBLSH). We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on the MNIST test dataset and the Gisette dataset. We discuss how our proposed method can be extended to random projections or even other hashing algorithms.

paragraphs: Sign random projections provide a fast way to estimate angular similarity and inner products between data. This paper asks whether those estimates can be improved using additional information while keeping the method practical. The proposed modification is described as inexpensive and straightforward to implement, making estimation quality the main target of the change.

The authors prove that their estimator has lower variance than standard sign random projections. Lower variance means less variability in the estimate due to the randomness involved in the procedure. The method can also be combined with other modifications of sign random projections, including Super-Bit LSH, allowing it to complement an existing variant.

Experiments on the MNIST test dataset and Gisette demonstrate the method’s effectiveness alongside the theoretical variance result. The paper also discusses extending the idea to random projections more generally or to other hashing algorithms. Those broader extensions are discussed as possibilities, while the demonstrated contribution is the improved estimator for the sign-random-projection setting.
summary.tldr: Additional information yields a practical sign-random-projection estimator with provably lower variance.

title: Improving Sign Random Projections With Additional Information

abstract: Future predictions on sequence data (e.g., videos or audios) require the algorithms to capture non-Markovian and compositional properties of high-level semantics. Context-free grammars are natural choices to capture such properties, but traditional grammar parsers (e.g., Earley parser) only take symbolic sentences as inputs. In this paper, we generalize the Earley parser to parse sequence data which is neither segmented nor labeled. This generalized Earley parser integrates a grammar parser with a classifier to find the optimal segmentation and labels, and makes top-down future predictions. Experiments show that our method significantly outperforms other approaches for future human activity prediction.

paragraphs: Predicting what happens next in video or audio requires understanding how meaningful events fit together over time. The relevant structure can extend beyond the immediate past and can combine smaller events into larger activities. Context-free grammars can express such structure, but conventional grammar parsers expect sequences that already contain discrete symbols.

The paper generalizes the Earley parser to sequences that have neither segment boundaries nor labels. It combines a grammar parser with a classifier to find the optimal segmentation and labeling. This connects the classifier's interpretation of the data with grammatical constraints on how the resulting events can fit together.

The integrated system also makes top-down predictions about future events using the grammar. Experiments on future human activity prediction show significant improvements over other approaches. The result supports combining recognition with structured sequence reasoning: the method uses an account of the larger activity both to interpret the observed sequence and to anticipate what may follow.
summary.tldr: A generalized Earley parser combines classification and grammar-based reasoning to segment unlabeled sequences and predict future human activities.

title: Generalized Earley Parser: Bridging Symbolic Grammars and Sequence Data for Future Prediction

abstract: We address the problem of finding influential training samples for a particular case of tree ensemble-based models, e.g., Random Forest (RF) or Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT). A natural way of formalizing this problem is studying how the model’s predictions change upon leave-one-out retraining, leaving out each individual training sample. Recent work has shown that, for parametric models, this analysis can be conducted in a computationally efficient way. We propose several ways of extending this framework to non-parametric GBDT ensembles under the assumption that tree structures remain fixed. Furthermore, we introduce a general scheme of obtaining further approximations to our method that balance the trade-off between performance and computational complexity. We evaluate our approaches on various experimental setups and use-case scenarios and demonstrate both the quality of our approach to finding influential training samples in comparison to the baselines and its computational efficiency.

paragraphs: To understand a prediction, it can be useful to ask which training examples most influenced it. One direct definition considers how the prediction would change if each example were removed and the model retrained. This paper develops ways to study that leave-one-out influence for gradient-boosted decision tree ensembles more efficiently.

The authors extend an influence-analysis framework previously used for parametric models to nonparametric boosted trees. Their extension assumes that the tree structures remain fixed. That assumption defines the scope of the analysis: the method studies changes within an established tree structure rather than accounting for every structural change that unrestricted retraining might produce.

The paper also introduces a general scheme for further approximations, allowing a tradeoff between computational complexity and performance. Experiments across different setups and use cases demonstrate both the quality of the influential-sample estimates relative to baselines and computational efficiency. The contribution makes training-example influence more accessible for boosted trees while explicitly retaining the fixed-structure condition on which the approach depends.
summary.tldr: Efficient influence estimates identify important training examples for boosted trees under a fixed-tree-structure assumption.

title: Finding Influential Training Samples for Gradient Boosted Decision Trees

abstract: We consider the problem of handling missing data with deep latent variable models (DLVMs). First, we present a simple technique to train DLVMs when the training set contains missing-at-random data. Our approach, called MIWAE, is based on the importance-weighted autoencoder (IWAE), and maximises a potentially tight lower bound of the log-likelihood of the observed data. Compared to the original IWAE, our algorithm does not induce any additional computational overhead due to the missing data. We also develop Monte Carlo techniques for single and multiple imputation using a DLVM trained on an incomplete data set. We illustrate our approach by training a convolutional DLVM on incomplete static binarisations of MNIST. Moreover, on various continuous data sets, we show that MIWAE provides extremely accurate single imputations, and is highly competitive with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: MIWAE addresses training deep latent variable models when the training data contain missing values. The method assumes missing-at-random data and adapts the importance-weighted autoencoder to optimize a potentially tight lower bound on the likelihood of the observed entries. This lets the learning objective directly target the available evidence.

The authors state that handling missing data introduces no additional computational overhead relative to the original importance-weighted autoencoder. They also develop Monte Carlo procedures for filling in missing values after training. These support both single imputation, which produces one completion, and multiple imputation, which produces several possible completions from the learned model.

The paper demonstrates training a convolutional model on incomplete static binarizations of MNIST. On several continuous datasets, it reports highly accurate single imputations that are strongly competitive with state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines learning from incomplete data and completing that data within the same generative modeling framework, with the missing-at-random assumption defining the stated training setting.
summary.tldr: MIWAE trains deep generative models on missing-at-random data and uses them for accurate single or multiple imputation without added missing-data training overhead.

title: MIWAE: Deep Generative Modelling and Imputation of Incomplete Data Sets

abstract: In this paper we show that generative adversarial networks (GANs) without restriction on the discriminative function space commonly suffer from the problem that the gradient produced by the discriminator is uninformative to guide the generator. By contrast, Wasserstein GAN (WGAN), where the discriminative function is restricted to 1-Lipschitz, does not suffer from such a gradient uninformativeness problem. We further show in the paper that the model with a compact dual form of Wasserstein distance, where the Lipschitz condition is relaxed, may also theoretically suffer from this issue. This implies the importance of Lipschitz condition and motivates us to study the general formulation of GANs with Lipschitz constraint, which leads to a new family of GANs that we call Lipschitz GANs (LGANs). We show that LGANs guarantee the existence and uniqueness of the optimal discriminative function as well as the existence of a unique Nash equilibrium. We prove that LGANs are generally capable of eliminating the gradient uninformativeness problem. According to our empirical analysis, LGANs are more stable and generate consistently higher quality samples compared with WGAN.

paragraphs: In a generative adversarial network, the discriminator must provide a useful gradient to guide the generator. The paper shows that unrestricted discriminator function spaces commonly produce gradients that fail to provide this guidance. It contrasts this with Wasserstein GANs, whose 1-Lipschitz restriction avoids the identified gradient problem.

The authors also examine a compact dual formulation of Wasserstein distance with a relaxed Lipschitz condition. They show that this relaxation can theoretically reintroduce uninformative gradients. Motivated by that distinction, they study a general formulation with Lipschitz constraints and introduce a family called Lipschitz GANs, or LGANs.

For LGANs, the paper establishes existence and uniqueness of the optimal discriminator and a unique Nash equilibrium. It also proves that the family is generally capable of eliminating the gradient uninformativeness problem. Empirical analysis reports greater stability and consistently higher sample quality than WGAN. The work therefore connects a restriction on the discriminator to both formal properties of the learning game and observed training behavior, while distinguishing theoretical guarantees from experimental comparisons.
summary.tldr: Lipschitz GANs constrain discriminators to address uninformative generator gradients, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements over WGAN.

title: Lipschitz Generative Adversarial Nets

abstract: Low rank matrix factorization is a fundamental building block in machine learning, used for instance to summarize gene expression profile data or word-document counts. To be robust to outliers and differences in scale across features, a matrix factorization step is usually preceded by ad-hoc feature normalization steps, such as tf-idf scaling or data whitening. We propose in this work to learn these normalization operators jointly with the factorization itself. More precisely, given a $d\times n$ matrix $X$ of $d$ features measured on $n$ individuals, we propose to learn the parameters of quantile normalization operators that can operate row-wise on the values of $X$ and/or of its factorization $UV$ to improve the quality of the low-rank representation of $X$ itself. This optimization is facilitated by the introduction of a new differentiable quantile normalization operator built using optimal transport, providing new results on top of existing work by Cuturi et al. (2019). We demonstrate the applicability of these techniques on synthetic and genomics datasets.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix factorization compresses a data matrix into a smaller representation. Before fitting it, practitioners often normalize features to address outliers and differences in scale. This paper makes normalization part of the optimization problem, learning it jointly with the factorization instead of fixing it through a separate preprocessing rule.

The method learns parameters of quantile-normalization operators that act row by row on the original feature matrix, its low-rank reconstruction, or both. The objective is to improve the quality of the resulting low-rank representation. This couples the transformation of feature values to the representation being fitted, so the normalization is chosen in relation to the factorization task.

The technical ingredient is a differentiable quantile-normalization operator built using optimal transport. Differentiability facilitates joint optimization of the normalization parameters and the factorization. The authors demonstrate applicability on synthetic and genomics datasets. The contribution is both a learnable alternative to ad hoc preprocessing and an operator that makes such coordinated learning possible within the proposed optimization framework.
summary.tldr: A differentiable optimal-transport operator lets quantile normalization be learned jointly with low-rank matrix factorization.

title: Supervised Quantile Normalization for Low Rank Matrix Factorization

abstract: In the paper, we propose a class of accelerated stochastic gradient-free and projection-free (a.k.a., zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe) methods to solve the constrained stochastic and finite-sum nonconvex optimization. Specifically, we propose an accelerated stochastic zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe (Acc-SZOFW) method based on the variance reduced technique of SPIDER/SpiderBoost and a novel momentum accelerated technique. Moreover, under some mild conditions, we prove that the Acc-SZOFW has the function query complexity of $O(d\sqrt{n}\epsilon^{-2})$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point in the finite-sum problem, which improves the exiting best result by a factor of $O(\sqrt{n}\epsilon^{-2})$, and has the function query complexity of $O(d\epsilon^{-3})$ in the stochastic problem, which improves the exiting best result by a factor of $O(\epsilon^{-1})$. To relax the large batches required in the Acc-SZOFW, we further propose a novel accelerated stochastic zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe (Acc-SZOFW*) based on a new variance reduced technique of STORM, which still reaches the function query complexity of $O(d\epsilon^{-3})$ in the stochastic problem without relying on any large batches. In particular, we present an accelerated framework of the Frank-Wolfe methods based on the proposed momentum accelerated technique. The extensive experimental results on black-box adversarial attack and robust black-box classification demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithms.

Moreover, under some mild conditions, we prove that the Acc-SZOFW has the function query complexity of $O(d\sqrt{n}\epsilon^{-2})$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point in the finite-sum problem, which improves the exiting best result by a factor of $O(\sqrt{n}\epsilon^{-2})$, and has the function query complexity of $O(d\epsilon^{-3})$ in the stochastic problem, which improves the exiting best result by a factor of $O(\epsilon^{-1})$. paragraphs: This paper studies constrained optimization when an algorithm can evaluate an objective but cannot directly access its gradients. It also avoids projection operations used to enforce constraints. The proposed methods combine these two properties within a zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe framework, targeting nonconvex objectives expressed either as finite sums or through stochastic observations.

The main method, Acc-SZOFW, combines SPIDER/SpiderBoost variance reduction with a new momentum acceleration technique. Under the stated mild conditions, it requires O(d√n ε⁻²) function queries for finite-sum problems and O(d ε⁻³) for stochastic problems to reach an ε-stationary point. Here, d represents dimension and n the finite-sum size. These guarantees concern approximate stationarity rather than finding a global optimum.

A second method, Acc-SZOFW*, uses STORM-based variance reduction to retain the stochastic query bound without large batches. The authors also generalize their momentum technique into an accelerated Frank-Wolfe framework. Experiments on black-box adversarial attacks and robust black-box classification support the efficiency of the proposed algorithms, connecting the query-complexity improvements to applications where gradient access is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Accelerated Frank-Wolfe methods reduce function-query costs for constrained nonconvex optimization without gradients or projections.

title: Accelerated Stochastic Gradient-free and Projection-free Methods

abstract: The deterministic CUR matrix decomposition is a low-rank approximation method to analyze a data matrix. It has attracted considerable attention due to its high interpretability, which results from the fact that the decomposed matrices consist of subsets of the original columns and rows of the data matrix. The subset is obtained by optimizing an objective function with sparsity-inducing norms via coordinate descent. However, the existing algorithms for optimization incur high computation costs. This is because coordinate descent iteratively updates all the parameters in the objective until convergence. This paper proposes a fast deterministic CUR matrix decomposition. Our algorithm safely skips unnecessary updates by efficiently evaluating the optimality conditions for the parameters to be zeros. In addition, we preferentially update the parameters that must be nonzeros. Theoretically, our approach guarantees the same result as the original approach. Experiments demonstrate that our algorithm speeds up the deterministic CUR while achieving the same accuracy.

The subset is obtained by optimizing an objective function with sparsity-inducing norms via coordinate descent. However, the existing algorithms for optimization incur high computation costs. This is because coordinate descent iteratively updates all the parameters in the objective until convergence. This paper proposes a fast deterministic CUR matrix decomposition. Our algorithm safely skips unnecessary updates by efficiently evaluating the optimality conditions for the parameters to be zeros. In addition, we preferentially update the parameters that must be nonzeros. Theoretically, our approach guarantees the same result as the original approach. paragraphs: CUR decomposition approximates a data matrix using selected columns and rows from the original matrix. Keeping those original components makes the approximation interpretable. In the deterministic approach studied here, selection is obtained by optimizing an objective with sparsity-inducing norms, but the coordinate-descent procedure can spend substantial time repeatedly updating parameters.

The paper accelerates this optimization by checking which updates are actually needed. It efficiently evaluates optimality conditions that identify parameters that should be zero, allowing unnecessary updates to be skipped safely. It also prioritizes updates to parameters that must be nonzero, directing computational effort toward components that matter to the solution.

The theoretical guarantee is that this change in update strategy preserves the result of the original approach. Experiments demonstrate faster deterministic CUR decomposition with the same accuracy. The value of the method is thus in making an existing interpretable approximation procedure cheaper to compute while retaining its solution guarantee, rather than obtaining speed through a less accurate decomposition.
summary.tldr: Safe skipping and prioritization of coordinate updates accelerate deterministic CUR decomposition while preserving the original result.

title: Fast Deterministic CUR Matrix Decomposition with Accuracy Assurance

abstract: Minimax optimization has found extensive applications in modern machine learning, in settings such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), adversarial training and multi-agent reinforcement learning. As most of these applications involve continuous nonconvex-nonconcave formulations, a very basic question arises—“what is a proper definition of local optima?” Most previous work answers this question using classical notions of equilibria from simultaneous games, where the min-player and the max-player act simultaneously. In contrast, most applications in machine learning, including GANs and adversarial training, correspond to sequential games, where the order of which player acts first is crucial (since minimax is in general not equal to maximin due to the nonconvex-nonconcave nature of the problems). The main contribution of this paper is to propose a proper mathematical definition of local optimality for this sequential setting—local minimax, as well as to present its properties and existence results. Finally, we establish a strong connection to a basic local search algorithm—gradient descent ascent (GDA): under mild conditions, all stable limit points of GDA are exactly local minimax points up to some degenerate points.

As most of these applications involve continuous nonconvex-nonconcave formulations, a very basic question arises—“what is a proper definition of local optima?” Most previous work answers this question using classical notions of equilibria from simultaneous games, where the min-player and the max-player act simultaneously. In contrast, most applications in machine learning, including GANs and adversarial training, correspond to sequential games, where the order of which player acts first is crucial (since minimax is in general not equal to maximin due to the nonconvex-nonconcave nature of the problems). paragraphs: Minimax learning problems involve one player minimizing an objective while another maximizes it. When the objective is nonconvex and nonconcave, the order of their decisions matters: reversing that order can change the problem. This paper asks what a local optimum should mean when the interaction is sequential.

Classical equilibrium notions used in earlier work describe simultaneous decisions. The authors introduce local minimax as a mathematical definition tailored to sequential interaction, motivated by applications such as adversarial training and GANs. They analyze its properties and establish existence results, providing a way to describe local solutions that respects the order of play.

The paper then connects this definition to gradient descent ascent, a basic local search procedure for minimax problems. Under mild conditions, its stable limit points correspond exactly to local minimax points, apart from certain degenerate points. This links the proposed solution concept to algorithmic behavior, while keeping the conditions and degeneracies central to the scope of the correspondence.
summary.tldr: Local minimax formalizes sequential local optimality and, under mild conditions and with degeneracies excepted, characterizes stable gradient descent-ascent limit points.

title: What is Local Optimality in Nonconvex-Nonconcave Minimax Optimization?

abstract: In this paper we address a variant of the continuous multi-armed bandits problem, called the threshold estimation problem, which is at the heart of many psychometric experiments. Here, the objective is to estimate the sensitivity threshold for an unknown psychometric function Psi, which is assumed to be non decreasing and continuous. Our algorithm, Dichotomous Optimistic Search (DOS), efficiently solves this task by taking inspiration from hierarchical multi-armed bandits and Black-box optimization. Compared to previous approaches, DOS is model free and only makes minimal assumption on Psi smoothness, while having strong theoretical guarantees that compares favorably to recent methods from both Psychophysics and Global Optimization. We also empirically evaluate DOS and show that it significantly outperforms these methods, both in experiments that mimics the conduct of a psychometric experiment, and in tests with large pulls budgets that illustrate the faster convergence rate.

paragraphs: Psychometric experiments often aim to identify a sensitivity threshold: a point on a function describing how responses change with a stimulus. This paper treats that task as a threshold estimation problem within continuous multi-armed bandits. The unknown psychometric function is assumed to be continuous and nondecreasing, so its response level does not fall as the stimulus increases.

The authors introduce Dichotomous Optimistic Search, or DOS, drawing on hierarchical bandit methods and black-box optimization. Its central appeal is that it is model free: it does not require choosing a particular model for the psychometric function. It still relies on the stated continuity and monotonicity assumptions and makes minimal additional assumptions about smoothness.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees that the authors describe as comparing favorably with recent approaches from psychophysics and global optimization. This matters because the method combines flexibility about the function’s shape with mathematical support for its threshold estimates, rather than relying solely on experimental performance.

The empirical evaluation reports significant improvements over those approaches in settings designed to mimic psychometric experiments. Separate tests with large sampling budgets illustrate faster convergence. Together, these findings support DOS as an efficient threshold estimation method in the evaluated settings, including when many observations are available to refine the estimate.
summary.tldr: Dichotomous Optimistic Search estimates perceptual thresholds with minimal assumptions about function shape, favorable theoretical guarantees, and stronger empirical performance than the compared methods.

title: Dichotomous Optimistic Search to Quantify Human Perception

abstract: Learning to flexibly follow task instructions in dynamic environments poses interesting challenges for reinforcement learning agents. We focus here on the problem of learning control flow that deviates from a strict step-by-step execution of instructions{—}that is, control flow that may skip forward over parts of the instructions or return backward to previously completed or skipped steps. Demand for such flexible control arises in two fundamental ways: explicitly when control is specified in the instructions themselves (such as conditional branching and looping) and implicitly when stochastic environment dynamics require re-completion of instructions whose effects have been perturbed, or opportunistic skipping of instructions whose effects are already present. We formulate an attention-based architecture that meets these challenges by learning, from task reward only, to flexibly attend to and condition behavior on an internal encoding of the instructions. We test the architecture’s ability to learn both explicit and implicit control in two illustrative domains—one inspired by Minecraft and the other by StarCraft—and show that the architecture exhibits zero-shot generalization to novel instructions of length greater than those in a training set, at a performance level unmatched by three baseline recurrent architectures and one ablation architecture.

paragraphs: Following instructions in a changing environment can require more than completing steps in order. An agent may need to revisit a step whose effect has been undone or skip one whose goal is already satisfied. Instructions can also explicitly demand branching and repetition. The paper studies learning both kinds of flexible control flow.

The proposed architecture uses attention over an internal encoding of the instructions. It learns which parts to attend to and how to condition its behavior on them using task reward alone. This allows control to move backward or forward through the instruction sequence as required by the instructions or by changes in the environment.

The authors test the architecture in two illustrative domains inspired by Minecraft and StarCraft. It generalizes without additional training to novel instructions longer than those used during training. Its performance in these tests exceeds that of three recurrent baselines and an ablated architecture. The results support attention as a useful mechanism for learning flexible instruction execution in the evaluated environments.
summary.tldr: An attention-based reinforcement learning agent learns to skip and revisit instruction steps and generalizes to longer unseen instructions in two domains.

title: Reinforcement Learning of Implicit and Explicit Control Flow Instructions

abstract: In this paper, we consider algorithm independent lower bounds for the problem of black-box optimization of functions having a bounded norm is some Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), which can be viewed as a non-Bayesian Gaussian process bandit problem. In the standard noisy setting, we provide a novel proof technique for deriving lower bounds on the regret, with benefits including simplicity, versatility, and an improved dependence on the error probability. In a robust setting in which the final point is perturbed by an adversary, we strengthen an existing lower bound that only holds for target success probabilities very close to one, by allowing for arbitrary target success probabilities in (0, 1). Furthermore, in a distinct robust setting in which every sampled point may be perturbed by a constrained adversary, we provide a novel lower bound for deterministic strategies, demonstrating an inevitable joint dependence of the cumulative regret on the corruption level and the time horizon, in contrast with existing lower bounds that only characterize the individual dependencies.

paragraphs: This paper studies fundamental limits on black-box optimization for functions with bounded norm in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The setting can be viewed as a non-Bayesian Gaussian process bandit problem. Its lower bounds describe difficulty inherent to the problem rather than shortcomings of a particular optimization algorithm.

For standard noisy observations, the authors introduce a proof technique that is simpler and more versatile and improves dependence on the allowed error probability. They then consider a robust setting where an adversary perturbs the final selected point. An existing lower bound is strengthened to cover any target success probability strictly between zero and one.

A separate robust setting permits a constrained adversary to perturb every sampled point. Here, the new lower bound applies to deterministic strategies and captures an unavoidable joint dependence of cumulative regret on corruption level and time horizon. This goes beyond bounds that describe those dependencies separately, clarifying how repeated sampling and adversarial interference combine to limit achievable performance.
summary.tldr: The paper strengthens lower bounds for noisy and adversarially perturbed kernel-bandit optimization, including joint corruption-and-horizon limits for deterministic strategies.

title: On Lower Bounds for Standard and Robust Gaussian Process Bandit Optimization

abstract: Influence maximization is the task of selecting a small number of seed nodes in a social network to maximize the spread of the influence from these seeds, and it has been widely investigated in the past two decades. In the canonical setting, the whole social network as well as its diffusion parameters is given as input. In this paper, we consider the more realistic sampling setting where the network is unknown and we only have a set of passively observed cascades that record the set of activated nodes at each diffusion step. We study the task of influence maximization from these cascade samples (IMS), and present constant approximation algorithms for this task under mild conditions on the seed set distribution. To achieve the optimization goal, we also provide a novel solution to the network inference problem, that is, learning diffusion parameters and the network structure from the cascade data. Comparing with prior solutions, our network inference algorithm requires weaker assumptions and does not rely on maximum-likelihood estimation and convex programming. Our IMS algorithms enhance the learning-and-then-optimization approach by allowing a constant approximation ratio even when the diffusion parameters are hard to learn, and we do not need any assumption related to the network structure or diffusion parameters.

paragraphs: Influence maximization selects a small set of starting nodes to spread influence widely through a network. Standard formulations assume the network and its diffusion parameters are available. This paper instead starts with an unknown network and passively observed cascades that record which nodes became active at each step.

The authors develop algorithms with constant-factor approximation guarantees under mild conditions on the distribution of initial seed sets. They also introduce a network inference method for learning structure and diffusion parameters from cascade data. Compared with prior solutions, this method requires weaker assumptions and avoids maximum-likelihood estimation and convex programming.

A central result is that useful influence optimization remains possible even when diffusion parameters are difficult to learn. The algorithms strengthen the learn-then-optimize approach by retaining a constant approximation guarantee in that situation. They require no assumptions about network structure or diffusion parameters, while still relying on the stated conditions on seed distributions. This separates the information needed for effective seed selection from the potentially harder task of accurately recovering every diffusion parameter.
summary.tldr: Observed diffusion cascades can support constant-factor influence maximization under seed-distribution conditions, even when diffusion parameters are hard to learn.

title: Network Inference and Influence Maximization from Samples

abstract: We consider the problem of learning structures and parameters of Continuous-time Bayesian Networks (CTBNs) from time-course data under minimal experimental resources. In practice, the cost of generating experimental data poses a bottleneck, especially in the natural and social sciences. A popular approach to overcome this is Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED). However, BOED becomes infeasible in high-dimensional settings, as it involves integration over all possible experimental outcomes. We propose a novel criterion for experimental design based on a variational approximation of the expected information gain. We show that for CTBNs, a semi-analytical expression for this criterion can be calculated for structure and parameter learning. By doing so, we can replace sampling over experimental outcomes by solving the CTBNs master-equation, for which scalable approximations exist. This alleviates the computational burden of sampling possible experimental outcomes in high-dimensions. We employ this framework to recommend interventional sequences. In this context, we extend the CTBN model to conditional CTBNs to incorporate interventions. We demonstrate the performance of our criterion on synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose experiments when learning a continuous-time Bayesian network from observations collected over time. The goal is to learn both the network structure and its parameters while using limited experimental resources. Choosing informative experiments matters because obtaining new data can be expensive in the natural and social sciences.

Bayesian optimal experimental design evaluates experiments through their possible outcomes, but accounting for all those outcomes becomes computationally difficult in high dimensions. The authors introduce a criterion based on a variational approximation to expected information gain. For these networks, they derive a partly analytical expression that replaces sampling experimental outcomes with solving the network’s master equation, for which scalable approximations are available.

The framework recommends sequences of interventions, supported by an extension to conditional continuous-time Bayesian networks that represents those interventions. Evaluations use synthetic and real-world data. The contribution is a more computationally manageable way to select informative experiments for both structure and parameter learning, with approximation central to making the calculation practical.
summary.tldr: A variational experimental-design criterion makes choosing informative interventions for continuous-time Bayesian networks more computationally manageable.

title: Active Learning of Continuous-time Bayesian Networks through Interventions

abstract: Recently Homomorphic Encryption (HE) is used to implement Privacy-Preserving Neural Networks (PPNNs) that perform inferences directly on encrypted data without decryption. Prior PPNNs adopt mobile network architectures such as SqueezeNet for smaller computing overhead, but we find naïvely using mobile network architectures for a PPNN does not necessarily achieve shorter inference latency. Despite having less parameters, a mobile network architecture typically introduces more layers and increases the HE multiplicative depth of a PPNN, thereby prolonging its inference latency. In this paper, we propose a \textbf{HE}-friendly privacy-preserving \textbf{M}obile neural n\textbf{ET}work architecture, \textbf{HEMET}. Experimental results show that, compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) PPNNs, HEMET reduces the inference latency by $59.3%\sim 61.2%$, and improves the inference accuracy by $0.4 % \sim 0.5%$.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption allows neural networks to perform inference directly on encrypted data without decrypting it. Designing a fast network for this setting requires attention to the costs of encrypted computation. This paper examines why using an ordinary mobile architecture does not necessarily produce a low-latency privacy-preserving network.

The authors identify a mismatch between parameter count and encrypted inference time. A mobile network may contain fewer parameters while introducing more layers. Those layers can increase multiplicative depth under homomorphic encryption, which in turn prolongs inference. Consequently, reducing model size alone does not reliably address the computational burden that matters in this setting.

HEMET is a mobile neural network architecture designed to be friendly to homomorphic encryption. In the reported experiments, it reduces inference latency by 59.3%–61.2% and improves inference accuracy by 0.4%–0.5% relative to the state-of-the-art privacy-preserving networks compared. The results show the practical value of matching architecture design to encrypted execution costs. They also explain why a network chosen for efficiency in ordinary computation may need a different design when its inputs remain encrypted.
summary.tldr: HEMET designs mobile networks around homomorphic-encryption costs, substantially reducing encrypted inference latency in reported experiments.

title: HEMET: A Homomorphic-Encryption-Friendly Privacy-Preserving Mobile Neural Network Architecture

abstract: This paper introduces the offline meta-reinforcement learning (offline meta-RL) problem setting and proposes an algorithm that performs well in this setting. Offline meta-RL is analogous to the widely successful supervised learning strategy of pre-training a model on a large batch of fixed, pre-collected data (possibly from various tasks) and fine-tuning the model to a new task with relatively little data. That is, in offline meta-RL, we meta-train on fixed, pre-collected data from several tasks and adapt to a new task with a very small amount (less than 5 trajectories) of data from the new task. By nature of being offline, algorithms for offline meta-RL can utilize the largest possible pool of training data available and eliminate potentially unsafe or costly data collection during meta-training. This setting inherits the challenges of offline RL, but it differs significantly because offline RL does not generally consider a) transfer to new tasks or b) limited data from the test task, both of which we face in offline meta-RL. Targeting the offline meta-RL setting, we propose Meta-Actor Critic with Advantage Weighting (MACAW). MACAW is an optimization-based meta-learning algorithm that uses simple, supervised regression objectives for both the inner and outer loop of meta-training. On offline variants of common meta-RL benchmarks, we empirically find that this approach enables fully offline meta-reinforcement learning and achieves notable gains over prior methods.
