paragraphs: This paper introduces offline meta-reinforcement learning: learning across tasks from fixed, previously collected data, then adapting to a new task using very little additional data. The stated adaptation setting uses fewer than five trajectories from the new task. Its motivation parallels pretraining and fine-tuning, with experience from several tasks preparing a model for rapid adaptation.

Keeping meta-training offline allows reuse of available training data and avoids potentially unsafe or expensive data collection during that phase. The problem nevertheless includes two requirements beyond ordinary offline reinforcement learning: transfer to unfamiliar tasks and adaptation with scarce test-task data. Both must be addressed while learning from a fixed collection of experience.

The proposed algorithm, MACAW, is an optimization-based meta-learning method that uses supervised regression objectives in both the inner and outer training loops. Experiments on offline versions of common meta-learning benchmarks show that it enables fully offline meta-reinforcement learning and achieves notable improvements over prior methods. The findings support this approach to learning transferable behavior from existing experience.
summary.tldr: MACAW learns from fixed multi-task experience and adapts to new reinforcement-learning tasks with fewer than five trajectories.

title: Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Advantage Weighting

abstract: We consider a stochastic contextual bandit problem where the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors is potentially large, however, only a sparse subset of features of cardinality $s_0 \ll d$ affect the reward function. Essentially all existing algorithms for sparse bandits require a priori knowledge of the value of the sparsity index $s_0$. This knowledge is almost never available in practice, and misspecification of this parameter can lead to severe deterioration in the performance of existing methods. The main contribution of this paper is to propose an algorithm that does not require prior knowledge of the sparsity index $s_0$ and establish tight regret bounds on its performance under mild conditions. We also comprehensively evaluate our proposed algorithm numerically and show that it consistently outperforms existing methods, even when the correct sparsity index is revealed to them but is kept hidden from our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper considers contextual bandits with many available features but only a small subset that affects rewards. A learner must make decisions while discovering which information is useful. Existing sparse-bandit methods commonly require the number of relevant features in advance, even though that quantity is rarely known in practice.

The proposed algorithm removes the need to supply this sparsity index. That matters because specifying the wrong number can severely degrade existing methods’ performance. Under conditions described as mild, the authors establish tight regret bounds, giving theoretical control over the accumulated cost of the algorithm’s decisions without assuming prior knowledge of the relevant feature count.

A comprehensive numerical evaluation reports that the method consistently outperforms existing approaches. The comparison even gives those approaches the correct sparsity index while withholding it from the proposed algorithm. These results support the practical value of adapting without that input, alongside the conditional theoretical guarantees. The contribution is specifically about learning in sparse high-dimensional bandits without requiring the sparsity level to be known beforehand.
summary.tldr: A sparse contextual-bandit algorithm achieves tight regret bounds without knowing how many features affect rewards.

title: Sparsity-Agnostic Lasso Bandit

abstract: Designing off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms is typically a very challenging task, because a desirable iteration update often involves an expectation over an on-policy distribution. Prior off-policy actor-critic (AC) algorithms have introduced a new critic that uses the density ratio for adjusting the distribution mismatch in order to stabilize the convergence, but at the cost of potentially introducing high biases due to the estimation errors of both the density ratio and value function. In this paper, we develop a doubly robust off-policy AC (DR-Off-PAC) for discounted MDP, which can take advantage of learned nuisance functions to reduce estimation errors. Moreover, DR-Off-PAC adopts a single timescale structure, in which both actor and critics are updated simultaneously with constant stepsize, and is thus more sample efficient than prior algorithms that adopt either two timescale or nested-loop structure. We study the finite-time convergence rate and characterize the sample complexity for DR-Off-PAC to attain an $\epsilon$-accurate optimal policy. We also show that the overall convergence of DR-Off-PAC is doubly robust to the approximation errors that depend only on the expressive power of approximation functions. To the best of our knowledge, our study establishes the first overall sample complexity analysis for single time-scale off-policy AC algorithm.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning must learn from data whose distribution differs from the distribution associated with the policy being optimized. Actor-critic methods can correct this mismatch using estimated density ratios. However, errors in those ratios and in the estimated value function can introduce substantial bias into the updates.

The paper proposes DR-Off-PAC, a doubly robust actor-critic method for discounted Markov decision processes. It uses learned auxiliary functions to reduce estimation errors. The actor and critics update simultaneously on a single timescale with constant stepsizes, avoiding the two-timescale or nested-loop organization used by prior algorithms discussed in the paper.

The authors analyze finite-time convergence and the number of samples needed to obtain an epsilon-accurate optimal policy. They also establish double robustness of overall convergence to approximation errors associated with the expressive power of the chosen function approximators. The contribution brings robustness analysis together with a simpler update schedule, which the paper identifies as more sample efficient than those prior structures. Its guarantees explicitly account for function-approximation error.
summary.tldr: DR-Off-PAC combines doubly robust estimation with simultaneous actor-critic updates and analyzes its convergence, sample complexity, and approximation errors.

title: Doubly Robust Off-Policy Actor-Critic: Convergence and Optimality

abstract: We analyze the properties of adversarial training for learning adversarially robust halfspaces in the presence of agnostic label noise. Denoting $\mathsf{OPT}_{p,r}$ as the best classification error achieved by a halfspace that is robust to perturbations of $\ell^{p}$ balls of radius $r$, we show that adversarial training on the standard binary cross-entropy loss yields adversarially robust halfspaces up to classification error $\tilde O(\sqrt{\mathsf{OPT}_{2,r}})$ for $p=2$, and $\tilde O(d^{1/4} \sqrt{\mathsf{OPT}_{\infty, r}})$ when $p=\infty$. Our results hold for distributions satisfying anti-concentration properties enjoyed by log-concave isotropic distributions among others. We additionally show that if one instead uses a non-convex sigmoidal loss, adversarial training yields halfspaces with an improved robust classification error of $O(\mathsf{OPT}_{2,r})$ for $p=2$, and $O(d^{1/4} \mathsf{OPT}_{\infty, r})$ when $p=\infty$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work showing that adversarial training provably yields robust classifiers in the presence of noise.

Our results hold for distributions satisfying anti-concentration properties enjoyed by log-concave isotropic distributions among others. We additionally show that if one instead uses a non-convex sigmoidal loss, adversarial training yields halfspaces with an improved robust classification error of $O(\mathsf{OPT}_{2,r})$ for $p=2$, and $O(d^{1/4} \mathsf{OPT}_{\infty, r})$ when $p=\infty$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work showing that adversarial training provably yields robust classifiers in the presence of noise.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to learn classifiers that withstand input perturbations, but incorrect labels complicate that goal. This paper studies linear decision boundaries, or halfspaces, with agnostic label noise. It measures performance relative to the best robust halfspace available for a specified perturbation radius, allowing the benchmark itself to have nonzero error.

For standard binary cross-entropy, the authors bound robust error by roughly the square root of that benchmark error for Euclidean perturbations. For maximum-coordinate perturbations, the bound also includes a factor of the dimension raised to one quarter. These guarantees require anti-concentration properties of the input distribution, satisfied by isotropic log-concave distributions among others.

Using a nonconvex sigmoidal loss improves the dependence from square-root to linear in the benchmark error, while retaining the dimension factor for maximum-coordinate perturbations. This makes the loss choice consequential for the provable quality of robust learning. The paper establishes that adversarial training can yield robust classifiers despite label noise within the analyzed setting, rather than requiring perfectly labeled data.
summary.tldr: Under anti-concentration assumptions, adversarial training learns noise-tolerant robust halfspaces, with stronger error guarantees from a sigmoidal loss.

title: Provable Robustness of Adversarial Training for Learning Halfspaces with Noise

abstract: The Contextual Graph Markov Model (CGMM) is a deep, unsupervised, and probabilistic model for graphs that is trained incrementally on a layer-by-layer basis. As with most Deep Graph Networks, an inherent limitation is the need to perform an extensive model selection to choose the proper size of each layer’s latent representation. In this paper, we address this problem by introducing the Infinite Contextual Graph Markov Model (iCGMM), the first deep Bayesian nonparametric model for graph learning. During training, iCGMM can adapt the complexity of each layer to better fit the underlying data distribution. On 8 graph classification tasks, we show that iCGMM: i) successfully recovers or improves CGMM’s performances while reducing the hyper-parameters’ search space; ii) performs comparably to most end-to-end supervised methods. The results include studies on the importance of depth, hyper-parameters, and compression of the graph embeddings. We also introduce a novel approximated inference procedure that better deals with larger graph topologies.

paragraphs: The Contextual Graph Markov Model learns probabilistic graph representations without supervision, training one layer at a time. A practical difficulty is choosing the size of the hidden representation in each layer. Searching over those sizes can require extensive model selection, as it does for many deep graph networks.

The paper introduces iCGMM, a Bayesian nonparametric extension that adapts each layer’s complexity during training to better fit the data distribution. This reduces the need to choose representation sizes through a separate search. The authors also develop an approximate inference procedure intended to handle larger graph topologies more effectively.

Across eight graph-classification tasks, iCGMM matches or improves the original model’s performance while reducing the hyperparameter search space. It also performs comparably to most evaluated end-to-end supervised methods. Additional studies examine depth, hyperparameters, and compression of graph embeddings. Together, these results support adapting representation complexity within training as a useful alternative to extensively searching over fixed layer sizes.
summary.tldr: iCGMM adapts graph-representation complexity during training, reducing model-selection demands while maintaining or improving evaluated performance.

title: The Infinite Contextual Graph Markov Model

abstract: We study reinforcement learning with linear function approximation where the transition probability and reward functions are linear with respect to a feature mapping $\boldsymbol{\phi}(s,a)$. Specifically, we consider the episodic inhomogeneous linear Markov Decision Process (MDP), and propose a novel computation-efficient algorithm, LSVI-UCB$^+$, which achieves an $\widetilde{O}(Hd\sqrt{T})$ regret bound where $H$ is the episode length, $d$ is the feature dimension, and $T$ is the number of steps. LSVI-UCB$^+$ builds on weighted ridge regression and upper confidence value iteration with a Bernstein-type exploration bonus. Our statistical results are obtained with novel analytical tools, including a new Bernstein self-normalized bound with conservatism on elliptical potentials, and refined analysis of the correction term. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first minimax optimal algorithm for linear MDPs up to logarithmic factors, which closes the $\sqrt{Hd}$ gap between the best known upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{H^3d^3T})$ in \cite{jin2020provably} and lower bound of $\Omega(Hd\sqrt{T})$ for linear MDPs.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning under a specific structural assumption: rewards and transition probabilities are linear in a feature representation of states and actions. The setting consists of finite episodes whose dynamics may vary across steps. Within this linear Markov decision process framework, the objective is efficient learning with regret close to the best achievable worst-case rate.

The proposed algorithm, LSVI-UCB+, combines weighted ridge regression with upper-confidence value iteration and a Bernstein-type exploration bonus. These components support learning value estimates while accounting for uncertainty during exploration. The proof introduces a new Bernstein self-normalized bound and a refined treatment of a correction term needed for the statistical analysis.

The resulting regret bound scales as H times d times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, where H is episode length, d is feature dimension, and T counts steps. It matches the stated lower bound to that precision, closing a square-root-of-Hd gap in prior upper bounds. The near-optimality claim applies to the specified linear MDP setting.
summary.tldr: LSVI-UCB+ achieves computationally efficient learning with regret matching the linear-MDP minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: Nearly Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Combinatorial Optimisation problems arise in several application domains and are often formulated in terms of graphs. Many of these problems are NP-hard, but exact solutions are not always needed. Several heuristics have been developed to provide near-optimal solutions; however, they do not typically scale well with the size of the graph. We propose a low-complexity approach for identifying a (possibly much smaller) subgraph of the original graph where the heuristics can be run in reasonable time and with a high likelihood of finding a global near-optimal solution. The core component of our approach is LeNSE, a reinforcement learning algorithm that learns how to navigate the space of possible subgraphs using an Euclidean subgraph embedding as its map. To solve CO problems, LeNSE is provided with a discriminative embedding trained using any existing heuristics using only on a small portion of the original graph. When tested on three problems (vertex cover, max-cut and influence maximisation) using real graphs with up to $10$ million edges, LeNSE identifies small subgraphs yielding solutions comparable to those found by running the heuristics on the entire graph, but at a fraction of the total run time. Code for the experiments is available in the public GitHub repo at https://github.com/davidireland3/LeNSE.

paragraphs: Graph-based combinatorial optimization often relies on heuristics because exact solutions are difficult to obtain. Even heuristics can become expensive on large graphs. LeNSE tackles this cost by searching for a smaller subgraph where an existing heuristic can run quickly while retaining a high likelihood of finding a near-optimal solution for the original problem.

Its central component is a reinforcement-learning algorithm that navigates possible subgraphs using a Euclidean embedding as a map. The embedding is trained with an existing heuristic applied to only a small part of the original graph. This combines learned selection of where to search with the problem-solving ability of established heuristics.

The authors test vertex cover, max-cut, and influence maximization on real graphs containing up to ten million edges. The selected subgraphs yield solutions comparable to applying the heuristics to the entire graph, at a fraction of the runtime. These are empirical results showing that a carefully selected smaller search region can preserve solution quality while substantially reducing the work required.
summary.tldr: LeNSE learns to select small subgraphs where existing optimization heuristics achieve comparable solutions much faster in the reported experiments.

title: LeNSE: Learning To Navigate Subgraph Embeddings for Large-Scale Combinatorial Optimisation

abstract: Despite the extensive studies on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), how to reliably sample high-quality images from their latent spaces remains an under-explored topic. In this paper, we propose a novel GAN latent sampling method by exploring and exploiting the hubness priors of GAN latent distributions. Our key insight is that the high dimensionality of the GAN latent space will inevitably lead to the emergence of hub latents that usually have much larger sampling densities than other latents in the latent space. As a result, these hub latents are better trained and thus contribute more to the synthesis of high-quality images. Unlike the a posterior "cherry-picking", our method is highly efficient as it is an a priori method that identifies high-quality latents before the synthesis of images. Furthermore, we show that the well-known but purely empirical truncation trick is a naive approximation to the central clustering effect of hub latents, which not only uncovers the rationale of the truncation trick, but also indicates the superiority and fundamentality of our method. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Byronliang8/HubnessGANSampling.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to choose GAN latent inputs that are likely to generate high-quality images. Its starting point is hubness in high-dimensional latent spaces: some latent points typically have much higher sampling densities than others. The authors argue that these hub latents receive better training and contribute more to high-quality synthesis.

The proposed sampling method uses this hubness information to identify promising latent inputs before images are generated. That timing is central to its efficiency: selection takes place in latent space, without first synthesizing a collection of images and then choosing the most appealing outputs. The method therefore makes latent selection part of the generation procedure itself.

The authors also interpret the familiar truncation trick as a simple approximation to the tendency of hub latents to cluster centrally. This supplies a rationale for an otherwise empirical technique and motivates using hubness more directly. Extensive experiments support the proposed sampling method's effectiveness, connecting the structure of the latent distribution to the quality of generated images.
summary.tldr: Hubness-based sampling identifies promising GAN latent inputs before image generation and explains the truncation trick through hub clustering.

title: Exploring and Exploiting Hubness Priors for High-Quality GAN Latent Sampling

abstract: Recent progress in state-only imitation learning extends the scope of applicability of imitation learning to real-world settings by relieving the need for observing expert actions. However, existing solutions only learn to extract a state-to-action mapping policy from the data, without considering how the expert plans to the target. This hinders the ability to leverage demonstrations and limits the flexibility of the policy. In this paper, we introduce Decoupled Policy Optimization (DePO), which explicitly decouples the policy as a high-level state planner and an inverse dynamics model. With embedded decoupled policy gradient and generative adversarial training, DePO enables knowledge transfer to different action spaces or state transition dynamics, and can generalize the planner to out-of-demonstration state regions. Our in-depth experimental analysis shows the effectiveness of DePO on learning a generalized target state planner while achieving the best imitation performance. We demonstrate the appealing usage of DePO for transferring across different tasks by pre-training, and the potential for co-training agents with various skills.

paragraphs: State-only imitation learning uses demonstrations without requiring access to the expert's actions. The paper argues that learning only a direct mapping from states to actions leaves the expert's target-planning behavior implicit. That can reduce flexibility when transferring knowledge to an agent whose available actions or transition dynamics differ from those of the demonstrator.

Decoupled Policy Optimization, or DePO, separates the policy into a high-level state planner and an inverse dynamics model. The planner determines target states, while the inverse dynamics component connects state transitions to actions. The method trains this structure using a decoupled policy gradient together with generative adversarial training, providing distinct components for planning and action realization.

The reported experiments show effective target-state planning, generalization into state regions outside the demonstrations, and the best imitation performance in the evaluated comparisons. The authors also demonstrate transfer across tasks through pre-training and discuss the potential to co-train agents with different skills. These findings support separating transferable planning knowledge from the dynamics-dependent process of choosing actions.
summary.tldr: DePO separates target-state planning from action realization to make state-only imitation more flexible and transferable.

title: Plan Your Target and Learn Your Skills: Transferable State-Only Imitation Learning via Decoupled Policy Optimization

abstract: In constrained reinforcement learning (RL), a learning agent seeks to not only optimize the overall reward but also satisfy the additional safety, diversity, or budget constraints. Consequently, existing constrained RL solutions require several new algorithmic ingredients that are notably different from standard RL. On the other hand, reward-free RL is independently developed in the unconstrained literature, which learns the transition dynamics without using the reward information, and thus naturally capable of addressing RL with multiple objectives under the common dynamics. This paper bridges reward-free RL and constrained RL. Particularly, we propose a simple meta-algorithm such that given any reward-free RL oracle, the approachability and constrained RL problems can be directly solved with negligible overheads in sample complexity. Utilizing the existing reward-free RL solvers, our framework provides sharp sample complexity results for constrained RL in the tabular MDP setting, matching the best existing results up to a factor of horizon dependence; our framework directly extends to a setting of tabular two-player Markov games, and gives a new result for constrained RL with linear function approximation.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning asks an agent to earn reward while also meeting requirements such as safety or budget limits. These additional objectives often lead to algorithms with machinery beyond ordinary reinforcement learning. This paper connects the problem to reward-free learning, where an agent learns how the environment changes without relying on a particular reward signal.

The connection matters because several objectives can share the same environment dynamics. Knowledge gathered without committing to one reward can therefore support decisions about multiple objectives. The authors propose a general procedure that uses a reward-free reinforcement learning solver to address both constrained learning and approachability problems, adding negligible overhead in the number of samples required.

With existing reward-free solvers, the framework yields sample-complexity guarantees for tabular decision processes that match the best existing results apart from a horizon-dependent factor. It also extends to tabular two-player Markov games and provides a new result with linear function approximation. These findings make reward-free learning a reusable foundation for several constrained decision problems.
summary.tldr: A general procedure converts reward-free reinforcement learning solvers into constrained-learning methods with negligible additional sample complexity.

title: A Simple Reward-free Approach to Constrained Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields (GNeRF) are one of the most promising real-world solutions for novel view synthesis, thanks to their cross-scene generalization capability and thus the possibility of instant rendering on new scenes. While adversarial robustness is essential for real-world applications, little study has been devoted to understanding its implication on GNeRF. We hypothesize that because GNeRF is implemented by conditioning on the source views from new scenes, which are often acquired from the Internet or third-party providers, there are potential new security concerns regarding its real-world applications. Meanwhile, existing understanding and solutions for neural networks’ adversarial robustness may not be applicable to GNeRF, due to its 3D nature and uniquely diverse operations. To this end, we present NeRFool, which to the best of our knowledge is the first work that sets out to understand the adversarial robustness of GNeRF. Specifically, NeRFool unveils the vulnerability patterns and important insights regarding GNeRF’s adversarial robustness. Built upon the above insights gained from NeRFool, we further develop NeRFool$^+$, which integrates two techniques capable of effectively attacking GNeRF across a wide range of target views, and provide guidelines for defending against our proposed attacks. We believe that our NeRFool/NeRFool$^+$ lays the initial foundation for future innovations in developing robust real-world GNeRF solutions. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/GATECH-EIC/NeRFool.

paragraphs: Generalizable neural radiance fields can render new scenes by conditioning on source views, making cross-scene use possible without building an entirely separate model for each scene. The paper identifies a potential security concern in this setup: source images may come from the internet or third parties and may contain adversarial perturbations.

NeRFool studies the resulting vulnerability patterns. The authors argue that existing robustness knowledge for neural networks may not transfer directly because these models involve three-dimensional structure and a distinctive collection of operations. Their investigation is intended to establish how adversarial robustness behaves in this setting and identify insights specific to generalizable radiance fields.

Building on that analysis, NeRFool+ combines two techniques that effectively attack rendering across a broad range of target views. The paper also provides guidelines for defending against the proposed attacks. Its contribution is an initial account of vulnerabilities and attack behavior, together with directions for defense. The authors frame this work as a foundation for future robust systems rather than a completed solution to generalizable radiance-field security.
summary.tldr: NeRFool analyzes adversarial vulnerabilities in generalizable radiance fields and develops attacks effective across many target views.

title: NeRFool: Uncovering the Vulnerability of Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields against Adversarial Perturbations

abstract: Population-based search has recently emerged as a possible alternative to Reinforcement Learning (RL) for black-box neural architecture search (NAS). It performs well in practice even though it is not theoretically well understood. In particular, whereas traditional population-based search methods such as evolutionary algorithms (EAs) draw much power from crossover operations, it is difficult to take advantage of them in NAS. The main obstacle is believed to be the permutation problem: The mapping between genotype and phenotype in traditional graph representations is many-to-one, leading to a disruptive effect of standard crossover. This paper presents the first theoretical analysis of the behaviors of mutation, crossover and RL in black-box NAS, and proposes a new crossover operator based on the shortest edit path (SEP) in graph space. The SEP crossover is shown theoretically to overcome the permutation problem, and as a result, have a better expected improvement compared to mutation, standard crossover and RL. Further, it empirically outperform these other methods on state-of-the-art NAS benchmarks. The SEP crossover therefore allows taking full advantage of population-based search in NAS, and the underlying theory can serve as a foundation for deeper understanding of black-box NAS methods in general.

paragraphs: Evolutionary neural architecture search maintains a population of candidate networks and can combine candidates through crossover. However, different graph encodings can describe the same underlying architecture. This many-to-one relationship creates the permutation problem: a crossover that operates on the encodings can disrupt useful structure because their apparent differences do not reliably reflect architectural differences.

The paper introduces a crossover operator based on a shortest edit path in graph space. It also provides a theoretical analysis of mutation, crossover, and reinforcement learning in black-box architecture search. Within that analysis, the proposed operator overcomes the permutation problem and has better expected improvement than mutation, standard crossover, and reinforcement learning.

Experiments on established architecture-search benchmarks also show the proposed crossover outperforming those alternatives. The theoretical result concerns expected improvement, rather than promising that every individual crossover will produce a better architecture. Together, the analysis and experiments support using graph-space relationships to make crossover more effective and to better understand the behavior of population-based architecture search.
summary.tldr: Shortest edit path crossover addresses equivalent graph encodings and improves expected and empirical performance in neural architecture search.

title: Shortest Edit Path Crossover: A Theory-driven Solution to the Permutation Problem in Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Explainability methods for NLP systems encounter a version of the fundamental problem of causal inference: for a given ground-truth input text, we never truly observe the counterfactual texts necessary for isolating the causal effects of model representations on outputs. In response, many explainability methods make no use of counterfactual texts, assuming they will be unavailable. In this paper, we show that robust causal explainability methods can be created using approximate counterfactuals, which can be written by humans to approximate a specific counterfactual or simply sampled using metadata-guided heuristics. The core of our proposal is the Causal Proxy Model (CPM). A CPM explains a black-box model $\mathcal{N}$ because it is trained to have the same actual input/output behavior as $\mathcal{N}$ while creating neural representations that can be intervened upon to simulate the counterfactual input/output behavior of $\mathcal{N}$. Furthermore, we show that the best CPM for $\mathcal{N}$ performs comparably to $\mathcal{N}$ in making factual predictions, which means that the CPM can simply replace $\mathcal{N}$, leading to more explainable deployed models.

paragraphs: Explaining a language model causally requires asking how its output would change under an appropriate counterfactual input. For an observed text, the exact counterfactual texts needed to isolate representation effects are unavailable. The paper investigates whether approximate counterfactuals can still support robust causal explanations, instead of abandoning counterfactual information altogether.

Its central proposal is the Causal Proxy Model, or CPM. A CPM learns to reproduce a black-box model's ordinary input-output behavior while developing internal representations that can be intervened on. Those interventions are trained to simulate the black box's counterfactual behavior. Approximate counterfactual texts can come from human-written edits or sampling heuristics guided by metadata.

This gives the proxy two connected responsibilities: matching factual predictions and supporting meaningful interventions for explanation. The authors also find that their best CPM makes factual predictions comparably to the original model. That result supports the possibility of deploying the proxy itself, making the model used for prediction more explainable while retaining comparable factual performance in the reported comparison.
summary.tldr: Causal Proxy Models use approximate counterfactual texts to imitate black-box predictions and support interventions for causal explanation.

title: Causal Proxy Models for Concept-based Model Explanations

abstract: Active clustering aims to boost the clustering performance by integrating human-annotated pairwise constraints through strategic querying. Conventional approaches with semi-supervised clustering schemes encounter high query costs when applied to large datasets with numerous classes. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Adaptive Active Aggregation and Splitting (A3S) framework, falling within the cluster-adjustment scheme in active clustering. A3S features strategic active clustering adjustment on the initial cluster result, which is obtained by an adaptive clustering algorithm. In particular, our cluster adjustment is inspired by the quantitative analysis of Normalized mutual information gain under the information theory framework and can provably improve the clustering quality. The proposed A3S framework significantly elevates the performance and scalability of active clustering. In extensive experiments across diverse real-world datasets, A3S achieves desired results with significantly fewer human queries compared with existing methods.

paragraphs: Active clustering uses strategically chosen human judgments about pairs of examples to improve how data are grouped. The challenge is making those judgments count: conventional methods can require too many queries when datasets are large and contain many classes. This paper develops A3S to improve clustering while reducing that annotation burden.

A3S begins with an initial grouping produced by an adaptive clustering algorithm. It then adjusts that grouping through aggregation and splitting, using pairwise constraints to guide the changes. Its adjustment strategy draws on an information-theoretic analysis of gains in normalized mutual information, connecting the choice of changes to a quantitative measure of clustering quality.

The authors provide a provable improvement result for their cluster adjustment and report extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets. In those evaluations, A3S reaches desired clustering results using substantially fewer human queries than existing methods. The contribution is therefore both a quality-driven way to refine clusters and evidence that this refinement can make active clustering more scalable.
summary.tldr: A3S strategically merges and splits initial clusters, improving clustering quality while requiring fewer human pairwise judgments in experiments.

title: A3S: A General Active Clustering Method with Pairwise Constraints

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, and organizations are racing to serve LLMs of varying sizes as endpoints for use-cases like chat, programming and search. However, efficiently serving multiple LLMs poses significant challenges for existing approaches due to varying popularity of LLMs. In the paper, we present MuxServe, a flexible spatial-temporal multiplexing system for efficient multiple LLM serving. The key insight behind is to colocate LLMs considering their popularity to multiplex memory resources, and leverage the characteristics of prefill and decoding phases to separate and flexibly colocate them to multiplex computation resources. MuxServe formally formulates the multiplexing problem, and proposes a novel placement algorithm and adaptive batch scheduling strategy to identify optimal colocations and maximize utilization. MuxServe designs a unified resource manager to enable flexible and efficient multiplexing. Evaluation results show that MuxServe can achieves up to $1.8\times$ higher throughput or processes $2.9\times$ more requests within $99%$ SLO attainment. The code is available at: https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/MuxServe.

paragraphs: Serving several language models efficiently is difficult when their popularity differs. Resource allocation must account for how much demand each model receives as well as the resources its requests consume. MuxServe addresses this problem by coordinating the placement and execution of multiple models so that memory and computation can be shared more effectively.

The system uses model popularity to guide colocation for memory sharing. It also distinguishes the prefill and decoding phases of inference, separating and flexibly colocating them according to their computational characteristics. A placement algorithm, adaptive batch scheduling, and a unified resource manager implement this approach around a formal formulation of the multiplexing problem.

The evaluation reports up to 1.8 times higher throughput, or 2.9 times as many processed requests while attaining service-level objectives for 99% of requests. These are reported evaluation outcomes, with the throughput figure explicitly an upper result. They show the potential value of scheduling around both model demand and inference phase when operating multiple language-model endpoints.
summary.tldr: MuxServe improves multi-LLM serving by coordinating model placement and scheduling around popularity, memory use, and inference phases.

title: MuxServe: Flexible Spatial-Temporal Multiplexing for Multiple LLM Serving

abstract: Robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) provide a framework for sequential decision-making that is robust to perturbations on the transition kernel. However, current RMDP methods are often limited to small-scale problems, hindering their use in high-dimensional domains. To bridge this gap, we present EWoK, a novel online approach to solve RMDP that Estimates the Worst transition Kernel to learn robust policies. Unlike previous works that regularize the policy or value updates, EWoK achieves robustness by simulating the worst scenarios for the agent while retaining complete flexibility in the learning process. Notably, EWoK can be applied on top of any off-the-shelf non-robust RL algorithm, enabling easy scaling to high-dimensional domains. Our experiments, spanning from simple Cartpole to high-dimensional DeepMind Control Suite environments, demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of the EWoK paradigm as a practical method for learning robust policies.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can be vulnerable when the environment’s transitions differ from those expected during training. Robust Markov decision processes address this uncertainty by accounting for perturbations to the transition kernel, which describes how actions lead to subsequent states. Existing methods often struggle to extend this framework beyond relatively small problems.

EWoK tackles that scaling challenge by estimating the worst transition kernel online and simulating adverse scenarios for the learning agent. Robustness is introduced through the scenarios the agent encounters. This leaves the policy-learning procedure flexible, rather than requiring specialized changes to its policy or value updates.

The authors present EWoK as a method that can be layered onto any off-the-shelf non-robust reinforcement learning algorithm. This modular design allows robust training to benefit from algorithms already suited to high-dimensional tasks. Experiments ranging from Cartpole to the DeepMind Control Suite demonstrate the approach’s practical effectiveness and applicability across environments of different complexity.
summary.tldr: EWoK trains robust policies by estimating and simulating adverse environment transitions while keeping the underlying reinforcement learning algorithm flexible.

title: Bring Your Own (Non-Robust) Algorithm to Solve Robust MDPs by Estimating The Worst Kernel

abstract: Large language models generate high-quality responses with potential misinformation, underscoring the need for regulation by distinguishing AI-generated and human-written texts. Watermarking is pivotal in this context, which involves embedding hidden markers in texts during the LLM inference phase, which is imperceptible to humans. Achieving both the detectability of inserted watermarks and the semantic quality of generated texts is challenging. While current watermarking algorithms have made promising progress in this direction, there remains significant scope for improvement. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel multi-objective optimization (MOO) approach for watermarking that utilizes lightweight networks to generate token-specific watermarking logits and splitting ratios. By leveraging MOO to optimize for both detection and semantic objective functions, our method simultaneously achieves detectability and semantic integrity. Experimental results show that our method outperforms current watermarking techniques in enhancing the detectability of texts generated by LLMs while maintaining their semantic coherence. Our code is available at https://github.com/mignonjia/TS_watermark.

paragraphs: Text watermarking modifies language-model generation so an automated detector can later recognize a statistical marker. Stronger markers can improve detection but may damage the meaning or fluency of the text. This paper treats that tension as a multi-objective optimization problem.

The proposed method uses lightweight networks to produce token-specific watermarking logits and splitting ratios. Its objectives explicitly address both detection and semantic quality, allowing the watermarking behavior to vary across tokens. The intended effect is to place detectable structure into generated text while preserving coherence rather than applying one uniform adjustment everywhere.

Experiments show better detectability than current watermarking methods while maintaining semantic coherence. The contribution is an adaptive generation-time watermark with an explicit quality objective. The abstract does not establish that every generated passage is detectable after arbitrary editing, nor that a detector can always distinguish all human and model writing; its claims concern the evaluated watermarking comparison.
summary.tldr: Token-specific multi-objective watermarking improves detection while preserving the reported semantic quality of generated text.

title: Token-Specific Watermarking with Enhanced Detectability and Semantic Coherence for Large Language Models

abstract: It is well known that LLMs cannot generalize well to long contexts whose lengths are larger than the training sequence length. This poses challenges when employing LLMs for processing long input sequences during inference. In this work, we argue that LLMs themselves have inherent capabilities to handles s long contexts without fine-tuning. To achieve this goal, we propose SelfExtend to extend the context window of LLMs by constructing bi-level attention information: the grouped attention and the neighbor attention. The grouped attention captures the dependencies among tokens that are far apart, while neighbor attention captures dependencies among adjacent tokens within a specified range. The two-level attentions are computed based on the original model’s self-attention mechanism during inference. With minor code modification, our SelfExtend can effortlessly extend existing LLMs’ context window without any fine-tuning. We conduct comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmarks and the results show that our SelfExtend can effectively extend existing LLMs’ context window length.

paragraphs: Language models often struggle when their input is longer than the sequences seen during training. SelfExtend explores whether an existing model can handle longer contexts through changes to inference alone. The authors argue that useful long-context capabilities are already present and can be accessed without fine-tuning the model.

The method constructs two levels of attention using the model’s original self-attention mechanism. Grouped attention captures relationships between tokens that are far apart. Neighbor attention handles relationships among nearby tokens within a specified range. Together, these mechanisms account for both distant context and local connections.

SelfExtend requires only minor code modifications and no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that it can effectively extend the context windows of existing language models. The contribution is therefore an inference-time strategy for making longer inputs usable with an already trained model. The findings support the proposed attention construction on the evaluated benchmarks without establishing that every model can process arbitrarily long inputs equally well.
summary.tldr: SelfExtend expands language-model context windows without fine-tuning by combining grouped attention for distant tokens with attention over nearby tokens.

title: LLM Maybe LongLM: SelfExtend LLM Context Window Without Tuning

abstract: A common approach to explaining NLP models is to use importance measures that express which tokens are important for a prediction. Unfortunately, such explanations are often wrong despite being persuasive. Therefore, it is essential to measure their faithfulness. One such metric is if tokens are truly important, then masking them should result in worse model performance. However, token masking introduces out-of-distribution issues, and existing solutions that address this are computationally expensive and employ proxy models. Furthermore, other metrics are very limited in scope. This work proposes an inherently faithfulness measurable model that addresses these challenges. This is achieved using a novel fine-tuning method that incorporates masking, such that masking tokens become in-distribution by design. This differs from existing approaches, which are completely model-agnostic but are inapplicable in practice. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by applying it to 16 different datasets and validate it using statistical in-distribution tests. The faithfulness is then measured with 9 different importance measures. Because masking is in-distribution, importance measures that themselves use masking become consistently more faithful. Additionally, because the model makes faithfulness cheap to measure, we can optimize explanations towards maximal faithfulness; thus, our model becomes indirectly inherently explainable.

paragraphs: Token-importance explanations claim to identify which words matter for a prediction, but a convincing explanation may misrepresent the model's behavior. One way to test it is to mask supposedly important tokens and check whether performance worsens. The problem is that masking can create inputs unlike those the model normally encounters, confusing the interpretation of the test.

This paper changes fine-tuning so that masked inputs belong to the model's intended input distribution. That makes masking a more suitable intervention for measuring explanation faithfulness. The approach builds this capability into the model, avoiding reliance on a separate proxy model for the measurement.

The authors apply the method to 16 datasets, use statistical tests to validate the distributional treatment of masking, and assess nine importance measures. Masking-based importance measures become consistently more faithful in their evaluation. Because faithfulness is also inexpensive to measure, explanations can be optimized against it. The contribution therefore connects model training, explanation evaluation, and explanation improvement within one approach.
summary.tldr: Fine-tuning with masking makes token-removal tests cheaper and more reliable for measuring and improving explanation faithfulness.

title: Faithfulness Measurable Masked Language Models

abstract: Most existing Large Language Model (LLM) benchmarks on scientific problem reasoning focus on problems grounded in high-school subjects and are confined to elementary algebraic operations. To systematically examine the reasoning capabilities required for solving complex scientific problems, we introduce an expansive benchmark suite SciBench for LLMs. SciBench contains a carefully curated dataset featuring a range of collegiate-level scientific problems from mathematics, chemistry, and physics domains. Based on the dataset, we conduct an in-depth benchmarking study of representative open-source and proprietary LLMs with various prompting strategies. The results reveal that current LLMs fall short of delivering satisfactory performance, with the best overall score of merely 43.22%. Furthermore, through a detailed user study, we categorize the errors made by LLMs into ten problem-solving abilities. Our analysis indicates that no single prompting strategy significantly outperforms the others and some strategies that demonstrate improvements in certain problem-solving skills could result in declines in other skills. We envision that SciBench will catalyze further developments in the reasoning abilities of LLMs, thereby ultimately contributing to scientific research and discovery.

paragraphs: Scientific reasoning benchmarks often emphasize high-school material and elementary algebra. SciBench broadens the evaluation to college-level mathematics, chemistry, and physics. Its purpose is to examine the abilities needed for more complex scientific problem solving through a carefully curated collection of problems across these domains.

The authors evaluate representative open-source and proprietary language models with several prompting strategies. The best overall score in their study is 43.22%, indicating substantial difficulty for the evaluated models. A detailed user study also organizes the models' errors into ten problem-solving abilities, giving a more informative view of performance than an overall score alone.

The prompting comparison finds no strategy that significantly outperforms the others overall. Some strategies improve particular abilities while reducing performance on others. This means prompt changes can produce uneven gains across the skills involved in scientific reasoning. SciBench contributes both a harder evaluation setting and an analysis of where performance breaks down, providing a basis for studying improvements in scientific problem solving.
summary.tldr: SciBench tests college-level scientific reasoning, finding a best evaluated score of 43.22% and no prompting strategy with a significant overall advantage.

title: SciBench: Evaluating College-Level Scientific Problem-Solving Abilities of Large Language Models

abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) for vision transformers (ViTs) has garnered significant attention due to its efficiency in compressing models. However, existing methods typically overlook the intricate interdependence between quantized weight and activation, leading to considerable quantization error. In this paper, we propose ERQ, a two-step PTQ approach meticulously crafted to sequentially reduce the quantization error arising from activation and weight quantization. ERQ first introduces Activation quantization error reduction (Aqer) that strategically formulates the minimization of activation quantization error as a Ridge Regression problem, tackling it by updating weights with full-precision. Subsequently, ERQ introduces Weight quantization error reduction (Wqer) that adopts an iterative approach to mitigate the quantization error induced by weight quantization. In each iteration, an empirically derived, efficient proxy is employed to refine the rounding directions of quantized weights, coupled with a Ridge Regression solver to curtail weight quantization error. Experimental results attest to the effectiveness of our approach. Notably, ERQ surpasses the state-of-the-art GPTQ by 22.36% in accuracy for W3A4 ViT-S.

paragraphs: ERQ is a post-training quantization method for compressing vision transformers. Quantization represents weights and activations at reduced numerical precision, introducing errors that can affect accuracy. The authors focus on the interaction between these two sources of error, arguing that existing methods often fail to account for their interdependence.

The method proceeds in two stages. Activation quantization error reduction first formulates compensation for activation errors as ridge regression, updating weights while they remain at full precision. Weight quantization error reduction then addresses errors from quantizing those weights. It iteratively adjusts weight-rounding directions using an empirically derived efficient proxy, together with a ridge-regression solver.

This sequence allows the weight adjustment to account for activation quantization before tackling the additional effects of weight quantization. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness. For the reported W3A4 ViT-S configuration, the abstract states that ERQ exceeds GPTQ by 22.36% in accuracy. That result pertains to the named configuration and illustrates the potential benefit of explicitly coordinating activation-error compensation with weight rounding.
summary.tldr: ERQ sequentially reduces activation and weight quantization errors to improve compressed vision transformers.

title: ERQ: Error Reduction for Post-Training Quantization of Vision Transformers

abstract: We design improved approximation algorithms for NP-hard graph problems by incorporating predictions (e.g., learned from past data). Our prediction model builds upon and extends the $\varepsilon$-prediction framework by Cohen-Addad, d’Orsi, Gupta, Lee, and Panigrahi (NeurIPS 2024). We consider an edge-based version of this model, where each edge provides two bits of information, corresponding to predictions about whether each of its endpoints belong to an optimal solution. Even with weak predictions where each bit is only $\varepsilon$-correlated with the true solution, this information allows us to break approximation barriers in the standard setting. We develop algorithms with improved approximation ratios for MaxCut, Vertex Cover, Set Cover, and Maximum Independent Set problems (among others). Across these problems, our algorithms share a unifying theme, where we separately satisfy constraints related to high degree vertices (using predictions) and low-degree vertices (without using predictions) and carefully combine the answers.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how predictions can improve approximation algorithms for difficult graph problems. The predictions may come from past data and provide partial information about an optimal solution. The authors extend an existing prediction framework to an edge-based setting, where each edge supplies two bits predicting whether its two endpoints belong to an optimal solution.

Even when each bit is only weakly correlated with the true solution, the authors show that this additional information can overcome approximation barriers from the standard setting. They develop improved approximation ratios for problems including MaxCut, Vertex Cover, Set Cover, and Maximum Independent Set. The result depends on the stated prediction model, which supplies information unavailable to ordinary algorithms.

A common strategy runs through the algorithms: use predictions to satisfy constraints associated with high-degree vertices, handle low-degree vertices without predictions, and carefully combine the two answers. This division explains how weak predictive information can still be useful. It concentrates that information on one part of the problem while retaining conventional algorithmic reasoning for the rest.
summary.tldr: Weak edge-based predictions enable improved approximation algorithms by guiding high-degree constraints while conventional methods handle low-degree vertices.

title: Improved Approximations for Hard Graph Problems using Predictions

abstract: While uncertainty estimation for graphs recently gained traction, most methods rely on homophily and deteriorate in heterophilic settings. We address this by analyzing message passing neural networks from an information-theoretic perspective and developing a suitable analog to data processing inequality to quantify information throughout the model’s layers. In contrast to non-graph domains, information about the node-level prediction target can increase with model depth if a node’s features are semantically different from its neighbors. Therefore, on heterophilic graphs, the latent embeddings of an MPNN each provide different information about the data distribution - different from homophilic settings. This reveals that considering all node representations simultaneously is a key design principle for epistemic uncertainty estimation on graphs beyond homophily. We empirically confirm this with a simple post-hoc density estimator on the joint node embedding space that provides state-of-the-art uncertainty on heterophilic graphs. At the same time, it matches prior work on homophilic graphs without explicitly exploiting homophily through post-processing.

paragraphs: Many graph uncertainty methods work best when connected nodes are similar, a property called homophily. Their performance can deteriorate on heterophilic graphs, where neighbors differ semantically. This paper studies that problem through an information-theoretic analysis of message-passing neural networks, examining what information their layers contain about a node's prediction target.

The authors develop an analogue of the data processing inequality suited to this setting. They show that information about the target can increase with depth when a node's features differ semantically from its neighbors. Consequently, representations at different layers can provide distinct information about the data distribution. This motivates considering those representations together when estimating epistemic uncertainty.

The proposed empirical implementation is a simple density estimator applied after training to the joint space of node embeddings. It achieves reported state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation on heterophilic graphs while matching previous work on homophilic graphs. It does so without post-processing that explicitly exploits homophily, supporting the broader design principle of combining information across layers.
summary.tldr: Combining node representations across layers improves uncertainty estimation on heterophilic graphs, supported by information-theoretic analysis and experiments.

title: Uncertainty Estimation for Heterophilic Graphs Through the Lens of Information Theory

abstract: Existing research on temporal knowledge graph completion treats temporal information as supplementary, without simulating various features of facts from a temporal perspective. This work summarizes features of temporalized facts from both diachronic and synchronic perspectives: (1) Diachronicity. Facts often exhibit varying characteristics and trends across different temporal domains; (2) Synchronicity. In specific temporal contexts, various relations between entities influence each other, generating latent semantics. To track above issues, we design a quaternion-based model, TeDS, which divides timestamps into diachronic and synchronic timestamps to support dual temporal perception: (a) Two composite quaternions fusing time and relation information are generated by reorganizing synchronic timestamp and relation quaternions, and Hamilton operator achieves their interaction. (b) Each time point is sequentially mapped to an angle and converted to scalar component of a quaternion using trigonometric functions to build diachronic timestamps. We then rotate relation by using Hamilton operator between it and diachronic timestamp. In this way, TeDS achieves deep integration of relations and time while accommodating different perspectives. Empirically, TeDS significantly outperforms SOTA models on six benchmarks.

paragraphs: Temporal knowledge-graph completion requires representing how facts depend on time. This paper separates two perspectives: diachronic information describes how facts vary across time, while synchronic information describes how relations influence one another within a particular temporal context. The authors argue that treating time as supplementary misses these distinct features.

TeDS represents both perspectives using quaternions. For synchronic modeling, it reorganizes time and relation quaternions into two combined representations and uses the Hamilton operator to model their interaction. For diachronic modeling, it maps time points to angles, applies trigonometric functions to form timestamp representations, and uses the Hamilton operator to rotate relations.

These operations integrate temporal information directly into the relation representations while preserving the distinction between change across time and interactions within a time context. Across six benchmarks, TeDS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models in the reported experiments. The results support using complementary temporal representations when completing knowledge graphs, with the model architecture explicitly designed around both kinds of temporal structure.
summary.tldr: TeDS uses quaternion representations to jointly model changes across time and interactions within temporal contexts for knowledge-graph completion.

title: TeDS: Joint Learning of Diachronic and Synchronic Perspectives in Quaternion Space for Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion

abstract: Safety aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to harmful fine-tuning attacks – a few harmful data mixed in the fine-tuning dataset can break the LLMs’s safety alignment. While several defenses have been proposed, our evaluation shows that existing defenses fail when some specific training hyper-parameters are chosen – a large learning rate or a large number of training epochs in the fine-tuning stage can easily invalidate the defense. To this end, we propose Antidote, a post-fine-tuning stage solution, which remains agnostic to the training hyper-parameters in the fine-tuning stage. Antidote relies on the philosophy that by removing the harmful parameters, the harmful model can be recovered from the harmful behaviors, regardless of how those harmful parameters are formed in the fine-tuning stage. With this philosophy, we introduce a one-shot pruning stage after harmful fine-tuning to remove the harmful weights that are responsible for the generation of harmful content. Despite its embarrassing simplicity, empirical results show that Antidote can reduce harmful score while maintaining accuracy on downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning can weaken a language model’s safety alignment even when only a small amount of harmful material enters the training dataset. This paper examines defenses against that problem and finds that their effectiveness can depend on training choices. In the authors’ evaluation, a large learning rate or many training epochs can invalidate existing defenses.

Antidote moves the intervention to after fine-tuning. It applies a single pruning stage intended to remove weights responsible for harmful outputs. The motivating idea is that removing harmful parameters can reduce harmful behavior regardless of how those parameters developed. Because the intervention occurs afterward, its design does not depend on the hyperparameters used during the fine-tuning stage.

Empirical results show that Antidote can lower harmful scores while preserving accuracy on downstream tasks. That finding supports post-training weight removal as a practical defense strategy in the evaluated settings. The abstract presents recovery through pruning as the method’s guiding philosophy, while the demonstrated outcome is a reduction in measured harmful behavior rather than a guarantee of complete safety.
summary.tldr: Antidote prunes harmful weights after fine-tuning, empirically reducing harmful behavior while maintaining downstream accuracy.

title: Antidote: Post-fine-tuning Safety Alignment for Large Language Models against Harmful Fine-tuning Attack

abstract: Speculative decoding (SPD) aims to accelerate the auto-regressive token generation process of a target Large Language Model (LLM). Some approaches employ a draft model with multiple heads to predict a sequence of future tokens, where each head handles a token in the sequence. The target LLM verifies the predicted sequence and accepts aligned tokens, enabling efficient multi-token generation. However, existing methods assume that all tokens within a sequence are equally important, employing identical head structures and relying on a single-generation paradigm, either serial or parallel. To this end, we theoretically demonstrate that initial tokens in the draft sequence are more important than later ones. Building on this insight, we propose Gumiho, a hybrid model combining serial and parallel heads. Specifically, given the critical importance of early tokens, we employ a sophisticated Transformer architecture for the early draft heads in a serial configuration to improve accuracy. For later tokens, we utilize multiple lightweight MLP heads operating in parallel to enhance efficiency. By allocating more advanced model structures and longer running times to the early heads, Gumiho achieves improved overall performance. The experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, fully validating its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/AMD-AIG-AIMA/Gumiho.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up autoregressive generation by having a draft model propose several future tokens for a target language model to verify. Multi-head draft models assign different prediction heads to positions in that proposed sequence. Gumiho questions the practice of giving every position the same architecture and treating all draft tokens as equally important.

The authors theoretically establish that earlier tokens matter more than later ones. Their hybrid design allocates more computation to those early predictions: sophisticated Transformer heads operate serially at the beginning of the draft. Later positions use lightweight multilayer perceptron heads that operate in parallel, favoring efficiency where additional prediction effort is less valuable.

This allocation connects architectural complexity and execution time to a token's position in the draft sequence. It combines careful early prediction with inexpensive later proposals, rather than using a uniform generation pattern throughout. Experiments report better performance than existing approaches, supporting the idea that unequal computational investment across draft positions can improve speculative decoding overall.
summary.tldr: Gumiho improves speculative decoding by using stronger serial heads for early tokens and lightweight parallel heads for later tokens.

title: Gumiho: A Hybrid Architecture to Prioritize Early Tokens in Speculative Decoding

abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence have been fueled by the development of foundation models such as BERT, GPT, T5, and Vision Transformers. These models are first pretrained on vast and diverse datasets and then adapted to specific downstream tasks, often with significantly less data. However, the mechanisms behind the success of this ubiquitous pretrain-then-adapt paradigm remain underexplored, particularly the characteristics of pretraining checkpoints that enhance downstream adaptation. We introduce a Bayesian model selection criterion, called the downstream free energy, which quantifies a checkpoint’s adaptability by measuring the concentration of nearby favorable parameters for a downstream task. We demonstrate that this Bayesian model selection criterion can be effectively implemented without access to the downstream data or prior knowledge of the downstream task. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence that the criterion reliably correlates with improved fine-tuning performance, offering a principled approach to predicting model adaptability.

paragraphs: Foundation models are pretrained on broad datasets and then adapted to particular tasks. This paper asks what makes a saved pretraining checkpoint a good starting point for that adaptation. The question concerns the checkpoint’s capacity to support later fine-tuning, including when the eventual task is not yet known.

The authors introduce downstream free energy, a Bayesian model selection criterion. It assesses adaptability through the concentration of nearby parameter settings that are favorable for a downstream task. The idea is to evaluate the neighborhood around a checkpoint: how much favorable parameter space is available near the starting model.

The authors show that the criterion can be implemented without downstream data or advance knowledge of the downstream task. They also report empirical evidence that its values reliably correlate with better fine-tuning performance. This makes the criterion a principled candidate for selecting checkpoints before adaptation begins. The stated evidence establishes a useful empirical relationship between the criterion and adaptability, rather than a guarantee that every selected checkpoint will perform best.
summary.tldr: Downstream free energy assesses a pretraining checkpoint’s adaptability without downstream data and empirically correlates with better fine-tuning.

title: A Bayesian Model Selection Criterion for Selecting Pretraining Checkpoints

abstract: Diffusion or score-based models recently showed high performance in image generation. They rely on a forward and a backward stochastic differential equations (SDE). The sampling of a data distribution is achieved by numerically solving the backward SDE or its associated flow ODE. Studying the convergence of these models necessitates to control four different types of error: the initialization error, the truncation error, the discretization error and the score approximation. In this paper, we theoretically study the behavior of diffusion models and their numerical implementation when the data distribution is Gaussian. Our first contribution is to derive the analytical solutions of the backward SDE and the probability flow ODE and to prove that these solutions and their discretizations are all Gaussian processes. Our second contribution is to compute the exact Wasserstein errors between the target and the numerically sampled distributions for any numerical scheme. This allows us to monitor convergence directly in the data space, while experimental works limit their empirical analysis to Inception features. An implementation of our code is available online.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples by numerically solving a reverse stochastic process or a related deterministic flow. Understanding their accuracy involves separating initialization, truncation, discretization, and score-approximation errors. This paper studies those sampling procedures when the target data distribution is Gaussian, creating a setting where the resulting distributions can be analyzed exactly.

The authors derive analytical solutions for both the backward stochastic differential equation and the probability-flow ordinary differential equation. They also prove that these solutions and their discretizations are Gaussian processes. This shared structure allows their analysis to connect the continuous mathematical model with the numerical procedure actually used to produce samples.

Within this Gaussian setting, the paper computes exact Wasserstein errors between the target distribution and numerically generated distributions for any numerical scheme. Those errors measure distributional discrepancy directly in the original data space. This gives a precise way to monitor convergence, whereas the empirical analyses described in the abstract rely on Inception features. The value of the Gaussian assumption is that it makes sampling error directly calculable rather than only indirectly assessed.
summary.tldr: For Gaussian data, exact diffusion solutions enable exact Wasserstein error calculations for numerical sampling schemes.

title: Diffusion models for Gaussian distributions: Exact solutions and Wasserstein errors

abstract: Efficient real-world deployments of large language models (LLMs) rely on Key-Value (KV) caching for processing and generating long outputs, reducing the need for repetitive computation. For large contexts, Key-Value caches can take up tens of gigabytes of device memory, as they store vector representations for each token and layer. Recent work has shown that the cached vectors can be compressed through quantization, pruning or merging, but these techniques often compromise quality towards higher compression rates. In this work, we aim to improve Key & Value compression by exploiting two observations: 1) the inherent dependencies between keys and values across different layers, and 2) the existence of high-compression methods for internal network states (e.g. attention Keys & Values). We propose AQUA-KV, an adaptive quantization for Key-Value caches that relies on compact adapters to exploit existing dependencies between Keys and Values, and aims to "optimally" compress the information that cannot be predicted. AQUA-KV significantly improves compression rates, while maintaining high accuracy on state-of-the-art LLM families. On Llama 3.2 LLMs, we achieve near-lossless inference at 2-2.5 bits per value with under $1%$ relative error in perplexity and LongBench scores. AQUA-KV is one-shot, simple, and efficient: it can be calibrated on a single GPU within 1-6 hours, even for 70B models.

paragraphs: Language models cache key and value vectors to avoid repeating computation while processing long contexts and generating outputs. Those caches can occupy tens of gigabytes because they retain information for each token and layer. AQUA-KV addresses the resulting memory burden by compressing cached representations while aiming to preserve the quality that aggressive compression often damages.

The method exploits dependencies among keys and values across layers. Compact adapters use those relationships to predict information already represented elsewhere, allowing compression to focus on information that cannot be predicted. This makes the approach adaptive to structure within the cache, rather than treating every cached vector as an independent object with equally novel content.

On Llama 3.2 models, the authors report near-lossless inference using 2–2.5 bits per value, with less than 1% relative error in perplexity and LongBench scores. Calibration takes 1–6 hours on one GPU, including for 70B models. These findings show a practical route to substantially smaller caches while retaining accuracy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: AQUA-KV compresses language-model caches by predicting shared information across layers and quantizing what remains.

title: Cache Me If You Must: Adaptive Key-Value Quantization for Large Language Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable reasoning abilities in various tasks such as mathematics and coding. However, recent studies indicate that even the best models lack true comprehension of their reasoning processes. In this paper, we explore how self-play can enhance the rationality of models in the reasoning process without supervision from humans or superior models. We design a $\textit{\textbf{C}ritic-\textbf{D}iscernment \textbf{G}ame} (\textbf{CDG})$ in which a prover first provides a solution to a given problem and is subsequently challenged by critiques of its solution. These critiques either aim to assist or mislead the prover. The objective of the prover is to maintain the correct answer when faced with misleading comments, while correcting errors in response to constructive feedback. Our experiments on tasks involving mathematical reasoning, stepwise error detection, self-correction, and long-chain reasoning demonstrate that CDG training can significantly improve the ability of well-aligned LLMs to comprehend their reasoning process.
