paragraphs: A model that can produce a solution still needs to judge whether criticism of that solution is valid. Accepting every correction can overturn a correct answer, while rejecting every correction prevents useful revision. This paper studies whether self-play can improve that judgment without supervision from humans or stronger models.

The proposed Critic-Discernment Game begins with a prover solving a problem. It then receives critiques that may be helpful or deliberately misleading. The prover’s objective depends on the situation: preserve a correct answer under misleading criticism, and repair an incorrect answer when the feedback is constructive. The training game therefore rewards selective responsiveness to criticism.

Experiments examine mathematical reasoning, identification of errors within reasoning steps, self-correction, and long reasoning chains. The authors report that CDG training can substantially improve well-aligned models’ comprehension of their own reasoning processes. The stated finding concerns this evaluated class of models and supports self-play as a way to improve how they assess and revise reasoning.
summary.tldr: The Critic-Discernment Game uses self-play to help well-aligned models accept useful critiques and resist misleading ones.

title: Improving Rationality in the Reasoning Process of Language Models through Self-playing Game

abstract: In recent years, while generative AI has advanced significantly in image generation, video generation continues to face challenges in controllability, length, and detail quality, which hinder its application. We present MimicMotion, a framework for generating high-quality human videos of arbitrary length using motion guidance. Our approach has several highlights. Firstly, we introduce confidence-aware pose guidance that ensures high frame quality and temporal smoothness. Secondly, we introduce regional loss amplification based on pose confidence, which reduces image distortion in key regions. Lastly, we propose a progressive latent fusion strategy to generate long and smooth videos. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in producing high-quality human motion videos. Videos and comparisons are available at https://tencent.github.io/MimicMotion.

paragraphs: Generating human motion videos requires control over movement, convincing visual detail, and consistency across frames. Video length adds another challenge because a useful sequence must remain smooth as it continues. MimicMotion is a framework for producing human videos of arbitrary length using motion guidance, with dedicated mechanisms addressing these related requirements.

The first mechanism is confidence-aware pose guidance, which incorporates pose confidence into guidance for frame quality and temporal smoothness. A second mechanism amplifies regional training losses according to pose confidence, reducing distortion in key image regions. These components make confidence information part of both the motion guidance and the emphasis placed on regional visual errors.

For longer sequences, the framework introduces progressive latent fusion to produce long, smooth videos. Its design therefore addresses local detail and continuity over time through separate but complementary components. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in generating high-quality human motion videos. The stated contribution is this combination of confidence-aware generation and a strategy specifically intended to extend video length while preserving smoothness.
summary.tldr: MimicMotion combines confidence-aware pose guidance, regional loss weighting, and latent fusion to generate long, smooth human motion videos.

title: MimicMotion: High-Quality Human Motion Video Generation with Confidence-aware Pose Guidance

abstract: The selective classifier (SC) has been proposed for rank based uncertainty thresholding, which could have applications in safety critical areas such as medical diagnostics, autonomous driving, and the justice system. The Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve (AURC) has emerged as the foremost evaluation metric for assessing the performance of SC systems. In this work, we present a formal statistical formulation of population AURC, presenting an equivalent expression that can be interpreted as a reweighted risk function. Through Monte Carlo methods, we derive empirical AURC plug-in estimators for finite sample scenarios. The weight estimators associated with these plug-in estimators are shown to be consistent, with low bias and tightly bounded mean squared error (MSE). The plug-in estimators are proven to converge at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ln(n)/n})$ demonstrating statistical consistency. We empirically validate the effectiveness of our estimators through experiments across multiple datasets, model architectures, and confidence score functions (CSFs), demonstrating consistency and effectiveness in fine-tuning AURC performance.

paragraphs: A selective classifier uses confidence rankings to decide which predictions to accept. Evaluating it therefore involves both the fraction of cases it handles and the risk among those cases. The area under the risk-coverage curve, or AURC, summarizes this relationship. This paper gives a formal statistical definition of AURC for the underlying population, providing a foundation for understanding what estimates from finite datasets represent.

The central result rewrites population AURC as a reweighted risk function. This connects the curve-based metric to an expression in which prediction errors receive particular weights. Using Monte Carlo methods, the authors construct plug-in estimators that replace population quantities with estimates from available samples. They show that the estimated weights are consistent, have low bias, and satisfy tight bounds on mean squared error.

The resulting AURC estimators converge at a rate of O(sqrt(ln(n)/n)), establishing consistency as sample size grows. Experiments across datasets, model architectures, and confidence scoring functions support their effectiveness, including for fine-tuning AURC performance. The contribution connects a widely used evaluation measure with explicit statistical guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper expresses population AURC as reweighted risk and develops finite-sample estimators with proven convergence guarantees.

title: A Novel Characterization of the Population Area Under the Risk Coverage Curve (AURC) and Rates of Finite Sample Estimators

abstract: Contemporary evaluation techniques are inadequate for agentic systems. These approaches either focus exclusively on final outcomes—ignoring the step-by-step nature of the thinking done by agentic systems—or require excessive manual labour. To address this, we introduce the Agent-as-a-Judge framework, wherein agentic systems are used to evaluate agentic systems. This is a natural extension of the LLM-as-a-Judge framework, incorporating agentic features that enable intermediate feedback for the entire task-solving processes for more precise evaluations. We apply the Agent-as-a-Judge framework to the task of code generation. To overcome issues with existing benchmarks and provide a proof-of-concept testbed for Agent-as-a-Judge, we present DevAI, a new benchmark of 55 realistic AI code generation tasks. DevAI includes rich manual annotations, like a total of 365 hierarchical solution requirements, which make it particularly suitable for an agentic evaluator. We benchmark three of the top code-generating agentic systems using Agent-as-a-Judge and find that our framework dramatically outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge and is as reliable as our human evaluation baseline. Altogether, we believe that this work represents a concrete step towards enabling vastly more sophisticated agentic systems. To help that, our dataset and the full implementation of Agent-as-a-Judge will be publically available at https://github.com/metauto-ai/agent-as-a-judge

paragraphs: Evaluating an agent only by its final output can miss important parts of how it solved a task. Examining the full process manually, however, requires substantial work. Agent-as-a-Judge addresses this problem by using an agentic system as the evaluator, extending language-model judging with capabilities for assessing intermediate steps and providing feedback throughout task execution.

These requirements give the evaluator a structured basis for assessing whether a solution meets its different obligations, rather than treating completion as one undifferentiated outcome.

The authors evaluate three leading code-generating agent systems. In this setting, Agent-as-a-Judge substantially outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge and matches the reliability of the human evaluation baseline. The findings support process-aware automated evaluation for these coding tasks and provide a concrete testbed for developing more capable agent evaluators.
summary.tldr: Agent-as-a-Judge evaluates agents’ intermediate work and matches a human evaluation baseline on a new AI coding benchmark.

title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents

abstract: Reinforcement learning has been widely applied to diffusion and flow models for visual tasks such as text-to-image generation. However, these tasks remain challenging because diffusion models have intractable likelihoods, which creates a barrier for directly applying popular policy-gradient type methods. Existing approaches primarily focus on crafting new objectives built on already heavily engineered LLM objectives, using ad hoc estimators for likelihood, without a thorough investigation into how such estimation affects overall algorithmic performance. In this work, we provide a systematic analysis of the RL design space by disentangling three factors: i) policy-gradient objectives, ii) likelihood estimators, and iii) rollout sampling schemes. We show that adopting an evidence lower bound (ELBO) based model likelihood estimator, computed only from the final generated sample, is the dominant factor enabling effective, efficient, and stable RL optimization, outweighing the impact of the specific policy-gradient loss functional. We validate our findings across multiple reward benchmarks using SD 3.5 Medium, and observe consistent trends across all tasks. Our method improves the GenEval score from $0.24$ to $0.95$ in $90$ GPU hours, which is $4.6\times$ more efficient than FlowGRPO and $2\times$ more efficient than the SOTA method DiffusionNFT without reward hacking.

title: Rethinking the Design Space of Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models: On the Importance of Likelihood Estimation Beyond Loss Design

abstract: Plug-and-Play diffusion prior (PnPDP) frameworks have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving imaging inverse problems by treating pretrained generative models as modular priors. However, we identify a critical flaw in prevailing PnP solvers (e.g., based on HQS or Proximal Gradient): they function as memoryless operators, updating estimates solely based on instantaneous gradients. This lack of historical tracking inevitably leads to non-vanishing steady-state bias, where the reconstruction fails to strictly satisfy physical measurements under heavy corruption. To resolve this, we propose Dual-Coupled PnP Diffusion (DC-PnPDP), which restores the classical dual variable to provide integral feedback, progressively enforce agreement between the data-consistency and prior. However, this rigorous geometric coupling introduces a secondary challenge: the accumulated dual residuals exhibit spectrally colored, structured artifacts that violate the Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) assumption of diffusion priors, causing severe hallucinations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Spectral Homogenization (SH), a frequency-domain adaptation mechanism that modulates these structured residuals into statistically compliant pseudo-AWGN inputs. This effectively aligns the solver’s rigorous optimization trajectory with the denoiser’s valid statistical manifold. Extensive experiments on CT and MRI reconstruction demonstrate that our approach resolves the bias-hallucination trade-off, achieving state-of-the-art fidelity with significantly accelerated convergence. The code is available at https://github.com/duchenhe/DC-PnPDP.

The authors identify a problem in prevailing solvers: updates based only on instantaneous gradients lack historical tracking, producing persistent disagreement with physical measurements under heavy corruption.

This connects stronger optimization feedback with the noise conditions expected by the denoiser. Experiments on CT and MRI report that the combined method resolves the bias–hallucination trade-off, achieves state-of-the-art fidelity, and converges significantly faster. Both components matter to the stated approach: accumulated feedback corrects bias, while residual adaptation addresses the resulting denoising mismatch.
summary.tldr: DC-PnPDP combines accumulated measurement feedback with spectral residual adaptation to improve diffusion-based CT and MRI reconstruction.

title: Plug-and-Play Diffusion Meets ADMM: Dual-Variable Coupling for Robust Medical Image Reconstruction

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models have achieved unprecedented success in zero-shot recognition by aligning visual features with broad semantic concepts. However, this semantic abstraction creates a critical vulnerability in open-world deployment: the "Hubris of Semantics", where models force-fit unknown anomalies into known categories with high confidence due to the lack of explicit negative knowledge. To address this Open-World Trustworthiness Paradox, we propose Immuno-VLM, a bio-inspired framework that adapts the biological principle of Immunological Negative Selection to high-dimensional latent spaces. Departing from traditional Open-Set Recognition methods that rely on passive density estimation or inefficient pixel-space outlier generation, Immuno-VLM leverages the generative reasoning of Large Language Models to actively hallucinate "Semantic Antibodies", textual descriptions of near-distribution outliers (e.g., look-alikes, contextual anomalies) that effectively bound the decision space of known classes. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K and four challenging OOD benchmarks reveal that Immuno-VLM establishes a new state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Immuno-VLM addresses a failure mode in recognizing unfamiliar visual inputs: broad semantic similarity can cause a model to assign an unknown anomaly to a familiar category with high confidence. The authors connect this behavior to a lack of explicit negative knowledge. Knowing what belongs to a category does not itself provide descriptions of nearby cases that should be excluded.

The framework takes inspiration from biological negative selection. It uses a language model’s generative reasoning to create textual descriptions of near-distribution outliers, such as look-alikes and contextual anomalies. These descriptions, called semantic antibodies, help bound known classes in the latent representation space without requiring outlier images to be generated in pixel space.

Experiments on ImageNet-1K and four out-of-distribution benchmarks report state-of-the-art results. The stated findings support actively constructing semantic counterexamples as a way to improve recognition of unfamiliar inputs. The distinctive contribution is using generated negative descriptions to refine category boundaries, addressing the same broad semantic abstraction that makes vision-language models useful for zero-shot recognition.
summary.tldr: Immuno-VLM generates textual descriptions of plausible outliers to help vision-language models distinguish unknown anomalies from familiar categories.

title: Immuno-VLM: Immunizing Large Vision-Language Models via Generative Semantic Antibodies for Open-World Trustworthiness

abstract: Diffusion-based camouflaged object detection (COD) has recently shown great potential. In contrast to existing approaches that rely on multiple sample steps to refine the predicted masks, we propose CODiff, which reformulates the diffusion process to enable one-step mask prediction while maintaining competitive accuracy. Specifically, we first establish the theoretical feasibility of one-step sampling for COD. Based on this, we design a dedicated network for one-step inference with a global semantic guidance mechanism to guide the denoising process globally and hierarchical condition integration blocks to provide fine-grained structural semantics. In addition, we design a straight-forward regularization to learn better intermediate features by bridging the representation gap between the condition backbone and the diffusion model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CODiff achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, improving MAE by over 22% on the challenging COD10K dataset. Code is available at https://github.com/KiiSooo/CODiff.

Diffusion approaches can refine these predicted masks over several sampling steps. CODiff reformulates the process to produce a mask in one step, aiming to retain strong detection accuracy while removing repeated sampling.

The paper first establishes theoretical feasibility for one-step sampling in this task. It then designs a network specifically for that setting. Global semantic guidance helps direct denoising using overall image meaning, while hierarchical condition integration supplies finer structural information. An additional regularizer improves intermediate features by reducing the representation gap between the conditioning backbone and the diffusion model.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, including an improvement of more than 22% in mean absolute error on COD10K. These findings show that, in the evaluated setting, one-step prediction can support strong mask accuracy. The architectural components explain how CODiff supplies both broad semantic guidance and detailed structure within that single inference step.
summary.tldr: CODiff predicts camouflaged-object masks in one diffusion step and reports state-of-the-art accuracy across multiple benchmarks.

title: CODiff: One-Step Diffusion Model for Camouflaged Object Detection

abstract: Automating the development of machine learning algorithms has the potential to unlock new breakthroughs. However, our ability to improve and evaluate algorithm discovery systems has thus far been limited by existing task suites. They suffer from many issues, such as: poor evaluation methodologies; data contamination; and containing saturated or very similar problems. Here, we introduce DiscoGen, a procedural generator of algorithm discovery tasks for machine learning, such as developing optimisers for reinforcement learning or loss functions for image classification. Motivated by the success of procedural generation in reinforcement learning, DiscoGen spans billions of tasks of varying difficulty and complexity from a range of machine learning fields. These tasks are specified by a small number of configuration parameters and can be used to optimise algorithm discovery agents (ADAs). We present DiscoBench, a fixed, small subset of DiscoGen tasks for principled evaluation of ADAs. Finally, we propose a number of ambitious, impactful research directions enabled by DiscoGen, and demonstrate its use for ADA optimisation through scaling experiments for automated prompt tuning. DiscoGen is released open-source.

Existing suites can contain overly similar or saturated problems, suffer from data contamination, and use weak evaluation methods. DiscoGen addresses this bottleneck through procedural generation of algorithm-discovery tasks.

Examples include developing reinforcement learning optimizers and image-classification loss functions. The generated tasks can be used to optimize algorithm discovery agents, supplying a broad task space for their development.

The authors also introduce DiscoBench, a small fixed subset intended for principled evaluation. This pairs a large configurable source of tasks with a stable benchmark for assessing agents. Scaling experiments in automated prompt tuning demonstrate one use of DiscoGen for agent optimization, and the generator is released openly. The contribution is infrastructure for studying discovery systems, with a demonstrated optimization use case and proposed directions for further research.
summary.tldr: DiscoGen generates billions of configurable algorithm-discovery tasks, while DiscoBench supplies a fixed subset for evaluating discovery agents.

title: Procedural Generation Of Algorithm Discovery Tasks in Machine Learning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can already draft plausible Triton kernels, yet most existing evaluations still focus on single-shot generation and underplay tool use and feedback. We introduce TritonGym, a benchmark and orchestration framework for evaluating agentic workflows in GPU code generation. TritonGym standardizes access to a set of code generation tools via function-calls, separating intrinsic model capability from workflow design and enabling fair, apples-to-apples comparison. The benchmark spans a maintained operator set, community samples, out-of-distribution tasks, and DSL extensions, ensuring both generality and extensibility. By providing a common orchestration and evaluation framework, TritonGym democratizes the development of GPU coding agents, supports practical adoption of agent-generated kernels, and facilitates progress on advanced agentic systems.

That leaves an incomplete picture of agents whose performance depends on the sequence of actions they take while developing code.

This common interface is designed to distinguish model capability from the contribution of workflow design. It gives researchers a more consistent basis for comparing different ways of organizing GPU coding agents and their interactions with tools.

Its task coverage includes a maintained operator set, community samples, out-of-distribution tasks, and domain-specific language extensions. These categories support both breadth and extensibility as coding requirements change. The contribution is evaluation infrastructure for studying agentic GPU programming, with the stated aim of making development more accessible and supporting practical adoption. The abstract emphasizes the framework's scope and purpose rather than reporting a performance ranking.
summary.tldr: TritonGym standardizes tools, tasks, and orchestration for comparing agentic workflows that generate Triton GPU kernels.

title: TritonGym: A Benchmark for Agentic LLM Workflows in Triton GPU Code Generation

abstract: Recent leaderboard-based evaluations of large language models aggregate user feedback by fitting a Bradley–Terry model to pairwise comparisons, producing a single global ranking based on a latent quality score. While appealing for its simplicity, this approach is incompatible with heterogeneous preferences: when LLMs are used across diverse tasks and use cases, users who favor fundamentally different model behaviors can be systematically misrepresented when collapsed into a single quality score. To address this issue, we study pluralistic leaderboards that aim to remain stable with respect to heterogeneous user populations. Drawing on ideas from social choice theory, we adapt the notion of local stability, which requires that no model outside the top-$k$ positions is collectively preferred to the top-$k$ set by more than $O(1/k)$ fraction of users. Building on techniques from the social choice literature, we design an alternative leaderboard mechanism that satisfies local stability while eliciting only $\widetilde{O}(k)$ pairwise comparisons per user, where $k$ is the size of the prefix for which stability is guaranteed. Using data from LMArena, we show that standard Bradley–Terry aggregation can violate local stability in practice, whereas our method provides substantially stronger stability guarantees.

paragraphs: A single language-model ranking can obscure genuine differences in what users want. Common leaderboards fit a Bradley–Terry model to pairwise preferences, assigning each model one underlying quality score. This paper argues that collapsing heterogeneous preferences into that score can systematically misrepresent users who favor different model behaviors or use cases.

The proposed alternative uses local stability, a concept adapted from social choice theory. For a top-k set, the requirement limits the fraction of users who collectively prefer an excluded model to that set to O(1/k). This evaluates whether the leading models adequately represent diverse preferences, instead of requiring all users' comparisons to fit a single shared quality scale.

The authors design a leaderboard mechanism that satisfies local stability while requesting only roughly k pairwise comparisons per user, up to logarithmic factors. Analysis of LMArena data shows that standard Bradley–Terry aggregation can violate the stability condition in practice. The alternative offers stronger stability guarantees for the chosen prefix size, giving the top of a leaderboard a formal connection to preference diversity.
summary.tldr: Pluralistic leaderboards provide a local-stability guarantee that better accommodates heterogeneous user preferences than a single global quality score.

title: Pluralistic Leaderboards

abstract: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) aim to learn universal patterns through large-scale pretraining on diverse graphs and generalize to open-world scenarios. While GFMs have garnered significant attention, existing works primarily focus on sigle-modal graphs. However, many real-world graphs are multimodal, consisting of structures alongside diverse features derived from modalities such as text and images. To date, exploration into Multimodal Graph Foundation Models (MGFMs) remains limited. Incorporating multimodal data provides a more comprehensive view, allowing models to learn richer semantics, thereby advancing GFMs. We are therefore motivated to explore MGFMs, where the core challenge lies in synergistically encoding structures and multimodal features to achieve effective cross-modal alignment and fusion. To this end, we propose a graph foundation model with Cross-modal Alignment and Modality-aware Expert fusion, CAME. Specifically, CAME first generates graph embeddings for each individual modality. We then introduce a multimodal multi-expert encoding mechanism, which includes a dimension-wise routing strategy to fuse multimodal information. Finally, we employ a cross-modal contrastive loss to train CAME, enabling the adaptive alignment and fusion across different modalities. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of CAME across multiple tasks and diverse multimodal graph datasets.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models aim to learn reusable patterns from many graphs. Much of this work considers graphs with only one kind of feature, while real graphs can combine connections with text, images, and other information. The challenge is to represent these sources together so that their meanings align and their complementary information remains useful.

CAME addresses this challenge by first producing a graph representation for each modality separately. A collection of expert components then combines these representations, with routing decisions made at the level of individual representation dimensions. This gives the fusion mechanism finer control over how it combines information than treating each modality as a single indivisible contribution.

Training uses a cross-modal contrastive objective to encourage alignment across modalities while learning how to fuse them. Experiments across multiple tasks and diverse multimodal graph datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The contribution is a coordinated approach to representing graph structure and heterogeneous features, making multimodal information part of the foundation model’s learning process.
summary.tldr: CAME combines modality-specific graph representations through expert routing and contrastive alignment to learn from multimodal graphs.

title: A Graph Foundation Model with Cross-Modal Alignment and Modality-Aware Expert Fusion for Multi-Modal Graphs

abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) possess unique characteristics distinct from natural language, yet existing EHR foundation models often rely on suboptimal NLP-based approaches. We propose a pretraining method tailored to EHRs’ distinct features. First, we introduce Pathology-Focused Binning, a density-based quantization strategy that prioritizes clinically significant numerical ranges over usual values. Second, to jointly capture both the exact timing of clinical events and the relative intervals between them, we propose Dual-Calendar Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE), which encodes absolute and relative temporal signals. Third, we introduce the Time-Conditioned Foreseeing (TCF) objective, aligning with clinical treatment planning to forecast events across multiple temporal horizons by explicitly modeling event timing. Our approach establishes a temporal generative EHR model that outperforms existing foundation models on eleven diverse downstream tasks—achieving up to a 54% improvement in AUPRC—and enables the generation of realistic, temporally consistent patient trajectories. Code is available at https://github.com/Pusheen-cat/TCF_PFM.

paragraphs: Electronic health records contain numerical measurements and events whose timing matters, making them different from ordinary language. The paper proposes pretraining tailored to those features. Its design addresses how clinical values are represented, how event timing is encoded, and what future events the model learns to predict.

Pathology-Focused Binning allocates attention to clinically significant numerical ranges through density-based quantization, rather than prioritizing usual values. Dual-Calendar Rotary Positional Embedding represents both absolute event times and relative intervals. The Time-Conditioned Foreseeing objective then forecasts events across multiple time horizons while explicitly modeling when they occur, aligning the prediction task with treatment planning.

Together, these components produce a temporal generative model for health records. The authors report improvements over existing foundation models on eleven downstream tasks, with gains of up to 54% in AUPRC. They also report generation of realistic patient trajectories that remain temporally consistent. The maximum metric improvement is task-dependent; the broader contribution is a pretraining approach that treats numerical significance and irregular timing as central properties of health records.
summary.tldr: TCF tailors health-record pretraining to clinically significant values and event timing, improving eleven downstream tasks and generating temporally consistent trajectories.

title: Time-Conditioned Foreseeing: An EHR-Specific Foundation Model for Irregular Dynamics and Calendrical Time

abstract: Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (mRAG) systems enable language models to answer knowledge-intensive queries with citation-supported responses across languages. Despite their growing use, an open questions is whether the mixture of different document languages impacts generation and citation behavior in unintended ways. To investigate this, we introduce a controlled methodology using model internals to measure language preference while holding other factors such as document relevance constant. Across eight languages and six open-weight models, we find that models preferentially cite English sources when queries are in English, with this bias amplified for lower-resource languages and for documents positioned mid-context. More crucially, we find that models sometimes trade-off document relevance for language preference, indicating that citation choices are not always driven by informativeness alone. Our findings shed light on how language models leverage multilingual context and influence citation behavior.

paragraphs: Multilingual retrieval-augmented generation lets a model answer questions using documents in several languages and cite its supporting sources. This paper investigates whether the language of a document influences citation choices independently of its usefulness. That distinction matters because a citation can appear informative while reflecting a preference for a particular language.

The authors introduce a controlled methodology using model internals to measure language preference while holding factors such as document relevance constant. Across eight languages and six open-weight models, they find a preference for citing English sources when questions are in English. The bias becomes stronger for lower-resource languages and for documents placed in the middle of the context.

The study also finds cases where models favor a preferred language over a more relevant document. This goes beyond a harmless tie-break between equally useful sources: informativeness does not always determine the selected citation. The results reveal a specific source-selection bias in the evaluated multilingual settings, showing that providing relevant multilingual evidence does not by itself ensure that a model will cite it according to relevance.
summary.tldr: Across the evaluated models, English-language queries can induce citation preferences that sometimes outweigh document relevance.

title: Linguistic Nepotism: Trading-off Quality for Language Preference in Multilingual RAG

abstract: Quantum hardware suffers from intrinsic device heterogeneity and environmental drift, forcing practitioners to choose between suboptimal non-adaptive controllers or costly per-device recalibration. We derive a scaling law lower bound for meta-learning showing that the adaptation gain (expected fidelity improvement from task-specific gradient steps) saturates exponentially with gradient steps and scales linearly with task variance, providing a quantitative criterion for when adaptation justifies its overhead. Validation on quantum gate calibration shows negligible benefits for low-variance tasks but $>$ 40% fidelity gains on two-qubit gates under extreme out-of-distribution conditions (10$\times$ the training noise), with implications for reducing per-device calibration time on cloud quantum processors. Further validation on classical linear-quadratic control confirms these laws emerge from general optimization geometry rather than quantum-specific physics. We further introduce a few-shot pre-adaptation protocol that estimates the optimal adaptation budget from $N =3–5$ probe steps within 3–19% relative error across out-of-distribution regimes.

paragraphs: Quantum devices differ from one another and drift over time, making controller adaptation potentially useful but costly. This paper asks when task-specific gradient steps justify that cost. It derives a scaling-law lower bound linking expected fidelity improvement to the number of adaptation steps and the variance among tasks.

These findings connect the value of adaptation to how strongly conditions differ across tasks.

The authors also introduce a preliminary probing procedure that estimates the optimal adaptation budget from three to five steps, achieving 3–19% relative error across out-of-distribution regimes. This offers a practical way to estimate how much adaptation to perform before committing to its full cost.
summary.tldr: A scaling-law lower bound and a short probing protocol help determine when controller adaptation merits its computational cost.

title: When Does Adaptation Win? Scaling Laws for Meta-Learning in Quantum Control

abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) recently emerged as a promising alternative to auto-regressive LLMs. The latest works further extended it to multimodal understanding and generation tasks. In this work, we propose LaViDa-R1, a multimodal, general-purpose reasoning dLLM. Unlike existing works that build reasoning dLLMs through task-specific reinforcement learning, LaViDa-R1 incorporates diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks in a unified manner. In particular, LaViDa-R1 is built with a novel unified post-training framework that seamlessly integrates supervised finetuning (SFT) and multi-task reinforcement learning (RL). It employs several novel training techniques, including answer-forcing, tree search, and complementary likelihood estimation, to enhance effectiveness and scalability. Extensive experiments demonstrate LaViDa-R1’s strong performance on a wide range of multimodal tasks, including visual math reasoning, reason-intensive grounding, and image editing.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models have expanded from language into multimodal understanding and generation. LaViDa-R1 investigates how to develop reasoning across those capabilities within one general-purpose model. The problem is broader than improving a single specialized task: the training framework must support diverse tasks involving both interpretation and generation.

The proposed post-training process combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning across multiple tasks. It also incorporates answer-forcing, tree search, and complementary likelihood estimation to improve training effectiveness and scalability. These techniques form part of a unified recipe, allowing the model's reasoning development to encompass several multimodal objectives together.

Experiments report strong performance across visual mathematical reasoning, grounding that requires substantial reasoning, and image editing. Those applications span understanding visual information, identifying relevant content, and producing requested changes. Their breadth supports the paper's claim that unified post-training can develop reasoning capabilities across different multimodal activities. The contribution is the integration of those activities into one diffusion-language-model training framework, extending beyond the task-specific reinforcement learning approach described in earlier work.
summary.tldr: LaViDa-R1 combines supervised fine-tuning and multi-task reinforcement learning to develop reasoning across multimodal understanding and generation.

title: Lavida-R1: Advancing Reasoning for Unified Multimodal Diffusion Language Models

abstract: While LLM-driven Neural Architecture Search (NAS) leverages exceptional code generation and reasoning, it suffers from a critical "Semantic-Physical Misalignment": LLMs prioritize high-level semantic plausibility but are agnostic to intrinsic physical dynamics such as gradient flow, whereas Zero-Cost Proxies (ZCPs) capture these local sensitivities but lack global semantic planning. To bridge this gap, we propose SAGE-NAS, a closed-loop evolutionary framework that synergizes an LLM-Based Semantic Agent with a Graph-Based Evaluator. Specifically, SAGE-NAS coordinates an LLM-driven Semantic Agent to construct candidate architectures by dynamically scheduling complementary sub-policies that balance exploitation with exploration. Furthermore, the framework integrates a Dual-Modality Graph Evaluator that serves as a rapid performance predictor by fusing ZCP statistics with topological features, and a State-Aware Behavioral Atlas that guides sparsity-driven exploration to escape local optima. Experiments demonstrate that SAGE-NAS achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple mainstream search spaces and downstream tasks, exhibiting a superior balance between search efficiency, model accuracy, and cross-task generalization capability.

paragraphs: Language models can propose plausible neural-network architectures, but plausibility does not capture how well signals and gradients behave inside those networks. Cheap performance proxies reveal some of these local properties but lack broad design reasoning. SAGE-NAS combines the two in a closed-loop evolutionary search framework for neural architectures.

A language-model agent constructs candidates while dynamically scheduling policies that balance exploring new designs with exploiting promising ones. A graph-based evaluator predicts performance by combining zero-cost proxy statistics with network topology. A state-aware behavioral atlas further guides exploration toward sparsely covered regions, helping the search move away from local optima.

Experiments across multiple search spaces and downstream tasks report state-of-the-art performance and a favorable balance of search efficiency, accuracy, and cross-task generalization. The approach matters because proposal generation and candidate evaluation contribute different information. Its feedback loop joins high-level architectural reasoning with structural and sensitivity-based evidence about whether a proposed design is likely to work well.
summary.tldr: SAGE-NAS couples language-model architecture proposals with graph-based performance feedback to improve neural architecture search.

title: SAGE-NAS: Synergizing LLM-Based Semantic Agent with Graph-Based Evaluator for Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Delayed outcomes are ubiquitous in online experimentation: treatment can affect whether an outcome occurs, when it occurs, and its realized value. To accommodate staggered entry while remaining robust to environmental nonstationarity and unit-level heterogeneity, we adopt a design-based perspective and target the sample cumulative reward in each arm as a function of calendar time. Our confidence sequences allow practitioners to continuously monitor the counterfactual incremental reward, such as revenue, that would have been realized by calendar time $t$ had all entered units been assigned to treatment rather than control. The main technical challenge is the choice of design-based filtration, complicated by the presence of asynchronous potential outcome times. We show that the IPW treatment-effect estimation error is not a martingale with respect to any filtration, while each arm-specific IPW estimation error is a martingale with respect to a carefully chosen arm-specific event-time filtration. We therefore construct a confidence sequence for the treatment effect by combining two arm-level confidence sequences with a union bound, and further demonstrate that this can outperform the traditional design-based variance upper bound. Finally, we characterize the class of augmentations for which the per-arm AIPW estimation error remains a martingale.

We show that the IPW treatment-effect estimation error is not a martingale with respect to any filtration, while each arm-specific IPW estimation error is a martingale with respect to a carefully chosen arm-specific event-time filtration. We therefore construct a confidence sequence for the treatment effect by combining two arm-level confidence sequences with a union bound, and further demonstrate that this can outperform the traditional design-based variance upper bound. Finally, we characterize the class of augmentations for which the per-arm AIPW estimation error remains a martingale.

paragraphs: In an online experiment, treatment can change whether an outcome happens, when it arrives, and its value. Participants may also enter at different times. This paper develops continuously valid uncertainty estimates for the cumulative reward that would have accrued by a calendar date if all entered participants had received treatment rather than control.

The approach uses the experiment’s randomization as the basis for inference, accommodating environmental changes and differences among participants. The technical obstacle is that the inverse-probability-weighted treatment-effect error is not a martingale with respect to any filtration. However, each arm’s estimation error is a martingale under a carefully chosen arm-specific event-time filtration, which specifies how information becomes available.

The authors therefore construct confidence sequences separately for treatment and control, then combine them through a union bound. They show that this approach can outperform the traditional design-based variance upper bound. They also characterize which augmentations preserve the per-arm martingale property for augmented inverse-probability weighting. These results provide a route to continuous monitoring despite asynchronous outcome arrivals.
summary.tldr: The paper builds anytime-valid treatment-effect confidence sequences by handling delayed outcomes separately within each randomized experimental arm.

title: Design-Based Anytime-Valid Inference for Randomized Experiments with Delayed Outcomes and Staggered Entry

abstract: Visual-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to predict actions directly from observations and language instructions, but their performance depends on large-scale, high-quality data and is limited by the scarcity of real-world robot action datasets. To facilitate VLA model learning with abundant unlabeled human videos, Latent Action Models (LAM) learn latent action representations from visual dynamics to provide additional supervision for VLA learning. However, LAM and VLA are typically trained separately, leaving LAM ungrounded during VLA training and VLA models constrained by frozen LAM representations. To address these issues, we propose Latent Action Representation Alignment (LARA), a plug-and-play framework that jointly optimizes LAM and VLA via representation alignment. This enables reciprocal benefits where LAMs learn with action trajectories to avoid spurious visual changes, while VLAs are regularized by forward dynamics learned within LAMs to reduce hallucinations of functionally ineffective trajectories. We demonstrate LARA’s versatility and effectiveness for pre-training, post-training enhancement of pre-trained VLA models, and LAM refinement, achieving an average of 10%, 5%, and 15% improvement over 3 simulation and 1 meticulously designed real-world robotic manipulation benchmarks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lmy1001/LARA.

paragraphs: Robotic vision-language-action models learn to turn observations and instructions into actions, but real robot action data are scarce. When these two models are trained separately, however, the latent representations stay fixed and cannot be corrected by the robot’s action-learning process.

Action trajectories help the latent action model distinguish meaningful action-related changes from distracting visual changes. In the other direction, its learned forward dynamics constrain the action model, reducing its tendency to generate trajectories that appear plausible but fail to accomplish useful physical effects.

The authors evaluate LARA for pretraining, enhancing pretrained action models, and refining latent action models. Across three simulation benchmarks and one real-world manipulation benchmark, they report average improvements of 10%, 5%, and 15% for these uses, respectively. The results support the value of reciprocal learning: each model supplies information that addresses a weakness in the other.
summary.tldr: LARA jointly aligns latent action and vision-language-action models so visual dynamics and robot trajectories improve each other.

title: LARA: Latent Action Representation Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: High-fidelity vehicle aerodynamics analysis is bottlenecked by costly CFD simulations. Neural surrogates accelerate prediction but lack inverse design capabilities, while existing generative optimization methods suffer from unstable convergence and frequent engineering constraint violations. We present UniDrag, a unified framework bridging multi-field aerodynamic prediction with robust differentiable shape optimization. Given a vehicle geometry, UniDrag predicts surface pressure, volume flow fields, drag coefficient $C_d$, and a streamwise build-up profile localizing drag contributions. Our architecture combines enhanced Physics-Sliced Attention (ePSA), Gated Expert Routing, and Modality-Protected Learning to prevent negative transfer across output modalities. At deployment, the frozen surrogate enables gradient-based optimization via Free-Form Deformation with engineering constraints. We introduce Expectation-over-Transformation to prevent adversarial exploitation of surrogate fragility. We curate a large-scale dataset of 15,000 vehicle geometries spanning four body types with GPU-accelerated LBM simulations. On this benchmark, UniDrag achieves $C_d$ prediction $R^2$ of 0.937 (+7.6% over baselines) and 13.7% mean CFD-verified drag reduction with 100% success rate and only 21.3 mm average displacement (0.46% vehicle length).

title: UniDrag: Unified Multi-Field Prediction and Robust Shape Optimization for Vehicle Aerodynamics

abstract: Continuous Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) serve as the fundamental continuous tokenizer for modern neural audio generation systems, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction while providing a compact, smooth latent space for downstream generative priors. However, continuous VAEs face a fundamental conflict when balancing compression rate, reconstruction fidelity, and latent space topology—a challenge we formalize as the Rate-Distortion-Regularity Trilemma. This trilemma stems from a critical topological mismatch: the prevailing isotropic Gaussian prior in standard VAEs imposes a flat latent geometry that fails to accommodate audio’s hierarchical nature, where low-frequency components are structured and compressible while high-frequency components are stochastic and incompressible, leading to disordered information packing where crucial semantic features are randomly interleaved with high-entropy noise. To resolve this challenge, we propose Structured Topology-Aware Regularization (STAR), a general training strategy that reshapes latent space geometry by imposing a growth-based constraint field, routing structural and textural information into channel subspaces with matching capacities. STAR is applicable to any VAE architecture and effectively resolves the trilemma, as demonstrated in CNN-based VAEs. To fully exploit STAR’s potential, we present STAR-VAE, combining STAR with a hybrid CNN-Mamba architecture that synergizes local feature extraction with linear-complexity global context modeling, achieving state-of-the-art performance. We further propose STAR-Gen, an LLM-based Flow Matching framework that leverages STAR-VAE’s structured latent space for high-fidelity generation without suffering from vector quantization artifacts. Empirical results demonstrate that STAR-VAE successfully resolves the trilemma, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity and enhanced semantic information preservation across diverse audio domains. The structured latent space improves both traditional diffusion models and our STAR-Gen paradigm, achieving state-of-the-art performance in text-to-audio generation. The project page is available at https://STAR-VAE.github.io.

paragraphs: Continuous audio autoencoders must compress sound, reconstruct it accurately, and provide a well-organized latent space for generation. It attributes the conflict to a mismatch between the usual isotropic Gaussian prior and audio’s hierarchy, where structured low-frequency information and stochastic high-frequency detail have different representation needs.

The strategy is presented as applicable across VAE architectures and demonstrated with convolutional VAEs. The authors also introduce STAR-Gen, an LLM-based flow-matching framework operating on the structured continuous representation. Experiments report state-of-the-art reconstruction, improved preservation of semantic information, and stronger text-to-audio generation with both diffusion models and STAR-Gen. These results support organizing the compressed space around audio structure to improve reconstruction and downstream generation together.
summary.tldr: STAR organizes audio latent spaces by structural and textural information, improving both reconstruction and text-to-audio generation.

title: STAR-VAE: Structured Topology-Aware Regularization for Audio Reconstruction and Generation

abstract: We present UGround, a Unified visual Grounding paradigm that dynamically selects intermediate layers across Unrolled transformers as "mask as prompt,” diverging from the prevailing pipeline that leverages the fixed last hidden layer as "$⟨\texttt{SEG}⟩$ as prompt.” UGround addresses two primary challenges posed by the prevailing paradigm: (1) its reliance on the fixed last hidden layer, which sequentially amplifies cumulative errors arising from layer-by-layer propagation without intermediate correction, and (2) its use of $⟨\texttt{SEG}⟩$ as a prompt, which implicitly projects textual embeddings into visual space without explicit spatial cues (e.g., coordinates). Central to UGround is Policy-Prompted Masking, which comprises two key components: Stochastic Skip Connection (SSC) and Mask as Prompt (MasP). SSC is a reinforcement learning policy that, via stochastic sampling, allows each $⟨\texttt{SEG}⟩$ token to slide across unrolled transformer layers, enabling dynamic layer selection at which it connects to the vision model (e.g., SAM) in a skip-connection fashion. Given the selected hidden layer, MasP uses the similarity map derived from the $⟨\texttt{SEG}⟩$ token and image tokens as a soft logit mask to prompt SAM for mask generation, offering explicit spatial cues through its activation regions. To validate the effectiveness of UGround, we, for the first time, have unified visual grounding within a single framework from an attribute perspective, spanning from traditional refer expression segmentation to newly proposed reasoning segmentation, single-target to multi-target, positive query to false premise (empty target). All codes are provided in the supplementary material.

paragraphs: Visual grounding connects a language request to the corresponding image region. A common approach uses a segmentation token’s final hidden representation to prompt a vision model. UGround targets two weaknesses in that design: errors can accumulate through successive layers, and a textual representation alone does not provide explicit spatial guidance.

Its Policy-Prompted Masking mechanism makes both the layer choice and the prompt more spatially useful. A reinforcement-learning policy stochastically selects which intermediate transformer layer supplies the segmentation token representation. The method then compares that representation with image tokens to form a similarity map. This map becomes a soft mask prompt for the vision model, providing activation regions that indicate where to look.

The framework covers referring-expression and reasoning segmentation, single and multiple targets, and false-premise requests whose correct target is empty. This breadth treats those cases as attributes within a unified grounding framework. The central contribution is a flexible connection between language processing and mask generation: the model can select an intermediate representation and translate it into explicit spatial evidence instead of relying on a fixed final-layer prompt.
summary.tldr: UGround dynamically selects transformer layers and turns language-image similarity into spatial mask prompts for unified visual grounding.

title: UGround: Towards Unified Visual Grounding with Unrolled Transformers

abstract: Thompson Sampling is one of the most widely used and studied bandit algorithms, known for its simple structure, low regret performance, and solid theoretical guarantees. Yet, in stark contrast to most other families of bandit algorithms, the exact mechanism through which posterior sampling (as introduced by Thompson) is able to "properly" balance exploration and exploitation, remains a mystery. In this paper, we show that the core insight to address this question stems from recasting Thompson Sampling as an online optimization algorithm. To distill this, we introduce a time invariant notion of regret that summarizes cumulative regret across horizons (through a regret bound), leading to a time invariant Bellman-optimal policy. It turns out that Thompson Sampling admits an online optimization form that mimics the structure of the Bellman-optimal policy, where greediness is regularized by a measure of residual uncertainty. When viewed through this new lens of online optimization, Thompson Sampling can be understood and improved in a principled manner, by comparing it against the Bellman-optimal benchmark.

paragraphs: Thompson Sampling is a widely used bandit algorithm with strong performance guarantees, yet its balance between exploration and exploitation has lacked a clear optimization interpretation. This paper recasts posterior sampling as online optimization to explain how uncertainty influences choices alongside the desire to obtain immediate reward.

The authors introduce a time-invariant notion of regret that summarizes cumulative regret across horizons through a regret bound. This leads to a time-invariant Bellman-optimal policy, providing a reference for decision-making. They then show that Thompson Sampling has an online optimization form resembling the structure of that policy, with greedy behavior regularized by residual uncertainty.

This interpretation makes the exploration mechanism explicit within an optimization objective. The paper does not identify Thompson Sampling with the Bellman-optimal policy; the structural relationship supplies a benchmark for understanding and improving it. Comparing the two offers a principled way to study how posterior sampling balances immediate gains against the uncertainty that remains during sequential learning.
summary.tldr: Thompson Sampling admits an online optimization interpretation in which residual uncertainty regularizes greedy choices.

title: What Does Thompson Sampling Optimize?

abstract: Neural networks trained with gradient-based methods exhibit a strong simplicity bias: they learn simpler statistical features of their data before moving to more complex features. Previous analyses of this phenomenon have largely focused on settings with (quasi-)isotropic inputs. In this work, we study the simplicity bias from a Fourier perspective, which allows us to include two key features of natural images in the analysis: approximate translation-invariance and power-law spectra. We first show experimentally that simple neural networks trained on image classification tasks first rely on amplitude information $-$ related to pair-wise correlations between pixels $-$ before exploiting phase information, which encodes edges and higher-order correlations. In view of this, we introduce a synthetic data model for translation-invariant inputs that allows precise control over amplitudes and phases while remaining tractable. We rigorously establish that for isotropic and high-dimensional inputs, classification based on phase information alone is a genuinely hard task: online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) cannot distinguish the structured inputs from noise within $n \ll N^3$ steps, but needs at least $n \gg N^3 \log^2{N}$ steps. In contrast, we show both experimentally and theoretically that power-law spectra can dramatically accelerate the speed of learning phase information, even if the spectra do not help with classification. Simulations with two-layer networks trained on textures and with deep convolutional networks on ImageNet and CIFAR100 confirm this non-trivial interaction between amplitudes and phases, providing mechanistic insights into how deep neural networks can learn natural image distributions efficiently.

summary.tldr: Fourier analysis shows how image amplitude structure can accelerate learning of phase information even without directly helping classification.

title: A Fourier perspective on the learning dynamics of neural networks: from sample complexities to mechanistic insights

abstract: We study reward-free and reward-agnostic exploration in episodic finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs), where an agent explores an unknown environment without observing external rewards. Reward-free exploration aims to enable $\epsilon$-optimal policies for any reward revealed after exploration, while reward-agnostic exploration targets $\epsilon$-optimality for rewards drawn from a small finite class. In the reward-agnostic setting, Li, Yan, Chen, and Fan (2024) achieve minimax sample complexity, but only for restrictively small accuracy parameter $\epsilon$. We propose a new algorithm that significantly relaxes the requirement on $\epsilon$. Our approach is novel and of technical interest by itself. Our algorithm employs an online learning procedure with carefully designed rewards to construct an exploration policy, which is used to gather data sufficient for accurate dynamics estimation and subsequent computation of an $\epsilon$-optimal policy once the reward is revealed. Finally, we establish a tight lower bound for reward-free exploration, closing the gap between known upper and lower bounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents that explore an unknown environment before receiving an external reward objective. In reward-free exploration, the collected information must support a near-optimal policy for any later reward. In reward-agnostic exploration, it only needs to support rewards from a small finite collection. The setting is episodic, finite-horizon Markov decision processes.

For the reward-agnostic case, an existing optimal sample-complexity result applies only under a restrictive requirement on the accuracy parameter. The authors propose an algorithm that substantially relaxes that requirement. It uses an online learning procedure with carefully constructed rewards to build an exploration policy, then gathers data for estimating the environment’s dynamics.

Once the external reward is revealed, those dynamics estimates support computation of a policy within the requested accuracy of optimal performance. The paper separately proves a tight lower bound for reward-free exploration, matching known upper bounds. These contributions clarify both how to explore efficiently for a restricted reward collection and the fundamental exploration cost when any reward may arrive later.
summary.tldr: The paper broadens an efficient reward-agnostic exploration guarantee and closes the known bounds gap for reward-free exploration.

title: Improved Bounds for Reward-Agnostic and Reward-Free Exploration

abstract: Diffusion Language Models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) models by enabling parallel and controllable generation. Within this family, Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) currently perform best but still underperform AR models in perplexity and lack key inference-time efficiency features, most notably KV caching. We introduce Esoteric Language Models (Eso-LMs), a new family of models that fuses AR and MDM paradigms, smoothly interpolating between their perplexities while overcoming their respective limitations. Unlike prior work, which uses transformers with bidirectional attention as MDM denoisers, we exploit the connection between MDMs and Any-Order autoregressive models and adopt causal attention. This design lets us (1) compute the exact likelihood of MDMs for the first time and, crucially, (2) allows exact KV caching for MDMs while preserving parallel generation over the full sequence length for the first time, significantly improving inference efficiency. Combined with an optimized sampling schedule, Eso-LMs establish a new state of the art on the speed-quality Pareto frontier for unconditional generation.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel, controllable generation, but the abstract identifies two disadvantages relative to autoregressive models: worse perplexity and missing inference optimizations, especially key-value caching. Eso-LMs connect these model families through any-order autoregression, creating a family that smoothly interpolates between their perplexities while retaining useful generation capabilities.

The architectural change is to use causal attention rather than the bidirectional attention typically employed by masked diffusion denoisers. By exploiting the connection to any-order autoregressive models, the authors make exact likelihood computation possible for masked diffusion models. They also enable exact key-value caching, allowing previously computed attention information to be reused while preserving parallel generation across the full sequence length.

Combined with an optimized sampling schedule, this design establishes a new reported state of the art on the speed-quality frontier for unconditional generation. The contribution joins tractable probability evaluation with an inference efficiency mechanism that masked diffusion had lacked. The stated performance result concerns the balance between generation speed and quality, making both aspects central to assessing the model family.
summary.tldr: Eso-LMs combine autoregressive and masked diffusion ideas to enable exact likelihoods, exact key-value caching, and efficient parallel generation.

title: Esoteric Language Models: A Family of Any-Order Diffusion LLMs

abstract: In gradient-based learning, a step size chosen in parameter units does not produce a predictable per-step change in function output. This often leads to instability in the streaming setting (i.e., batch size$=1$), where stochasticity is not averaged out and update magnitudes can momentarily become arbitrarily big or small. Instead, we propose intentional updates: first specify the intended outcome of an update and then solve for the step size that approximately achieves it. This strategy has precedent in online supervised linear regression via Normalized Least Mean Squares (NLMS) algorithm, which selects a step size to yield a specified change in the function output proportional to the current error. We extend this principle to streaming deep reinforcement learning by defining appropriate intended outcomes: Intentional TD aims for a fixed fractional reduction of the TD error, and Intentional Policy Gradient aims for a bounded per-step change in the policy, limiting local KL divergence. We propose practical algorithms combining eligibility traces and diagonal scaling. Empirically, these methods yield state-of-the-art streaming performance, frequently performing on par with batch and replay-buffer approaches.

paragraphs: A learning rate specifies how far model parameters move, but that movement does not determine a predictable change in the model’s output. This becomes troublesome in streaming reinforcement learning, where each update uses one example and random fluctuations are not averaged across a batch. Update effects can consequently become extremely large or small.

Intentional updates reverse the usual choice: specify the desired behavioral change first, then solve approximately for a step size that achieves it. Building on a principle used in online linear regression, Intentional TD targets a fixed fractional reduction in temporal-difference error. Intentional Policy Gradient instead targets a bounded policy change by limiting local KL divergence.

The practical algorithms combine these targets with eligibility traces and diagonal scaling. Experiments report state-of-the-art streaming performance, frequently matching approaches that use batches or replay buffers. The findings suggest that controlling the intended effect of each update can make learning from individual experiences more stable and effective. The step-size calculation is approximate, and parity with batch methods is reported frequently rather than universally.
summary.tldr: Intentional updates choose learning rates to approximately achieve specified changes in prediction error or policy behavior during streaming reinforcement learning.

title: Intentional Updates for Streaming Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study black-box optimization of Lipschitz functions under noisy evaluations. Existing adaptive discretization methods implicitly avoid suboptimal regions but do not provide explicit certificates of optimality or measurable progress guarantees. We introduce Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP), which maintains an explicit active set $A_t$ of potentially optimal points via confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelopes. Any point outside $A_t$ is certifiably suboptimal with high probability, and under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension $\alpha$, we prove Vol$(A_t)$ shrinks at a controlled rate yielding sample complexity $Õ(\varepsilon^{-(2+\alpha)})$. We develop three extensions: CGP-Adaptive learns $L$ online with $O(\log T)$ overhead; CGP-TR scales to $d > 50$ via trust regions with local certificates; and CGP-Hybrid switches to GP refinement when local smoothness is detected. Experiments on 12 benchmarks ($d \in [2, 100]$) show CGP variants match or exceed strong baselines while providing principled stopping criteria via the computable gap proxy $\varepsilon_t$.

Rather than merely concentrating evaluations in promising regions, it maintains an explicit set of points that could still be optimal. Points removed from this set are certified as suboptimal with high probability.

The method combines uncertainty estimates with Lipschitz envelopes to update this active set. Under a margin condition involving the near-optimality dimension alpha, the authors bound how quickly its volume shrinks and obtain sample complexity of approximately epsilon raised to minus two minus alpha, ignoring logarithmic factors. Extensions learn the Lipschitz constant online, use trust regions to handle dimensions above 50 with local certificates, or switch to Gaussian-process refinement when local smoothness is detected. Across 12 benchmarks spanning dimensions two to 100, the variants match or outperform strong baselines. Their distinctive contribution is making elimination and progress measurable alongside optimization performance.
summary.tldr: Certificate-Guided Pruning optimizes noisy Lipschitz functions while explicitly certifying eliminated regions and providing measurable stopping criteria.

title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

abstract: Knowledge Base Question Answering (KBQA) challenges models to bridge the gap between natural language and strict knowledge graph schemas by generating executable logical forms. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced this field, current approaches often struggle with a dichotomy of failure: they either generate hallucinated queries without verifying schema existence or exhibit rigid, template-based reasoning that mimics synthesized traces without true comprehension of the environment. To address these limitations, we present KBQA-R1, a framework that shifts the paradigm from text imitation to interaction optimization via Reinforcement Learning. Treating KBQA as a multi-turn decision process, our model learns to autonomously navigate the knowledge base using a structured action space, refining its reasoning strategies based on concrete execution feedback rather than static supervision. Furthermore, we introduce Referenced Rejection Sampling (RRS), a data synthesis method that resolves cold-start challenges by strictly aligning reasoning traces with ground-truth action sequences. Extensive experiments on WebQSP, GrailQA, and GraphQuestions demonstrate that KBQA-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/KBQA-R1-814F.

paragraphs: Answering questions with a knowledge base requires translating ordinary language into executable queries that respect the database’s schema. A plausible-looking query can fail if it refers to nonexistent schema elements. The paper also identifies a different problem: models can copy rigid reasoning templates without adequately responding to the knowledge base they are actually using.

KBQA-R1 trains the model through reinforcement learning in a multi-turn decision process. A structured set of actions lets it navigate the knowledge base, and execution feedback informs its reasoning strategy. This makes interaction with the environment part of learning how to answer, rather than relying solely on imitation of prewritten traces.

To initialize this process, Referenced Rejection Sampling generates training data whose reasoning traces strictly follow ground-truth action sequences. This addresses the cold-start problem before interaction-based optimization. Experiments on WebQSP, GrailQA, and GraphQuestions report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support combining carefully aligned initial traces with feedback from actual execution to improve knowledge-base question answering.
summary.tldr: KBQA-R1 learns to answer knowledge-base questions through structured interactions and execution feedback, achieving state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks.

title: KBQA-R1: Reinforcing Large Language Models for Knowledge Base Question Answering

abstract: Recent reinforcement-learning frameworks for visual perception policy usually incorporate intermediate reasoning chains expressed in natural language. Empirical observations indicate that such purely linguistic intermediate reasoning often reduces performance on perception tasks. We argue that the core issue lies not in reasoning per se but in the form of reasoning: while these chains perform semantic reasoning in an unstructured linguistic space, visual perception requires reasoning in a spatial and object-centric space. In response, we introduce Artemis, a perception-policy learning method that performs structured visual reasoning, where each intermediate step is represented as a (label, bounding-box) pair capturing a verifiable visual state. This design enables explicit tracking of intermediate states, direct supervision for proposal quality, and avoids ambiguity introduced by language-based reasoning. Building upon verifiable and spatially grounded reasoning chains, Artemis provides a unified architecture for diverse perceptual tasks, without requiring the task-specific designs relied upon by prior perceptual policy models. Trained using grounding and detection sampeles in natural image domains, Artemis generalizes to counting and geometric perception tasks. At its core, a spatially grounded, object-centric chain rule provides a principled foundation for scalable and general perceptual policies.

paragraphs: Artemis investigates why adding intermediate reasoning can hurt visual perception. The authors argue that the representation of reasoning matters: free-form language describes meaning, while perception requires keeping track of objects and their spatial locations. Their approach makes those visual states explicit throughout the reasoning process.

Each intermediate step consists of an object label and a bounding box. This gives the model a concrete proposal that can be checked and supervised directly. A chain of these proposals records how the model progresses through the image, reducing the ambiguity of verbal descriptions. The method builds perception policies around a spatial, object-centered chain rule and uses one architecture across different perceptual tasks.

The model is trained with grounding and detection examples from natural images and generalizes to counting and geometric perception tasks. These findings support structured visual reasoning as a useful basis for broader perception policies. The contribution is both a way to represent intermediate decisions and a way to make their quality directly assessable during learning.
summary.tldr: Artemis represents visual reasoning as sequences of object labels and bounding boxes, supporting perception policies that generalize across tasks.

title: Artemis: Structured Visual Reasoning for Perception Policy Learning

abstract: Entity tracking (ET), the ability to keep track of states, is a fundamental skill that underlies complex reasoning. An increasing amount of work investigates how transformer language models (LMs) solve entity binding without state changes. However, there is limited understanding of how non-toy LMs address ET problems of realistic difficulties expressed in natural language. To this end, we investigate the mechanisms underlying ET in more complex scenarios featuring multiple state-changing operations. We find that LMs do not incrementally track world states across tokens or query-relevant states across layers, but simply aggregate relevant information in parallel at the last token when the query becomes evident. We further investigate mechanisms of individual operations (PUT, REMOVE, MOVE) to characterize this non-incremental ET mechanism. Surprisingly, LMs implement the REMOVE operation with a fragile global suppression tag; this global removal mechanism predicts various failure modes that we confirm behaviorally. We provide a mechanistic solution of nullifying this tag to partially address this issue. Overall, our findings reveal that LMs solve a fundamentally sequential task using a non-sequential strategy. More broadly, our work illustrates how behavioral and mechanistic analyses can fruitfully interact. Behavioral results inform mechanistic hypotheses, and insights from mechanistic analyses help build stronger behavioral evaluations by predicting failure modes missing from existing evaluations.

It combines observations of model behavior with analysis of the internal mechanisms responsible.

summary.tldr: The studied language models track changing entities through parallel information aggregation, with a fragile removal mechanism that predicts observable failures.

title: Do Language Models Track Entities Across State Changes?

abstract: Even for the gradient descent (GD) method applied to neural network training, understanding its optimization dynamics, including convergence rate, iterate trajectories, function value oscillations, and especially its implicit acceleration, remains a challenging problem. We analyze nonlinear models with the logistic loss and show that the steps of GD reduce to those of generalized perceptron algorithms (Rosenblatt, 1958), providing a new perspective on the dynamics. This reduction yields significantly simpler algorithmic steps, which we analyze using classical linear algebra tools. Using these tools, we demonstrate on a minimalistic example that the nonlinearity in a two-layer model can provably yield a faster iteration complexity $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d})$ compared to $\Omega(d)$ achieved by linear models, where $d$ is the number of features. This helps explain the optimization dynamics and the implicit acceleration phenomenon observed in neural networks. The theoretical results are supported by extensive numerical experiments. We believe that this alternative view will further advance research on the optimization of neural networks.
