paragraphs: Even ordinary gradient descent can have complicated behavior when used to train nonlinear models. Its trajectories, oscillating objective values, and sometimes unexpectedly fast progress remain difficult to explain. This paper develops a different mathematical description of those dynamics by connecting gradient descent with generalized perceptron algorithms.

For the nonlinear models studied with logistic loss, the authors show that gradient descent steps reduce to simpler perceptron-style updates. This representation makes classical linear algebra tools available for analyzing the training process. The point is to expose structure in familiar gradient descent dynamics through an equivalent, more tractable description.

On a minimal example, the analysis proves that nonlinearity in a two-layer model can reduce iteration complexity to roughly the square root of the feature count, ignoring logarithmic factors, compared with a linear lower bound for linear models. Extensive numerical experiments support the theoretical results. The demonstrated acceleration belongs to the analyzed example, but it provides a concrete explanation of how model nonlinearity itself can contribute to faster optimization without introducing an explicit acceleration mechanism.
summary.tldr: A perceptron-based view of gradient descent explains how nonlinearity can provably accelerate optimization in a minimal two-layer example.

title: Gradient Descent as a Perceptron Algorithm: Understanding Dynamics and Implicit Acceleration

abstract: We study ridge regression and ridge-regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) under $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy via output perturbation. In classical private ERM, the ridge parameter simultaneously controls statistical regularization and the estimator’s global sensitivity. Larger regularization reduces the DP noise scale but increases bias. So choosing the tuning parameter becomes a privacy–accuracy bottleneck. We propose a framework that makes these two roles explicit by decoupling regularization into (i) a statistical penalty $\alpha$, defining the target ridge/ERM solution, and (ii) a privacy-stabilization parameter $c$, used only to enforce a curvature floor and hence a tight sensitivity bound. We apply this framework to ridge regression, where $c$ is used to boost the minimum eigenvalue of the empirical Gram matrix. We derive an explicit bias–variance–DP-variance risk decomposition and characterize optimal $(\alpha,c)$ in several regimes, yielding sharp tuning guidance and improved accuracy relative to single-parameter regularization. Finally, we extend the same decoupling principle to general ridge-regularized ERM. We support the theory with simulations.

paragraphs: Private regression often adds noise to a fitted estimator to protect individual data contributions. Regularization then serves two purposes: it shapes the statistical solution and limits how much that solution can change when data changes. Increasing regularization can reduce the privacy noise required, but it also increases bias. A single tuning parameter must therefore negotiate competing demands.

This paper separates those roles. A statistical penalty, alpha, defines the target regularized solution, while a privacy-stabilization parameter, c, enforces a lower bound on curvature and controls sensitivity. For ridge regression, the stabilization raises the minimum eigenvalue of the empirical Gram matrix. The framework applies to output perturbation under epsilon-delta differential privacy.

The authors derive a risk decomposition separating bias, ordinary variance, and variance from privacy noise. They characterize optimal parameter choices in several regimes and report improved accuracy compared with single-parameter regularization. Simulations support the theory, and the same separation principle extends to more general ridge-regularized empirical risk minimization. The contribution is a clearer, more flexible way to tune privacy and statistical behavior.
summary.tldr: Separating statistical regularization from privacy stabilization provides sharper tuning guidance and improved accuracy for private ridge regression and related estimators.

title: Decoupling Regularization and Privacy in Differentially Private Ridge Regression and ERM

abstract: Effectively retrieving, reasoning, and understanding multimodal information remains a critical challenge for agentic systems. Traditional Retrieval-augmented Generation (RAG) methods rely on linear interaction histories, which struggle to handle long-context tasks, especially those involving information-sparse yet token-heavy visual data in iterative reasoning scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce VimRAG, a framework tailored for multimodal Retrieval-augmented Reasoning across text, images, and videos. Inspired by our systematic study, we model the reasoning process as a dynamic directed acyclic graph that structures the agent states and retrieved multimodal evidence. Building upon this structured memory, we introduce a Graph-Modulated Visual Memory Encoding mechanism, with which the significance of memory nodes is evaluated via their topological position, allowing the model to dynamically allocate high-resolution tokens to pivotal evidence while compressing or discarding trivial clues. To implement this paradigm, we propose a Graph-Guided Policy Optimization strategy. This strategy disentangles step-wise validity from trajectory-level rewards by pruning memory nodes associated with redundant actions, thereby facilitating fine-grained credit assignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VimRAG consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse multimodal RAG benchmarks.

paragraphs: An agent reasoning over retrieved images and videos can accumulate a long history that consumes many tokens while containing relatively little useful evidence. VimRAG addresses this problem by organizing agent states and retrieved material into a changing directed acyclic graph. The graph provides structured memory across text, images, and videos.

Its visual-memory encoding mechanism uses a node’s position in the graph to assess its significance. Important evidence receives more high-resolution tokens, while less useful clues are compressed or discarded. This makes the allocation of visual detail depend on how evidence participates in the reasoning structure, rather than simply retaining everything in a linear interaction history.

The framework also introduces graph-guided policy optimization. By pruning memory nodes linked to redundant actions, it separates the validity of individual steps from rewards assigned to the complete reasoning trajectory. This supports more precise credit assignment during training. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across diverse multimodal retrieval-augmented generation benchmarks, supporting structured memory as a useful basis for both context management and policy learning.
summary.tldr: VimRAG uses a graph of reasoning states and evidence to allocate visual tokens and improve learning from multimodal retrieval.

title: Navigating Massive Visual Context in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Multimodal Memory Graph

abstract: We provide the first study of the problem of finding differentially private (DP) second-order stationary points (SOSP) in stochastic (non-convex) minimax optimization. Existing literature either focuses only on first-order stationary points for minimax problems or on SOSP for classical stochastic minimization problems. This work provides, for the first time, a unified and detailed treatment of both empirical and population risks. Specifically, we propose a purely first-order method that combines a nested gradient descent–ascent scheme with SPIDER-style variance reduction and Gaussian perturbations to ensure privacy. A key technical device is a block-wise ($q$-period) analysis that controls the accumulation of stochastic variance and privacy noise without summing over the full iteration horizon, yielding a unified treatment of both empirical-risk and population formulations. Under standard smoothness, Hessian-Lipschitzness, and strong concavity assumptions, we establish high-probability guarantees for reaching an $(\alpha,\sqrt{\rho_\Phi \alpha})$-approximate second-order stationary point with $\alpha = \mathcal{O}( (\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3})$ for empirical risk objectives and $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{n^{1/3}} + (\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n\varepsilon})^{1/2})$ for population objectives, matching the best known rates for private first-order stationarity.

paragraphs: This paper studies privacy-preserving optimization problems in which one set of variables is minimized while another is maximized. It seeks approximate second-order stationary points, a stronger local condition than merely making the gradient small. The work treats both empirical objectives built from a dataset and population objectives representing the underlying data distribution.

The proposed algorithm uses only first-order information. It combines nested gradient descent and ascent, SPIDER-style variance reduction, and Gaussian perturbations for differential privacy. Its analysis groups iterations into blocks to control accumulated sampling variance and privacy noise, avoiding a direct accumulation across the entire iteration horizon.

Under smoothness, Hessian-Lipschitzness, and strong concavity assumptions, the authors establish high-probability second-order stationarity guarantees. The empirical accuracy parameter scales as (√d/(nε))^(2/3), while the population rate includes n^(-1/3) plus (√d/(nε))^(1/2), where d, n, and ε represent dimension, sample size, and privacy level. These rates match the best known private first-order stationarity rates, showing that the stronger local guarantee is attainable at those accuracy scales in the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: A first-order private minimax algorithm achieves conditional second-order stationarity guarantees matching the best known private first-order accuracy rates.

title: Finding Differentially Private Second Order Stationary Points in Stochastic Minimax Optimization

abstract: Existing coding benchmarks evaluate language models (LMs) on concrete, well-specified tasks such as fixing bugs or writing tests. However, human programmers do not spend all day addressing isolated GitHub issues. Instead, real-world software development is grounded in the pursuit of high-level goals. Evaluating whether LMs can iteratively develop code to accomplish open-ended objectives without explicit guidance remains an open challenge. We introduce CodeClash, a benchmark where LMs compete in multi-round tournaments to build the best codebase for achieving a competitive objective. Each round proceeds in two parts: agents edit their code, then their codebases compete head-to-head in a code arena that determines winners based on objectives like score maximization, resource acquisition, or survival. Models must decide for themselves how to improve their code both absolutely and against their opponents. We run 1680 tournaments to evaluate 8 LMs across 6 arenas, revealing how models exhibit diverse development styles and share fundamental limitations in strategic reasoning. Models also struggle with long-term codebase maintenance; repositories become progressively messy and redundant. Top models lose every round against expert human programmers. We open-source CodeClash to advance the study of autonomous, goal-oriented code development.

paragraphs: CodeClash evaluates whether language models can improve software toward an open-ended goal without receiving a precise list of changes. Instead of presenting a single bug or test-writing task, it puts models in repeated competitions. Each model must decide which code changes could improve its results and how to respond to competing implementations.

Every tournament round has an editing phase followed by a head-to-head contest between codebases. The arenas reward objectives such as maximizing a score, acquiring resources, or surviving. This structure connects development choices to observable competitive outcomes while requiring agents to maintain and revise a codebase across rounds. Success involves both absolute improvement and adaptation to opponents.

The study runs 1,680 tournaments involving eight models across six arenas. It finds varied development styles but shared weaknesses in strategic reasoning and sustained maintenance, with repositories becoming increasingly messy and redundant. In the reported comparisons, top models lose every round against expert human programmers. The benchmark exposes gaps between completing clearly specified coding tasks and autonomously directing a longer development effort.
summary.tldr: CodeClash tests autonomous software improvement through repeated competitions, revealing weaknesses in model strategy and long-term code maintenance.

title: CodeClash: Benchmarking Goal-Oriented Software Engineering

abstract: Multimodal representation learning aims to construct a shared embedding space in which heterogeneous modalities are semantically aligned. Despite strong empirical results, InfoNCE-based objectives introduce inherent conflicts that yield distribution gaps across modalities. In this work, we identify two conflicts in the multimodal regime, both exacerbated as the number of modalities increases: (i) an alignment–uniformity conflict, whereby the repulsion of uniformity undermines pairwise alignment, and (ii) an intra-alignment conflict, where aligning multiple modalities induces competing alignment directions. To address these issues, we propose a principled decoupling of alignment and uniformity for multimodal representations, providing a conflict-free recipe for multimodal learning that simultaneously supports discriminative and generative use cases without task-specific modules. We then provide a theoretical guarantee that our method acts as an efficient proxy for a global Hölder divergence over multiple modality distributions, and thus reduces the distribution gap among modalities. Extensive experiments on retrieval and UnCLIP-style generation demonstrate consistent gains.

paragraphs: Multimodal representation learning places different kinds of data in a shared space so that related content aligns. This paper identifies two conflicts in InfoNCE-based training that can leave the modalities separated. Both become more pronounced as additional modalities are included, making the problem especially relevant beyond a simple pair of input types.

The first conflict is between alignment and uniformity: spreading representations apart can work against bringing matching examples together. The second occurs within alignment itself, as matching several modalities introduces competing directions. The authors propose separating alignment and uniformity to remove these identified conflicts while supporting both discriminative and generative uses without task-specific modules.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the method is an efficient proxy for a global Hölder divergence across modality distributions, providing a connection to reducing their distribution gap. Experiments on retrieval and UnCLIP-style generation report consistent gains. Together, the analysis and results suggest that coordinating the training objectives can improve a shared representation's usefulness for both finding related content and generating content.
summary.tldr: Decoupling alignment and uniformity addresses competing multimodal training signals and improves retrieval and generation.

title: Towards Uniformity and Alignment for Multimodal Representation Learning

abstract: Language models famously improve under a smooth scaling law, but some specific capabilities exhibit sudden breakthroughs in performance. Advocates of "emergence" view these capabilities as unlocked at a specific scale, but others attribute breakthroughs to superficial metric thresholding effects. We propose that breakthroughs are instead driven by continuous changes in the probability distribution of training outcomes when performance is bimodally distributed across random seeds. We show that different random seeds can produce either smooth or emergent scaling trends in synthetic length generalization tasks, multiple choice question answering, and grammatical generalization. We reveal that sharp breakthroughs in metrics are produced by underlying continuous changes in their distribution across seeds. These distributions may become abruptly bimodal at a capacity threshold—but this threshold appears at scales well before most seeds achieve breakthrough. Our observations hold true even under continuous loss metrics, confirming that random variation must be considered when predicting a model’s performance from its scale.

paragraphs: Some language-model abilities appear to improve abruptly as model scale increases, despite smoother overall scaling trends. Explanations have included capabilities becoming available at a particular scale and evaluation metrics creating artificial thresholds. This paper investigates a different source of apparent breakthroughs: variation in training outcomes across random seeds.

The authors examine synthetic length generalization, multiple-choice question answering, and grammatical generalization. Different seeds can yield either smooth improvement or apparently emergent behavior. The paper connects sharp metric changes to continuous shifts in the distribution of outcomes across seeds, especially when that distribution has two distinct modes.

The distribution itself may become abruptly bimodal at a capacity threshold, but that threshold appears well before most seeds achieve a breakthrough. The observed effects also persist with continuous loss metrics, so they cannot be explained solely by thresholded evaluation scores. These findings make random training variation relevant to scaling predictions: a model's size can affect the likelihood of reaching a capability, while individual runs need not display the same progression.
summary.tldr: Apparent capability breakthroughs can arise from changing probabilities of training outcomes across random seeds as models scale.

title: Random Scaling of Emergent Capabilities

abstract: Diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models, leveraging simultaneous denoising to enable global planning and iterative refinement. These properties make dLLMs attractive for long-context generation. However, deploying dLLMs faces a prohibitive memory barrier, as existing inference systems are inefficient for the diffusion paradigm. We observe that current inference systems are misaligned with dLLMs. Unlike autoregressive models, whose memory footprint is dominated by the KV-Cache, dLLMs are bottlenecked by transient activations rematerialized per step. Moreover, generic memory reuse mechanisms lack the global visibility to handle dynamic memory peaks of dLLMs, which alternate between logits and feed-forward networks. To address these challenges, we present Mosaic, a memory-efficient inference system that shifts dLLM execution from local, static management to a global, dynamic paradigm. Mosaic integrates (i) a mask-only logits kernel eliminating redundant activation materialization, (ii) a lazy chunking optimizer using online heuristics to tame dynamic memory peaks, and (iii) a global memory manager leveraging virtual addressing to mitigate memory fragmentation. Evaluations show that Mosaic reduces the memory peak-to-average ratio by 2.71$\times$ on average and increases the maximum inference sequence length on identical hardware by 15.30–32.34$\times$. Crucially, Mosaic is training-free and preserves exact model outputs, while reducing end-to-end latency by 2.5%–55.4%. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/flashserve/Mosaic.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models repeatedly denoise many positions, supporting iterative refinement and global planning. Their inference memory demands differ from those of autoregressive models: temporary activations recreated during each step are a major bottleneck. Memory peaks also shift between logits and feed-forward networks, making local, static memory management poorly suited to this execution pattern.

Mosaic coordinates memory globally and adapts to these changing peaks. A mask-only logits kernel avoids redundant activation materialization, a lazy chunking optimizer uses online heuristics to control peak demand, and a global manager uses virtual addressing to reduce fragmentation. Together, these components address the amount, timing, and organization of memory use.

End-to-end latency falls by 2.5%–55.4%. The system requires no training and preserves exact model outputs. Thus, the demonstrated context-length gains concern what the inference system can accommodate through execution and memory improvements.
summary.tldr: Mosaic reorganizes diffusion language model inference memory to support 15.30×–32.34× longer sequences while preserving exact outputs.

title: Mosaic: Unlocking Over 30$\times$ Context Length for Diffusion LLMs Inference via Global Memory Planning and Dynamic Peak Taming

abstract: Audio-Visual Segmentation (AVS) targets pixel level localization of sounding emitting objects in videos. However, existing models rely on dense cross-modal attention with quadratic computational cost, limiting their suitability for resource efficient deployment. Most efficiency oriented methods focus on backbone reduction and overlook the interaction module as the primary bottleneck. This paper proposes LightAVSeg, a lightweight framework that replaces heavy attention with a decoupled design for semantic filtering and spatial grounding, resulting in interaction costs that scale linearly with spatial resolution. Furthermore, we introduce an auxiliary alignment loss to enforce semantic consistency during training with zero inference overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LightAVSeg achieves a new state-of-the-art among lightweight methods: with 20.5M parameters ( 1/7 of AVSegFormer), it reaches 50.4 mIoU on the MS3 benchmark and enables efficient inference on a mobile processor.

paragraphs: Audio-visual segmentation identifies the pixels belonging to objects that emit sound in a video. Connecting audio and image information can be expensive when models use dense cross-modal attention. The paper argues that this interaction module is a major bottleneck that efficiency efforts focused on shrinking the backbone can overlook.

LightAVSeg replaces heavy attention with separate mechanisms for semantic filtering and spatial grounding. These handle which content is relevant to the sound and where that content appears. The resulting interaction cost grows linearly with spatial resolution. An auxiliary alignment loss encourages semantic consistency during training without adding work during inference.

The model contains 20.5 million parameters, about one-seventh of AVSegFormer's size, and reaches 50.4 mIoU on the MS3 benchmark. The authors report a new state of the art among lightweight methods and efficient inference on a mobile processor. These results connect the interaction-module redesign to a practical combination of segmentation quality, smaller model size, and resource-efficient deployment.
summary.tldr: LightAVSeg separates semantic filtering from spatial grounding to reduce audio-visual interaction cost, achieving strong lightweight segmentation results and mobile inference.

title: LightAVSeg: Lightweight Audio-Visual Segmentation

abstract: Intermediate token generation (ITG), where a model produces output before the solution, has become a standard method to improve the performance of language models on reasoning tasks. These intermediate tokens have been called "reasoning traces" or even "thinking traces" – implicitly anthropomorphizing the traces, and implying that these traces resemble steps a human might take when solving a challenging problem, and as such can provide an interpretable window into the operation of the model’s thinking process to the end user. In this position paper, we present evidence that this anthropomorphization isn’t a harmless metaphor, and instead is quite dangerous – it confuses the nature of these models and how to use them effectively, and leads to questionable research. We call on the community to avoid such anthropomorphization of intermediate tokens.
originalAbstract: Intermediate token generation (ITG), where a model produces output before the solution, has become a standard method to improve the performance of language models on reasoning tasks. These intermediate tokens have been called "reasoning traces" or even "thinking traces" – implicitly anthropomorphizing the traces, and implying that these traces resemble steps a human might take when solving a challenging problem, and as such can provide an interpretable window into the operation of the model’s thinking process to the end user. In this position paper, we present evidence that this anthropomorphization isn’t a harmless metaphor, and instead is quite dangerous – it confuses the nature of these models and how to use them effectively, and leads to questionable research. We call on the community to avoid such anthropomorphization of intermediate tokens.

paragraphs: Language models often generate text before giving a final solution, a practice the paper calls intermediate token generation. This can improve performance on reasoning tasks. The authors question the common habit of labeling that text as a record of the model’s reasoning or thinking, because those terms imply a particular interpretation of what the text reveals.

Calling the output a thinking trace suggests that it resembles the steps a person would take and provides an understandable view into the model’s internal process. The paper presents evidence that this anthropomorphic interpretation is consequential. The authors argue that it confuses users about the nature of language models and how to use them effectively.

The paper also connects that confusion to questionable research and calls for the community to avoid anthropomorphic terminology for intermediate tokens. Its distinction is between the performance benefit of producing intermediate output and the interpretation placed on that output. Recognizing the benefit does not itself establish that the generated text is an interpretable account of human-like thinking.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that calling intermediate model output “thinking” misleads users and researchers about what that output reveals.

abstract: Graph-based methods for semi-supervised learning have recently been shown to be promising for combining labeled and unlabeled data in classification problems. However, inference for graphbased methods often does not scale well to very large data sets, since it requires inversion of a large matrix or solution of a large linear program. Moreover, such approaches are inherently transductive, giving predictions for only those points in the unlabeled set, and not for an arbitrary test point. In this paper a new approach is presented that preserves the strengths of graph-based semisupervised learning while overcoming the limitations of scalability and non-inductive inference, through a combination of generative mixture models and discriminative regularization using the graph Laplacian. Experimental results show that this approach preserves the accuracy of purely graph-based transductive methods when the data has “manifold structure,” and at the same time achieves inductive learning with significantly reduced computational cost.
originalAbstract: Graph-based methods for semi-supervised learning have recently been shown to be promising for combining labeled and unlabeled data in classification problems. However, inference for graphbased methods often does not scale well to very large data sets, since it requires inversion of a large matrix or solution of a large linear program. Moreover, such approaches are inherently transductive, giving predictions for only those points in the unlabeled set, and not for an arbitrary test point. In this paper a new approach is presented that preserves the strengths of graph-based semisupervised learning while overcoming the limitations of scalability and non-inductive inference, through a combination of generative mixture models and discriminative regularization using the graph Laplacian. Experimental results show that this approach preserves the accuracy of purely graph-based transductive methods when the data has “manifold structure,” and at the same time achieves inductive learning with significantly reduced computational cost.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses relationships among labeled and unlabeled examples to help classify them. The paper identifies two obstacles to using these methods more broadly. Their inference can require a large matrix inversion or a large linear program, and their predictions are typically restricted to the unlabeled points already included in the problem.

Harmonic mixtures combine a generative mixture model with discriminative regularization based on the graph Laplacian. The mixture model supplies a model-based route to prediction, while the graph component retains information about relationships among examples. This combination is designed to support predictions for arbitrary new test points and reduce the computational burden associated with purely graph-based inference.

The experiments show that the method preserves the accuracy of graph-based transductive approaches when the data has manifold structure. In the same setting, it achieves inductive prediction with significantly lower computational cost. The result supports combining these two modeling approaches when the aim is to retain graph-based learning benefits while extending prediction beyond a fixed collection of unlabeled examples.
summary.tldr: Harmonic mixtures combine mixture models and graph regularization to predict new examples efficiently while preserving graph-based accuracy on data with manifold structure.

title: Harmonic mixtures: combining mixture models and graph-based methods for inductive and scalable semi-supervised learning

abstract: Discriminative training of graphical models can be expensive if the variables have large cardinality, even if the graphical structure is tractable. In such cases, pseudolikelihood is an attractive alternative, because its running time is linear in the variable cardinality, but on some data its accuracy can be poor. Piecewise training (Sutton & McCallum, 2005) can have better accuracy but does not scale as well in the variable cardinality. In this paper, we introduce piecewise pseudolikelihood, which retains the computational efficiency of pseudolikelihood but can have much better accuracy. On several benchmark NLP data sets, piecewise pseudolikelihood has better accuracy than standard pseudolikelihood, and in many cases nearly equivalent to maximum likelihood, with five to ten times less training time than batch CRF training.
originalAbstract: Discriminative training of graphical models can be expensive if the variables have large cardinality, even if the graphical structure is tractable. In such cases, pseudolikelihood is an attractive alternative, because its running time is linear in the variable cardinality, but on some data its accuracy can be poor. Piecewise training (Sutton & McCallum, 2005) can have better accuracy but does not scale as well in the variable cardinality. In this paper, we introduce piecewise pseudolikelihood, which retains the computational efficiency of pseudolikelihood but can have much better accuracy. On several benchmark NLP data sets, piecewise pseudolikelihood has better accuracy than standard pseudolikelihood, and in many cases nearly equivalent to maximum likelihood, with five to ten times less training time than batch CRF training.

paragraphs: Training a discriminative graphical model can be expensive when each variable has many possible values, even if the graph itself permits tractable computation. Pseudolikelihood is appealing because its running time grows linearly with the number of values per variable. However, the paper notes that its accuracy can be poor on some data.

Piecewise training offers another tradeoff: it can improve accuracy, but its cost scales less favorably with the number of possible values. The authors introduce piecewise pseudolikelihood to combine useful properties of these approaches. The proposed training method retains pseudolikelihood's computational efficiency while allowing substantially better predictive accuracy.

On several natural-language-processing benchmarks, piecewise pseudolikelihood achieves better accuracy than standard pseudolikelihood. In many cases, its accuracy is nearly equivalent to maximum-likelihood training, while training takes five to ten times less time than batch CRF training. These findings show a favorable speed–accuracy tradeoff on the evaluated tasks. They support an efficient alternative when large variable cardinalities make conventional training costly, without asserting that the accuracy match holds in every case.
summary.tldr: Piecewise pseudolikelihood improves on standard pseudolikelihood accuracy while substantially reducing training time relative to batch CRFs on NLP benchmarks.

title: Piecewise pseudolikelihood for efficient training of conditional random fields

abstract: In this paper we perform an empirical evaluation of supervised learning methods on high dimensional data. We evaluate learning performance on three metrics: accuracy, AUC, and squared loss. We also study the effect of increasing dimensionality on the relative performance of the learning algorithms. Our findings are consistent with previous studies for problems of relatively low dimension, but suggest that as dimensionality increases the relative performance of the various learning algorithms changes. To our surprise, the methods that seem best able to learn from high dimensional data are random forests and neural nets.
originalAbstract: In this paper we perform an empirical evaluation of supervised learning methods on high dimensional data. We evaluate learning performance on three metrics: accuracy, AUC, and squared loss. We also study the effect of increasing dimensionality on the relative performance of the learning algorithms. Our findings are consistent with previous studies for problems of relatively low dimension, but suggest that as dimensionality increases the relative performance of the various learning algorithms changes. To our surprise, the methods that seem best able to learn from high dimensional data are random forests and neural nets.

paragraphs: This paper examines how supervised learning methods perform when examples have many input dimensions. Its focus is comparative: the authors ask whether the relative strengths of learning algorithms change as dimensionality increases. That question matters because a method that performs well with relatively few input dimensions may occupy a different position when the representation becomes much larger.

The evaluation uses three measures: accuracy, AUC, and squared loss. These provide different perspectives on prediction quality, so the comparison is not organized around a single performance score. The study also explicitly investigates increasing dimensionality, connecting changes in algorithm performance to the size of the input representation.

For relatively low-dimensional problems, the findings agree with earlier studies. At higher dimensions, however, the relative performance of the methods appears to shift. Random forests and neural networks seem best able to learn from the high-dimensional data examined. This is an empirical finding about the study's comparisons, providing evidence that conclusions drawn from lower-dimensional evaluations may not carry over unchanged.
summary.tldr: The evaluation suggests that algorithm rankings change with dimensionality, with random forests and neural networks appearing strongest on the high-dimensional data studied.

title: An empirical evaluation of supervised learning in high dimensions

abstract: A good distance measure for time series needs to properly incorporate the temporal structure, and should be applicable to sequences with unequal lengths. In this paper, we propose a distance measure as a principled solution to the two requirements. Unlike the unconventional feature vector representation, our approach represents each time series with a summarizing smooth curve in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and therefore translate the distance between time series into distances between curves. Moreover we propose to learn the kernel of this RKHS from a population of time series with discrete observations using Gaussian process-based non-parametric mixed-effect models. Experiments on two vastly different real-world problems show that the proposed distance measure leads to improved classification accuracy over the conventional distance measures.
originalAbstract: A good distance measure for time series needs to properly incorporate the temporal structure, and should be applicable to sequences with unequal lengths. In this paper, we propose a distance measure as a principled solution to the two requirements. Unlike the unconventional feature vector representation, our approach represents each time series with a summarizing smooth curve in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and therefore translate the distance between time series into distances between curves. Moreover we propose to learn the kernel of this RKHS from a population of time series with discrete observations using Gaussian process-based non-parametric mixed-effect models. Experiments on two vastly different real-world problems show that the proposed distance measure leads to improved classification accuracy over the conventional distance measures.

paragraphs: Comparing time series requires more than comparing collections of measurements: the temporal structure matters, and sequences may have different lengths. This paper proposes a distance measure designed to address both requirements. Its approach represents each observed series by a smooth curve, making comparisons between sequences into comparisons between those curves.

The curves belong to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS, which supplies the mathematical setting for measuring their distances. The paper also proposes learning the kernel that defines this space from a population of discretely observed time series. It does so using Gaussian process-based nonparametric mixed-effect models, connecting the distance representation to information learned across the available series.

Experiments on two very different real-world problems show improved classification accuracy compared with conventional distance measures. The findings support the proposed representation on those tasks rather than establishing a universal ranking of distances. The methodological contribution is the combination of smooth temporal summaries, support for unequal sequence lengths, and a kernel learned from the population being modeled.
summary.tldr: Representing time series as smooth curves in a learned kernel space supports unequal lengths and improves classification on two real-world problems.

title: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space framework for pairwise time series distances

abstract: We present a new view of Gaussian belief propagation (GaBP) based on a representation of the determinant as a product over orbits of a graph. We show that the GaBP determinant estimate captures totally backtracking orbits of the graph and consider how to correct this estimate. We show that the missing orbits may be grouped into equivalence classes corresponding to backtrackless orbits and the contribution of each equivalence class is easily determined from the GaBP solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this multiplicative correction factor can be interpreted as the determinant of a backtrackless adjacency matrix of the graph with edge weights based on GaBP. Finally, an efficient method is proposed to compute a truncated correction factor including all backtrackless orbits up to a specified length.

We show that the GaBP determinant estimate captures totally backtracking orbits of the graph and consider how to correct this estimate. We show that the missing orbits may be grouped into equivalence classes corresponding to backtrackless orbits and the contribution of each equivalence class is easily determined from the GaBP solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this multiplicative correction factor can be interpreted as the determinant of a backtrackless adjacency matrix of the graph with edge weights based on GaBP. Finally, an efficient method is proposed to compute a truncated correction factor including all backtrackless orbits up to a specified length.

paragraphs: This paper examines the determinant estimate produced by Gaussian belief propagation through a graph-based representation. It expresses the determinant as a product of contributions from graph orbits. This perspective makes it possible to ask which contributions the belief-propagation estimate includes and which ones require a correction.

The authors show that the estimate captures totally backtracking orbits. They organize the missing orbits into equivalence classes associated with backtrackless orbits, and show that each class's contribution can be obtained readily from the existing Gaussian belief-propagation solution. The correction therefore builds on quantities already provided by that solution.

They further identify the multiplicative correction as the determinant of a backtrackless adjacency matrix whose edge weights depend on belief propagation. For computation, they propose an efficient truncated correction that includes every backtrackless orbit up to a chosen length. The contribution is both an interpretation of the original estimate and a systematic correction procedure, with the truncated calculation explicitly limited by the selected orbit length.
summary.tldr: An orbit-product view identifies missing contributions in Gaussian belief-propagation determinant estimates and provides a systematic correction.

title: Orbit-product representation and correction of Gaussian belief propagation

abstract: We consider a sequential decision problem where the rewards are generated by a piecewise-stationary distribution. However, the different reward distributions are unknown and may change at unknown instants. Our approach uses a limited number of side observations on past rewards, but does not require prior knowledge of the frequency of changes. In spite of the adversarial nature of the reward process, we provide an algorithm whose regret, with respect to the baseline with perfect knowledge of the distributions and the changes, is $O(k \log(T))$, where $k$ is the number of changes up to time $T$. This is in contrast to the case where side observations are not available, and where the regret is at least $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$.
originalAbstract: We consider a sequential decision problem where the rewards are generated by a piecewise-stationary distribution. However, the different reward distributions are unknown and may change at unknown instants. Our approach uses a limited number of side observations on past rewards, but does not require prior knowledge of the frequency of changes. In spite of the adversarial nature of the reward process, we provide an algorithm whose regret, with respect to the baseline with perfect knowledge of the distributions and the changes, is $O(k \log(T))$, where $k$ is the number of changes up to time $T$. This is in contrast to the case where side observations are not available, and where the regret is at least $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decisions when reward distributions stay fixed for intervals but change at unknown times. Neither the distributions nor their change points are known to the learner. The proposed approach uses a limited number of additional observations of past rewards and does not require advance knowledge of how frequently changes occur.

Its guarantee concerns regret, measured against a baseline that knows both the reward distributions and when they change. The authors provide an algorithm with regret O(k log(T)), where k is the number of changes by time T. The dependence on both quantities matters: the bound grows logarithmically with the time horizon and linearly with the number of changes.

The abstract contrasts this result with a lower bound of Ω(√T) when side observations are unavailable. The comparison identifies additional access to past rewards as a consequential resource in the stated problem. Despite the adversarial character of the reward process, the algorithm can obtain the stated bound without knowing the change frequency beforehand.
summary.tldr: Limited side observations enable O(k log(T)) regret for piecewise-stationary rewards without advance knowledge of the change frequency.

title: Piecewise-stationary bandit problems with side observations

abstract: Standard Gaussian processes (GPs) model observations' noise as constant throughout input space. This is often a too restrictive assumption, but one that is needed for GP inference to be tractable. In this work we present a non-standard variational approximation that allows accurate inference in heteroscedastic GPs (i.e., under input-dependent noise conditions). Computational cost is roughly twice that of the standard GP, and also scales as O(n^3). Accuracy is verified by comparing with the golden standard MCMC and its effectiveness is illustrated on several synthetic and real datasets of diverse characteristics. An application to volatility forecasting is also considered.
originalAbstract: Standard Gaussian processes (GPs) model observations' noise as constant throughout input space. This is often a too restrictive assumption, but one that is needed for GP inference to be tractable. In this work we present a non-standard variational approximation that allows accurate inference in heteroscedastic GPs (i.e., under input-dependent noise conditions). Computational cost is roughly twice that of the standard GP, and also scales as O(n^3). Accuracy is verified by comparing with the golden standard MCMC and its effectiveness is illustrated on several synthetic and real datasets of diverse characteristics. An application to volatility forecasting is also considered.

paragraphs: Standard Gaussian-process regression assumes that observation noise has the same magnitude throughout the input space. The paper addresses situations where that assumption is too restrictive because noise changes with the input. Modeling this variation produces a heteroscedastic Gaussian process, but makes inference harder than in the constant-noise formulation.

The authors introduce a nonstandard variational approximation that permits accurate inference with input-dependent noise. Its computational cost is roughly twice that of a standard Gaussian process, while retaining cubic scaling in the number of observations. This offers a quantified tradeoff: a more flexible noise model at a higher computational cost, without changing the stated scaling order.

Accuracy is assessed through comparison with Markov chain Monte Carlo, used as a reference for inference quality. Experiments on varied synthetic and real datasets illustrate effectiveness, and the paper also considers volatility forecasting. The contribution is a practical approximate-inference method that lets the model account for changing observation noise while keeping its computational requirements closely related to those of standard Gaussian-process regression.
summary.tldr: A variational approximation enables accurate Gaussian-process regression with input-dependent noise at roughly twice the standard computational cost.

title: Variational Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Regression
